This is particularly useful when analysing large multi-omics datasets (i.e. with many omics layers or with a large number of features).

It must be noted that feature prefiltering is critical for the overall computational requirements of the pipeline, as reducing the size of the omics datasets will ensure a shorter running time and smaller memory requirement for all subsequent steps. In addition, prefiltering has been shown to improve the integration results by reducing the noise present in the data, which also reduces the risk of overfitting, and by reducing the imbalance between datasets, as the largest omics datasets would otherwise dominate the integration results (Sathyamoorthi et al. 2025, Subramanian et al. 2020, Rohart et al. 2017, Perez-Riverol et al. 2017). Therefore, it is strongly recommended to reduce the size of each omics dataset prior to integration.

text: [4 Discussion] We present moiraine, an R package for constructing reproducible multi-omics integration analysis pipelines. moiraine enables users to import omics datasets and associated features and samples metadata, without any restriction on the type or number of datasets that can be included. These datasets can then be inspected, transformed and pre-filtered; a number of options are made available, but custom steps can easily be implemented in the analysis pipeline. moiraine handles the conversion of the multi-omics dataset into whatever input format is required for one of the supported integration methods, namely sPLS, sO2PLS, DIABLO, MOFA or MEFISTO, allowing the user to focus on data integration rather than data wrangling

text: [Background] Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with a complex etiology, posing significant challenges for early diagnosis and treatment. Distinct from normal cognitive aging, AD is defined by hallmark neuropathological features, including the aggregation of amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques and neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) (DeTure and Dickson 2019). These pathological changes initially appear in the entorhinal cortex (Ent) and hippocampus (HPC), key areas for memory and learning, before spreading to broader cortical and subcortical regions (Trejo-Lopez et al. 2022). Understanding the spatiotemporal progression of AD pathology is critical for identifying early biomarkers and developing targeted interventions.

title: Entorhinal Cholecystokinin in Alzheimer’s Disease: Its Earliest Vulnerability and Rescue Effects Across Different Disease Stages in a Mouse Model
text: [Background] The medial temporal lobe (MTL), which includes the HPC, Ent, and adjacent cortical regions such as the perirhinal and postrhinal cortices, plays a central role in memory formation. Bilateral resection of the MTL in humans results in severe anterograde amnesia and profound memory deficits in patients (Squire 2009). Although brain atrophy occurs gradually during normal aging, the process accelerates markedly in AD, with the MTL being specifically vulnerable (Chauveau et al. 2021). These brain regions show early AD-related pathology, including Aβ deposition, tau aggregation, synaptic loss, and neuronal death, ultimately resulting in their progressive volume reduction (Jack et al. 1998)

Furthermore, patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) frequently display early deficits in spatial navigation, suggesting functional disruption within the Ent-HPC circuit, one of the first neural networks affected in AD (Hort et al. 2007). text: [Distinct Spatiotemporal Trajectories of Brain Volume in 3xTg-AD Mice: Rapid Entorhinal Atrophy and Early Hippocampal Growth Arrest] Identifying region-specific brain atrophy patterns is critical for early detection and intervention of AD. As an important region regulating learning and memory, MTL is known to be particularly vulnerable to early neurodegeneration (Chauveau et al. 2021). To systematically characterize these changes, we investigated global and region-specific brain volume changes in 3xTg-AD and WT mice across multiple ages.

section: Distinct Spatiotemporal Trajectories of Brain Volume in 3xTg-AD Mice: Rapid Entorhinal Atrophy and Early Hippocampal Growth Arrest
text: [Distinct Spatiotemporal Trajectories of Brain Volume in 3xTg-AD Mice: Rapid Entorhinal Atrophy and Early Hippocampal Growth Arrest] We first quantified the whole-brain dimensions, including anteroposterior (AP) length, mediolateral (ML) width, and dorsoventral (DV) thickness, in WT and 3xTg-AD mice at 2, 5, 7, 12, and 18 months of age. Given the large workload of this comprehensive stereoscopic analysis across multiple ages, we initially characterized volume changes using male mice. In 3xTg-AD mice, all three dimensions followed a similar trajectory: a slight increase up to 7 months of age, reflecting normal postnatal brain development, followed by progressive shrinkage. By 18 months, all measures were significantly reduced in 3xTg-AD mice compared to WT controls (Fig. 1C, E, F), indicating a transition from early developmental growth to later neurodegeneration in overall brain size.

text: [Distinct Spatiotemporal Trajectories of Brain Volume in 3xTg-AD Mice: Rapid Entorhinal Atrophy and Early Hippocampal Growth Arrest] Next, we examined volume changes in the cerebral cortex and MTL subregions. Significant atrophy across the cerebral cortex emerged in 3xTg-AD mice at 12 and 18 months, indicating widespread degeneration in late AD stages (Fig. 1G and S1A-B). Notably, MTL subregions showed distinct temporal patterns of volume loss. text: [Distinct Spatiotemporal Trajectories of Brain Volume in 3xTg-AD Mice: Rapid Entorhinal Atrophy and Early Hippocampal Growth Arrest] Hippocampal volume also displayed distinct developmental trajectories between genotypes. In WT mice, hippocampal volume increased steadily during early postnatal stages and stabilized thereafter, indicating normal postnatal development (Hammelrath et al. 2016; Zhang et al. 2005; Calabrese et al. 2013). In 3xTg-AD mice, however, hippocampal growth was impaired early in development, leading to significantly smaller volume by 5 months of age relative to WT controls (Figs. 1K and 16.54 mm3 in 3xTg-AD vs. 18.99 mm3 in WT; 12.9% decrease, P = 0.0119). These findings imply that the smaller hippocampal volume in 3xTg-AD mice stems from an early neurodevelopmental growth arrest, rather than from the progressive degenerative atrophy seen in the Ent.

text: [Distinct Spatiotemporal Trajectories of Brain Volume in 3xTg-AD Mice: Rapid Entorhinal Atrophy and Early Hippocampal Growth Arrest] To conclude, morphological analysis of 3xTg-AD brains revealed distinct region-specific volume changes during AD progression. The Ent showed rapid progressive atrophy, while the HPC exhibited early growth arrest (Fig. 1M). These findings suggest that the AD pathogenesis in this model may involve not only progressive neurodegeneration, but also early neurodevelopmental defects. Furthermore, the late-stage atrophy observed in multiple brain regions (PrC, POR, PFC) indicates progressive disease spread throughout the brain.

text: [Discussion] Glial responses in the Ent were distinct. Astrocytes exhibited early and persistent atrophy with weak spatial associations with Aβ plaques or tau tangles. This impaired reactivity probably exacerbates localized aggregation of neurotoxic proteins, reduces synaptic coverage in the Ent, and impairs neuronal communication (Chung et al. 2015). Microglia in the Ent were reactive and closely associated with pathological aggregates, suggesting that microglia are involved in synaptic remodeling through protective clearance mechanisms and potentially synaptic pruning (Ohyagi et al. 2005; Franco-Bocanegra et al. 2019).

text: [Discussion] In contrast to the progressive entorhinal atrophy, the HPC in 3xTg-AD mice exhibited a distinct phenotype of early developmental growth arrest and impaired neurogenesis, particularly within the vulnerable DG. This observation carries several important implications. First, it suggests that the hippocampal deficit in this model may originate from an early-life impairment in circuit assembly or maturation, rather than solely from a later degenerative process. Second, the severe impairment of adult neurogenesis, a key source of hippocampal plasticity, likely compromises the circuit’s capacity for adaptive rewiring from the outset, predisposing it to functional failure even before significant neuron loss (Aniol et al. 2022; Kawles et al. 2023)

title: Entorhinal Cholecystokinin in Alzheimer’s Disease: Its Earliest Vulnerability and Rescue Effects Across Different Disease Stages in a Mouse Model
text: [Discussion] . Astrocytic activation emerged later, with marked hypertrophy observed in both WT and 3xTg-AD mice by 18 months. In WT mice, this may be a compensatory response to the age-related increasing oxidative stress and metabolic burden (Clarke et al. 2018). In AD mice, this activation likely serves a protective function, enhancing clearance of neurotoxic proteins and maintaining homeostasis (Fuller et al. 2009; Cabral-Miranda et al. 2025).

title: Entorhinal Cholecystokinin in Alzheimer’s Disease: Its Earliest Vulnerability and Rescue Effects Across Different Disease Stages in a Mouse Model
text: [Discussion] Collectively, our results revealed two distinct pathological trajectories in the 3xTg-AD mouse brain: a severe, early-onset progressive degeneration in the Ent characterized by the vulnerability of both neurons and astrocytes, and a pathological phenotype in the HPC marked by early neurogenesis deficits, arrested growth, and distinct glial responses. These patterns underscore the need for region-targeted strategies in AD.

title: Entorhinal Cholecystokinin in Alzheimer’s Disease: Its Earliest Vulnerability and Rescue Effects Across Different Disease Stages in a Mouse Model
text: [Discussion] These region-specific cascades reflect both conserved and model-divergent features of AD pathophysiology. The early, severe entorhinal atrophy and loss of layer II excitatory neurons directly parallel the established vulnerability of this region in human AD, as shown by neuroimaging and post-mortem studies (Jack et al. 1998; Gómez-Isla et al. 1996). In contrast, the hippocampal phenotype diverges: it shows a developmental growth impairment rather than the progressive atrophy typical of late-stage human AD. This aligns with observations in other amyloidogenic models (e.g., APP/PS1 mice, Delatour et al. 2006), suggesting a shared model-specific developmental component

title: Entorhinal Cholecystokinin in Alzheimer’s Disease: Its Earliest Vulnerability and Rescue Effects Across Different Disease Stages in a Mouse Model
text: [Discussion] . 2006), suggesting a shared model-specific developmental component. Furthermore, we observed divergent glial responses within this AD model: decreased astrocytic reactivity in the atrophying Ent alongside robust microglial activation in the HPC. Although widespread gliosis is a hallmark of both human AD and many mouse models, the regional difference in glial engagement within the same brain we observed is less commonly reported. This regional disparity indicates that neuroinflammatory responses are highly context-dependent, shaped by local pathology and disease stage. Consequently, glia-targeting therapeutic strategies may need to be tailored not only to cell type but also to the specific pathological environment of each affected brain region.

title: Entorhinal Cholecystokinin in Alzheimer’s Disease: Its Earliest Vulnerability and Rescue Effects Across Different Disease Stages in a Mouse Model
text: [Discussion] The early and specific downregulation of entorhinal CCK is a key finding of our study, aligning with growing evidence for impaired CCK signaling in AD pathogenesis. Human post-mortem studies show reduced cortical CCK immunoreactivity in AD (Mazurek and Beal 1991; Perry et al. 1981), while higher cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) CCK levels correlate with reduced AD risk, better cognition, and greater grey matter volume (Plagman et al. 2019). Transcriptomic analyses further identify downregulated CCK receptors in AD brains (Hokama et al. 2014; Lin et al. 2014). Complementing this, AD animal models like APP/PS1 mice exhibit reduced hippocampal CCK mRNA (Liu et al. 2021).

title: Entorhinal Cholecystokinin in Alzheimer’s Disease: Its Earliest Vulnerability and Rescue Effects Across Different Disease Stages in a Mouse Model
text: [Discussion] We found that CCK downregulation in the Ent of 3xTg-AD mice at 7 months precedes widespread cortical atrophy and correlates with the onset of hippocampal synaptic dysfunction. This early loss, occurring prior to overt neuronal death and potentially stemming from activity-dependent mechanisms (Li et al. 2014; Chen et al. 2013), was followed by progressive CCK/CCK-BR reduction across brain regions by 12 months. Based on the Ent’s early vulnerability and the specific downregulation of CCK, a key neuropeptide for synaptic modulation and memory, we hypothesized that this deficit would disrupt entorhinal control over its downstream hippocampal and cortical targets, thereby contributing to cognitive decline (Lee and Soltesz 2011; Rehfeld 2021; Li et al. 2014; Chen et al. 2013)

title: Entorhinal Cholecystokinin in Alzheimer’s Disease: Its Earliest Vulnerability and Rescue Effects Across Different Disease Stages in a Mouse Model
text: [Discussion] . 2014; Chen et al. 2013). This rationale guided our focus on assessing and rescuing synaptic function in the HPC and neocortex, the primary recipients of entorhinal projections. We therefore hypothesized that deficient entorhinal CCK signaling disrupts its control over downstream hippocampal and cortical targets. Critically, administering CCK-BR agonists restored synaptic plasticity and cognition in these downstream regions, demonstrating that compensating for entorhinal CCK deficiency can effectively reverse network-level dysfunction and providing a mechanistic link between CCK loss and early circuit impairment in AD.

title: Entorhinal Cholecystokinin in Alzheimer’s Disease: Its Earliest Vulnerability and Rescue Effects Across Different Disease Stages in a Mouse Model
text: [Discussion] To evaluate the therapeutic potential of CCK for AD, we treated 3xTg-AD mice at different ages with CCK-4, a natural CCK-BR agonist. We found that CCK-4 significantly improved recognition memory, motor learning, and cortical and hippocampal LTP across mild to severe AD stages. These therapeutic effects verify that CCK-4 enhances synaptic plasticity and neural network connectivity, addressing key pathological features of AD. However, the poor pharmacokinetic properties of CCK-4, including its short plasma half-life (less than 1 min in rodents) and low bioavailability, hinder its clinical translation and application (Koulischer et al. 1982). To overcome these limitations, we developed HT-267, a novel CCK-4 analogue with optimized pharmacological properties

text: [Discussion] . 1982). To overcome these limitations, we developed HT-267, a novel CCK-4 analogue with optimized pharmacological properties. HT-267 exhibits enhanced CCK-BR binding affinity, increased potency, a substantially extended half-life, and favourable rescue effects on cognition and neuroplasticity of aged 3xTg-AD mice (Zhang et al. 2024). The 90-day treatment with HT-267 in 3xTg-AD mice significantly improved their cognitive function and synaptic plasticity. Meanwhile, HT-267 enhanced synaptic scaffolding, as indicated by increased PSD-95 expression in hippocampal dendrites and cortical neurons (Chen et al. 2011; Sturgill et al. 2009)

Together, these findings support that pharmacological activation of CCK-BR can mitigate synaptic deficits and cognitive decline in AD, and HT-267 represents a promising drug candidate for maintaining neural circuit function and delaying AD progression. Future studies should focus on elucidating the exact molecular mechanisms underlying CCK-BR-mediated neuroprotection, evaluating the long-term safety and efficacy of CCK-BR agonist applications, and exploring combination strategies to maximize the therapeutic potential of CCK-based therapies in AD.

text: [Discussion] Some limitations in this study warrant consideration. First, regarding anatomical quantification, the regional volume changes were quantified using ex vivo stereology on histological sections. Although this approach was important for achieving direct spatial correlations between atrophy, cellular pathology, and molecular alterations within the same tissue, it lacks the precision and longitudinal capacity of in vivo imaging techniques such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Future MRI studies could refine these anatomical findings. Second, regarding therapeutic mechanisms, the systemic (intraperitoneal) delivery of CCK-4 and HT-267, though effective, acts globally. This precludes attributing the rescue effects definitively to the Ent versus other brain regions

Regarding causal neural circuits, although our data strongly link entorhinal CCK downregulation to downstream synaptic deficits, the definitive role of entorhinal CCK neurons remains to be established. Cell-type-specific neuromodulatory approaches (e.g., chemogenetics) to selectively manipulate entorhinal CCK neuronal activity could determine if this population is sufficient to elicit or rescue the observed circuit-level dysfunctions.

title: Entorhinal Cholecystokinin in Alzheimer’s Disease: Its Earliest Vulnerability and Rescue Effects Across Different Disease Stages in a Mouse Model
text: [Conclusions] This study strengthens the evidence that the Ent is a critical early site of degeneration in AD, and that downregulation of CCK constitutes an early molecular signature of AD pathogenesis. We established the rescue effects of CCKBR agonists on cognitive, synaptic, and motor impairments across mild to severe AD progression stages. Additionally, we confirmed that long-term treatment with the optimized analogue HT-267, initiated at a young age in 3xTg-AD mice, decelerates the progression of cognitive and synaptic deficits compared to VEH-treated controls. Taken together, these findings position CCK as a potential biomarker for early AD detection, and the CCK-BR as a promising therapeutic target for modifying disease course.

Baicalin (BAI), a natural compound with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-cancer properties, has shown cardioprotective effects in DOX-treated animal cardiac models, but its impact on human cardiomyocytes remains unexplored. title: Protective effect of Baicalin against doxorubicin-induced cytotoxic and electrophysiological damage in human iPSC-cardiomyocytes
text: [Introduction] Doxorubicin (DOX) is an anthracycline drug with strong therapeutic effects in the treatment of multiple cancers1. However, its clinical application is limited due to the DOX-induced cardiotoxicity (DIC) that impacts patient prognosis and survival2–5. Acute DOX cardiotoxicity manifests after a single treatment and is associated with transient electrophysiological abnormalities such as conduction alterations and arrhythmias, occurring from seconds up to 48 h post-administration6–8. Chronic DIC, associated with the cumulative lifetime dose, can lead to irreversible alterations such as chronic dilated cardiomyopathy with decreased left ventricular ejection fraction, occasionally resulting in fatal outcomes4,6

text: [Introduction] . This form of DIC is difficult to predict and clinically manage because it may appear several years after treatment cessation9,10. Based on the increasing number of cancer survivors who have received DOX treatment, the study of DIC is of great interest, and currently, no suitable biomarkers to enable early detection or the development of effective treatment strategies are available11,12.

title: Protective effect of Baicalin against doxorubicin-induced cytotoxic and electrophysiological damage in human iPSC-cardiomyocytes
text: [Introduction] DIC is associated with oxidative stress, cardiomyocyte morphological changes, cell death, and apoptosis13–17. In particular, cardiomyocytes are very susceptible to DOX-induced oxidative damage due to their relatively lower level of antioxidant enzymes, and it has been hypothesized that alterations in membrane function, due to DOX-induced oxidative damage, may be responsible for many of the observed ECG changes17,18. Moreover, cardiomyocytes have a lower ability to regenerate, so they are potentially more susceptible to the long-term adverse effects of DOX17–19. DIC is also associated with alterations in the expression and organization of troponins and with direct myofibril damage and sarcomere disorganization15,16.

text: [Introduction] The DOX-induced molecular and structural alterations in the cardiac muscle could still occur in clinically asymptomatic patients, leading to a progressive weakening of the heart muscle, which may appear much later in life2–5. Management of DOX effects requires continuous monitoring and cardioprotective therapies based on antioxidant drugs or agents such as dexrazoxane, a ROS-reducing agent18–22. However, clinical practice guidelines support its use only in a specific subset of patients, excluding many others who might benefit from a novel therapeutic strategy that needs to be established21,22.

text: [Introduction] Several studies, in the last few years, have focused on natural compounds in preventing the adverse effects of DOX23. In particular, flavonoids belong to the polyphenol compounds extracted from several plant species and represent a class of molecules with antioxidant properties that could mitigate DIC23–26. Among these, Baicalin (BAI), a molecule extracted from S. baicalensis Georgi, is a natural bioactive compound with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-cancer activities27–35. Different preclinical studies performed on animal models have provided evidence that baicalin could be a promising therapeutic agent for cardiovascular protection via inflammation regulation, inhibition of oxidative stress, and reduction of cardiomyocyte apoptosis36–39

text: [Introduction] The human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) have revolutionized human cardiac disease and cardiotoxicity research, representing an in vitro human cardiac system for studying arrhythmia, cardiomyopathies, and to test cardiotoxicity both in short and long-term drug treatments40–45.

text: [Introduction] In this study, we use an integrated analytical approach combining cytotoxicity assays with hiPSC-CM–based multielectrode array (MEA) technology to investigate the structural and electrophysiological protective effects of BAI against acute and long-term DOX-induced cardiotoxicity. Our data revealed that Baicalin confers both structural and functional cardioprotection through multiple complementary mechanisms, including anti-apoptotic, antioxidant effects, structural preservation, and stabilization of electrophysiological activity of hiPSC-CMs. These results underscore the potential of BAI as a cardioprotective agent and provide a strong rationale for further translational research in the context of chemotherapy-associated cardiac risk.

text: [Discussion] In the current study, we demonstrated the protective effects of BAI, a natural flavonoid with antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, and anticancer activities, against DOX-induced cardiotoxicity in a representative human cardiac model.

title: Protective effect of Baicalin against doxorubicin-induced cytotoxic and electrophysiological damage in human iPSC-cardiomyocytes
text: [Discussion] A hallmark of DOX-induced cardiac injury is the induction of cardiomyocyte death, and the apoptotic pathway is one of the most well-characterized programmed cell death pathways involved in DIC, as demonstrated in both in vivo and in vitro cardiac models12,13. Consistent with this, our results show that both acute and long-term DOX treatments induced a significant decrease in viability and an increase in apoptotic cell death in hiPSC-CMs. Moreover, a significant increase in intracellular ROS levels was observed in DOX-treated hiPSC-CMs, in line with previous studies17–20

title: Protective effect of Baicalin against doxorubicin-induced cytotoxic and electrophysiological damage in human iPSC-cardiomyocytes
text: [Discussion] . Moreover, a significant increase in intracellular ROS levels was observed in DOX-treated hiPSC-CMs, in line with previous studies17–20. In particular, in our experimental conditions, a nuclear CellRox signal was observed after DOX 1 µM for 24 h, consistent with acute oxidative and genotoxic stress, which is further supported by the concomitant increase in nuclear γ-H2AX foci, indicating DNA double-strand break formation under high-dose, short-term DOX exposure. Interestingly, our study indicates that BAI can contrast all these DOX cytotoxic effects both in acute and long-term treatments, with a marked protective effect obtained with BAI 10 µM and 25 µM doses

text: [Discussion] . These results suggest a potent anti-apoptotic and antioxidative BAI activity in our human in vitro model, in agreement with previous data reported in cardiac animal models27–39,46.

title: Protective effect of Baicalin against doxorubicin-induced cytotoxic and electrophysiological damage in human iPSC-cardiomyocytes
text: [Discussion] Oxidative stress is widely accepted as a key factor of DOX-induced apoptosis8,12–14. Notably, BAI at 10 µM markedly reduced acute DOX-induced cell death and apoptosis, despite only a moderate decrease in total ROS levels. In addition, long-term exposure to 0.3 µM DOX induced significant cell death and apoptosis, despite relatively low ROS levels production, probably reflecting a chronic sublethal stress rather than the acute oxidative overload observed at higher DOX concentrations. These findings suggest that the anti-apoptotic effect of BAI may be mediated not only by attenuation of DOX-induced ROS production, but also by additional mechanisms, potentially including the preservation of DNA integrity, as reported in previous studies47,48

text: [Discussion] . According to this hypothesis, the analysis of the effects of BAI on DNA integrity by immunofluorescence staining of γH2AX-positive cardiomyocytes demonstrated that BAI significantly inhibits DOX-induced genotoxic stress.

title: Protective effect of Baicalin against doxorubicin-induced cytotoxic and electrophysiological damage in human iPSC-cardiomyocytes
text: [Discussion] DOX-induced oxidative stress and apoptosis in hiPSC-CMs ultimately impair their structural integrity and function. Previous studies have shown that even low therapeutic DOX doses (< 0.5 µM) can markedly alter the cardiac sarcomeric organization, a key factor in maintaining normal contractility and myocardial function, and may contribute to the delayed malfunctioning of human cardiomyocytes of chronic DIC15,16,43. In line with this evidence, the long-term DOX treatment induced a marked sarcomeric disarray in iPSC-CMs. Interestingly, BAI 10 µM and 25 µM co-treatment was able to significantly preserve the α-actinin and troponin organization, suggesting a protective role of this natural compound against the cardiac structural alterations associated with the DOX-induced delayed cardiotoxicity.

title: Protective effect of Baicalin against doxorubicin-induced cytotoxic and electrophysiological damage in human iPSC-cardiomyocytes
text: [Discussion] In addition to its cytotoxic effects, DOX has also been associated with several functional alterations in humans, including arrhythmias, sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, T wave flattening, abnormalities of the QT interval, and atrio-ventricular nodal block2–5. Consistent with these clinical observations, in vitro studies indicated that DOX alters the electrophysiological properties of hiPSC-CMs with both acute and long-term effects on electrophysiological parameters, and the DOX-induced adverse effects on cardiac function can be detected in real-time with the MEA system41–45,49,50. These alterations include the modulation of corrected field potential duration, beat period, conduction velocity, and spike amplitude, and are correlated to a doxorubicin-induced cytotoxicity41–45,49,50

title: Protective effect of Baicalin against doxorubicin-induced cytotoxic and electrophysiological damage in human iPSC-cardiomyocytes
text: [Discussion] . In the present study, for the first time, we demonstrate that BAI is able to improve the DOX-induced electrophysiological alterations in a human cardiac model. In particular, a marked BAI protective effect was observed against the DOX-induced reduction of FPDc, BP, Spike Amplitude, Conduction Velocity, and APD90, after 3 days of DOX 0.3 μM exposure. These results are not associated with iPSC-CMs cell death or detachment, as demonstrated by the simultaneous viability evaluation performed with the impedance assay.

title: Protective effect of Baicalin against doxorubicin-induced cytotoxic and electrophysiological damage in human iPSC-cardiomyocytes
text: [Discussion] All these parameters are commonly altered in models of DOX-induced cardiotoxicity, and this is associated with ROS overproduction, cytoskeletal disorganization, and sarcomeric disarray, all of which compromise myocardial architecture and function, increasing the arrhythmic risk and contractile dysfunction41–43,51–56. In our experimental conditions, despite the onset of electrophysiological changes recorded after long-term DOX exposure, no detachment or cell death was observed. Therefore, we could not exclude that other mechanisms involving the regulation of ion channels could be associated to the long-term DOX-mediated alteration of iPSC-CMs electrophysiology

text: [Discussion] . However, the stabilization obtained with BAI co-treatment suggests a functional benefit associated with either the maintenance of cardiomyocyte structural integrity or the improvement of cardiomyocyte excitability and conduction.

title: Protective effect of Baicalin against doxorubicin-induced cytotoxic and electrophysiological damage in human iPSC-cardiomyocytes
text: [Discussion] Our results suggest that BAI may represent a novel cardioprotective agent in the human heart, able to avoid the acute and delayed DIC. Notably, the most protective effects of BAI were observed at concentrations of 10 µM and 25 µM. These doses were selected for their anticancer properties demonstrated in several human cancer cell models25–33. Therefore, the potential therapeutic use of BAI together with DOX could not only mitigate DIC but also improve drug anticancer activity.

title: Protective effect of Baicalin against doxorubicin-induced cytotoxic and electrophysiological damage in human iPSC-cardiomyocytes
text: [Discussion] Despite the promising findings, our study has some limitations. The hiPSC-CMs provide a relevant human-based model for studying DOX cardiotoxicity. However, they do not fully recapitulate the complexity of the adult human heart. Therefore, to confirm BAI efficacy and safety in a more complex physiological environment, further validation in preclinical and clinical studies is required. Another limitation of our study is the use of a single hiPSC line (iCell-CMs). Although this model is widely adopted for preclinical cardiotoxicity testing, the intrinsic variability between lines underscores the need for validation in additional hiPSC-CM models, in particular for the electrophysiological analysis

text: [Discussion] . For instance, the FPDc reduction observed after DOX exposure in our study is consistent with previous findings in iCell-CMs, whereas other cardiac models have reported FPDc prolongation41–45,57. Moreover, several clinical studies have reported a prolongation of the QT interval in patients treated with DOX2–7. These discrepancies likely reflect limitations of hiPSC-CM models, which may arise from factors such as the absence of innervation, differences in cell composition (e.g., the proportion of ventricular, atrial, and nodal cardiomyocytes), variations in maturation, ion channel expression, and drug exposure

text: [Discussion] Moreover, although BAI exerted strong protective effects at 10 and 25 µM in hiPSC-CMs, it should be noted that these concentrations are relatively high, and BAI is characterized by limited bioavailability, and these concentrations are pharmacologically challenging, potentially restricting its translational application58,59. Therefore, further preclinical studies will be necessary to optimize new strategies for formulation (e.g., nanoparticle encapsulation, prodrugs, structural analogs), delivery, and the development of derivatives with improved pharmacokinetic properties before considering clinical applications.

title: Protective effect of Baicalin against doxorubicin-induced cytotoxic and electrophysiological damage in human iPSC-cardiomyocytes
text: [Discussion] Finally, although our results demonstrated cardioprotective BAI effects in a human cardiac model against oxidative stress, apoptosis, sarcomere disorganization, and electrophysiological alterations, the precise molecular mechanisms underlying these effects require further investigation. In particular, additional experiments will be necessary to clarify this finding and to determine whether BAI’s protective effect is primarily associated with the prevention of DOX uptake into cardiomyocytes or instead with the modulation of downstream stress pathways.

title: Protective effect of Baicalin against doxorubicin-induced cytotoxic and electrophysiological damage in human iPSC-cardiomyocytes
text: [Discussion] In conclusion, integrating hiPSC-CM-based MEA technology with cytotoxicity assays enabled the detection of both cardiotoxic and cardioprotective effects, reinforcing the value of human in vitro cardiac models for evaluating drug-induced cardiotoxicity and identifying novel protective compounds. This combined analytical approach revealed that baicalin confers both structural and functional cardioprotection of a human cardiac cell model, likely through multiple complementary mechanisms, including anti-apoptotic, antioxidant effects, structural preservation, and stabilization of electrophysiological activity

text: [Discussion] . Overall, our findings highlight the effectiveness of Baicalin, particularly at 10 µM and 25 µM concentrations, in mitigating doxorubicin-induced cardiac damage, supporting its potential translational value as a promising cardioprotective agent during chemotherapy.

title: Protective effect of Baicalin against doxorubicin-induced cytotoxic and electrophysiological damage in human iPSC-cardiomyocytes
text: [MEA analysis] The local extracellular action potential (LEAP) induction experiments were performed to measure the 90% Action Potential Duration (APD90). LEAP signals were induced in iCell cardiomyocytes 72 h after DOX (0.3 µM) and BAI (1, 10, and 25 µM) and vehicles (H2O and DMSO) treatments and then recorded for 3 min. In each well, all electrodes were used for LEAP induction. APD90 (ms) was analyzed using the Cardiomyocyte Analysis Tool software version 2.2.7 and AxIS Metric Plotting Tool version 2.2.5 (Axion Biosystem). For LEAP analysis, data were obtained from two independent experiments performed in quadruplicate (n = 8).

title: Protective effect of Baicalin against doxorubicin-induced cytotoxic and electrophysiological damage in human iPSC-cardiomyocytes
text: [Statistical analysis] Data are presented as mean value ± SEM. Data from multiple independent groups of samples (control, DOX-alone, DOX plus BAI 1 µM, DOX plus BAI 10, and DOX plus BAI 25 µM) were compared using two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test, using GraphPad Prism software (version 10.6.0). The statistical significance was accepted for p < 0.01.

title: The COVID-19 pandemic has not influenced survival outcomes of head and neck cancer squamous cell carcinomas in the West of Scotland: a retrospective cohort study
text: [abstract] The COVID-19 pandemic posed significant disruptions to healthcare worldwide. This study aimed to assess if the COVID-19 pandemic affected short-term survival outcomes of patients with head and neck cancer squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) in the west of Scotland.

title: The COVID-19 pandemic has not influenced survival outcomes of head and neck cancer squamous cell carcinomas in the West of Scotland: a retrospective cohort study
text: [abstract] A retrospective cohort analysis was conducted using regional centre data. Patients diagnosed with HNSCC during pre-pandemic (June-October 2019), intra-pandemic (June-October 2020) and post(peak)-pandemic (June-October 2022) were compared. Demographic, behavioural, clinical, and survival data were analysed using Kaplan-Meier curves, Cox-regression, and logistic-regression for stage at diagnosis.

title: The COVID-19 pandemic has not influenced survival outcomes of head and neck cancer squamous cell carcinomas in the West of Scotland: a retrospective cohort study
text: [abstract] A total of 707 patients were included. While the 2020 cohort exhibited an increase in advanced-stage disease (67.5% p = 0.01), no statistically significant difference in overall survival was observed across the study period (p = 0.22). Cox-regression showed no associations between year of diagnosis and mortality, even after multivariable adjustment for confounders. Survival was strongly associated with age, performance status, stage, and HPV status among oropharynx cancers. Socioeconomic inequalities persisted, with the poorest survival among those from the most socioeconomically deprived areas (p = 0.02).

title: The COVID-19 pandemic has not influenced survival outcomes of head and neck cancer squamous cell carcinomas in the West of Scotland: a retrospective cohort study
text: [abstract] While an increase in advanced-stage HNSCC diagnoses was observed in the West of Scotland during 2020, short-term survival outcomes remained comparable to pre- and post-pandemic.

title: The COVID-19 pandemic has not influenced survival outcomes of head and neck cancer squamous cell carcinomas in the West of Scotland: a retrospective cohort study
text: [Introduction] Head and neck cancer (HNSCC), commonly defined as cancers of the oral cavity, pharynx and larynx, is associated with poor survival at advanced stages[1]. Research has emphasised that timely diagnosis and treatment are crucial for achieving optimal survival and quality of life outcomes[2]. The COVID-19 pandemic, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, inflicted great stress and disruptions on healthcare systems worldwide, including the UK[3, 4]. In the acute phases of the pandemic in 2020 and 2021, public health guidance advised primary and secondary care medical and dental care services to postpone all non-urgent face-to-face consultations and elective procedures. The population was advised not to access healthcare unless for urgent or emergency care.

title: The COVID-19 pandemic has not influenced survival outcomes of head and neck cancer squamous cell carcinomas in the West of Scotland: a retrospective cohort study
text: [Introduction] Delays and declines in the number of referrals to head and neck units were subsequently observed across the UK[5–7]. These were accompanied by concerns that the reduced quantity of referrals would result in an increased burden of advanced-stage disease, with detrimental prognostic implications[8].

title: The COVID-19 pandemic has not influenced survival outcomes of head and neck cancer squamous cell carcinomas in the West of Scotland: a retrospective cohort study
text: [Introduction] A subsequent rapid review and meta-analysis of the wider international literature suggested a shift towards advanced-stage diagnoses associated with the COVID-19 pandemic[9]. Currently, there is little research assessing the longitudinal effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on HNSCC survival outcomes. Using retrospective data collected from routinely diagnosed and treated cohorts, this analysis aimed to identify if HNSCC survival in the west of Scotland was adversely affected by the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: The COVID-19 pandemic has not influenced survival outcomes of head and neck cancer squamous cell carcinomas in the West of Scotland: a retrospective cohort study
text: [Methods] Local clinical NHS Caldicott Guardian and University of Glasgow ethical (Project number 200240340) approvals were obtained. HNSCC cases were identified from the regional multidisciplinary team (MDT) database, which records all new HNSCC cases in the west of Scotland region. This west of Scotland cancer network region serves a population of 2.5 million people (approximately 46% of the Scottish population)[10]. Demographic, behavioural and clinical data were collected from electronic patient records. This retrospective cohort analysis was conducted as per the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) framework[11].

title: The COVID-19 pandemic has not influenced survival outcomes of head and neck cancer squamous cell carcinomas in the West of Scotland: a retrospective cohort study
text: [Inclusion and exclusion criteria] Participants were defined as patients with histologically confirmed squamous cell carcinomas of the oral cavity (C00.3 - C00.9, C02–C05), oropharynx (C01, C02.4, C09, C10, C14), larynx (C32), nasopharynx (C11), Hypopharynx (C12, C13) and other overlapping sites (C14.8)[12, 13]. Participants were excluded if they had diagnoses of recurrent cancers, tumours of the thyroid or salivary glands, or haematological cancers of the head and neck.

title: The COVID-19 pandemic has not influenced survival outcomes of head and neck cancer squamous cell carcinomas in the West of Scotland: a retrospective cohort study

This latter period constituted a time where most public health measures (including mask-wearing and travel restrictions) had been relaxed in Scotland following the rollout of the national vaccination programme and declines in COVID-19 incidence, although the World Health Organisation did not declare an official end to the global pandemic until the 5th of May 2023[14, 15]. text: [Sociodemographic data] Patients among cohorts were of a similar mean age at the time of diagnosis (65.2 (2019), 64.7 (2020) and 65.4 (2022) years old). Most patients were male (71.4%, n = 505) across all three cohorts (p = 0.14). A strong socioeconomic gradient was observed, with 39% of patients living in SIMD-1 (20% most socioeconomically deprived) areas. This remained true across the study duration (46.0% (2019), 32.9% (2020), and 38.1% (2022)). A reduction in the proportion of patients from lower SES backgrounds (SIMD-1, 20% most deprived) was observed in 2020 (p = 0.01).

text: [Clinical data] Advanced-stage disease was observed among 59.8% of patients (Table 1). Specifically, the pandemic cohort had a higher proportion of advanced-stage disease (67.5%) compared with the 2019 (56.9%) and 2022 cohorts (59.0%).

title: Sustainable hard water treatment using talc derived magnesium silicate zeolite evaluated by statistical physics and field validation in Siwa Oasis
text: [abstract] Groundwater in Egypt’s Siwa Oasis exhibits extreme hardness (total ≈ 3312.6 mg/L as CaCO3; Mg2+ ≈ 609.5 mg/L, Ca2+ ≈ 325.4 mg/L), far above guideline values and problematic for health and infrastructure. We report a sustainable softening approach using magnesium-silicate zeolite (Mg.ZA) synthesized from natural talc via alkali fusion (550 °C, 5 h) and mild hydrothermal conversion, producing LTA-type crystallinity with mesoporosity and high surface area (187 m2/g). Performance was evaluated under batch and fixed-bed (continuous-flow) conditions and interpreted with statistical-physics modeling. In batch at pH 7, Mg.ZA achieved 268.8 mg/g (Ca2+) and 206.9 mg/g (Mg2+), following pseudo-first-order kinetics and Langmuir isotherms, indicating physisorption-dominated, near-monolayer uptake

title: Sustainable hard water treatment using talc derived magnesium silicate zeolite evaluated by statistical physics and field validation in Siwa Oasis
text: [abstract] . First, in alkaline conditions, the formation of metal hydroxide species (e.g., Ca(OH)₂, Mg(OH)₂) reduces the concentration of free divalent ions in solution, thereby limiting their availability for adsorption62. These values are consistent with those reported for magnesium-silicate and zeolite-A–type materials in similar adsorption systems. text: [Regeneration and recyclability of Mg.ZA] The regeneration and recyclability of the synthesized magnesium silicate zeolite (Mg.ZA) were investigated under batch conditions to assess its stability and potential for repeated use. Five successive adsorption–desorption cycles were carried out using 100 mL of 100 mg/L Ca2+ or Mg2+ solutions at pH 7 and 293 K. text: [Conclusions] This study addresses the critical issue of water hardness in Egypt’s Siwa Oasis, where groundwater exhibits exceptionally high levels of calcium and magnesium—reaching 609.5 mg/L (Mg2+) and 325.4 mg/L (Ca2+), resulting in a total hardness of approximately 3312.6 mg/L as CaCO3. title: Sustainable hard water treatment using talc derived magnesium silicate zeolite evaluated by statistical physics and field validation in Siwa Oasis
text: [Conclusions] Although Mg–ZA demonstrated strong performance for hard-water treatment, further optimization is required to support large-scale and long-term application. Key challenges include improving the energy efficiency of the fusion process, enhancing selective removal of both Ca2+ and Mg2+, and maintaining structural and chemical stability during repeated regeneration cycles. text: [abstract] Effective precision oncology demands integration of pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) profiling with tumor-specific genomic features. Here, we present a personalized treatment model using a patient-derived Networking Organoid Culture System (NOCS) composed of intestinal, liver, and kidney organoids differentiated from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) of an NF1-mutant breast cancer patient. This multi-organoid system enabled individualized assessment of drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. Integrative genomic and pathway analyses uncovered therapeutic vulnerabilities, including responsiveness to a novel exon skipping therapy targeting NF1

These findings establish a clinically relevant framework that integrates multi-organ PK/PD modeling with genotype-driven therapeutic strategies, highlighting the potential of combining targeted gene correction with small-molecule therapy for personalized treatment. text: [Introduction] Neurofibromin (NF1) mutations define a clinically and biologically distinct subset of breast cancers (BCs) associated with aggressive behavior and limited response to targeted therapies.1 NF1 encodes a Ras GTPase-activating protein (Ras-GAP) that negatively regulates Ras signaling, and its inactivation leads to sustained activation of Ras and downstream PI3K/AKT and MAPK pathways.2–4 Loss-of-function mutations in NF1 promote tumor proliferation, survival, and therapeutic resistance, and have emerged as poor-prognosis genomic alterations across multiple solid tumors, including BC.5–10 Despite the availability of pathway inhibitors, patients with NF1-mutant tumors rarely achieve durable responses due to feedback reactivation and pathway redundancy

Exon skipping can restore the open reading frame in pre-mRNA by removing deleterious exons, allowing the production of a truncated but functional neurofibromin protein.11 Although this approach is under active investigation in neuromuscular disorders, its application to oncogenic Ras regulation remains largely unexplored.12–14

text: [Introduction] A major barrier to evaluating such genotype-corrective therapies lies in the lack of preclinical platforms that faithfully capture both patient-specific drug responses and systemic pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD). Organoids derived from patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) now enable the in vitro modeling of various tissues, including the intestine, liver, and kidney.15–18 However, individual organoids lack the capacity to simulate integrated absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) processes observed in vivo19.

text: [Introduction] To address this, multi-organ microphysiological systems (MPSs)—including networking cell culture systems (NCCS) and organ-on-a-chip technologies—have been developed to support dynamic inter-organ crosstalk.20–23 When integrated with patient-specific iPSC-derived organoids, these platforms can model systemic drug behavior within a genetically relevant context, offering a new avenue for functional precision oncology.24–26

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
text: [Introduction] Here, we report the development of a patient-specific, iPSC-derived multi-organ PK/PD evaluation platform for NF1-mutant breast cancer. Using iPSCs derived from a patient tumor harboring an NF1 mutation, we generated intestinal, hepatic, and renal organoids and incorporated them into an NOCS-based MPS. We applied this system to evaluate antisense oligonucleotide therapy in combination with small-molecule inhibitors, demonstrating the identification of a patient-optimized treatment (Paxalisib) with synergistic efficacy when paired with NF1 exon skipping. This study establishes a mechanistically grounded, translational framework for integrating drug metabolism, genomic repair, and individualized therapy selection in genetically defined breast cancer.

section: Identification of patient-specific molecular characteristics in primary cells isolated from BC patient 1 tissue
text: [Identification of patient-specific molecular characteristics in primary cells isolated from BC patient 1 tissue] To evaluate the genetic similarity between patient tissues and isolated primary cells, tumor and normal tissues and their corresponding primary cells were analyzed using WES. Normal tissues and derived cells were 96.2% genetically similar, while tumor tissues and derived cells were 97.7% genetically similar. In the tumor tissue, we identified a loss-of-function mutation in NF1 (c.165_166insCT, p.I55fsX) and gain-of-function mutations in PIK3CA (c.3139 C > T, p.H1047Y) and ERBB2/HER2 (c.2711 A > T, p.D904V) (Fig. 5e). We therefore investigated alterations in the downstream NF1-RAS, PI3K-AKT, and MEK-ERK signaling pathways, and found that tumor-derived primary cells exhibited increased activation of these pathways compared to their normal counterparts (Fig. 5f–g).

section: Exon skipping of the NF1 mutant in BC patient 1-derived primary cells as a potential therapy
text: [Exon skipping of the NF1 mutant in BC patient 1-derived primary cells as a potential therapy] To improve drug responsiveness in patients with BC harboring NF1 mutations, we assessed exon-skipping therapy as an advanced personalized therapeutic strategy. WES identified a novel frameshift mutation in exon 2 of NF1, c.165_166insCT (p.I55fsX), which was located in a highly conserved region (Supplementary Fig. 6a). We identified exonic splicing enhancer (ESE) and silencer sites within NF1 exon 2 using the Human Splicing Finder and selected candidate antisense oligonucleotides (AONs) targeting ESE sites (Supplementary Fig. 6b). Because AON-binding sites within double-stranded RNA regions may be inaccessible, reducing exon-skipping efficacy, we analyzed the RNA secondary structure of exon 2 and designed AONs to bind to loop or single-stranded regions (Supplementary Figs. 6c and 5h)

text: [NOCS for PK/PD assessment of precision therapeutics] The NOCS was developed to closely replicate in-vivo organ connectivity and physiological fluid dynamics, providing a dynamic microenvironment that supports nutrient transport, drug metabolism, and waste elimination. By integrating multi-organ interactions in a controlled fluidic system, NOCS offers a robust platform for evaluating drug absorption, metabolism, and efficacy in a physiologically relevant context.

text: [NOCS for PK/PD assessment of precision therapeutics] In previous studies,20 NCCS were implemented as closed systems (Supplementary Fig. 7a, left), limiting their ability to accurately replicate in vivo PK profiles, particularly for drugs cleared primarily by the kidneys. Compounds, such as Acyclovir and Chlorothiazide, characterized by minimal hepatic metabolism and predominant renal clearance, failed to exhibit physiologically relevant clearance patterns in the closed configuration. This limitation was likely due to metabolite accumulation and the absence of continuous medium exchange, which are essential for mimicking systemic drug elimination. The semi-open system, named NOCS, introduced here yielded PK profiles for these drugs that more closely mirrored in-vivo behavior, indicating improved simulation of metabolic and excretory processes

text: [Patient 1-specific PD evaluation of combination therapy in NF1-mutant BC using the NOCS platform] To validate the therapeutic synergy in vivo, primary breast tumor cells from the NF1 patient were subcutaneously implanted into nude mice. Lenti-U7-AON2/12 for NF1 exon skipping was intratumorally delivered when tumors reached ~50 mm³, followed by oral Paxalisib treatment every three days (Supplementary Fig. 11a). Consistent with NOCS results, combined NF1-AON and Paxalisib treatment markedly suppressed xenograft tumor growth and weight, reduced proliferation, and increased apoptosis compared to either monotherapy, as shown by active caspase-3 staining (Supplementary Fig. 11b–e), without significant changes in body weight or histopathological abnormalities in major organs (Supplementary Fig. 11f–h)

text: [Discussion] We developed and validated a NOCS, a multi-organ MPS that enables dynamic inter-organ interaction and recapitulates systemic PK and PD in a patient-specific context. By incorporating iPSC-derived organoids from an NF1-mutant patient with BC into a dynamic microfluidic circuit, we successfully established NOCS models mimicking patient-relevant drug absorption, metabolism, distribution, and excretion with high physiological fidelity. Compared to conventional organ-on-a-chip systems,29 the NOCS platform supports the integration of fully matured, tissue-specific organoids across multiple compartments

text: [Discussion] Despite the strengths of this study, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the work focused on iPSCs derived from a single breast cancer patient harboring an NF1 mutation. This patient-specific design inevitably limits broad generalizability across diverse genetic backgrounds. However, the primary aim of the study was to establish the technical feasibility and translational relevance of the NOCS platform for integrating patient-derived intestine, liver, kidney, and tumor compartments into a unified PK/PD evaluation system. Importantly, even within this single-patient setting, the platform consistently captured functionally meaningful differences in drug metabolism and therapeutic response, demonstrating its capacity to resolve patient-specific pharmacological heterogeneity

text: [Discussion] In conclusion, we established a NOCS, a patient-specific, multi-organ in-vitro PK/PD platform integrating tailored organoids for precision medicine. We proposed a personalized therapeutic strategy combining exon skipping with targeted inhibition and aligned with the patient’s genetic and physiological profiles. As a scalable and translationally relevant system, NOCS provides a powerful tool to guide individualized drug selection and dosing based on genotype-specific responses.

section: Identification of the NF1 mutant allele in BC Patient 1-derived hiPSCs
text: [Identification of the NF1 mutant allele in BC Patient 1-derived hiPSCs] To validate the genetic background of the NF1 mutation in BC patient-derived hiPSCs compared to BC tissues, genomic DNA was extracted from normal and patient-derived hiPSCs using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (QIAGEN, #69504, Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The exon 2 region of NF1 was amplified by PCR, and the PCR products were cloned into a TA cloning vector. After TA cloning, the NF1 mutation in patient-derived hiPSCs was verified by sequencing, and the results were compared to the WES analysis of the patient tissue. WES analysis was conducted by Theragen Bio (Suwon, Republic of Korea) using standard next-generation sequencing technology.

section: Generation of small intestine organoid (IO) from hiPSCs and isolation of ISCs
text: [Generation of small intestine organoid (IO) from hiPSCs and isolation of ISCs] The differentiation of human normal and BC patient 1-derived iPSCs into hIOs, and the isolation of proliferative ISCs, were performed as previously described.27 Briefly, hiPSCs were differentiated into DE by treatment with 100 ng/mL Activin A (Novus Biologicals) for 3 days in RPMI 1640 medium with increasing concentrations of fetal bovine serum (FBS). The DE cells were then cultured in RPMI 1640 medium with 2% FBS, 500 ng/mL FGF4 (PeproTech), and 500 ng/mL WNT3A (R&D Systems) to form mid-hindgut cells. These cells formed 3D spheres, which were embedded in Matrigel (Corning Inc.) and cultured in hIO medium [Advanced DMEM/F-12, 2% B-27, 100 ng/mL EGF, and 100 ng/mL Noggin].

section: Generation of small intestine organoid (IO) from hiPSCs and isolation of ISCs
text: [Generation of small intestine organoid (IO) from hiPSCs and isolation of ISCs] For ISC isolation, hIOs were removed from Matrigel and gently pipetted to eliminate residual fragments. Organoids were digested in 1 mL of 0.25% trypsin-EDTA for 5 minutes at 37 °C and dissociated into small clumps. Digestion was stopped with 10 mL of ISC basal medium [Advanced DMEM/F-12 with 2mM L-glutamine, 15 mM HEPES, and 1% P/S], followed by centrifugation at 800 × g for 3 minutes. The pellet was resuspended in ISC growth medium containing 1 μM Jagged-1 (Anaspec) and 10 μM Y27632 (Tocris Bioscience), along with 2% B-27, 10 nM [Leu15]-Gastrin I, 100 ng/mL WNT3A, EGF, and Noggin, 500ng/mL R-Spondin 1, 500 nM A83-01 (Tocris Bioscience), 10 μM SB202190, 2.5 μM PGE2, 1mM N-acetyl L-cysteine, and 10 mM nicotinamide (Sigma-Aldrich), prepared in ISC basal medium

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
section: Generation of hIECs model using ALI culture
text: [Generation of hIECs model using ALI culture] To generate the hIECs model, ISCs were seeded onto 12-well transwell plates to establish polarized cultures. Transwell membranes were pre-coated with 1% Matrigel in cold ISC basal medium and incubated for 1 hour at 37 °C. ISCs were washed with PBS, dissociated using 0.25% trypsin-EDTA for 8 minutes at 37 °C, and centrifuged. A total of 3.5 × 10⁵ cells were seeded into each insert with ISC growth medium. After reaching confluency, the apical medium was removed to initiate ALI conditions, and the basal medium was replaced every 2 days. ALI cultures were maintained for 6–10 days to promote epithelial differentiation. Detailed information on the reagents used for liver organoid generation is provided in Supplementary Table 4.

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
text: [Generation of hLOs from hiPSCs] Differentiation of human normal and BC patient 1-derived iPSCs into hepatic-like organoids (hLOs) was performed as previously described.28 Briefly, iPSCs were treated with 100 ng/mL Activin A (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in RPMI 1640 with 2% B-27 for 6 days to induce DE. For HE induction, DE cells were cultured for 4 days under hypoxic conditions in RPMI 1640 with 2% B-27 minus insulin (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific), 25 ng/mL BMP4, and 10 ng/mL bFGF (PeproTech)

text: [Generation of hLOs from hiPSCs] . Detached HE cells were embedded in Matrigel and cultured in hepatic medium (HM) composed of advanced DMEM/F12 with 1% P/S, 1 mM GlutaMax, 1 mM HEPES, 1% N-2, 2% B-27 without vitamin A, 1% ITS, 50 ng/mL EGF, 25 ng/mL HGF, 10 ng/mL bFGF, 10 ng/mL Oncostatin M (R&D Systems), 5 μM A83-01, 10 μM forskolin (Sigma-Aldrich), 1mM N-acetyl L-cysteine, 10 nM Leu15-gastrin I, 10 mM nicotinamide, and 100 nM dexamethasone (Sigma-Aldrich). Organoids were expanded in Matrigel domes with HM refreshed every 2–3 days and passaged weekly at a 1:4–1:10 ratio.

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
text: [Generation of hLOs from hiPSCs] For differentiation, one day post-passaging, HM was replaced with expansion medium (EM), composed of advanced DMEM/F12 with 1% P/S, 1 mM GlutaMax, 1 mM HEPES, 1% N-2, 2% B-27 without vitamin A, 50 ng/mL EGF, 25 ng/mL HGF, 100 ng/mL FGF10, 1mg/mL R-spondin 1, 25 ng/mL BMP7 (PeproTech), 5 μM A83-01, 10 μM forskolin, 1mM N-acetyl L-cysteine, 10 mM nicotinamide, and 10 nM Leu15-gastrin I. After 3 days in EM, the medium was replaced with differentiation medium (DM) containing advanced DMEM/F12, 1% P/S, 1 mM GlutaMax, 1 mM HEPES, 1% N-2, 2% B-27 with vitamin A, 25 ng/mL HGF, 0.5 μM A83-01, 100 ng/mL FGF19 (PeproTech), 100 ng/mL BMP7, 1mM N-acetyl L-cysteine, 10 nM Leu15-gastrin I, and 3 μM dexamethasone. Organoids were maintained in DM for 6 days with medium changes every 2 days

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
text: [Generation of KOs from iPSCs] To generate KOs, human normal and BC patient 1-derived iPSCs were seeded on Matrigel-coated flasks and cultured in mTeSR1 medium (STEMCELL Technologies, #85850). When cells reached ~30–40% confluency (day 1–2), primitive streak (PS) induction was initiated using Advanced RPMI 1640 (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with antibiotic–antimycotic (Gibco, #15240062), NEAAs, GlutaMax, B-27, and 8 μM CHIR99021 (Tocris Bioscience) for 4 days. For BC iPSCs, 1 μM Y-27632 was also included.

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
text: [Generation of KOs from iPSCs] From days 5–7, cells were treated with 100 ng/mL FGF9 (PeproTech), 1 μg/mL heparin (Sigma-Aldrich), and 0.1 μM RA (Sigma-Aldrich, days 5–6 only) to induce intermediate mesoderm (IM). IM cells were dissociated using Accutase (STEMCELL Technologies, #07920), and 1 × 10⁵ cells/well were seeded into ultra-low attachment 96-well plates (Corning, #CLS7007), centrifuged (800 × g, 2 min), and cultured with FGF9, heparin, and 5 μM Y-27632 for 1 day. Aggregates (5–6/well) were transferred to collagen-coated transwell inserts (Corning, #3491), treated with 5 μM CHIR99021 for 1 h, then cultured in differentiation medium containing 100 ng/mL FGF9 and 100 ng/mL BMP7 (PeproTech) for 10–14 days with daily medium changes, avoiding overflow onto the apical surface.47

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
section: Generation of hKORTECs Model from hKTOs
text: [Generation of hKORTECs Model from hKTOs] KO-derived iPSCs were dissociated using Gentle Cell Dissociation Reagent (STEMCELL Technologies, #100-0485) for 10 min at 37 °C. Tubular segments and single cells were embedded in Matrigel and cultured in DMEM/F12 supplemented with 1.5% B-27, 1 μM N-acetyl L-cysteine, 5 μM A83-01, 100ng/mL R-spondin 1, 50 ng/mL FGF10 (PeproTech), 50 ng/mL EGF, 50 ng/mL BMP7, and 10 μM Y-27632. Medium was changed every 2 days, and tubule-like organoids appeared within 7–14 days. Organoids were passaged weekly.

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
section: Generation of hKORTECs Model from hKTOs
text: [Generation of hKORTECs Model from hKTOs] For hKORTECs, ~250,000 cells from tubule organoids were seeded onto SPLInsert™ Hanging 24-well plates (SPL Life Science, #36124) and cultured in kidney tubule organoid medium. Upon confluency, the apical medium was removed to initiate ALI conditions while preventing overflow onto the membrane. Reagent details are provided in Supplementary Table 4.

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
section: Generation of BC patient 1-derived tumor spheroid model
text: [Generation of BC patient 1-derived tumor spheroid model] Primary multicellular cells were isolated from the tumor and matched normal breast tissues obtained from patients with breast cancer. Cells were cultured in Mammary Epithelial Growth Medium (MEGM; Lonza, Basel, Switzerland, # CC-3150) supplemented with 1 μM forskolin, 1 μM RepSox, 1 μM Y-27632, 10 ng/mL recombinant human R-Spondin1, and 2% Matrigel (Corning Inc., #354234). Cell suspensions were placed in 15-mL SFU tubes (SPL Life Science, #911604) and subjected to rotation culture at 37 °C in 5% CO₂ incubator for 48 hours to induce multicellular aggregate formation. Following aggregation, cell clusters were embedded in a 3D extracellular matrix composed of type I collagen (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, #A10644-01) and Matrigel mixed at a 7:3 volume ratio

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
section: Generation of BC patient 1-derived tumor spheroid model
text: [Generation of BC patient 1-derived tumor spheroid model] . The embedded aggregates were transferred into ultra-low attachment 6-well plates (Corning Inc., # CLS3471) and maintained in suspension culture with MEGM for an additional 3–5 days at 37 °C under 5% CO₂. The resulting spheroids were used for subsequent functional and histological analyses.

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
section: In vitro three germ layer differentiation
text: [In vitro three germ layer differentiation] To assess the differentiation potential, BC patient-derived iPSCs were detached using 1 mg/mL Collagenase Type IV and 1 mg/mL Dispase II (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, #17105041). The cell colonies were transferred to Petri dishes (SPL Life Science) and cultured in embryoid body (EB) differentiation medium containing DMEM/F-12 and 10% KSR for 5 days. Formed EBs were then re-plated onto 5% Matrigel-coated 4-well plates (Thermo Fisher Scientific, #167063) and cultured for an additional 10 days.

section: In vitro three germ layer differentiation
text: [In vitro three germ layer differentiation] Cells were subsequently analyzed for germ layer-specific differentiation by immunostaining, the proportion of positive cells was quantified using ImageJ (version 1.53e), and RT-qPCR using ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm markers. Antibody and primer details are provided in Supplementary Tables 5 and 7.

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
text: [Immunocytochemical analysis] hiPSCs and organoids were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde at 4 °C overnight, then washed with PBS (Welgene). Samples were incubated with primary antibodies at 4 °C overnight, followed by Alexa Fluor®-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at 25 °C in the dark. Organoids were washed with PBS containing 0.05% Tween-20 between steps. Nuclei were stained with Hoechst 33342 (Invitrogen) and slides mounted using Fluoromount™ Aqueous Mounting Medium (Sigma-Aldrich, #F4680). Images were captured using a confocal microscope (LSM 800, ZEISS) or EVOS FL Auto microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and analyzed with ImageJ (version 1.53e).

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
text: [Alkaline phosphatase (AP) staining and Immunostaining] hiPSCs were stained using the AP Detection Kit (Sigma-Aldrich) following the manufacturer’s instructions. For immunostaining, cells were washed with PBS and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min at 25 °C, followed by permeabilization with PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100 for 15 min. After blocking with 4% BSA (Bovogen Biologicals, Keilor East, VIC, Australia, #BSAS-AU) for 1 h at 25 °C, cells were incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C. The next day, samples were washed with PBS containing 0.05% Tween-20 and incubated with fluorescence-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at 25 °C. Nuclei were stained with DAPI (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA, USA, #564907) and visualized using a fluorescence microscope (IX71, Olympus Corporation, Tokyo, Japan)

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
section: RNA preparation, cDNA synthesis, and quantitative real-time PCR
text: [RNA preparation, cDNA synthesis, and quantitative real-time PCR] Total RNA from hiPSCs and differentiated cells was extracted using the RNeasy Mini Kit (QIAGEN, #74106). cDNA was synthesized using the SuperScript™ IV First-Strand Synthesis System (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific, #18091200). qPCR was performed using SYBR™ Green PCR Master Mix (Applied Biosystems, Thermo Fisher Scientific, #43-091-55) on a 7500 Fast Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems). Gene expression levels were analyzed using the ΔΔCt method. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 7.

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
section: Short tandem repeat (STR) analysis and Karyotype analysis
text: [Short tandem repeat (STR) analysis and Karyotype analysis] Genomic DNA was extracted from breast cancer fibroblasts and hiPSCs using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit. STR analysis was performed by HumanPass Inc. (Seoul, Republic of Korea), and G-banding karyotype analysis of cultured hiPSCs was conducted by GenDix Inc. (Seoul, Republic of Korea).

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
text: [TEER Measurement] To assess barrier integrity and functionality of the hIEC and KORTEC models, TEER was measured using an epithelial volt/ohm meter (EVOM2, World Precision Instruments, Sarasota, FL, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. TEER was assessed both to evaluate the functional properties of the models and to determine the impact of drug treatment on epithelial barrier toxicity.

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
text: [Dextran uptake assay] To evaluate the paracellular permeability of the hIECs model, FITC-conjugated dextrans (4 kDa, Chondrex Inc., #4013; 40 kDa, Chondrex Inc., #4009) were used. The hIEC models were washed with PBS and treated with HBSS (Thermo Fisher Scientific, #14025092) containing 6.25 μM of each FITC-dextran in the apical compartment. After a 30-minute incubation at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 incubator, the basal solution was collected for fluorescence analysis using a multi-mode microplate reader (SpectraMax i3x, Molecular Devices).

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
text: [Dextran uptake assay] For the hKORTECs model, FITC-labeled dextran (3 kDa, Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific, #D3306) was added to the apical compartment at a final concentration of 0.1 mg/ml. At 30, 60, 120, 240, and 360 minutes, 100 μl of medium was collected from both apical and basolateral compartments. Fluorescence intensity was measured using a multi-mode microplate reader.

section: Measurement of ALB, AST, and ALT
text: [Measurement of ALB, AST, and ALT] To quantify ALB, ALT, and AST, organoid culture supernatants were collected after 24 hours, and the concentrations of secreted ALB, ALT, and AST were measured using Human Albumin (Bethyl Laboratories, Montgomery, TX, USA), ALT (Abcam, Cambridge, UK), and AST (Abcam) ELISA kits according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Absorbance was measured using a microplate reader. A list of the ELISA kits used in this study is provided in Supplementary Table 6.

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
text: [Uptake of CLF] To measure CLF polarity, organoids were removed from the Matrigel by washing with PBS and incubated with culture medium supplemented with 10 μg/ml CLF (Corning Inc.) and 1 μg/ml Hoechst 33342 for 30 minutes at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 incubator. After incubation, the dye was removed, and the DhLOs were gently washed twice with cold PBS containing calcium and magnesium (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, #10010023). Culture medium was then added, and the DhLOs were photographed under a confocal microscope (LSM 800, ZEISS).

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
section: Measurement of cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme and CYP450 reductase (CPR) activity assay
text: [Measurement of cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme and CYP450 reductase (CPR) activity assay] CPR activity in the hIECs was evaluated using the Cytochrome P450 Reductase Assay Kit (Abcam, #ab204704) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Standard and reaction wells were prepared with appropriate volumes of samples, inhibitors, or controls, followed by the addition of reaction mix and 20 mM G6P solution. After 30 minutes of incubation at 25 °C, CPR activity was measured using a colorimetric microplate reader.

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
section: Measurement of cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme and CYP450 reductase (CPR) activity assay
text: [Measurement of cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme and CYP450 reductase (CPR) activity assay] To assess CYP enzyme activity in the DhLOs model, specific CYP enzymes were induced with inducers: 20 μM rifampicin for CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, and CYP3A4, and 100 μM omeprazole for CYP1A2. CYP family activity was analyzed using a P450-Glo assay kit (Promega Corporation) and measured with a GloMax Navigator Microplate Luminometer (Promega Corporation). The results were normalized to total cell count using a TC20 Automated Cell Counter (Bio-Rad Laboratories) and expressed as enzyme activity per 1 × 10⁶ cells.

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
section: Assessment of Albumin Uptake and MRP2/4 Transport Function in the hKORTECs
text: [Assessment of Albumin Uptake and MRP2/4 Transport Function in the hKORTECs] For albumin uptake assessment, FITC-labeled albumin (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific, #A23015) was added to the apical compartment at a final concentration of 0.2 mg/ml. After 6 hours, samples were collected from both the apical and basolateral compartments, and the fluorescence was measured using a multi-mode microplate reader.

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
section: Assessment of Albumin Uptake and MRP2/4 Transport Function in the hKORTECs
text: [Assessment of Albumin Uptake and MRP2/4 Transport Function in the hKORTECs] For the MRP2/4 transport assay, 10 μM CDFDA (Sigma-Aldrich, #21879) ± 20 μM MK-571 (Sigma-Aldrich, #M7571) in serum-free medium was added to the basolateral compartment, and serum-free medium ± 20 μM MK-571 was added to the apical compartment. Cells were incubated at 37 °C for 2 hours, and samples were collected from the basolateral compartment and the fluorescence was measured using a multi-mode microplate reader.

title: Personalized pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic guided therapy via an induced pluripotent stem cell–derived multi-organoid platform in NF1-mutant breast cancer
section: Functional analysis of drug transporters in hKORTECs
text: [Functional analysis of drug transporters in hKORTECs] For nephrotoxicity and drug transporter activity assays, hKORTECs were exposed to 20 μM cisplatin (Sigma-Aldrich) with/without 1 mM cimetidine (Sigma-Aldrich) for 24 hours and the apoptosis profile was examined in the hKORTECs. For the apoptosis assay, cells were harvested and incubated with 100 μl of Muse Annexin V & Dead Cell Reagent (Millipore, Bedford, MA, USA) for 20 minutes at room temperature. Apoptosis was determined using the Muse Cell Analyzer (Millipore), and the statistics were presented as percentages of the cells that were alive, apoptotic, or dead.

text: [Tissue Processing] Human breast tumor and normal tissues, mouse xenografts, and major organs were fixed in 10% formalin (Sigma-Aldrich, #HT501128) for 4–6 hours at 25 °C. The tissues were then placed in cassettes, thoroughly washed with water, and stored in 70% ethanol at 4 °C overnight until further processing. Tissue processing was performed according to a standard protocol, which included sequential dehydration steps: 80% ethanol for 1 hour at 25 °C, followed by 90% ethanol for 1 hour, 95% ethanol for 1 hour, and two rounds of 100% ethanol for 1 hour each. This was followed by three xylene treatments, each for 1 hour at 25 °C. Finally, tissues were infiltrated with paraffin wax overnight at 65 °C

text: [Tissue Processing] . This was followed by three xylene treatments, each for 1 hour at 25 °C. Finally, tissues were infiltrated with paraffin wax overnight at 65 °C. Paraffin-embedded tissue samples were sectioned into 5–7 μm thick slices using a rotary microtome (Epredia, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Epredia™ HM 325) and mounted onto silane-coated histological slides (MUTO CHEMICALS CO., #5116-20 F, Tokyo, Japan) to enhance tissue adhesion.

text: [Immunohistochemical (IHC) Analysis] Paraffin-embedded tissue slides were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated through graded ethanol. Endogenous peroxidase activity was blocked with 0.3% H₂O₂, followed by permeabilization with PBST (1× PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100). Antigen retrieval was performed in 10 mM sodium citrate buffer with 0.05% Tween 20 using a microwave. After blocking with 2% normal horse serum, slides were incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C. Following PBST washes, biotinylated secondary antibodies were applied, followed by ABC reagent (Vector Laboratories, Inc., Newark, CA, USA, #PK-400) and DAB substrate (Vector Laboratories, Inc., #SK-4105). Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI. Images were captured using an inverted microscope (IX71, Olympus) and analyzed with cellSense software
