text: [Review objectives] The purpose of this scoping review is to provide an overview of the current state of ST utilization along with different AI-driven workflows for studying OPMDs and to highlight emerging opportunities for leveraging ST and AI to improve lesion classification and identification of high-risk cases, along with current limitations and open challenges.

text: [Materials and methods] Search strategy A literature search was conducted using seven different electronic search engines: Springer, Embase (Elsevier), Cochrane Library (Wiley), EBSCOhost, IEEE Xplore, PubMed, and Google Scholar. The search followed the PRISMA guidelines for scoping reviews. In addition to using the search terms combined with logical operators such as "OR" for union, "AND" ("&") for intersection, and "-" for negation, we also searched the reference lists of the relevant articles to perform a more thorough literature search. Specific search terms were tailored for each database. To capture the latest developments in this area, we limited our search to studies published between January 2014 and early May 2025 when our search was conducted

text: [Notable studies] The ten notable studies demonstrated the use of spatial transcriptomics and/or proteomics to investigate H&N cancers, particularly HPV-positive SCC, de-novo SCC and SCC associated with OPMDs. However, they leveraged ST technology in the context of different study designs and objectives. Two studies [29, 30] applied ST to corroborate immune checkpoints identified a priori and studied via immunohistochemistry (IHC). This study design had the advantage that ST, which is expensive, could be applied to a smaller number of representative samples from the larger cohort. Seven studies applied ST to characterize gene expression across tissue types and/or the tumor microenvironment (TME) more broadly

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] . Seven studies applied ST to characterize gene expression across tissue types and/or the tumor microenvironment (TME) more broadly. Of these studies, one [31] investigated treatment resistance with a longitudinal case study, two [32, 33] investigated malignant transformation with a cross-sectional study design, which [33] also presents a spatial atlas, and four [34–37] investigated the role of spatial architecture in H&N SCC. The study by [35], in particular, trained an ML model on ST data to predict whether spots are at the “leading edge” of a tumor and then applied this model to different (non-H&N SCC) cancer types. The final notable study [38] was developed a cell-death-related risk score on publicly available bulk and scRNA-seq data and then generated ST for risk score validation

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] . Overall, the ten notable studies identified gene expression signatures with prognostic and therapeutic implications, as discussed in more depth below.

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] Noda et al. [29] utilized imaging approach to characterize the distribution and, in some regions, the mutual exclusivity, of immune checkpoint ligands (e.g., PD-L1 and B7-H4) within H&N SCC. The study involved IHC scoring of a large cohort. Transcript–protein concordance was validated by ST sequencing (Visium) of six representative H&N SCC paired samples, with squamous intraepithelial neoplasia and normal oral mucosa. Spatial mapping of CD274 expression corroborated immunostaining, showing the strongest enrichment in invasive H&N SCC regions, identified based on histology. ST also corroborated the presence of PD-L1 mRNA and protein expression in the PD-L1–high zones identified from the IHC, supporting the biological relevance of transcript-level measurements for checkpoint stratification.

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] Noda et al. [30] expanded upon their original study [29], investigating B7-H4 (VTCN1) as an alternative immune checkpoint target in H&N SCC, characterized by Low PD-L1 or immune-checkpoint-inhibitor-resistance. As in the group’s first paper, they combined ST (Visium) and multiplex IHC experiments on H&N SCC samples with paired squamous intraepithelial neoplasia and normal oral mucosa. Spatial maps revealed a mutually exclusive VTCN1–CD274 pattern in 83% of cases, with CD8A down-regulated in VTCN1-positive regions, indicating immune-suppressive niches. These transcriptomic findings corroborated IHC, showing reciprocal B7-H4/PD-L1 staining across tumor cores

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] . These transcriptomic findings corroborated IHC, showing reciprocal B7-H4/PD-L1 staining across tumor cores. Clinically, the authors proposed B7-H4 as a promising antibody–drug-conjugate target for PD-L1-negative or immune-checkpoint-inhibitor-resistant H&N SCC. Unlike the other studies that aimed to broadly characterize spatial patterns of disease progression, the two investigations by Noda et al. focused on evaluating an IHC marker that had been identified a priori. Because their goal was to validate this targeted IHC finding rather than explore global spatial gene-expression heterogeneity, their analytical pipeline appropriately relied on conventional differential-expression and pathway analyses rather than ML/DL based discovery approaches.

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] Iwasa et al. [31] used GeoMx digital spatial profiling to study spatial changes in gene expression and TME compartments from a single patient with SCC who acquired resistance to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy (nivolumab). Tumor samples collected pre- and post- resistance, along with normal tissue. The workflow involved selecting tumor, stromal, and normal regions of interest (PanCK ±), performing whole-transcriptome profiling, and comparing samples using differential expression and Reactome pathway enrichment within the GeoMx platform

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] . These analyses revealed that, prior to immunotherapy, the initial tumor exhibited strong expression of antigen presentation and interferon-gamma signaling genes, whereas after resistance, these pathways were suppressed and replaced by dominant epigenetic reprogramming signatures including overexpression of PRMTs, HDACs, DNMT1, and EZH2 accompanied by downregulation of MHC class I molecules. Concurrently, the TME shifted from protein synthesis-related activity to G protein-coupled receptors and olfactory receptor signaling, indicating stromal reprogramming

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] . Overall, these results suggest that immune escape in SCC might be driven by epigenetic suppression of antigen presentation and altered stromal signaling, highlighting potential therapeutic targets to restore immunogenicity and overcome resistance, although the conclusions of this study may be limited by the single-patient, observational design and possible therapy-specific effects.

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] Sun et al. [33] investigated the transformation of precancerous lesions to oral SCC. scRNA-seq and ST sequencing (Visium) was applied to biopsies from nine patients, including normal mucosa, dysplastic tissue adjacent to the malignant SCC lesions, and tumoral tissues. Segmentation of these regions was performed by a pathologist based on the histological images. Transcriptionally distinct zones were defined via unsupervised clustering and marker gene identification. Clusters were used in pathway enrichment analyses. Cell–cell communication was characterized with CellphoneDB [39]

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] . Clusters were used in pathway enrichment analyses. Cell–cell communication was characterized with CellphoneDB [39]. These analyses identified initiation-associated epithelial and fibroblast signatures, immune and stromal cell reprogramming (especially immune‑inhibitory monocytes and pro-tumor signaling pathways such as VEGF), all spatially localized to precancerous zones. Validation, performed via functional modeling in mice, suggests that targeting the identified pathways (e.g., anti‑PD‑1, anti‑TGFβ) may prevent malignant progression, informing future early‑intervention strategies. Lastly, the study provided an integrative single-cell and ST atlas, capturing the cellular and molecular changes underlying SCC initiation from normal mucosa to dysplastic epithelium to early tumor

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] Zhi et al. [32] also explored malignant transformation with a cross-sectional design, like the study by Sun et al. [33], but focusing on oral submucous fibrosis (OSF), an entity classified as a high-risk OPMD. ST sequencing (Visium) was applied to 4 OSF-SCC transformed samples and 1 conventional SCC sample (no OSF) as a control. Regions of interest, generated via unsupervised clustering, were annotated based on marker genes. After, differential gene expression and pathway analyses were conducted. The results were overlaid with spatial metabolomics data to assign metabolic programs to tissue zones, a unique aspect of this study

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] . The results were overlaid with spatial metabolomics data to assign metabolic programs to tissue zones, a unique aspect of this study. This analysis enabled the delineation of inflammatory stem-like cells (ISCs) undergoing partial epithelial–mesenchymal transition (pEMT) within the in-situ carcinoma region, eventually acquiring fibroblast-like phenotypes and participating in collagen deposition. This ISC > pEMT > CAF (Cancer Associated Fibroblasts) path mirrors biological transitions suspected in high-risk OPMDs. Importantly, the enrichment of polyamine metabolism and presence of tertiary lymphoid structures suggest both diagnostic and therapeutic relevance, supporting the utility of ST in identifying metabolic vulnerabilities and immunologic context

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] Shaikh et al. [34] investigated the spatial distribution and role of fibroblast and myeloid cells subtypes driving lymph node metastasis. Their study analyzed H&N SCC samples from 23 gingivo-buccal SCC patients, applying both ST and IHC. After ST profiling (GeoMx) in selected regions of interest across tumor–stromal interfaces, spatial deconvolution (unsupervised learning) was to assess cell-type composition per spot. Standard methods for differential gene expression, gene set variation, and protein–protein interaction networks were applied. Overall, the analyses identified functional organization of tumor-stromal interfaces as a critical zone for metastasis progression

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] . Overall, the analyses identified functional organization of tumor-stromal interfaces as a critical zone for metastasis progression. These are regions within 200 μm of the tumor edge, where intermediate fibroblasts, myeloid-derived cells, and neutrophils accumulate near tumor regions, while CAF and extracellular matrix genes (e.g., FN1 and COL5A1) localize toward stromal ends, especially in lymph node–positive cases. They observed that intermediate fibroblasts transition into CAFs and migrate outward, contributing to extracellular matrix remodeling and immune suppression, suggesting this spatial reorganization and stromal activation may promote an immune-suppressive microenvironment favoring cancer invasion and lymphatic spread

Instead, Liu et al. leveraged scRNA-seq and ST (Visium), along with publicly available bulk and scRNA-seq data. Data integration enabled tumor immune microenvironment identification as well as per spot metabolic activity calculations with scMetabolism. Unsupervised clustering was performed on these spatial regions, and then clusters were classified into hyper-, normal-, or hypo-metabolic niches

Lastly, cell–cell communication was evaluated in these regions to delineate the coordinate work axis of epithelia cells, inflammatory CFAs, and regulatory T cells.

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] Arora et al. [35] investigated spatial architecture in oral SCC, identifying a transcriptionally conserved leading-edge zone associated with tumor aggressiveness and poor prognosis. ST sequencing (Visium) was applied to samples from 10 oral SCC patients. After unsupervised clustering, marker genes were used to label clusters as “tumor core”, “leading edge”, or “transitory”. Distinct and consistent spatial architectures between tumor core and leading edge were identified via differential gene expression, functional enrichment, pathway, and regulatory analyses [note that publicly available scRNA-seq data was leveraged for cell type deconvolution, as in Liu et al. [37]

text: [Notable studies] . [37]. RNA velocity and kinetic modeling was used to trace cell fate trajectories in the oral SCC HPV-negative samples, leading to the identification of gene signatures and differences associated with aggressive forms of oral SCC. Lastly, the annotated ST data was used to train models for predicting whether a spot was tumor core or leading edge. The application of these models to publicly available ST data for 17 different cancer types revealed that tumor core tended to be tissue-specific but leading edge had conserved gene expression profiles across cancer types, suggesting a potential common mechanism for tumor progression

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] . This study marks an important step toward automating ST annotation through AI, demonstrating that learned architectural patterns can be transferred across tissue types and that spatial profiling can yield predictive spatial biomarkers. This zonal dissection could be directly applicable in OPMDs to stratify regions at highest risk of malignant transformation, although the limited number of samples used to train the model may limit the robustness of such inferences, underscoring the need for large, annotated ST data sets to enable reliable model training and generalization.

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] Zhang et al. [36] exclusively utilized publicly available data, making it distinct from the previously discussed notable studies. ST data were taken from the previously discussed study by Arora et al. [35] and scRNA-seq were data taken from [40] and [41]. Data integration was performed with the ML method RCTD [22]. This analysis revealed associations between epithelial cell subtypes and their interaction with normal-like CAFs and tumor invasiveness. Additionally, the identification of integrin and IGF1-mediated crosstalk provided mechanistic insight into epithelial-stromal interactions driving invasiveness, in concordance with Shaikh et al. [34]

text: [Notable studies] . [34]. This framework could be utilized to investigate other cell types and interactions associated with tumorigenesis in OPMDs, for example peri epithelial lymphocytes in OED have been reported to be significant for malignant transformation prediction [42]. Critically, this framework can utilize existing scRNA-seq or ST data, reducing the need for data generation, which can be prohibitively expensive for ST.

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] Pan et al. [38] also made use of publicly available data, like Zhang et al. [36]. Specifically, they leveraged bulk and ScRNA-seq data from both HPV-related and conventional oral SCC samples to train a consensus cell death-related risk score model. This risk score was validated with ST data (Visium) generated from tissue sections of laryngeal SCC from two patients and one normal larynx control patient. ST analyses revealed that high risk scores were also associated with TGF-β signaling pathways and that the interfaces between malignant cells and immune cells were enriched for high-risk scores. Unrelated to the ST validation, high risk scores were predictive of worse overall survival

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] . Unrelated to the ST validation, high risk scores were predictive of worse overall survival. Future studies could investigate the utility of such risks to OPMDs, which enable spatially resolved modeling of cell death, for early prediction of malignant transformation. Lastly, it is worth noting that this study evaluated whether learned patterns from one data generation modality translate another, similar to Arora et al.’s [35] who attempted transfer from oral SCC to other cancer types.

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] To summarize, the ten notable studies summarized above differ in their scope, analytical framework, and biological focus but are united by a common theme: spatial information is crucial for exposing the spatial interplay of cell types, signaling networks, and microenvironmental states that drive malignant transformation or cancer progression in OPMDs and H&N SCC. In many studies, joint ST and scRNA-seq data, often including data from public repositories, was also critical for combating trade-offs in spatial and molecular resolution [e.g. [35–37]]. Strong molecular signal (sequencing depth) in particular, is critical for robust inference of metabolic or immune activity

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] . [35–37]]. Strong molecular signal (sequencing depth) in particular, is critical for robust inference of metabolic or immune activity. Another common theme is the growing emphasis on multi-modal data [e.g., ST and IHC [29, 30]] and multi-omics data [e.g., ST and spatial metabolomics; e.g. [32]]. Integrated data analyses provided complementary perspectives on tissue organization, revealing that the tumor–stromal interface is not a static boundary but a dynamic and interactive zone where fibroblast reprogramming, immune exclusion, and metabolic heterogeneity converge to drive malignant progression. These results underscore that understanding OPMD and H&N SCC progression requires viewing the tissue as a coordinated ecosystem rather than isolated cell populations.

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] Multi-omics and multi-modal studies naturally intersect with the growing use of ML and AI to further enhance the interpretive and predictive power of spatial data. The study by Arora et al. [35] illustrates how ML can extract latent spatial patterns and predict molecular phenotypes from high-dimensional ST datasets, whereas the study by Pan et al. [38] demonstrates models trained on non-spatial transcriptomic data can be used to stratify prognostic risk in ST. DL algorithms, in particular, hold promise for integrating histopathological imaging, gene expression, and clinical metadata to derive holistic, multi-modal representations of tumor biology, enabling scalable and automated insights into OPMD and H&N SCC progression.

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Notable studies] Lastly, only one study leveraged a longitudinal design [31], and the only two studies to explicitly investigate malignant transformation from lesions [32, 33] used a cross-sectional approach. Longitudinal or temporally reconstructed spatial analyses may be needed to directly study how metabolic rewiring, stromal differentiation, and immune modulation unfold over time and to evaluate causality and directionality in disease progression. We expect this to be especially important in the context of OPMDs where malignant transformation is a slow and spatially heterogeneous process. This motivates us to present a conceptual framework for investigating malignant transformation of OPMDs.

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Study design and sample selection] A major challenge to study design is OPMD conditions are relatively rare, and biopsies are invasive and sometimes infeasible, creating challenges in curating sufficiently large and diverse datasets that are needed to power for downstream analyses. Longitudinal sampling is another critical yet challenging aspect of study design. Ideally such studies would involve temporal tracking by collecting serial biopsies taken from the same anatomical site in the same patient at multiple time points, to capture the evolving transcriptional landscape during transformation. However, prospective sampling techniques are often logistically and ethically restricted

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Study design and sample selection] . However, prospective sampling techniques are often logistically and ethically restricted. A more practical and immediately feasible alternative is to leverage retrospective collection of archived Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded specimens. Retrospective studies are greatly enabled by FFPE-compatible ST platforms, which enable spatial profiling of preserved tissue. With these technological advances, retrospective studies may enable temporal reconstruction of disease evolution and provide an attainable pathway for studying dynamic molecular changes leading to malignant transformation in OPMDs. However, retrospective studies will be fundamentally limited by the speed at which RNA degrades

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Study design and sample selection] . However, retrospective studies will be fundamentally limited by the speed at which RNA degrades. Even with advanced preservation techniques, RNA can degrade quickly, leading to extremely poor ST quality data; thus, a critical first step in retrospective ST analyses is evaluation of RNA quality e.g. with RNAScope. Another critical consideration in applying ST to OPMDs is identifying retrospective cases that underwent malignant transformation within the same site that was initially biopsied, indicated by long-term follow-up of the OPMD with clinical- and histopathology-proven diagnosis. Furthermore, within each tissue section, it is essential to precisely select regions of interest that include both tumoral tissue, zones of malignant transformation, and adjacent normal tissue

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Study design and sample selection] . This is particularly important for identifying differentially expressed genes among disease tissues. Researchers must also account for technical constraints of the ST platform, for example, Visium HD slides allow for only two 6.5 × 6.5 mm capture areas per slide which limits the amount of tissue that can be included.

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Lineage tracing] Regardless of the longitudinal study design, the future trajectories of biopsies lesions are unknown. Cell lineage tracing [43, 44], in conjunction with ST [45, 46], present a promising path forward to studying cellular trajectories across time and space. This technology, which is currently only leveraged within the context of xenographs [47] and mouse models [43, 44], could be used to spatial validate findings from traditional study designs. The idea is to apply genome editing, for example CRISPR Cas systems, to induce heritable mutations at target sites in the genome over time. The induced mutations can be captured via scRNA-seq or ST, along with gene expression data, and then used to reconstruct cell lineage trees

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Lineage tracing] . The induced mutations can be captured via scRNA-seq or ST, along with gene expression data, and then used to reconstruct cell lineage trees. Leaves of the tree are labeled by cells or spots, the case of ST, have associated gene expression data, enabling spatial–temporal analyses of gene expression evolution [48, 49], cell state trajectories [50] and cell differentiation [51]. This approach, without ST, has been successfully used to study tumor evolution and metastasis in mouse models [43, 44]. Despite these exciting advances, lineage tracing technologies are still in their nascency

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
text: [Lineage tracing] . Despite these exciting advances, lineage tracing technologies are still in their nascency. It is currently difficult to ensure the phylogenetic signal is sufficient for reconstructing an accurate and sufficiently resolved cell lineage tree and there can be data quality challenges as in non-lineage tracing ST studies [52].

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
section: Utilization of AI methods and risk stratification
text: [Utilization of AI methods and risk stratification] AI models are commonly used for ST analyses, but another important direction of research is their application for stratifying malignant transformation risks, providing an objective transformation prediction tool that can be leveraged in the clinic. Several studies suggest that this is feasible. Two have employed DL-based image segmentation to analyze clinical images of various types of OPMDs [53, 54], demonstrating its applicability to classification different OPMD subtypes and prediction of malignant transformation rates, after incorporating clinical metadata [53, 54]. Relatedly, DL models trained and applied on scanned WSIs can detect subtle histopathological features associated with an increased risk of malignant transformation [42, 55]

title: Spatial transcriptomics and artificial intelligence: a scoping review of emerging applications in head and neck pathology
section: Utilization of AI methods and risk stratification
text: [Utilization of AI methods and risk stratification] . Such models could serve as an aiding tool to alert pathologists of the potential of malignant transformation. We anticipate that combining ML/DL approaches with multi-model data, from clinical imaging, histopathology, and spatial omics, will further improve malignant transformation prediction, and ongoing advances in AI and multi-modal data integration indicate that an implementation is becoming increasingly feasible.

Our review identified just 10 studies that met the inclusion–exclusion criteria. This research predominantly focused on characterizing the TME, rather than the molecular events driving malignant transformation. A more detailed investigation into the spatial and transcriptional changes that occur as OPMDs progress to invasive cancer is essential for identifying early biomarkers and potential intervention targets.

First, training and validating ML models, and DL models in particular, requires ultra-large data sets with ground truth annotations and standardized metadata. The lack of such data sets in H&N pathology, and limited access to standardized metadata presents a major challenge. Relatedly, annotation variability compounds the problem where inconsistent labeling across pathologists introduces noise into training data and undermines reproducibility. text: [abstract] Emerging evidence indicates that elevated systemic iron levels and dysregulated iron metabolism are closely associated with the pathogenesis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Observational studies have linked iron overload (e.g., hereditary hemochromatosis) to an increased risk of HCC, potentially mediated through iron-induced oxidative stress, DNA damage, and chronic inflammatory responses. However, the causal relationship between specific iron-related factors—such as organ-specific iron accumulation, systemic iron metabolism disorders, or exogenous iron exposure (dietary/drug iron)—and HCC development remains unconfirmed.

text: [Introduction] Iron is mainly stored in hemoglobin, and excess iron is stored in the liver parenchyma as ferritin. Iron plays a crucial role in the human body as a cofactor for various proteins and enzymes, which can provide energy for cells, promote cell proliferation, and repair damaged tissues [6]. When the content of iron exceeds the normal range of the human body, it will encourage the excess iron to undergo a Fenton reaction, producing excessive reactive oxygen species(ROS) and other peroxides(Lipid hydroperoxides (LOOH), protein peroxides, and nucleic acid peroxides) to damage cells [7]. It has been shown that cancer cells require the involvement of iron during the stages of tumor development, survival, dissemination, and metastasis [8]

text: [Discussion] . Iron is an essential trace element in the human body. When the body’s iron content exceeds the safe limit, it leads to the denaturation of ferritin, which stores iron, and iron ions are released into the cytoplasm of hepatocytes [19]. Excessive iron deposition induces hepatic injury, with growing evidence supporting iron overload as an independent risk factor for primary liver cancer [20, 21]. Emerging evidence further implicates hepatic iron overload as a cofactor in hepatocarcinogenesis, particularly in the context of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), where iron synergizes with lipotoxicity to amplify oxidative DNA damage [22].

text: [Discussion] In this study, we applied the MR approach to in-depth analysis of pooled genetic data from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to assess the potential causal association between human iron levels and the risk of HCC. The results reveal a significant causal relationship between liver iron content and the occurrence of HCC. On the one hand, the excessive accumulation of iron in hepatocytes can strongly drive oxidative stress response, break the redox homeostasis in cells, and put cells in a state of stress damage. On the other hand, iron accumulation also induces abnormal activation of the cell death program and forced disturbance of liver regeneration

title: IMP2 enhances M2 macrophage polarization via LKB1-AMPK-mediated mitochondrial dynamics and fatty acid β-oxidation to ameliorate diabetic osteoporosis
text: [abstract] A reduction in M2 macrophage polarization is a key pathogenic contributor to diabetic osteoporosis (DOP). In this study, we revealed that IMP2 affects mitochondrial dynamics and fatty acid β-oxidation (FAO) via the LKB1-AMPK pathway, influencing the M2 polarization pattern and thereby improving DOP. Leveraging Cre-loxp technology, we generated macrophage-specific IMP2 knockout mice. Under diabetic settings, IMP2 knockout further disrupted M2 macrophage polarization and intensified bone deterioration. Mechanistically, IMP2 enhances LKB1 mRNA stability through the N6-methyladenosine (m6A) pathway, activating the LKB1-AMPK signaling cascade. This pathway promotes mitochondrial fusion and boosts FAO, fueling M2 macrophage polarization

title: IMP2 enhances M2 macrophage polarization via LKB1-AMPK-mediated mitochondrial dynamics and fatty acid β-oxidation to ameliorate diabetic osteoporosis
text: [Introduction] DOP is a common skeletal complication of diabetes, marked by reduced bone mass, decreased bone microstructure, and a substantially heightened fracture risk [1, 2]. Over 35% of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) suffer from bone loss, with roughly 20% meeting the diagnostic criteria for osteoporosis [1]. Despite its prevalence, the pathogenesis of DOP remains incompletely understood, and clinical treatment options are limited, underscoring the urgent need to identify novel regulatory targets and therapeutic strategies.

title: IMP2 enhances M2 macrophage polarization via LKB1-AMPK-mediated mitochondrial dynamics and fatty acid β-oxidation to ameliorate diabetic osteoporosis
text: [Introduction] Macrophages, an important component of the immune system, play pivotal roles in bone metabolism and inflammation regulation [3, 4]. They can differentiate into functionally distinct subtypes through polarization: pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages and anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages [5, 6]. In the context of diabetes, the reduction in M2 macrophages weakens their anti-inflammatory and tissue-repair capabilities [7–9]. Our previous research has demonstrated that M2 macrophages secrete TGF-β, promoting the osteogenic differentiation of BMSCs [10]. Therefore, modulating macrophage polarization, particularly promoting M2 polarization, could offer a new avenue for improving DOP.

title: IMP2 enhances M2 macrophage polarization via LKB1-AMPK-mediated mitochondrial dynamics and fatty acid β-oxidation to ameliorate diabetic osteoporosis
text: [Introduction] Epigenetics exerts crucial regulatory effects on M2 macrophages. Among epigenetic modifications, RNA modifications, especially m6A methylation, profoundly influence polarization process by dynamically regulating RNA fate [11–13]. As one of the most abundant chemical modifications on eukaryotic mRNA, m6A methylation is formed by methyltransferase complexes, which can be reversibly removed by demethylases, and recognized by “readers” proteins (such as the IGF2BP family). This process regulates the stability, splicing, transport, and translation efficiency of target mRNA, playing a central role in physiological and pathological processes like cell differentiation, metabolic adaptation and immune response [14]

text: [Introduction] . Insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA-binding protein 2 (IMP2/IGF2BP2), a key reader in the m6A process, is abnormally expressed in T2DM, obesity and cancer [15]. IMP2 is closely related to macrophage polarization, serving as a key regulator [15, 16]. Knocking out IMP2 reduces M2 macrophage polarization and exacerbates inflammatory bowel disease [17]; however, the mechanism by which IMP2 regulates M2 macrophages in DOP remains unclear.

title: IMP2 enhances M2 macrophage polarization via LKB1-AMPK-mediated mitochondrial dynamics and fatty acid β-oxidation to ameliorate diabetic osteoporosis
text: [Introduction] Recent studies indicate that the macrophage polarization is closely linked to mitochondrial dynamics and metabolic status [6, 18]. Mitochondria, the core cellular organelles for energy metabolism, regulate cellular functional state through fusion-fission dynamics. Enhanced fusion supports the polarization of M2 macrophages, while excessive fission induces the M1 pro-inflammatory phenotype [19]. FAO, an important metabolic pathway, generates acetyl coenzyme A, replenishes the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and significantly elevates oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and ATP production, promoting M2 macrophage polarization [20]

title: IMP2 enhances M2 macrophage polarization via LKB1-AMPK-mediated mitochondrial dynamics and fatty acid β-oxidation to ameliorate diabetic osteoporosis
text: [Introduction] . In diabetes, high glucose levels induce mitochondrial dynamics imbalance, reducing fusion and causing functional damage [21, 22], as well as a decrease in FAO [23], thereby inhibiting M2 macrophage polarization. Although the impact of mitochondrial function and metabolic status on M2 macrophage polarization is confirmed, the common epigenetic pathways remain unclear.

title: IMP2 enhances M2 macrophage polarization via LKB1-AMPK-mediated mitochondrial dynamics and fatty acid β-oxidation to ameliorate diabetic osteoporosis
text: [Introduction] The LKB1-AMPK signaling pathway is central to cellular energy sensing and metabolic regulation [24], playing crucial roles in maintaining mitochondrial function [25, 26] and lipid metabolism [27, 28]. LKB1 phosphorylates and activates AMPK, which maintains mitochondrial dynamic balance and enhances FAO [28, 29]. In the high glucose environment of diabetes, the LKB1-AMPK pathway activity is often inhibited [30], potentially contributing to mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic disorders. Previous studies have shown that m6A modification is involved in regulating the expression of LKB1 [31, 32], whether IMP2 participates in metabolic and immune regulation by modulating the expression or activity of pathway-related molecules remains unknown.

text: [Introduction] Therefore, we hypothesize that in DOP, IMP2 may target the LKB1-AMPK signaling pathway to influence macrophage mitochondrial dynamic balance and FAO level, thereby promoting the polarization of M2 macrophage and ultimately improving bone metabolism imbalance. By combining in vitro and in vivo experiments, we aim to elucidate the molecular mechanism of IMP2 in DOP, providing a theoretical foundation for the development of targeted immunometabolic therapeutic strategies.

These included an insulin resistance test (Figure S1A), IHC staining for insulin receptors in insulin-target organs (i.e., skeletal muscle and liver) (Figure S1B), immunofluorescence assays demonstrating impaired GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane in the liver and skeletal muscle cells of STZ-induced mice (Figure S1C), as well as WB analysis of the p-AKT/AKT ratio in the insulin signaling pathway (Figure S1D). Subsequently, the characteristic bone destruction associated with diabetes was confirmed. Histological analysis revealed that compared to the control (CON) group, femoral HE staining in the T2DM group displayed typical osteoporotic features, including a reduced number of trabecular bones, increased structural sparsity, and an enlarged bone marrow cavity (Figure 1A). The expression level of CD206, a surface marker specific to M2 macrophages, was notably diminished in the bone marrow of T2DM mice (Figure 1B). Dual immunofluorescence labeling further demonstrated that the co-expression of CD206 and IMP2 in the bone marrow tissue of the T2DM group was significantly lower than that in the CON group, a finding corroborated by Pearson correlation coefficient analysis (Figure 1C)

text: [Osteogenesis disorders in a diabetic environment were accompanied by reduced M2 macrophage271 polarization and downregulated IMP2 expression] In in vitro experiments, we selected 30 mM glucose based on the CCK8 assay to mimic the diabetic microenvironment (Figure S1E). Under high glucose conditions, the polarization balance between M1 and M2 macrophages was disrupted, with increased expression levels of M1 macrophage markers (CD86, iNOS and IL-6) (Figure S1F) and decreased expression levels of M2 macrophage markers (CD163,ARG-1, TGF-β, and IL-10) (Figure 1H-I, S1G), indicating impaired M2 polarization capacity. Notably, high glucose significantly downregulated IMP2 expression at both transcriptional and translational levels during M2 polarization of RAW264.7 cells (Figure 1J-L)

section: IMP2 knockout led to a further reduction in M2 macrophages in T2DM mice and exacerbated osteogenesis disorder in DOP mice
text: [IMP2 knockout led to a further reduction in M2 macrophages in T2DM mice and exacerbated osteogenesis disorder in DOP mice] To delve deeper into IMP2 regulation and its impact on bone mass, we generated macrophage-specific IMP2 knockout mice using the Cre-loxp system and confirmed successful knockout (Figure S2A-B). Micro-CT and HE staining revealed an increase in bone mass in macrophage IMP2 knockout mice (Figure 2A-B). Immunohistochemistry demonstrated a notable reduction in the number of CD206 positive M2 macrophages in the femurs of IMP2f/f, Cre mice (Figure 2C). Analysis of osteogenic-related factors showed lower expression levels of ALP and RUNX2 in the IMP2f/f, Cre group compared to the non-knockout group (Figure 2D-E)

In the diabetic context, IMP2 knockout further suppressed M2 macrophage polarization and exacerbated osteogenesis disorders. Specifically, Micro-CT and HE staining revealed significantly lower bone mass and reduced bone trabeculae in IMP2f/f, Cre+T2DM mice compared to IMP2f/f+T2DM mice (Figure 2A-B). section: IMP2 regulated M2 macrophage polarization to improve osteogenic dysfunction induced by high glucose levels
text: [IMP2 regulated M2 macrophage polarization to improve osteogenic dysfunction induced by high glucose levels] The previous results have shown that high glucose environment suppresses IMP2 expression and impedes M2 macrophage polarization. To further elucidate IMP2’s regulatory role in M2 macrophage polarization, we first overexpressed IMP2 using a plasmid (Igf2bp2 (NM_183029) pLV3-CMV-MCS- 3xFLAGCopGFP-Puro) and confirmed the transfection efficiency at both the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 3A-D). In in vitro experiments, IMP2 overexpression alone enhanced the expression of M2 macrophage markers (CD163, CD206, ARG-1) and anti-inflammatory cytokines (TGF-β, and IL-10) (Figure S3A-C), and also promoted the osteogenesis-promoting effect of M2 macrophages on BMSCs (Figure S3D)

text: [IMP2 regulated mitochondrial fusion to improve its dysfunction in M2 macrophages induced by high glucose levels] Mitochondrial dynamics and function directly influence cell status and differentiation [41]. Mito-Tracker staining and TEM observations revealed distinct mitochondrial phenotypes among groups, RAW264.7 cells in the high glucose induction group exhibited significantly shortened mitochondrial length, reduced fusion, mitochondrial swelling and disruption of the inner membrane structure (Figure 4A-B, D). text: [IMP2 promotes M2 macrophage polarization by regulating FAO] Mitochondrial metabolic status has a direct bearing on macrophage polarization. Further metabolic analysis revealed that during M2 polarization induced by IL-4 and IL-13, macrophages exhibited increased ATP production (Figure 5A). title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [abstract] Tumorigenesis and progression are driven by dysregulated genes and signaling pathways, with cellular metabolic reprogramming being a hallmark that supports neoplastic growth. Alanyl-tRNA Synthetase 1 (AARS1), a key enzyme with dual roles in metabolism and gene expression regulation, has emerged as a critical focus in cancer and disease research. As a member of the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (AARS) family, AARS1 canonically catalyzes the attachment of alanine to its cognate transfer RNA (tRNA) to ensure fidelity in protein synthesis. Emerging evidence reveals non-canonical roles of AARS1 in tumor biology, including regulation of metabolic reprogramming, cell proliferation, apoptosis, and intracellular signal sensing—all of which directly impact tumor growth and patient prognosis

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [abstract] . Beyond cancer, dysregulated AARS1 (via abnormal expression or pathogenic mutations) is linked to a spectrum of non-malignant disorders, including Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease (a hereditary peripheral neuropathy), adult-onset leukoencephalopathy, recurrent acute liver failure, and sulfide dysplasia. These associations arise from disrupted cellular homeostasis and impaired physiological functions caused by AARS1-mediated pathway dysregulation. Notably, AARS1’s ability to sense lactate and catalyze lysine lactylation—a newly identified post-translational modification (PTM)—represents a novel mechanism linking metabolic dysregulation to disease pathogenesis

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [abstract] . Dysregulated AARS1 contributes to tumor initiation, progression, metastasis, and treatment resistance, while its mutations drive the onset of several neurodegenerative and metabolic disorders. Unraveling the molecular mechanisms of AARS1, particularly its lactylation-related functions, will deepen our understanding of cellular metabolism in disease and identify novel therapeutic targets for precise diagnosis and treatment of tumors and other disorders. Furthermore, AARS1 holds significant promise as a diagnostic biomarker and therapeutic target, offering new avenues for precision medicine in both oncology and non-malignant conditions.

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Introduction] Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (AARSs) are a family of evolutionarily conserved enzymes that serve as the “molecular link” between genetic code and protein synthesis. By catalyzing the covalent attachment of specific amino acids to their corresponding transfer RNAs (tRNAs), AARSs ensure the accurate translation of mRNA into functional proteins—an essential process for maintaining cellular homeostasis across all living organisms [1]. Over the past three decades, research has expanded beyond the canonical translational roles of AARSs, uncovering their non-canonical functions in cell signaling, metabolism, and stress response—many of which are dysregulated in disease [2, 3].

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Introduction] Alanyl-tRNA Synthetase 1 (AARS1), a member of the AARS family, has gained increasing attention due to its unique dual roles in protein synthesis and disease pathogenesis. In tumor cells, AARS1 exhibits two pivotal non-canonical functions: acting as an intracellular lactate sensor and catalyzing lysine lactylation—a Post-Translational Modification (PTM) first identified in 2019 that regulates metabolism, gene expression, and cell fate in cancer [4, 5]. This lactylation-mediated mechanism provides a direct link between the Warburg effect (aerobic glycolysis in tumors) and malignant progression, offering a new lens to understand metabolic reprogramming in cancer [5, 6].

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Introduction] Beyond oncology, AARS1 is implicated in multiple non-malignant disorders. Pathogenic mutations in the AARS1 gene are a well-established cause of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2 N (CMT2N), an inherited peripheral neuropathy characterized by progressive motor and sensory dysfunction [7–9]. Additionally, AARS1 mutations have been linked to adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP), recurrent acute liver failure, and sulfide dysplasia—highlighting its pleiotropic roles in maintaining nervous system and metabolic homeostasis [10–13].

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Introduction] Despite these advances, critical gaps remain in our understanding of AARS1, particularly concerning the precise atomic details of its lactate-sensing ability, the complete repertoire of its lactylation substrates beyond well-studied transcription factors, and the nuanced tissue-specific mechanisms by which AARS1 mutations drive diverse non-cancer diseases. This review comprehensively summarizes the molecular biology of AARS1, its lactylation-mediated functions in tumors, and its role in non-malignant disorders

section: Structural features: conservation and domain specialization
text: [Structural features: conservation and domain specialization] AARS1 is highly evolutionarily conserved, with >60% amino acid sequence identity between Escherichia coli and human orthologs—reflecting its essential role in protein synthesis ADDIN EN.CITE (3, 14). In humans, the AARS1 gene is localized to chromosome 16q22.1 and encodes a 968-amino acid polypeptide with three functionally distinct domains (Figure 1), each critical to its canonical and non-canonical functions:

text: [Aminoacylation domain (residues 1–455)] This N-terminal domain is the catalytic core of AARS1, responsible for recognizing alanine and its cognate tRNA (tRNA^Ala). It contains a conserved ATP-binding pocket and a tRNA^Ala recognition motif that ensures specific aminoacylation—key to preventing translational errors [3, 14]. Pathogenic mutations in this domain (e.g., N71Y, G102R) disrupt catalytic activity, though some mutations (e.g., R329H) spare aminoacylation while driving CMT2N via alternative mechanisms [9, 15].

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Editing domain (residues 456–757)] Also known as the “proofreading domain,” this central region hydrolyzes misactivated amino acids (e.g., serine, glycine) or mismatched aminoacyl-tRNAs (e.g., Ser-tRNA^Ala) to maintain translational fidelity [16, 17]. Loss-of-editing activity (e.g., due to the E688G mutation) leads to protein misfolding and neurodegeneration, as observed in ALSP [12]. Notably, this domain also contains a lactate-binding site that mediates AARS1’s non-canonical role as a lactate sensor [5].

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [C-terminal domain (residues 758–968)] This domain, also called the oligomerization domain, facilitates AARS1 dimerization and contains a conserved nuclear localization signal (NLS). In normal cells, AARS1 is predominantly cytoplasmic; however, in tumors, the NLS mediates nuclear translocation—enabling AARS1 to regulate transcription and DNA damage repair [5, 18]. Mutations in this domain (e.g., E788A, D893N) disrupt AARS1’s subcellular localization and interaction with neuropilin 1 (NRP1), a key driver of CMT2N [9].

section: Canonical function: ensuring translational fidelity in protein synthesis
text: [Canonical function: ensuring translational fidelity in protein synthesis] Under physiological conditions, AARS1’s primary role is to mediate alanine incorporation into nascent proteins via a two-step ATP-dependent reaction (Fig. 2):

text: [Amino acid activation] AARS1 binds alanine and ATP, catalyzing the formation of an alanyl-AMP intermediate (with release of pyrophosphate, PPi). This step is driven by ATP hydrolysis and is highly specific—ensuring only alanine is activated [3, 14].

For example, the T606I mutation in the editing domain impairs proofreading, leading to accumulation of misfolded proteins and white matter lesions in ALSP patients [12].

section: Aberrant AARS1 expression: a marker of malignant progression
text: [Aberrant AARS1 expression: a marker of malignant progression] Across multiple tumor types, AARS1 is consistently upregulated at both the mRNA and protein levels—correlating with advanced disease and poor prognosis (Table 1). This overexpression is driven by oncogenic signaling pathways (e.g., MYC, PI3K/AKT) that promote metabolic reprogramming and protein synthesis in tumors [5, 18].

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
section: Aberrant AARS1 expression: a marker of malignant progression
text: [Aberrant AARS1 expression: a marker of malignant progression] In breast cancer, for example, AARS1 overexpression is observed in 72% of invasive ductal carcinomas, and patients with high AARS1 levels have a 3.2-fold higher risk of distant metastasis compared to those with low expression [5]. In leukemia, AARS1 upregulation promotes drug resistance by enhancing lactate metabolism and DNA damage repair—enabling tumor cells to survive genotoxic stress [6].

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
section: Nuclear translocation of AARS1: a switch to oncogenic functions
text: [Nuclear translocation of AARS1: a switch to oncogenic functions] In normal cells, AARS1 is primarily cytoplasmic (where it mediates translation). In tumors, however, AARS1 undergoes partial nuclear translocation—driven by activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway, which phosphorylates AARS1’s C-terminal domain and enhances NLS activity [5, 18]. Nuclear AARS1 exerts two key oncogenic functions:

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Transcriptional regulation] Nuclear AARS1 binds to the promoters of oncogenes (e.g., YAP, c-MYC) and tumor suppressors (e.g., p53), modulating their expression. For example, in gastric cancer, nuclear AARS1 lactylates YAP, promoting its nuclear retention and transcriptional activity—driving cell proliferation and invasion [18].

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [DNA damage repair] AARS1 interacts with DNA repair proteins (e.g., MRE11, BRCA1) in the nucleus, enhancing homologous recombination (HR) repair. This reduces the efficacy of DNA-damaging agents (e.g., cisplatin), contributing to chemoresistance [6, 19].

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [DNA damage repair] Notably, nuclear AARS1 levels correlate with tumor grade: in high-grade lung adenocarcinomas, 65% of cells show nuclear AARS1 localization, compared to only 12% in low-grade tumors [5]. This suggests that AARS1 nuclear translocation is a late event in malignant progression.

section: AARS1-mediated lysine lactylation: a link between metabolism and oncogenesis
text: [AARS1-mediated lysine lactylation: a link between metabolism and oncogenesis] The Warburg effect (aerobic glycolysis) in tumors leads to excessive lactate accumulation (10–20 mM in the tumor microenvironment, vs. 1–2 mM in normal tissues) [4, 5]. AARS1 senses this lactate and catalyzes lysine lactylation—a PTM that regulates protein function by altering charge, structure, or protein-protein interactions [4–6]. Beyond its prominent role in cancer, lysine lactylation has also been observed in non-malignant contexts, including histone modifications mediated by HDAC1, underscoring its widespread biological relevance [20].

text: [Mechanism of AARS1-mediated lactylation] AARS1’s ability to switch between canonical aminoacylation and non-canonical lactylation is a remarkable example of metabolic plasticity. This shift is mechanistically linked to its aminoacylation domain, which possesses a binding site capable of accommodating both alanine and lactate. The reaction proceeds via two ATP-dependent steps, analogous to its canonical function (Fig. 3):

text: [Mechanism of AARS1-mediated lactylation] Lactate Activation and Competitive Binding: In the presence of ATP, AARS1 can bind either alanine or lactate. When lactate levels are low, AARS1 primarily binds alanine, forming alanyl-AMP, which is then transferred to tRNA^Ala for protein synthesis. However, under conditions of high lactate concentration, such as those found in the tumor microenvironment, lactate competes effectively with alanine for binding within the aminoacylation domain [5, 6]. This competitive binding event is crucial: high lactate levels shift the equilibrium towards the formation of a lactate-AMP intermediate

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Mechanism of AARS1-mediated lactylation] Step 1: Lactate Activation and Formation of Lactate-AMP Intermediate. Under conditions of high lactate concentration, characteristic of the tumor microenvironment, lactate competes with alanine for binding within the aminoacylation domain of AARS1. In the presence of ATP, AARS1 catalyzes the activation of lactate, forming a high-energy lactate-AMP intermediate, analogous to the alanyl-AMP intermediate formed during canonical aminoacylation. This activation step involves the transfer of the adenylate moiety from ATP to lactate, with the concomitant release of pyrophosphate (PPi). The ability of AARS1’s active site to accommodate lactate and utilize ATP for its activation is a key aspect of its metabolic sensing capability.

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Mechanism of AARS1-mediated lactylation] Step 2: Lactate Transfer to Substrate Proteins. The activated lactyl group from the lactate-AMP intermediate is then covalently transferred to the ε-amino group of specific lysine residues on substrate proteins, resulting in the formation of lactylated proteins and the release of AMP.

text: [Mechanism of AARS1-mediated lactylation] Proteomic studies have identified > 500 lactylation substrates of AARS1 in tumor cells, including transcription factors (p53, YAP), metabolic enzymes (PKM2, LDHA), and DNA repair proteins (MRE11) [5, 6, 18, 19]. These substrates are involved in cell cycle regulation, metabolism, and stress response—key pathways for tumor survival. It is important to acknowledge that proteomic studies, while powerful for initial identification, can sometimes yield false positives. Therefore, rigorous validation of high-confidence lactylation targets using orthogonal assays, such as in vitro lactylation assays with purified recombinant AARS1 and specific peptides or proteins, is crucial

section: Lactylation of p53: a canonical oncogenic mechanism
text: [Lactylation of p53: a canonical oncogenic mechanism] The tumor suppressor p53 is a major AARS1 lactylation substrate. In normal cells, p53 is activated by DNA damage, inducing expression of downstream target genes (e.g., p21, Bax) that trigger cell cycle arrest or apoptosis [5, 6]. In tumors, AARS1 lactylates p53 at two key residues in its DNA-binding domain: K120 and K139 (Fig. 4): (1) Disrupted DNA Binding: Lactylation of K120 (a residue critical for p53-DNA interaction) reduces p53’s affinity for target gene promoters by 4–5-fold [5] (2). Impaired Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation (LLPS): p53 forms nuclear condensates via LLPS to enhance its transcriptional activity. Lactylation of K139 disrupts these condensates, further inhibiting p53 function [5]

section: Lactylation of p53: a canonical oncogenic mechanism
text: [Lactylation of p53: a canonical oncogenic mechanism] . Lactylation of K139 disrupts these condensates, further inhibiting p53 function [5]. In patients with wild-type p53 (≈ 50% of human cancers), AARS1 expression and p53 lactylation levels are inversely correlated with overall survival. For example, in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with wild-type p53, high AARS1/p53 lactylation is associated with a 2.8-fold higher risk of death compared to low levels [5]. This highlights AARS1-mediated p53 lactylation as a critical mechanism of tumor suppressor inactivation in cancer.

section: Lactylation of p53: a canonical oncogenic mechanism
text: [Lactylation of p53: a canonical oncogenic mechanism] AARS1-mediated p53 lactylation inhibits its tumor suppressor function. Lactylation at K120 disrupts p53-DNA binding, while lactylation at K139 impairs LLPS. Both effects reduce p53 transcriptional activity, preventing expression of downstream tumor suppressor genes (e.g., p21, Bax) and promoting tumor cell survival

section: Lactylation of metabolic enzymes and DNA repair proteins
text: [Lactylation of metabolic enzymes and DNA repair proteins] Beyond transcription factors like p53 and YAP, AARS1-mediated lactylation targets a diverse array of proteins involved in critical cellular processes, including metabolism and DNA damage repair. This broad substrate specificity underscores the pervasive influence of lactylation in cancer biology.

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
section: Lactylation of metabolic enzymes and DNA repair proteins
text: [Lactylation of metabolic enzymes and DNA repair proteins] For example, PKM2 (Pyruvate Kinase M2), a key glycolytic enzyme that plays a central role in the Warburg effect, has been identified as a lactylation substrate. Lactylation of PKM2 can modulate its enzymatic activity and its role in promoting tumor cell proliferation and survival. While the precise functional consequences of PKM2 lactylation are still being elucidated, it suggests that lactylation may directly impact metabolic flux and tumor energetics.

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
section: Lactylation of metabolic enzymes and DNA repair proteins
text: [Lactylation of metabolic enzymes and DNA repair proteins] Furthermore, MRE11, a component of the MRN complex essential for DNA double-strand break repair, is another significant lactylation substrate. AARS1-mediated lactylation of MRE11 has been shown to enhance its recruitment to DNA damage sites and promote homologous recombination repair [19, 22]. This enhances the DNA repair capacity of cancer cells, contributing to resistance against genotoxic chemotherapy.

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
section: Lactylation of metabolic enzymes and DNA repair proteins
text: [Lactylation of metabolic enzymes and DNA repair proteins] These examples, spanning metabolic enzymes and DNA repair proteins, highlight that AARS1-mediated lactylation extends far beyond transcriptional regulation, impacting fundamental cellular processes that are critical for tumor initiation, progression, and treatment resistance. This broad spectrum of substrates provides a more holistic view of lactylation’s role in cancer, demonstrating its capacity to fine-tune diverse cellular pathways.

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
section: Interplay with other metabolic post-translational modifications (PTMs)
text: [Interplay with other metabolic post-translational modifications (PTMs)] While the focus has been on lactylation, it is crucial to consider how this modification might intersect with other prevalent metabolic PTMs, such as acetylation and succinylation. These modifications, also occurring on lysine residues, can influence protein function by altering charge and interaction networks. It is plausible that lactylation may compete with acetylation or succinylation for binding to the same lysine residues on certain substrates, thereby modulating the functional outcome of these competing modifications. Alternatively, lactylation could act in concert with or antagonize other PTMs, creating complex regulatory layers that govern protein activity and cellular fate [23, 24]

text: [AARS1 mutations in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT)] CMT disease is the most common inherited peripheral neuropathy (prevalence: 1 in 2500), with CMT2N (a subtype caused by AARS1 mutations) accounting for 2–5% of cases [7–9]. AARS1 mutations in CMT2N are diverse, affecting all three domains—but their pathogenicity is not driven by loss of aminoacylation activity (unlike canonical AARS1 dysfunction). Instead, two key mechanisms have been identified:

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Aberrant interaction with neuropilin 1 (NRP1)] NRP1 is a transmembrane receptor that mediates neurotrophic signaling (via binding to vascular endothelial growth factor A, VEGF-A). All CMT2N-associated AARS1 mutations (e.g., R329H, N71Y, E788A) enhance AARS1-NRP1 binding—displacing VEGF-A and blocking neurotrophic signaling [9, 15, 25]. Recent structural studies have provided key insights into the interaction between AARS1 and NRP1, revealing how specific mutations disrupt the normal functional interplay and lead to aberrant signaling cascades [5]. This leads to axonal degeneration, demyelination, and progressive motor and sensory dysfunction (e.g., muscle weakness, numbness in extremities)

text: [Aberrant interaction with neuropilin 1 (NRP1)] . This leads to axonal degeneration, demyelination, and progressive motor and sensory dysfunction (e.g., muscle weakness, numbness in extremities). For example, the R329H mutation—identified in 8 CMT families across 4 countries—does not alter AARS1’s aminoacylation activity but increases its affinity for NRP1 by 3-fold, leading to severe axonal loss in peripheral nerves [9, 15].

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Disrupted axonal transport] AARS1 mutations (e.g., G102R in the aminoacylation domain) impair its interaction with microtubule-associated proteins (e.g., tau), disrupting axonal transport of tRNAs and proteins. This leads to reduced protein synthesis in axon terminals, contributing to neuronal degeneration [8, 26].

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Disrupted axonal transport] Clinical phenotypes of CMT2N vary by mutation but typically include early-onset (childhood/adolescence) progressive weakness, reduced reflexes, and electrophysiological evidence of axonal neuropathy (e.g., reduced motor nerve conduction velocity < 45 m/s) [7, 25]. Notably, some patients with the R329H mutation present with reversible white matter lesions, which may mimic stroke or encephalitis—highlighting the need for genetic testing to avoid misdiagnosis [15].

section: AARS1 in neurodegenerative and white matter diseases
text: [AARS1 in neurodegenerative and white matter diseases] Beyond CMT2N, AARS1 mutations drive other neurological disorders by disrupting protein homeostasis and ER stress responses:

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
section: Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP)
text: [Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP)] ALSP is a rare neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, dysarthria, and white matter lesions. A homozygous non-synonymous mutation (AARS1: NM_001605:exon14:c.1817 C > T:p.Thr606Ile) in the editing domain of AARS1 was identified as a causative factor in a Chinese family with ALSP [12]. This mutation impairs AARS1’s proofreading activity, leading to accumulation of mischarged Ser-tRNA^Ala and misfolded proteins. The resulting ER stress activates the PERK-eIF2α pathway, triggering neuronal apoptosis and white matter degeneration [12, 17]. Clinical manifestations in affected individuals included progressive blurred vision, hypertonia, and severe emaciation (BMI 13.36)—consistent with widespread neuronal loss [12].

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Zebrafish models of neurodegeneration] Zebrafish with a homozygous ars1^cq71/cq71 mutation (orthologous to human AARS1) exhibit defects in neural progenitor cell (NPC) maintenance. The mutation activates the ER stress-induced PERK signaling pathway, which upregulates nfe2l2b (encoding Nrf2). Nrf2 then binds to the p53 promoter, driving p53-mediated NPC apoptosis [27]. This leads to reduced neurogenesis and progressive neurodegeneration—mimicking human AARS1-related white matter disease. Notably, pharmacological inhibition of PERK reversed NPC loss in zebrafish, suggesting a potential therapeutic strategy for human disorders [27].

section: AARS1 in metabolic and rare diseases
text: [AARS1 in metabolic and rare diseases] AARS1 dysfunction also contributes to non-neurological disorders, primarily via impaired protein synthesis and metabolic dysregulation:

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Recurrent acute liver failure] The first case of AARS1-related liver disease was reported in a child with two missense mutations (p.Leu298Gln and p.Arg751Gly) in the aminoacylation domain [8]. These mutations reduced AARS1 protein stability (by 40%) and enzymatic activity (by 60%) in fibroblasts, leading to impaired protein synthesis in hepatocytes. Clinical manifestations included recurrent acute liver failure (ALT/AST > 1000 U/L), coagulopathy, and hyperammonemia—requiring liver transplantation at age 5 [10]. This case highlights AARS1’s critical role in maintaining liver function, likely via supporting the high protein synthesis demands of hepatocytes.

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Sulfide dysplasia] Sulfide dysplasia is a rare disorder characterized by abnormal sulfur metabolism and connective tissue defects. AARS1 mutations (e.g., p.Arg751Gly) reduce its ability to interact with cysteine synthase—an enzyme involved in cysteine (a precursor of sulfur-containing molecules) synthesis. This leads to reduced cysteine levels, impaired sulfide metabolism, and connective tissue abnormalities (e.g., joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility) [13]. While the mechanism is not fully elucidated, it suggests a novel non-canonical role of AARS1 in metabolic pathway crosstalk.

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Structural basis of lactate sensing] While AARS1 is known to bind lactate, the atomic structure of the AARS1-lactate complex has not been resolved. This structural information is critical for understanding how lactate binding induces conformational changes that allosterically switch AARS1 from its canonical aminoacylation role to its non-canonical lactyltransferase activity. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) studies of AARS1 in complex with lactate, ATP, and potential protein substrates could reveal detailed atomic interactions. Such structural insights will be pivotal for the rational design of highly specific inhibitors targeting its lactyltransferase function [5, 6]

text: [Structural basis of lactate sensing] . Such structural insights will be pivotal for the rational design of highly specific inhibitors targeting its lactyltransferase function [5, 6]. In fact, recent advances in frozen EM have provided high-resolution structures for other aminoacyl tRNA synthetases, such as leurs, to form complexes with their homologous tRNAs and ligands, such as leurs ligand structures. These studies demonstrate the ability of cryo em in elucidating ligand induced conformational dynamics and substrate recognition mechanisms in AARS family. Applying a similar frozen EM method to aars1 can obtain valuable insights about its lactic acid binding capsule and the subsequent allosteric transformation controlling its dual enzyme activity [28].

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Full spectrum of lactylation substrates] To date, only ~ 500 AARS1 lactylation substrates have been identified (via proteomics in cancer cells) [5, 18]. However, the full spectrum distribution of AARS1 lactylated substrate under different physiological and pathological conditions, including non cancerous tissues, remains to be further studied. Systematic screening in these different cellular environments is essential for revealing tissue-specific substrates. Identification of these substrates will clarify the effects of aars1 mediated lactylation in various cellular processes and disease mechanisms.

title: The role of Alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 lactylation in tumors and other diseases
text: [Tissue-specific regulation of AARS1] AARS1’s function varies by cell type (e.g., lactylation in tumors vs. translation in normal cells), but the regulatory mechanisms (e.g., post-translational modifications, cofactors) driving this specificity are unknown. Emerging technologies such as single cell RNA sequencing and spatial proteomics provide powerful tools for mapping AARS1 expression, localization and interaction groups in a cell type specific manner. Understanding these regulatory networks is essential to analyze the role of aars1 and formulate targeted treatment interventions.
