text: [Raman measurements] A dedicated reference database (Supplementary Material-Reference Library) was created for the most common drug samples and fillers currently circulating in Canada. The reference library was continuously updated throughout the project as new psychoactive substances or fillers were detected by other means.

title: Street drug monitoring with networked spectrometers powered by machine learning: a pilot study in Ontario, Canada
text: [Raman measurements] The collected spectra are uploaded in real-time to the cloud and analyzed by ML models. The reference spectra were used by the ML model to determine the contribution of each individual component. All networked spectrometers operated through a web-based dashboard specifically designed for use by site staff with minimal or no scientific background. Thus, data were collected from sites in real-time and centralized by the project team, enabling geographic monitoring of street drug trends across participating locations.

title: Street drug monitoring with networked spectrometers powered by machine learning: a pilot study in Ontario, Canada
text: [Raman measurements] Results are downloaded back to the instrument in real-time, providing immediate feedback from the first collected spectrum. The results are averaged until the last spectra is collected. All spectra are stored in a secured server (Amazon Web Services) and are subsequently used to improve ML analysis. During the collection of the spectra, the participants are invited to complete a survey including demographics, expected content of the sample and anticipated consumption-related behavior of the participant. A calibration procedure enables the autofocusing of the laser beam to maximize the signal from the surface sample. This enhances the accuracy, spatial resolution, and reliability of the collected spectral map and enables clear visualization.

title: Street drug monitoring with networked spectrometers powered by machine learning: a pilot study in Ontario, Canada
text: [Machine learning processing] The Raman instruments automate spectral processing and classification through cloud-based ML algorithms. Raman preprocessing involves several critical steps to ensure an accurate interpretation of the spectra. This includes spectral smoothing and denoising, baseline correction and normalization. An adaptive smoothness penalized least squares (asPLS) was used for baseline correction and a sinc kernel approach was used for smoothing/denoising. After these steps, the spectra are ready for further analysis and machine learning classification. Proper baseline correction and smoothing are essential to highlight the true Raman peaks, ensuring subsequent identification and semi-quantification of substances through spectral analysis

title: Street drug monitoring with networked spectrometers powered by machine learning: a pilot study in Ontario, Canada
text: [Machine learning processing] . The associated software used a neural network (NN), a type of ML, to interpret the intricate patterns found in spectral data. This network consists of multiple neural layers that extract features from the input spectra used for the classification. By training on a comprehensive dataset of known substances, the NN learns to recognize the unique spectral signatures of various compounds, allowing it to distinguish between them. The architecture is optimized for real-time processing, ensuring that results are delivered to participants almost immediately. The limit of detection (LOD) and limit of quantification (LOQ) for fentanyl were determined using a 3-component mixture (fentanyl, mannitol, caffeine) made in the laboratory

text: [Sample preparation] For HPLC–MS experiments, samples collected from the sites were ground to be homogenized. Subsequently, 3 to 7 mg of the samples were dissolved in 5 ml of a mixture of methanol: acetonitrile: water (2.5: 1.5: 1) followed by sonicating for 10 min to ensure complete dissolution. Afterwards, the solution was filtered through a 0.2 µm filter to remove any insoluble impurities that could potentially interfere with the chromatographic separation or damage the instrument. The obtained solution was then diluted 50-fold with water and injected into the HPLC–MS system. The collected data was acquired using Agilent MassHunter Workstation and was processed using TOF qualitative and quantitative data analysis software (Agilent Technologies, Inc., Santa Clara CA).

text: [Raman spectra] Raman spectra for the most common substances are reported in Fig. 4. As can be observed, each compound possesses a distinct vibrational fingerprint arising from its molecular structure that is used as the basis for molecular identification [30]. Nonetheless, in Fig. 5, the Raman spectra of cocaine and benzoylecgonine (the main metabolite of cocaine) [31], have overlapped vibrational modes due to common structural characteristics. Initially, the ML model overestimated the concentration of cocaine in some samples due to the presence of benzoylecgonine. Because benzoylecgonine was not yet included in the spectral database, the model misclassified it as cocaine, leading to inflated quantification results

text: [Raman spectra] . After benzoylecgonine was added to the database, the reported concentrations of cocaine aligned more closely with the values obtained through HPLC–MS analysis. This scenario illustrates both a limitation and an advantage of the ML classification: when a structurally similar compound is absent from the database, the model may attribute its signature to the closest available analog. However, this limitation can readily be addressed by regular updates to the Raman spectral library. text: [Composition trend change in Ontario] The World Health Organization has reported approximately 600,000 deaths yearly due to opioid poisonings [32]. Fentanyl, a highly potent synthetic opioid, has shown a substantial increase in prevalence since 2016. A significant number of fatal overdoses are related to fentanyl and its analogs. In 2023, 82% of all accidental overdose deaths were attributed to fentanyl. Benzodiazepines and xylazine are studied as compounds of interest due to their synergistic respiratory depressant influence on opioids which yield higher overdose risks. Naloxone is less effective in alleviating the effects of these drugs because they act on different receptors than fentanyl, which creates the need for alternative overdose treatments [33]

text: [Impact of awareness and scans at public health sites] The participants were asked to provide feedback about the information provided by the analytical results and decisions around consumption of their substance. From measurements performed on 7752 samples, 3902 participants reported on their decision of how they were responding to the outcome of their result, as summarized in Fig. 11. These findings point to the potential public health impacts of this drug-checking service. Notably, 21.9% (3902) of reporting participants stated they would choose to discard their sample entirely after receiving their results. An additional 16.8% of reporting participants stated a choice to reduce their intended dose—both actions that would likely reduce the risk of overdose or adverse events

title: Street drug monitoring with networked spectrometers powered by machine learning: a pilot study in Ontario, Canada
text: [Conclusion] By analyzing 7752 street drugs collected from 5120 participants of varying ages and genders across Ontario, this pilot study is the most comprehensive investigation of street drugs conducted in Ontario thus far. This study utilized a dedicated network of Raman spectrometers to provide real-time street drug analysis in Ontario, with the primary objective of enhancing public health and reducing overdose risks. Although these devices are not designed to perform at the level of research laboratory instruments such as HPLC–MS, they offer immediate feedback to the participants which is critical for influencing positive consumption-related changes, as reported by 38% of the participants

text: [Conclusion] . The LOD and LOQ were determined for the Raman measurements as well as the deviation of the results with respect to HPLC–MS measurements. Overall, the performance of Raman spectroscopy offers an interesting alternative that can be used in conjunction with research grade instrumentation, thus improving harm reduction strategies and public health interventions. The integrated network connectivity—through a web-based dashboard—and the use of simultaneous ML models to interpret complex Raman spectra, provide key benefits such as real-time updates and continuous improvement in model efficiency. The network also offers the possibility to monitor the geographic mobility of substances between distinct geographic locations.

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [abstract] Corticosteroids have long been used as immunomodulatory agents in viral respiratory infections, but their role in influenza and COVID-19 remains controversial. While both diseases share overlapping pathogenic mechanisms involving hyperinflammation and immune dysregulation, clinical evidence suggests divergent outcomes in response to corticosteroid therapy.

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [abstract] This review critically examines the evidence regarding corticosteroid use in influenza and COVID-19, focusing on their impact on mortality, disease progression, and secondary infections.

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [abstract] A narrative review was conducted including randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses, and major observational studies published between 2000 and 2025. Data were analyzed comparatively for influenza (seasonal and pandemic strains) and SARS-CoV-2 infection.

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [abstract] In influenza, most studies associate corticosteroid administration—particularly at high doses or prolonged courses—with increased mortality, delayed viral clearance, and higher rates of secondary bacterial pneumonia. Conversely, in COVID-19, randomized trials such as RECOVERY demonstrated that low-to-moderate doses of dexamethasone significantly reduce mortality in patients requiring oxygen or mechanical ventilation, without clear benefit in mild disease. These opposing outcomes highlight the importance of timing, dosing, and patient selection, reflecting distinct immunopathological trajectories between the two infections.

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [abstract] Corticosteroid therapy exerts context-dependent effects in viral pneumonia. While detrimental in most cases of influenza, it is beneficial in severe COVID-19 when guided by systemic inflammation. Future strategies should focus on personalized and real-time immune monitoring to tailor immunomodulatory interventions to each patient’s inflammatory and virological status.

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [Introduction] Corticosteroids, long utilized in critical care, have been frequently administered to critically ill patients, particularly those developing acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) or severe septic shock [1–3]. In severe community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), the use of corticosteroids is theoretically supported by the anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties of glucocorticoids, which may counteract the uncontrolled local and systemic inflammation—often described as a “cytokine storm”—that characterizes severe lung injury. This exaggerated innate immune response involves intense trafficking of macrophages and neutrophils, along with the abundant release of highly cytotoxic mediators and proinflammatory cytokines in the lung parenchyma [4]

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [Introduction] The role of corticosteroids in severe CAP has been extensively studied, particularly in bacterial etiologies. Evidence from randomized controlled trials supports their use in selected patients with severe disease and an exaggerated systemic inflammatory response, demonstrating benefits such as reduced time to clinical stability and shorter ICU stays [6–8]. However, when the etiology is viral—especially in influenza or SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia—the role of corticosteroids becomes more complex and pathogen-specific.

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [Corticosteroids in severe influenza pneumonia] Influenza virus infections, particularly novel or pandemic strains such as H1N1, H7N9, and H5N1, can cause substantial influenza-related critical illness and mortality [7]. Severe manifestations typically include viral pneumonitis and ARDS [7]. Despite standard care options, including neuraminidase inhibitors and admission to intensive care units (ICUs) for supportive treatment, morbidity and mortality remain high [7]. In this context, the efficacy and safety of adjunctive corticosteroid therapy in severe influenza pneumonia remain highly debated, largely due to the lack of well-conducted randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Most available evidence derives from observational studies, which are inherently susceptible to bias

A recent RCT including severe CAP has been published, 658 patients were included and 536 received a fixed 7-days hydrocortisone treatment. However, the low number of included patients with influenza CAP included it does not allow for concrete conclusions to be drawn in this etiological subgroup [8].

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [Association with mortality] Among hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT) recipients with seasonal influenza limited to upper respiratory tract disease, high-dose corticosteroids (> 1 mg/kg/day) were associated with prolonged viral shedding but not with worse clinical outcomes such as progression to lower respiratory disease (LRD), hypoxemia, or death [13]. Interestingly, low-to-moderate doses appeared to trend toward a protective effect against LRD, suggesting that corticosteroid impact may vary depending on patient population (immunocompromised vs. general critical illness).

text: [Association with mortality] Observational studies face substantial challenges in adjusting for baseline and time-dependent confounders. For instance, a Canadian ICU study of 607 H1N1pdm09 patients demonstrated that while crude mortality was higher in the steroid group (25.5% vs. 16.4%), the association disappeared after accounting for time-dependent variables via marginal structural modeling. Nevertheless, steroid use conferred no clinical benefit [10].

text: [Corticosteroids in specific contexts] Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD): A retrospective analysis of acute decompensated COPD (AECOPD) hospitalizations in Switzerland (2012–2017) found no evidence of worse outcomes among patients with concurrent or confirmed influenza compared to those without. Most AECOPD patients likely received corticosteroids as standard care, suggesting this practice is safe in this subset, possibly because airway obstruction and inflammation—major determinants of disease severity—are effectively reduced by steroids [23].

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [Corticosteroids in specific contexts] Drug–Drug Interactions (Oseltamivir): Oseltamivir remains the cornerstone antiviral for severe influenza pneumonia, reducing hospitalization duration and improving outcomes when administered within 48 h of symptom onset [24, 25]. Co-administration of dexamethasone with oseltamivir slightly reduced systemic exposure to oseltamivir carboxylate in healthy volunteers, though this effect was deemed clinically insignificant [26].

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [Limitations and future directions] Most existing evidence derives from retrospective or prospective observational studies, which are prone to substantial methodological weaknesses—particularly confounding by indication, dosage, timing, and comorbidities [27]. Clinicians often reserve corticosteroids for the most critically ill patients, potentially biasing outcomes against the intervention. Although advanced statistical techniques such as propensity score matching and marginal structural modeling attempt to address these biases, unmeasured confounders remain problematic [10].

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [Limitations and future directions] Current WHO guidelines advise against routine systemic corticosteroid use in severe or progressive influenza illness, except in specific circumstances such as septic shock requiring vasopressors or suspected adrenal insufficiency [28].

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [Limitations and future directions] Given the inconsistent findings and low-quality evidence, there is broad consensus on the urgent need for randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials to clarify the efficacy and safety of corticosteroids in severe influenza pneumonia. The ongoing FLUDEX trial in Spain aims to evaluate low-dose dexamethasone (6 mg/day for 7 days) combined with oseltamivir in hospitalized patients with severe influenza [29]. The results of such trials will be critical to refining clinical guidelines regarding timing, dose, and duration of corticosteroid therapy in this population.

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [Conclusion] Overwhelming observational evidence and meta-analyses indicate that adjunctive corticosteroid therapy in critically ill patients with influenza pneumonia—particularly when administered early or at high doses for ARDS—is associated with increased mortality and infectious complications. While corticosteroids have a strong biological rationale for modulating hyperinflammation, current clinical data do not support their routine use as adjunctive therapy in influenza pneumonia. Clinicians should exercise extreme caution with this intervention, recognizing its potential for harm, pending confirmation from high-quality randomized controlled trials.

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [Corticosteroids in severe SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia] The outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic had a major impact worldwide. Most cases were mild or asymptomatic, but up to 10% of patients required hospitalization and oxygen therapy, and many of them presented with severe ARDS and needed respiratory support and ICU admission [30, 31]. The development of ARDS was characterized by an unusual severity and an atypical response to the standard treatment [32]. During the first half of 2020, while health systems around the world were overwhelmed, researchers and healthcare professionals were trying to gather information to understand the pathophysiology of that unknown virus.

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [Corticosteroids in severe SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia] The abrupt onset of ARDS and findings such as high levels of circulating cytokines and inflammatory biomarkers, lymphopenia, and mononuclear infiltration of lungs or lymph nodes suggested a macrophage activation syndrome-like condition as the key in COVID-19-induced organ dysfunction [33, 34]. Subsequent investigations ruled out this hypothesis, as interleukin-6 levels were much lower in COVID-19 patients than in other critical illnesses such as bacterial sepsis [35, 36]

text: [Corticosteroids in severe SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia] . Latest evidence suggests a defect in host immunity, with a profound depletion in the number of effector immune cells and severe functional defects in T cell and monocyte function [36] which leads to a poor control of viral replication [37], overregulation of the pro- and anti-inflammatory response, endothelial dysfunction, and organ failure.

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [Corticosteroids in severe SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia] Based on the cytokine storm hypothesis, most therapeutic efforts in the first months of 2020 were directed to block proinflammatory cytokines or inhibit the inflammatory signaling cascade using drugs such as corticosteroids. Corticosteroids, given their lipophilicity, cross the host cell membrane and bind to glucocorticoid receptors present in the cell cytoplasm, which initiates a series of immune cell responses that lead to a decrease in gene transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1, IL-2, IL-6, IL-8, TNF and IFN-γ, increase the gene expression of the anti-inflammatory cytokine mediator IL-10, and inhibit neutrophil adhesion to endothelial cells and activation of macrophages [38, 39].

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [Corticosteroids in severe SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia] Corticosteroids have played a controversial role in viral pneumonia, and many studies have failed to demonstrate a benefit in other diseases closely related to COVID-19, such as severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS-CoV-1) or Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS), where corticosteroid treatment even decreased viral RNA clearance [40, 41]. With the difficulties added by the pandemic, most studies in COVID-19 did not define standard treatment protocols or homogeneous criteria for the selection of patients. Moreover, most of the studies focused on mortality and did not report data on analytical, microbiological, or respiratory evolution

First reports from China between January and March 2020 found no differences in the incidence of clinical deterioration, cure rate, ICU admission, hospitalization duration, and in-hospital mortality with the adjuvant corticosteroid treatment [42].

title: The role of corticosteroids in severe viral pneumonia: lessons from COVID-19 and influenza
text: [Corticosteroids in severe SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia] The RECOVERY trial marked a turning point in recommendations regarding the use of corticosteroids in critically ill COVID-19 patients [43]. This controlled, open-label trial was conducted in the United Kingdom from March 19 to June 8, 2020. 2,104 patients who were hospitalized with COVID-19 were randomized to receive dexamethasone 6 mg/d for 10 days, and 4,321 patients were randomized to receive usual care (8% of them received dexamethasone as part of their clinical care). Mortality at 28 days was significantly lower in the dexamethasone group (22.9% vs. 25.7%; rate ratio, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.75 to 0.93; p < 0.001). There was a trend showing the greatest benefit among patients undergoing invasive mechanical ventilation (29.3% vs. 41.4%; rate ratio, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.81)

text: [Other viruses] The utilization of systemic corticosteroids for viral pneumonia caused by pathogens other than COVID-19 or influenza remains highly debated and largely unsupported by definitive outcome data from rigorous randomized controlled trials. Glucocorticoids were widely employed as adjuvant therapy during severe coronavirus outbreaks, such as SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) and MERS (Middle East Respiratory Syndrome) [71]. However, observational studies correlated steroid use with detrimental effects, including decreased cellular immunity (CD4, CD8, and CD3 reduction), increased secondary infections, prolonged viral shedding, and increased 30-day mortality [72, 73]

text: [Conclusion] The divergent effects of corticosteroids in influenza and SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia could hypothetically be explained by differences in viral pathogenesis and host immune dynamics. In influenza, viral replication peaks early, accompanied by a rapid and essential type I interferon response that limits viral spread. Corticosteroid administration during this phase blunts the antiviral immune response, could delay viral clearance, and predispose to secondary bacterial infections [78]. Conversely, severe SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia is characterized by a delayed interferon response followed by a prolonged hyperinflammatory phase marked by cytokine dysregulation, endothelial injury, and diffuse alveolar damage [79]

text: [Conclusion] . In this context, corticosteroids could mitigate the exaggerated immune response without significantly impairing viral control. Thus, while corticosteroids exacerbate disease severity in influenza by suppressing early antiviral defense, they improve outcomes in COVID-19 by attenuating late, dysregulated inflammation.

text: [Conclusion] In any case, a personalized and real-time approach that evaluates both the inflammatory and immune status, together with the direct viral effects, is more likely to enable tailored immunomodulation according to each patient’s needs at any given time.

text: [abstract] 4-(Methylnitrosamino)-1-(3-pyridyl)-1-butanone (NNK) is a potent tobacco-specific nitrosamine that has been widely recognized as a major carcinogen contributing to smoking-related lung diseases. Although its involvement in lung cancer has been extensively studied, the underlying pathogenic mechanisms by which NNK contributes to the development of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) remain unclear.

title: Integrated network toxicology and multi-omics analysis reveals the role of tobacco-specific carcinogen NNK in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis pathogenesis
text: [abstract] In this study, potential IPF-related targets of NNK were identified through integrating multiple public databases. Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analyses were performed to uncover key biological processes associated with NNK-induced IPF. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) combined with machine learning approaches was employed to screen for core regulatory genes. Furthermore, molecular docking and 100-nanosecond molecular dynamics simulations were utilized to assess the binding interactions between NNK and candidate target proteins. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and immune infiltration analyses were also performed to validate gene expression patterns and characterize the immune microenvironment.

Six hub genes (BCHE, CD38, MMP7, PLA2G2A, ST6GAL1, and TIMP1) were identified as potential key diagnostic biomarkers.

The identified core genes and associated pathways provide novel insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying smoking-related IPF and offer promising targets for future therapeutic strategies.

title: Integrated network toxicology and multi-omics analysis reveals the role of tobacco-specific carcinogen NNK in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis pathogenesis
text: [Discussion] Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a highly heterogeneous interstitial lung disease characterized by a poor prognosis. Despite its relatively low global prevalence, IPF is associated with a high mortality rate. Current therapeutic options, such as pirfenidone and nintedanib, are limited to slowing disease progression and do not reverse the underlying pathological changes [20–22]. Therefore, gaining a deeper insight into the molecular mechanisms driven by environmental exposures is essential to pave the way for identifying new therapeutic targets.

title: Integrated network toxicology and multi-omics analysis reveals the role of tobacco-specific carcinogen NNK in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis pathogenesis
text: [Discussion] Epidemiological data indicate that smoking is one of the most well-established environmental risk factors for IPF, with over 60% of patients having a history of smoking [8, 23]. Multiple carcinogens present in cigarette smoke are believed to contribute to alveolar epithelial cell injury, fibroblast activation, and disruption of immune homeostasis [24]. Among these carcinogens is the tobacco-specific nitrosamine NNK, which is a significant carcinogen produced during nicotine metabolism. NNK has been shown to induce chronic inflammation and fibrotic changes in lung tissue following long-term exposure [25]. Although NNK has been extensively studied as a promoter of lung cancer, its network toxicological mechanisms in the development of IPF have yet to be fully elucidated.

title: Integrated network toxicology and multi-omics analysis reveals the role of tobacco-specific carcinogen NNK in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis pathogenesis
text: [Discussion] This study explores the potential pathogenic mechanisms of NNK in IPF from a systems biology perspective. The convergence of multiple databases suggests that NNK disrupts lung tissue homeostasis and fibrotic processes by inducing oxidative stress, interfering with the cell cycle, and activating the FoxO pathway. Through the integration of expression networks and the development of machine learning models, six key genes—BCHE, CD38, MMP7, PLA2G2A, ST6GAL1, and TIMP1—were identified; all exhibited strong predictive performance and clinical discrimination. Immune infiltration analysis indicates that these genes may play a role in remodeling the immune microenvironment by influencing the infiltration of immune cells such as B cells and T cells, thereby accelerating IPF progression.

text: [Discussion] Among them, the gene MMP7 stands out for its pivotal role in IPF. Numerous studies have confirmed its significantly elevated expression levels in plasma from IPF patients as well as in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) and lung tissues; this elevation is closely associated with disease severity [26]. MMP7 is primarily expressed by lung epithelial cells, macrophages, and fibroblasts. It facilitates fibroblast proliferation and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling during fibrosis through mechanisms such as cleaving E-cadherin or activating pro-HB-EGF [27, 28]. Additionally, polymorphisms within its promoter region may enhance transcription activity, potentially exacerbating disease progression [29]

This pathway may also contribute to the neuro-immuno-fibrotic crosstalk observed in IPF. text: [Conclusion] Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a fatal disease strongly associated with cigarette smoking, yet the specific fibrotic mechanisms of the tobacco-specific nitrosamine NNK have remained elusive. In this study, we combined systems biology predictions with robust in vitro and in vivo validation to demonstrate that NNK significantly exacerbates pulmonary fibrosis by upregulating MMP7. We observed that NNK exposure dose-dependently increased MMP7 expression in human lung fibroblasts and aggravated tissue remodeling in bleomycin-treated mice, confirming MMP7 as a critical downstream effector. Crucially, our receptor blocking experiments confirmed that this pro-fibrotic response is mediated through the α7-nAChR signaling pathway

text: [abstract] Acute lung injury (ALI) can initiate early epithelial remodeling that may precede pulmonary fibrosis, with EMT of alveolar epithelial cells implicated in this acute phase. While mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC)-derived exosomes exhibit repair potential, their conventional culture conditions fail to mimic the hypoxic microenvironment of ALI. Here, we explored the therapeutic effects and regulatory mechanisms of hypoxia-preconditioned bone marrow MSC-derived exosomes (HExos) in LPS-induced ALI with early epithelial remodeling.

text: [abstract] BMSCs were characterized via osteogenic/adipogenic differentiation and flow cytometry. Exosomes derived under normoxia (NExos) and hypoxia (HExos) were isolated and validated using nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and Western blot. An LPS-induced ALI mouse model was employed to evaluate exosome efficacy. Through integrated miRNA sequencing, luciferase reporter assays, and gain-/loss-of-function experiments, we examined a working model involving the miR-486a-5p/Skp2/GATA4 axis.

text: [abstract] HExos markedly alleviated LPS-induced acute lung injury and early-stage collagen deposition. Mechanistically, HExos were enriched with miR-486a-5p, which directly targeted Skp2, thereby reducing Skp2-mediated ubiquitin–proteasome degradation of GATA4 and attenuating EMT-like changes. Notably, miR-486a-5p mimics reversed EMT-like changes in alveolar epithelial cells, while its knockdown abolished the protective effect.

text: [Background] Acute Lung Injury (ALI) and its severe form, Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), are devastating clinical conditions with high morbidity and mortality rates [1–3]. Pathologically, they involve diffuse alveolar damage, excessive pulmonary inflammation, and alveolar epithelial cell (AEC) apoptosis [4]. Persistent or recurrent injury may disrupt repair mechanisms, potentially leading to irreversible pulmonary fibrosis—a major clinical challenge due to its poor reversibility, adverse impact on patient prognosis, and significant quality-of-life burden [5]. Thus, developing novel therapies to halt fibrosis progression holds critical clinical value.

title: Hypoxia-preconditioned mesenchymal stromal cell–derived exosomes attenuate LPS-induced acute lung injury and early epithelial remodeling in mice: evidence for a miR-486a-5p–Skp2–GATA4 axis
text: [Background] Recent studies highlight the pivotal role of alveolar epithelial cell epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in pulmonary fibrosis progression [6]. Deciphering EMT’s molecular mechanisms could revolutionize therapeutic strategies for ALI-associated fibrosis. Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) have emerged as promising candidates for lung disease treatment [7], demonstrating exceptional efficacy against ALI and fibrosis [8, 9]. Current evidence indicates MSC therapy primarily functions through paracrine signaling [10], where secreted growth factors, anti-inflammatory mediators, and bioactive compounds multi-targetedly ameliorate ALI pathology: enhancing epithelial repair, reducing vascular leakage, improving alveolar clearance, and regulating immune responses [9, 11].

title: Hypoxia-preconditioned mesenchymal stromal cell–derived exosomes attenuate LPS-induced acute lung injury and early epithelial remodeling in mice: evidence for a miR-486a-5p–Skp2–GATA4 axis
text: [Background] Exosomes, the principal paracrine effectors of MSCs, are nanosized vesicles (50–150 nm) formed through multivesicular body-plasma membrane fusion, featuring a distinctive bilayer membrane structure [12, 13]. These natural carriers efficiently deliver bioactive cargo (proteins, mRNAs, miRNAs) and mediate critical intercellular communication [14]. Compared with whole-cell transplantation, exosome therapy retains comparable therapeutic effects while offering superior advantages including minimal immunogenicity and enhanced safety [15]

title: Hypoxia-preconditioned mesenchymal stromal cell–derived exosomes attenuate LPS-induced acute lung injury and early epithelial remodeling in mice: evidence for a miR-486a-5p–Skp2–GATA4 axis
text: [Background] The oxygen microenvironment critically regulates MSC functionality [18, 19]with conventional normoxic culture conditions failing to recapitulate physiological oxygen levels [20]. Hypoxic preconditioning potently enhances MSC proliferation, migration, viability, and therapeutic efficacy [21, 22]. While hypoxia-primed MSCs demonstrate superior anti-fibrotic effects in renal fibrosis models compared to normoxic counterparts [21], their exosomal functions in pulmonary fibrosis remain elusive. We hypothesize that hypoxic preconditioning may amplify exosomal anti-fibrotic effects through cargo optimization.

title: Hypoxia-preconditioned mesenchymal stromal cell–derived exosomes attenuate LPS-induced acute lung injury and early epithelial remodeling in mice: evidence for a miR-486a-5p–Skp2–GATA4 axis
text: [Background] As pivotal exosomal effectors, miRNAs play central roles in ALI and fibrosis regulation [23–25]. Notably, miR-486a-5p and related miRNAs constitute 43–59% of BMSC exosomal content [26], with miR-486a-5p specifically attenuating pulmonary fibrosis via TGF-β1 pathway inhibition [27].Mechanistically, the ubiquitin-proteasome system—particularly the SCF-Skp2 complex—modulates fibrotic progression [28–30]. Skp2 deficiency alleviates renal fibrosis [31], and its inhibitors show therapeutic promise for pulmonary fibrosis [32]. Our bioinformatics analysis identifies transcription factor GATA4 as a novel Skp2 substrate, with GATA4 implicated in multi-organ fibrosis [33, 34], suggesting the miR-486a-5p/Skp2/GATA4 axis as a potential regulatory cascade.

title: Hypoxia-preconditioned mesenchymal stromal cell–derived exosomes attenuate LPS-induced acute lung injury and early epithelial remodeling in mice: evidence for a miR-486a-5p–Skp2–GATA4 axis
text: [Discussion] Pulmonary fibrosis is a progressive interstitial lung disease marked by aberrant epithelial repair and matrix deposition, often leading to respiratory failure. Current antifibrotic treatments slow decline but rarely reverse disease, highlighting the need to target early remodeling. In a mouse model of LPS-associated acute lung injury with early remodeling, hypoxia-preconditioned mesenchymal stromal cell–derived exosomes were associated with reduced injury and remodeling. Our findings support a preliminary working model in which exosomal miR-486a-5p constrains Skp2 and preserves GATA4 abundance to limit EMT-like changes, suggesting a potential avenue for exosome-based modulation of epithelial remodeling.

text: [Discussion] Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs), as multipotent stromal cells, hold immense potential in regenerative medicine [41]. However, clinical deployment faces formidable barriers: cryopreservation hurdles, functional heterogeneity, alloimmune responses, oncogenic potential, and ethical controversies. Notably, MSC-derived exosomes (MSC-Exos) serve as bioactive nanovesicles that faithfully transmit parental cell signals, thereby harnessing MSC-like therapeutic benefits while evading cell-based therapy risks [42].

title: Hypoxia-preconditioned mesenchymal stromal cell–derived exosomes attenuate LPS-induced acute lung injury and early epithelial remodeling in mice: evidence for a miR-486a-5p–Skp2–GATA4 axis
text: [Discussion] Physiological oxygen tension (1–14% O₂) is markedly lower than standard in vitro culture conditions (21% O₂). Intriguingly, hypoxic preconditioning has been demonstrated to enhance MSC therapeutic potency [43] by augmenting their paracrine activity. Supporting this concept, MSC-derived exosomes were recently shown to mitigate radiation-induced lung injury [44], prompting our hypothesis that hypoxia-preconditioned exosomes (HExo) would exhibit superior therapeutic efficacy to normoxic exosomes (Exo) in acute lung injury (ALI).

text: [Discussion] Experimental validation revealed that while HExo and Exo shared comparable physical characteristics (NTA assay), HExo demonstrated enhanced cellular uptake efficiency in lung epithelial cells (MLE-12). In LPS-induced EMT models, HExo potently reversed the characteristic downregulation of the epithelial marker E-cadherin and aberrant upregulation of the mesenchymal marker vimentin [45]. Consistently, in vivo studies established that HExo not only attenuated alveolar inflammation and pathological collagen deposition but also preserved lung histoarchitecture.

title: Hypoxia-preconditioned mesenchymal stromal cell–derived exosomes attenuate LPS-induced acute lung injury and early epithelial remodeling in mice: evidence for a miR-486a-5p–Skp2–GATA4 axis
text: [Discussion] Emerging mechanistic evidence has shown that MSC exosomes exert their therapeutic effects primarily through miRNA delivery. For instance, miR-142 confers radioprotection in intestinal injury [46], miR-125b-5p enhances renal tubular repair [47], and miR-125a-5p attenuates myocardial injury by modulating macrophage polarization and angiogenesis [48]. These findings collectively provide potential explanations for the enhanced efficacy of HExo.Nevertheless, the miRNA cargo profile of mouse bone marrow MSC-derived HExos and its functional impact on EMT-like changes in MLE-12 cells remain unexplored.

title: Hypoxia-preconditioned mesenchymal stromal cell–derived exosomes attenuate LPS-induced acute lung injury and early epithelial remodeling in mice: evidence for a miR-486a-5p–Skp2–GATA4 axis
text: [Discussion] Our small RNA sequencing revealed that miR-486a-5p was remarkably enriched in HExos relative to Exos and was effectively internalized by MLE-12 cells, suggesting its pivotal role in mediating the superior bioactivity of HExos. Functional validation demonstrated that miR-486a-5p mimics suppressed EMT-like changes progression in alveolar epithelial cells, whereas knockdown of miR-486a-5p in BMSCs-HExos substantially compromised its EMT-inhibitory effects. These data establish that exosomal transfer of miR-486a-5p to injured MLE-12 cells constitutes the core mechanism underlying BMSCs-HExos’ protective action.

title: Hypoxia-preconditioned mesenchymal stromal cell–derived exosomes attenuate LPS-induced acute lung injury and early epithelial remodeling in mice: evidence for a miR-486a-5p–Skp2–GATA4 axis
text: [Discussion] To delineate the downstream pathway, we employed bioinformatics prediction followed by experimental verification, identifying Skp2 as a bona fide target of miR-486a-5p via dual-luciferase reporter assays. Notably, Skp2, an F-box protein component of the SCF ubiquitin ligase complex, is ubiquitously expressed across tissues (heart, kidney, liver, etc.) and orchestrates diverse processes including cell cycle progression and fibrosis by governing the turnover of key substrates (e.g., p27, FOXO1) [28, 49]. Relevant to our findings, Skp2 has been implicated in TGF-β1-induced EMT and E-cadherin ubiquitination [50]. Further investigation revealed that Skp2 may target GATA4, a transcription factor linked to cellular senescence and fibrogenesis, for ubiquitin-mediated degradation.

title: Hypoxia-preconditioned mesenchymal stromal cell–derived exosomes attenuate LPS-induced acute lung injury and early epithelial remodeling in mice: evidence for a miR-486a-5p–Skp2–GATA4 axis

Collectively, these findings support a working model in which HExos deliver miR-486-5p to downregulate Skp2, preserving GATA4 abundance and attenuating EMT-like remodeling.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [abstract] Fatphobia is a form of discrimination that negatively impacts physical and mental health. Adolescents in health-related technical education are both exposed to and capable of reproducing fatphobia. This study aimed to analyze the perceptions of adolescent students in professional technical health courses regarding fatphobia and its relationship with social media.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [abstract] This qualitative study was conducted with 24 adolescents aged 14 to 18 years enrolled in Nursing and Aesthetics technical programs at a public technical school in Fortaleza, Brazil. Two focus group sessions were held, one for each program, using a semi-structured guide. Sessions were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using Descending Hierarchical Classification with the IRaMuTeQ software. The analysis sought to identify thematic patterns based on the frequency and association of textual segments. The study followed established qualitative reporting criteria to ensure transparency and rigor.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [abstract] Five thematic classes emerged: (1) Recognition and reproduction of fatphobia; (2) Experience of fatphobia; (3) Social construction of the “ideal body”; (4) The fat body and the reinterpretation of health; and (5) Influence of social media and use of digital filters. Students recognized the existence and harmful effects of fatphobia but also acknowledged reproducing stigmatizing comments and behaviors. Students demonstrated nuanced views about the relationship between body size and health, challenging weight-centered biomedical interpretations. Social media emerged as a powerful driver of unrealistic aesthetic expectations.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [abstract] Adolescents in technical health training recognize fatphobia as both an individual and structural issue, shaped by social norms and amplified by social media. Although they express empathy toward people with larger bodies, many simultaneously reproduce weight-stigmatizing practices. Technical-vocational schools represent formative spaces where fatphobia is simultaneously reproduced and questioned, making them key environments for integrating educational interventions that promote body diversity, challenge weight-based prejudice, and support the development of more inclusive future health professionals.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Introduction] Fatphobia, understood as prejudice and bias directed at people with bodies categorized as fat, impacts individuals’ physical, psychological, and social health [1]. It is a form of discrimination that affects adults, children, and adolescents alike [2], and is reproduced through scientific discourse and institutional practices, manifesting in various contexts, such as educational settings [3], social media [4], and healthcare services [5]

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Introduction] . In this study, we adopt the following conceptual distinctions: “fatphobia” refers to the sociocultural and political structures that devalue fat bodies and uphold thinness as a normative ideal [1]; and “obesity” and “overweight” are used strictly as biomedical categories [2], mentioned when referring to dominant clinical discourses or institutional classifications.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Introduction] In the healthcare field, fatphobia influences interactions between healthcare professionals and patients with fat bodies, resulting in delayed diagnoses, reduced quality of care, and adverse health outcomes [6]. The use of stigmatizing language and the belief that weight is entirely controllable through individual effort compromise the therapeutic bond and hinder treatment adherence, even among children and adolescents [7]. As a result, overweight individuals often delay or avoid seeking medical care, even when faced with serious and treatable conditions, due to fear of judgment or previous negative experiences [8].

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Introduction] The literature indicates that professionals recognize limitations in their competencies to address larger bodies, reporting insecurity and inadequate educational training [9]. Education about fatphobia and obesity is limited in both content and depth in the curricula of health professional training programs. These programs still do not adequately address the multifactorial determinants of body weight, the psychosocial implications of fatphobia, or practical strategies to reduce it [3, 10].

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Introduction] Fatphobia among undergraduate health students is present even at the beginning of their studies, with negative weight stereotypes attributed primarily to personal flaws or lack of willpower [11–13]. A study comparing health students at different stages of their studies found that students with lower educational levels (high school) were more likely to show fatphobia than those pursuing or completing a master’s degree [10]. However, a systematic literature review indicates that the influence of education on fatphobia remains inconclusive, as studies have shown conflicting results [14].

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Introduction] On social media, adolescents are more exposed to fatphobia, with this exposure influenced by both the time spent using the platform and the type of content consumed by this audience [15]. Furthermore, the idealization of thin bodies on social media intensifies body dissatisfaction, negatively impacting adolescents’ physical and mental health [16].

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Introduction] Adolescents in professional training in the health field are a target group for further study, as they are most affected by social media exposure and will also be future care agents capable of reproducing or modifying fatphobic practices. Therefore, this study aimed to analyze the perceptions of adolescent students in professional technical courses in the health field regarding fatphobia and its relationship with social media. Our interpretation is guided by the understanding that such perceptions are not merely descriptive but are embedded in broader processes of subjectivation, symbolic violence, and professional socialization within health training contexts.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Methods] This is a qualitative study guided by the theoretical framework of Transdisciplinary Studies of Fat Corporalities in Brazil, an epistemological field that questions the structural prejudice sustained by the biomedical paradigm of obesity and proposes new ways of understanding fat bodies [17, 18]. The Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) checklist was used as methodological guidance to improve the structure and credibility of this study [19]. The project was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the University of Fortaleza, under ruling No. 5,885,073.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Methods] The research was conducted in the city of Fortaleza, the capital of the state of Ceará, located in the Northeast region of Brazil. Participants included students from a technical-vocational high school enrolled in Nursing and Aesthetics programs. In the state of Ceará, secondary technical training is predominantly offered by State Schools of Vocational Education. These institutions integrate the high school curriculum with full-time technical training, with a focus on professional qualifications.

This category advances the theoretical discussion by demonstrating how symbolic violence operates through digital platforms, shaping identity and reinforcing aesthetic norms among future health professionals.

text: [Influence of social media and use of digital filters] The organization of the categories presented does not imply that they are independent; rather, it serves as a descriptive strategy to highlight the interconnections and overlaps among them. For instance, the recognition of fatphobia (Class 1) coexists with its reproduction through digital culture (Class 5), while resistance to dominant health and beauty narratives (Classes 3 and 4) emerges in tension with normalized stigma expressed in daily interactions (Class 2).

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] Adolescents recognize the negative impacts of fatphobia and acknowledge it as a structural phenomenon, reinforced by social media, while also admitting to reproducing fatphobic discourses. This duality of perceptions highlights the internalization of aesthetic standards and the development of critical consciousness, possibly influenced by adolescence itself and the educational context in health programs. These perceptions are not isolated opinions but are shaped by the socialization processes of technical health education, which both challenge and reinforce fatphobic discourse

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] . Unlike prior studies focused on university-level students, our findings show that these dynamics begin earlier: students in technical programs, though not yet exposed to full clinical practice, already negotiate professional values influenced by biomedical models and aesthetic ideals.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] Students identified that fatphobic behaviors are often naturalized and interpreted as “jokes” or harmless comments. This situation is similar to Pierre Bourdieu’s [22] concept of symbolic violence, which describes subtle forms of domination based on the unconscious acceptance of values and hierarchies imposed by the dominant culture. In the context of fatphobia, this violence is related to practices such as attributing negative characteristics to people with fat bodies (e.g., lack of self-control or incompetence), which become socially acceptable and even legitimized [23].

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] Reports of personal or witnessed experiences of discrimination in public and family spaces reinforce that fatphobia acts as a form of everyday violence. Family members, especially parents and siblings, can be common sources of fatphobia, often manifested through criticism, judgment, jokes, and weight-related teasing [24]. In public spaces, the lack of physical adaptations causes embarrassment and limits participation in common activities, such as accessing health services, leisure, and transportation. Therefore, people with larger bodies often avoid public environments or situations where they may be exposed to judgment or physical inadequacy [8, 25, 26]

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] . Interpreting these experiences through the lens of symbolic violence highlights how fatphobia operates not only through overt discrimination, but also through normalized practices that remain unquestioned within everyday social and educational contexts.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] The coexistence of empathy and complicity in students’ statements suggests that technical training environments both expose and reproduce fatphobia. While students begin to reflect critically on fatphobic experiences, their narratives also reveal a lack of institutional framing to support that reflection. This highlight missed opportunities within technical curricula to foster more inclusive understandings of body size and health [17]. These patterns are also shaped by adolescence, a developmental period when body identity is still being constructed and is influenced by social norms and peer belonging [27]

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] . This suggests that, without intentional pedagogical intervention, technical education risks reinforcing social norms that pathologize fat bodies at the moment when students are beginning to form their professional and moral identities.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] While some students demonstrate empathy and question weight-based norms, they also reproduce stigmatizing attitudes, revealing an ambivalent stance shaped by early professional socialization. This contradiction suggests that the process of becoming a health professional is tied to subjectivation, whereby students internalize institutional norms that both challenge and sustain fatphobic discourse. Although critical awareness begins to emerge, it remains fragile due to the lack of pedagogical support. These patterns align with prior research showing that health education often overlooks the psychosocial dimensions of fatphobia and the complex determinants of body weight [10]

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] . Additionally, the hidden curriculum, comprising implicit norms and values, can reinforce dominant ideologies within training environments [28, 29]. Without pedagogical efforts to deconstruct fatphobic norms, technical health training may inadvertently serve as a site for the reproduction of fatphobia.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] As an early entry point into the health field, technical training introduces not only practical competencies but also implicit notions of body image within healthcare. This context intensifies key tensions (empathy versus stigma reproduction, and critical discourse versus everyday practice) by immersing students in dominant health discourses before they develop the critical awareness necessary to question them. Therefore, curricular design at the technical level should not be limited to clinical content but must actively engage with social and structural determinants of health, including fatphobia.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] The ideal of a thin and curvy body is evident in adolescents’ statements. This standard, known as slim-thick, is considered more harmful to mental health than the traditional thin ideal, as it requires the simultaneous pursuit of thinness and curves, a goal difficult to achieve without invasive interventions or unhealthy practices [30]. The search for this type of body is influenced by advertising, social media, and digital influencers, leading teenagers, especially females, to seek not only thinness but also curves in specific areas of the body [31]. The prominence of the slim-thick ideal in students’ narratives underscores how aesthetic norms penetrate health training spaces, conflicting with inclusive and health-centered professional values.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] By pointing out that weight should not be the sole indicator of health, adolescents demonstrate an affinity with approaches such as Health At Every Size (HAES), which proposes a non-pathologizing understanding of fat bodies and emphasizes person-centered care rather than weight [30]. Body weight alone is not a reliable marker of health. Weight-based measures, such as the Body Mass Index (BMI), are independent of key metabolic markers (e.g., blood pressure, lipid profile, and glycated hemoglobin); thus, people with the same weight may present different metabolic health profiles [32]. Strategies that prioritize healthy behaviors and well-being are considered more effective for promoting comprehensive health [33]

text: [Discussion] . Strategies that prioritize healthy behaviors and well-being are considered more effective for promoting comprehensive health [33]. This challenges the reductionist logic of the biomedical model and opens space for understandings of health that resist the pathologization of fat bodies.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] Adolescents report routinely using digital filters on social media to enhance desired physical characteristics, indicating a link between the beauty standards promoted on these platforms and dissatisfaction with self-image. The practice of manipulating photos with filters influences adolescents to negatively compare their bodies to edited versions of themselves or others [34]. Digital influencers intensify this process by promoting the “ideal body” as a consumer product, supposedly attainable through weight-loss products and restrictive eating habits, and by associating it with health, beauty, and happiness [35]

Constant exposure to this content contributes to the naturalization of unrealistic aesthetic standards, hindering the appreciation of body diversity and perpetuating fatphobia [36]. This highlights the need to critically address digital cultures within health education, as unexamined exposure to idealized imagery may reinforce fatphobic attitudes about bodies and health.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] It is possible to observe the attempt to resignify their own image, as indicated by statements that recognize their own beauty and the natural diversity of bodies. Body-positive content (a movement that promotes self-compassion and body acceptance) is growing on social media and is associated with increased positive self-image thinking [37–39]. A study with adolescents and young adults revealed that these groups recognize the relevance of body-positive posts for self-acceptance, although some still demonstrate resistance to this content due to internalized beauty ideals [40]. This coexistence of discourses highlights the complexity of social media interactions and their role in shaping divergent perceptions regarding the body.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] Our study contributes to the literature by showing how technical-vocational schools may act as formative spaces where normative discourses around bodies are established and reinforced. This has important implications for early professional identity formation, particularly in health-related fields where body ideals are often implicitly associated with notions of competence and self-discipline. Without targeted pedagogical interventions, these biases may be internalized and carried into future healthcare practice.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] Like all qualitative research, this study does not aim to generalize its findings but rather to offer an in-depth understanding of adolescent perceptions within a specific institutional and cultural context. Some limitations should be acknowledged. The focus group format may have introduced social desirability bias, as participants might have moderated their responses due to the presence of peers or researchers, particularly when addressing sensitive topics such as body image and fatphobia. The predominantly female composition of the sample may have influenced the themes that emerged, especially those related to beauty standards and social media use

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] . The institutional affiliation of the researchers with health education programs may have shaped the discussions, reinforcing professional or normative perspectives. These contextual factors should be considered when interpreting the findings, as they may have influenced both the content and tone of participants’ responses. Additionally, the research was conducted in only one public technical school in Fortaleza, in Northeast Brazil, where specific cultural values and aesthetic norms may prevail, which may limit the transferability of results to other regions or educational settings; therefore, the findings may not be transferable to settings with different sociocultural perceptions of body image and fatphobia.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] Despite these limitations, the use of focus groups and analysis with the IRaMuTeQ software enabled greater depth in interpreting the statements, revealing symbolic aspects of fatphobia that would be difficult to capture through quantitative approaches. This study offers analytically insights into an understudied educational context, highlighting processes that are likely present, though variably expressed, in other technical health training settings.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Conclusion] Adolescents undergoing technical training in healthcare recognize the existence and impacts of fatphobia, both individually and structurally. While demonstrating critical awareness of the discrimination faced by fat people, participants also recognize their own participation in the reproduction of fatphobic practices. The influence of social media, particularly through the use of filters and the propagation of difficult-to-achieve aesthetic standards, was recognized as an important factor in the construction of self-image and the perception of the ideal body, reinforcing discriminatory behaviors.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Conclusion] The adolescents’ statements highlight the need for educational approaches that promote respect for body diversity and the deconstruction of fatphobia. Vocational schools, as spaces for professional and critical training, can be a strategic environment for developing more inclusive and anti-discriminatory care practices. It is essential that these institutions incorporate content and pedagogical practices that enable future professionals to recognize and avoid fatphobic practices within healthcare settings.

title: RT–ICI therapy induces a distal immunometabolic axis that shapes systemic macrophage polarization and enhances local T cell immunity
text: [abstract] Colorectal cancer (CRC) liver metastases remain refractory to immunotherapy due to a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Here, we conducted a prospective clinical study enrolling 18 patients with microsatellite-stable CRC liver metastases treated with high-dose radiotherapy (RT) followed by anti–PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitors (RT–ICI). Integrative analysis of single-cell RNA-sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and peripheral immune profiling revealed that RT–ICI therapy reprograms both tumor-intrinsic and immune compartments. RT triggered the emergence of an APOA2⁺ tumor cell state characterized by enhanced lipid metabolic activity and transient elevation of circulating HDL

title: RT–ICI therapy induces a distal immunometabolic axis that shapes systemic macrophage polarization and enhances local T cell immunity
text: [Introduction] Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains one of the most common and deadly malignancies worldwide [1], with liver metastasis being the predominant cause of cancer-related mortality [2]. Although immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), particularly PD-1 blockade, have demonstrated durable clinical benefit in CRC [3], the vast majority of patients with microsatellite-stable (MSS) CRC—including those with liver metastases—exhibit minimal response to PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitors [4]. This poor efficacy has been attributed to an immunosuppressive liver microenvironment characterized by T cell exclusion, abundant tumor-associated macrophages, and impaired antigen presentation [5].

title: RT–ICI therapy induces a distal immunometabolic axis that shapes systemic macrophage polarization and enhances local T cell immunity
text: [Introduction] Radiotherapy (RT) has emerged as a potent immunomodulatory modality capable of converting “cold” tumors into “hot” immune-reactive lesions [6]. Recent work in lung cancer suggests RT–ICI induces CXCL16–CXCR6 recruitment of CXCL13⁺ CD8 T cells [7]. Beyond its cytotoxic effects, RT enhances tumor immunogenicity by inducing the release of tumor-associated antigens (TAAs), upregulating MHC class I molecules, and facilitating dendritic cell maturation and T cell priming [8]. These effects provide a strong rationale for combining RT with ICIs to sensitize otherwise resistant MSS CRC to immunotherapy. Indeed, preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials suggest that RT–ICI combination therapy can elicit systemic immune responses and overcome resistance in selected MSS CRC patients [9].

title: RT–ICI therapy induces a distal immunometabolic axis that shapes systemic macrophage polarization and enhances local T cell immunity
text: [Introduction] Recent evidence has underscored the importance of lipid metabolism in shaping immune responses within the tumor microenvironment [10]. Lipid accumulation can impair cytotoxic T cell function [11], promote regulatory phenotypes in macrophages, and establish immunosuppressive niches [12]. Among lipid regulators, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and its sensor, liver X receptor alpha (LXRα), play central roles in maintaining lipid homeostasis [13] and modulating innate immune signaling [14]. LXRα forms a functional heterodimer with retinoid X receptor alpha (RXRA) [15], which binds to LXR response elements in genes governing cholesterol efflux, lipid metabolism, and macrophage polarization—such as CETP [16] and CD5L [17]

title: RT–ICI therapy induces a distal immunometabolic axis that shapes systemic macrophage polarization and enhances local T cell immunity
text: [Introduction] In this study, we investigated the systemic and local consequences of RT–ICI combination therapy in MSS CRC patients with liver metastases using single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, lipid profiling, and immune phenotyping. We discovered that RT–ICI treatment induced a tumor subpopulation with elevated APOA2 expression, driving increased HDL biosynthesis and a transient rise in circulating HDL. This HDL surge activated the LXR–RXRA pathway in CETP+ macrophages at distant sites, promoting M2-like immunosuppressive polarization—an effect we term a “distal immunometabolic response.” Concurrently, RT–ICI enhanced intratumoral cytotoxicity by expanding pro-inflammatory CD8+ T cell subsets, which co-localized with chemokine-producing macrophages

text: [RT–ICI combination prolongs survival and suppresses tumor progression in patients with CRC liver metastases] Tumor burden was assessed by CT imaging at baseline and post-treatment. Lesions located within the high-dose RT field exhibited substantial regression, with all measurable lesions decreasing in size by more than 50% (Fig. 1B-C). Flow cytometric analysis of peripheral blood revealed significant post-treatment immunological changes, characterized by a decrease in the proportion of lymphocytes and a concurrent increase in neutrophils; conversely, proportions of monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils remained relatively stable (Fig. 1D-H). Collectively, these findings suggest that RT-ICI therapy modulates systemic immune cell composition, which may contribute to enhanced anti-tumor responses.

text: [RT–ICI combination therapy enhances lipid metabolism in tumor cells] To elucidate the remodeling of the tumor microenvironment by RT–ICI therapy, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing on paired pre- and post-treatment tumor samples. Unsupervised clustering defined nine major cell lineages (Fig. 1I, Fig. S1A-B), with re-clustering of epithelial cells identifying seven distinct subpopulations (Fig. 1J-L). Comparative analysis revealed no significant changes in chromosomal copy number variations (CNVs) following treatment (Fig. 1M).

text: [RT–ICI combination therapy enhances lipid metabolism in tumor cells] However, Gene Ontology (GO) analysis highlighted a profound metabolic shift in post-treatment tumor cells, characterized by the upregulation of lipid transport and localization pathways (Fig. 1N). Simultaneously, we observed enrichment in antigen processing and T cell activation pathways. These data align with the established immunomodulatory role of RT in priming CD8 + T cell responses via tumor-associated antigen release, suggesting that treated tumor cells actively support adaptive immunity. Metabolic profiling further confirmed this reprogramming, showing enhanced fatty acid elongation, degradation, and ether lipid metabolism (Fig. S2C).

text: [RT–ICI combination therapy enhances lipid metabolism in tumor cells] To link these intratumoral changes to systemic physiology, we examined biochemical parameters (Fig. 2E-N, Fig. S4). While post-treatment serum amylase decreased, HDL levels remained unchanged at the endpoint. We postulated a dynamic compensatory mechanism; indeed, longitudinal analysis revealed a transient yet significant spike in serum HDL during treatment (Fig. 2L). Thus, RT-ICI therapy appears to drive intratumoral APOA2 upregulation and HDL biogenesis, leading to transient systemic effects subject to homeostatic regulation.

text: [RT–ICI combination therapy promotes infiltration of pro-inflammatory cytotoxic T cells] To explore IT_T differentiation, we performed pseudotime trajectory analysis of T cell populations pre- and post-treatment (Fig. 3H). Post-treatment T cells formed a coherent developmental trajectory, whereas pre-treatment T cells displayed fragmented trajectories with multiple disconnected modules (Fig. S5D). In the post-treatment group, two dominant trajectories originated from CCR7⁺ naïve T cells: one leading to cytotoxic T cells, and the other to FOXP3⁺ regulatory T cells (Fig. 3I). Examination of exhaustion markers along pseudotime revealed that HAVCR2 and PDCD1 expression did not increase with T cell maturation, suggesting that RT–ICI therapy suppresses T cell exhaustion, consistent with the effects of immune checkpoint blockade (Fig. 3J)

text: [RT–ICI combination therapy reshapes Spatial and molecular cell–cell communication networks] To explore how combination therapy alters intercellular signaling dynamics, we performed cell–cell communication analysis across distinct cell populations before and after treatment. Globally, both the number and intensity of intercellular interactions increased significantly following RT–ICI therapy (Fig.S7A). Notably, CETP⁺ macrophages (CETP_Ma), inflammatory–toxic T cells (IT_T), and GZMB⁺ effector T cells (GZMB_T) exhibited markedly higher interaction strength with a broad range of other cell types post-treatment (Fig. 6A). Quantitative contribution analysis further revealed that IT_T and GZMB_T cells were major contributors to the overall signaling network after therapy, with both increased outgoing and incoming signal strengths (Fig.S7B).

text: [RT–ICI combination therapy reshapes Spatial and molecular cell–cell communication networks] To validate these findings spatially, we applied RCTD-based deconvolution to Visium spatial transcriptomics data. Two annotation outcomes emerged: the first primarily identified stromal populations with limited immune cell resolution (Fig.S10A), while the second annotated diverse immune cell subsets (Fig.S10B). This discrepancy may stem from the co-localization of immune cells with dense stromal components in the tumor, along with the limited spatial resolution and capture efficiency of the 10x Visium platform—particularly for sparse or migratory immune cells.

text: [RT–ICI combination therapy reshapes Spatial and molecular cell–cell communication networks] Neighborhood enrichment analysis further revealed that CXCL10_Ma macrophages exhibited spatial proximity to multiple T cell subsets (Fig. 6C). Spatial visualization confirmed co-localization of CXCL10_Ma, IT_T, and GZMB_T populations (Fig. 6D), suggesting that macrophage-derived CXCL chemokines may directly recruit cytotoxic and inflammatory T cells to exert anti-tumor effects in situ. These findings highlight a reinforced pro-inflammatory circuit induced by RT–ICI therapy, coordinating innate and adaptive immunity within the tumor microenvironment.

text: [RT–ICI combination therapy reshapes Spatial and molecular cell–cell communication networks] Interestingly, CETP_Ma macrophages, despite being expanded post-treatment, showed consistently low neighborhood enrichment scores across cell types (Fig. 6E). Spatial mapping revealed that, although CETP_Ma infiltration increased post-therapy (in agreement with scRNA-seq data), these cells were predominantly located outside of the irradiated tumor region (Fig. 6F). Given our earlier observation of transient HDL elevation in circulation after radiotherapy, we hypothesize a systemic feedback mechanism: radiotherapy enhances APOA2⁺ tumor cell–derived HDL production, which circulates and activates LXR signaling in distant macrophages, leading to M2 polarization and CETP⁺ macrophage expansion

text: [Discussion] In this study, we systematically dissected the immunometabolic landscape of colorectal cancer (CRC) liver metastases under RT–ICI combination therapy using single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics. Our findings highlight a dual impact of this treatment strategy: it locally enhances anti-tumor immunity while simultaneously inducing a distal immunometabolic remodeling program that may modulate systemic immune responses.

text: [Discussion] A major discovery was the emergence of an APOA2⁺ tumor cell subpopulation after RT–ICI therapy. These cells exhibited elevated lipid metabolism, including enhanced fatty acid elongation, ether lipid synthesis, and reverse cholesterol transport. The upregulation of APOA2 and associated HDL pathway genes (e.g., APOA1, APOC1, APOC3) suggests a therapy-induced reprogramming of tumor lipid metabolism. Given prior studies linking CNVs to tumor aggressiveness, this suggests that RT–ICI therapy does not substantially alter tumor malignancy at the genomic level [24]
