text: [Discussion] Paradoxically, our data also revealed the expansion of CETP⁺ M2-like macrophages (CETP_Ma)—an immunosuppressive myeloid population—following treatment. CETP_Ma expressed high levels of canonical M2 markers (CD163, MRC1), immunosuppressive genes (TIMD4, CXCL12), and LXR target genes (CETP, CD5L), and exhibited enrichment in pathways such as ERK1/2 signaling and negative regulation of lymphocyte activation. These molecules are well-established mediators of M2 polarization: CD5L (AIM) promotes lipid accumulation and enhances anti-inflammatory macrophage polarization [25]. CD163, a scavenger receptor, is a prototypical M2 marker involved in hemoglobin clearance and IL-10 production [26]

title: RT–ICI therapy induces a distal immunometabolic axis that shapes systemic macrophage polarization and enhances local T cell immunity
text: [Discussion] . CD163, a scavenger receptor, is a prototypical M2 marker involved in hemoglobin clearance and IL-10 production [26]. TIMD4 (TIM4), often associated with phagocytic clearance of apoptotic cells, contributes to a tolerogenic macrophage phenotype [27]. CXCL12 (SDF-1) facilitates immune suppression by recruiting regulatory T cells and M2-like macrophages [28]. MRC1 (CD206), a mannose receptor, promotes tissue repair and is upregulated during alternative macrophage activation [29]. Transcription factor analysis pinpointed selective activation of LXRα (NR1H3) and RXRA in this subset, suggesting that circulating HDL—elevated transiently during treatment—activates the LXR/RXR axis in macrophages, promoting their polarization toward an M2-like state.

text: [Discussion] Strikingly, spatial transcriptomics revealed that CETP_Ma was predominantly localized outside irradiated tumor regions. Coupled with the transient rise in serum HDL levels post-RT, this led us to propose a “distal immunometabolic effect”: RT-induced HDL from APOA2⁺ tumor cells circulate to distant sites, where it engages LXR signaling in macrophages, inducing CETP expression and M2 polarization. This may facilitate immune suppression and tumor growth at non-irradiated lesions, representing a potential mechanism of systemic immune escape despite local immune activation.

title: RT–ICI therapy induces a distal immunometabolic axis that shapes systemic macrophage polarization and enhances local T cell immunity
text: [Discussion] Our results have both mechanistic and translational implications. First, they highlight the metabolic-immune crosstalk initiated by RT–ICI therapy, revealing how tumor-derived lipid cues can shape systemic immunity. Second, the identification of CETP_Ma as a spatially distinct, prognostically adverse population suggests that targeting the HDL–LXR–CETP axis may mitigate unintended immunosuppression and improve treatment efficacy. Third, the spatial co-localization of CXCL10_Ma, IT_T, and GZMB_Teff underscores the therapeutic value of reinforcing localized immune hubs while minimizing distal immune dampening.

text: [Discussion] However, this study has several limitations. The sample size, though prospectively collected and paired, remains modest (n = 18), which may limit the generalizability of certain findings. Second, while our spatial transcriptomic analysis revealed key cellular relationships, the limited resolution of the 10x Visium platform—especially in densely fibrotic liver tissue—may underestimate immune cell infiltration. Third, while we inferred LXR activation based on gene expression and regulon analysis, functional validation (e.g., ChIP–seq or LXR inhibition assays) is warranted to confirm causality. Lastly, the precise role of CETP⁺ macrophages in promoting distal immune escape remains to be tested in vivo, possibly through lineage tracing or HDL transfer models

Among the 18 patients enrolled in the phase I trial, paired plasma samples during treatment were available for only 4 individuals, all of whom showed increased HDL levels following RT–ICI therapy. In parallel, single-cell and spatial transcriptomic profiling performed in another 4 patients demonstrated enrichment of APOA2⁺ tumor cells and induction of downstream LXR–CETP–associated metabolic programs within the tumor microenvironment. text: [Discussion] In summary, our study reveals that RT–ICI therapy orchestrates a complex immunometabolic reprogramming in CRC liver metastases, characterized by localized T cell activation and distal macrophage-mediated immune modulation. These findings underscore the need to consider spatial and metabolic heterogeneity in immunotherapy response, and they nominate the HDL–LXR–CETP axis as a potential target to synergize with RT–ICI therapy and overcome distal resistance.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [abstract] The differentiation of macrophages into foam cells is a hallmark of atherosclerotic plaques, and macrophage polarization is a key driver of disease progression, yet the underlying genetic mechanisms remain poorly understood. We employed summary data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) combined with transcriptomic validation to explore causal relationships and validate findings at the tissue level.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [abstract] We integrated multi-omics data, including DNA methylation (mQTLs), gene expression (eQTLs), and protein expression (pQTLs), from GeneCards and GWAS summary statistics from FinnGen and UK Biobank. SMR and colocalization analyses were used to identify causal associations. Tissue-specific validation was conducted using eQTL data from artery tissues, and transcriptome analysis was performed using GEO datasets to confirm gene expression patterns in atherosclerotic tissues, followed by confirmation in clinical samples. The function of key genes were explored using Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analysis.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [abstract] SMR and colocalization analyses identified 41 methylation sites, 2 genes (DNMT3A and DLGAP5), and 1 protein associated with atherosclerosis. Specifically, methylation site cg10130446 in DLGAP5 was negatively correlated with atherosclerosis, while sites cg08485187 and cg17742416 in DNMT3A were positively associated. Tissue-specific validation revealed that SIRT6 gene expression was linked to atherosclerosis risk in aortic and tibial artery tissues. Transcriptome analysis from GEO database and blood samples confirmed elevated DLGAP5 and SIRT6 expressions.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [abstract] This study integrates SMR with transcriptomic validation to reveal causal links between macrophage polarization-related genes and atherosclerosis. Key genes DNMT3A, DLGAP5, and SIRT6 were identified as significant candidate regulatory factors. Tissue-specific validation and GEO-based transcriptome analysis provided robust evidence supporting these findings, highlighting the importance of macrophage polarization in atherosclerosis pathogenesis and offering new insights for therapeutic intervention.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Background] Atherosclerosis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by lipid accumulation in large arteries [1]. As the leading cause of cardiovascular diseases, it accounts for approximately one-third of global deaths, with increasing prevalence worldwide [2–4]. Despite established risk factors such as hyperlipidemia and hypertension [5], the persistent burden of AS underscores the urgent need to elucidate its underlying mechanisms.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Background] Macrophages are crucial immune cells involved in the inflammatory response associated with atherosclerosis [6]. Upon entering the arterial intima, monocytes differentiate into macrophages and can adopt different functional phenotypes based on the local microenvironment. These phenotypes are broadly categorized into M1 and anti-inflammatory (M2) macrophages [6–8]. The balance between M1 and M2 macrophages plays a pivotal role in the progression or regression of atherosclerotic lesions. Advanced single-cell sequencing technologies have revealed the heterogeneity of macrophage populations within atherosclerotic plaques, highlighting the complexity of macrophage polarization and its impact on disease pathology [9]

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Background] Genes involved in macrophage polarization, encompassing those encoding cytokines, transcription factors, and receptors, have been implicated in the modulation of atherosclerotic processes [11]. Notably, key transcriptional regulators such as NF-κB, STAT1, and PPAR-γ play pivotal roles in orchestrating the M1/M2 balance [12]. Previous investigations, ranging from Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) to Mendelian Randomization (MR) analyses, have consistently detected associations between these inflammatory mediators and atherosclerosis [13, 14]. However, a critical limitation in current literature is the conflation of general inflammatory signaling with the specific genetic drivers of macrophage polarization

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Background] . For instance, while loci such as NFKB1 or PPARG are robustly linked to atherosclerosis, their extensive involvement in broad systemic immune responses makes it difficult to pinpoint whether their pathogenicity stems specifically from the modulation of macrophage polarization mechanisms or merely from generalized systemic inflammation [15, 16]. Consequently, the precise causal architecture—specifically, whether genetic variations within the polarization machinery directly drive atherogenesis independent of systemic inflammatory burdens—remains incompletely elucidated.

text: [Background] Mendelian randomization (MR) is an innovative analytical approach that leverages genetic variants as instrumental variables to infer causal relationships between exposures and outcomes. Unlike observational studies, MR is robust to reverse causation and minimizes confounding, thereby significantly enhancing the accuracy and reliability of its findings [17]. Building on this foundation, summary data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) has emerged as a powerful extension of MR. SMR enables researchers to explore genetic associations between various molecular traits—such as gene expression, DNA methylation, or protein levels—and diseases of interest using large-scale genomic datasets [18]

text: [Background] . By utilizing top cis-quantitative trait loci (cis-QTLs) as exposure variables, SMR achieves greater statistical power, especially when analyses are conducted with independent samples of substantial size. Prior research has demonstrated the efficacy of SMR in identifying and validating pathogenic genes linked to atherosclerosis [19]. Therefore, this approach provides a comprehensive perspective of causal inference between targeted genes and the disease.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Background] Given the crucial role of macrophage polarization in atherosclerosis, this study aimed to identify potential macrophage polarization-related genes in the disease using SMR methods. Using comprehensive multi-omics analysis, this study aims to reveal the complex genetic factors behind atherosclerosis and macrophage polarization. We expect that these findings will not only increase the understanding of the mechanism of the disease, but also provide important theoretical guidance for the development of precision treatment programs and personalized medical pathways.

We also explored the potential causal associations between mQTL and eQTL by framing mQTL as the exposure variable and eQTL as the outcome variable. text: [Summary-data-based MR analysis] . This method integrates all SNPs in a window centered on the QTL ± 500 kb in SMR analysis, whose p value is less than the default value 5.0 × 10− 8, and the LD r2 value of top-related SNPs is less than the default value 0.9. To distinguish between pleiotropic effects and linkage, we applied the heterogeneity in dependent instruments (HEIDI) test. A P-HEIDI value greater than 0.05 indicates that the observed associations are unlikely due to pleiotropy. By setting thresholds of P_SMR_multi < 0.05, P_SMR < 0.05, and P-HEIDI > 0.05, we identified results that met these criteria for further colocalization analyses among mQTL, eQTL, and pQTL, as well as for integration analysis.

text: [Summary-data-based MR analysis] Our analytic framework was rigorously designed to satisfy the three core assumptions of Mendelian randomization: relevance, independence, and exclusion restriction. The relevance assumption was ensured by selecting top cis-QTLs with genome-wide significance (P < 5.0 × 10− 8) as instrumental variables, guaranteeing a strong association with the exposure. To address the independence and exclusion restriction assumptions, we applied the HEIDI test to distinguish true causality from linkage disequilibrium (LD) or horizontal pleiotropy. A P-HEIDI > 0.05 was strictly used as the criterion to filter out pleiotropic signals, thereby supporting the inference that the genetic instruments affect atherosclerosis risk solely through the target molecular traits.

section: Multi-omics integration and gene prioritization strategy
text: [Multi-omics integration and gene prioritization strategy] To systematically identify key genes, we employed a hierarchical prioritization strategy. First, genes were screened for significant causal associations (P_SMR < 0.05) in at least one omics level (mQTL, eQTL, or pQTL), with pleiotropy excluded by the HEIDI test (P_HEIDI > 0.05). Second, we prioritized candidates showing consistent evidence across multiple omics layers, specifically focusing on the intersection of mQTL, eQTL, and pQTL hits. Finally, these candidates were rigorously validated using tissue-specific eQTL data and clinical differential expression analysis to confirm their biological relevance.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Discussion] This study investigated the causal relationships between macrophage polarization-related genetic factors and atherosclerosis using SMR approach. We integrated genetic data from mQTL, eQTL, and pQTL analyses to identify key genes associated with atherosclerosis. Upon integrating the multi-omics data, we identified two genes associated with atherosclerosis risk: DNMT3A and DLGAP5. Additionally, the expression of the SIRT6 gene demonstrated a significant association with atherosclerosis risk in both aortic and tibial artery tissues. Transcriptomic analysis using further confirmed the elevated expression of DLGAP5 and SIRT6 in atherosclerosis patients, supporting their role in disease progression.

text: [Discussion] Among the key genes identified, DLGAP5 and DNMT3A stood out with robust evidence linking them to atherosclerosis. DLGAP5 is known to function as an oncoprotein, playing significant roles in multiple cancer types by promoting cell proliferation, migration, and invasion [29]. Specifically, in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), DLGAP5 exhibits high expression levels compared to normal liver tissues, and its elevated expression correlates with poor clinical outcomes and tumor immune cell infiltration, indicating its potential role in modulating the tumor microenvironment [30]. Furthermore, studies have shown that DLGAP5 promotes gallbladder cancer (GBC) progression and induces macrophage M2 polarization through the activation of the cAMP pathway, enhancing tumor growth and metastasis [31]

Notably, DLGAP5 knockdown suppresses viability and proliferation while enhancing apoptosis and disrupting the cell cycle, which implies its critical role in ovarian cancer pathogenesis [32]. Although direct evidence linking DLGAP5 to macrophage polarization in ovarian cancer is limited, the gene’s impact on cancer development and immune response suggests a possible indirect effect on the tumor-associated macrophages. Collectively, although direct evidence linking DLGAP5 with atherosclerosis is lacking, current findings suggests that DLGAP5 may modulate macrophage polarization and therefore results in various disease

Our study indicated that DLGAP5’s methylation site cg10130446 demonstrated a significant negative association with atherosclerosis risk, suggesting that higher methylation levels at this site reduce DLGAP5 expression, which in turn lowers disease risk. Furthermore, the elevated expression of DLGAP5 was confirmed in atherosclerotic tissues and blood samples. text: [Discussion] DNMT3A, a methyltransferase critical for de novo DNA methylation, has emerged as a key regulator in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis through its epigenetic modifications that influence gene expression and cellular function. Mutations in DNMT3A associated with clonal hematopoiesis promote a pro-inflammatory state in macrophages, leading to increased activation of inflammatory pathways and accelerated atherosclerotic lesion development, a mechanism comparable to that observed with TET2 mutations [33]. DNMT3A also impacts m6A RNA methylation, a key post-transcriptional regulatory mechanism, which may influence endothelial cell adhesion and smooth muscle cell proliferation, contributing to plaque formation and instability [34]

text: [Discussion] . Additionally, loss-of-function mutations in DNMT3A are linked to altered DNA methylation patterns in macrophages, which promote inflammasome activation and cytokine secretion, amplifying chronic inflammation in atherosclerotic plaques [35]. Furthermore, DNMT3A deficiency leads to several potentially pro-atherogenic phenotypes in various immune cell populations, including pro-inflammatory activation of mast cells [36], increased IFNγ production by T cells, and reduced immunosuppressive function in myeloid-derived suppressor cells. Conversely, DNMT3A inhibition has been shown to increase IL-13 expression in T cells and limit type I interferon production in macrophages, which could protect against atherosclerosis development [37, 38]

SIRT6, a member of the sirtuin family of NAD-dependent deacetylases, has been shown to play a crucial role in various cardiovascular pathologies [39, 40]. SIRT6 is unique due to its chromatin-associated deacetylase activity, which imparts several protective effects similar to those of SIRT1 [41–43]. These include inhibition of heart failure and slowing down the aging process in mice [44, 45]

text: [Discussion] In this study, we employed SMR analysis to investigate the causal relationship between macrophage polarization-related genes and atherosclerosis. Utilizing a multi-omics strategy—encompassing methylation, gene expression, and protein levels—we aimed to construct a regulatory network that elucidates the synergistic roles of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis progression. text: [Discussion] . While our study employs a multi-omics approach to investigate the relationship between macrophage polarization-related genes and atherosclerosis, several limitations must be considered. Firstly, the study’s observational nature restricts our ability to definitively establish causality. Secondly, the key genes identified in blood eQTL analyses were not validated by tissue-specific studies, underscoring the need for future research to bridge this gap. Importantly, our analysis relies heavily on aggregate-level data from populations predominantly of European ancestry, which may limit the generalizability of our findings to other ethnic groups

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Conclusions] In conclusion, this study explored the potential role of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis through SMR combined with multi-omics analysis, and discussed the possible mechanism of three crucial genes, DLGAP5, DNMT3A and SIRT6 associated with the disease. These findings not only highlight the complex role of epigenetic regulation in disease progression, but also suggest that future studies should aim to uncover the complex interactions between these genes, aiming to fully elucidate the pathophysiological mechanisms by which macrophage polarization and atherosclerosis are intertwined. This might potentially provide a theoretical basis for understanding the genetic architecture of the disease and prioritizing candidate genes for future experimental validation.

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [abstract] T cells cooperate with the intestinal microbiota to coordinate antimicrobial defense, but whether this crosstalk arose as an independent innovation in mammals or represents an evolutionarily conserved feature of vertebrate immunity remains unknown.

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [abstract] Using the teleost Nile tilapia as a model, we demonstrate that both systemic and localized infection with Edwardsiella piscicida induce enteritis, correlated with robust intestinal T cell responses. Selective T cell depletion triggered excessive expression of proinflammatory cytokines, impaired mucosal architecture, and diminished host resistance to infection, underscoring the essential role of T cells in gut immunity. Strikingly, T cell depletion also caused profound alterations in gut microbial composition, characterized by a sharp decline in beneficial taxa such as Cetobacterium and the expansion of opportunistic pathogens including Klebsiella and Acinetobacter, indicating that T cells are required to maintain microbiome homeostasis

Conversely, broad-spectrum antibiotic eradication of the microbiota provoked hyperproliferation of intestinal T cells and barrier disruption, revealing reciprocal regulation between T cells and commensals. From the gut content, we isolated a C. somerae strain SH518, whose dietary supplementation for 6–8 weeks enhanced the activation, proliferation, and effector function of intestinal T cells, preserved mucosal homeostasis during E. piscicida challenge, and even boosted systemic T cell immunity in the spleen.

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [abstract] Collectively, these findings demonstrate that teleost T cells engage in bidirectional interactions with gut microbiota to orchestrate both antimicrobial defense and mucosal homeostasis. We therefore propose that T cell–microbiota cooperation represents an evolutionarily ancient strategy predates terrestrial adaptation, offering new insights into the coevolution of mucosal T cell immunity and microbiome.

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [Background] The gut microbiota represents one of the most influential ecological partners of vertebrates, shaping host physiology and immunity through a complex and reciprocal dialogue rather than a simple symbiotic association [1]. In mammals, accumulating evidence has demonstrated that intestinal microbes regulate immunity by guiding lymphocyte development [2], inducing regulatory T cells (Tregs) [3] and secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) [4], reinforcing epithelial barrier integrity, and promoting tolerance to commensals while enabling defense against pathogens [5]

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [Background] . Conversely, the adaptive immune system actively sculpts microbial communities [6]: secretory IgA selectively coats commensals to establish immune exclusion [4], and T cells orchestrate mucosal homeostasis by balancing Treg-mediated tolerance with effector T cell-driven pathogen clearance [3]. Notably, T cell deficiency results in more profound dysbiosis than B cell deficiency [7], underscoring T cells as central regulators of gut microbial equilibrium. This bidirectional co-evolution between microbiota and adaptive lymphocytes has provided a cornerstone for the immunological success and evolutionary radiation of jawed vertebrates.

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [Background] Teleost fish, an early-diverging lineage of jawed vertebrates possessing adaptive immunity, offer a unique window into the evolutionary origins of microbiota–immune interactions [8, 9]. While significant progress has been made in elucidating the role of fish B cells in mucosal immunity—particularly IgM- [10] and IgT-mediated [11] regulation of microbiota and barrier defense—the relationship between intestinal T cells and the microbiota remains entirely unexplored in teleosts. Whether the coordination between T cells and intestinal microbiota represents a strategy independently acquired by mammals or a gradually evolved mechanism common to all vertebrates remains largely unknown

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [Background] The teleost intestine retains structural features shaped by aquatic living and evolutionary ancestry. Its architecture is simple, lacking Peyer’s patches or microfold cells [13], which limits the temporal window for antigen-presenting cells to sample luminal antigens. The mucus barrier consists of a single layer, in contrast to the stratified mammalian system, thereby exposing T cells more directly to microbial antigens. Moreover, teleosts host intestinal microbial loads up to three orders of magnitude greater than mammals, dominated by Proteobacteria including pathogenic genera such as Vibrio [14]

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [Background] Here, using Nile tilapia as a model, we provide the first evidence that intestinal T cells in teleosts mount pathogen-specific responses and orchestrate local inflammatory processes. Through T cell depletion, gut microbiota disruption, and bacterial infection models, integrated with 16S rDNA sequencing, we reveal that T cells are indispensable for shaping microbial community composition and maintaining intestinal immune equilibrium. Furthermore, dietary supplementation with Cetobacterium, a T cell-regulated commensal, enhances host resistance to infection through modulating T cell activation and effector functions, highlighting a reciprocal interaction in which commensal microbes reinforce T cell responses

text: [Background] . Together, these findings establish T cells as central architects of gut immune–microbiota homeostasis in an early vertebrate lineage. By uncovering the dual role of intestinal T cells—coordinating defense against pathogens while sustaining microbial balance—our study illuminates a conserved framework of host–microbiota interaction that predates terrestrial adaptation and highlights the evolutionary origins of T cell-mediated mucosal immunity.

text: [Local infectious and chemical enteritis drive intestinal T cell responses] To further establish the link between intestinal inflammation and gut T cell responses, a TNBS-induced chemical enteritis model was employed. By day 4 post-exposure, the foregut displayed villus tip edema and structural disruption, while the hindgut was characterized by dense inflammatory cell infiltration (Fig. 3A). During the acute phase (day 1), markedly increased MPO activity indicated a neutrophil-dominated response, which subsequently declined by day 4, coinciding with lymphocyte expansion (Fig. 3B, S2L, S2M). text: [Gut dysbiosis causes spontaneous T-cell response and intestinal inflammation] Building on the finding that T cells shape microbial community composition, we next examined the reciprocal influence of gut microbiota on host T-cell immunity. To this end, tilapia were subjected to broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment with ampicillin (Amp) and kanamycin (Kan) by daily oral gavage for 14 consecutive days to disrupt intestinal microbial communities. Antibiotic exposure markedly reduced overall bacterial abundance (Fig. 6A), confirming effective depletion of gut microbiota. Concomitantly, pronounced mucosal damage was observed, including epithelial disorganization and inflammatory cell infiltration in both foregut and hindgut (Fig. 6B, C), indicating that microbial perturbation precipitated local inflammation

text: [T cell depletion perturbs gut microbiota with a marked decline in Cetobacterium] To delineate microbial taxa regulated by T cells, we reanalyzed 16S rDNA sequencing data from T cell-depleted tilapia. This collapse was accompanied by the expansion of opportunistic or pathogenic genera, including Acinetobacter, Klebsiella, Citrobacter, and Exiguobacterium (Fig. 7A). text: [Discussion] . This interpretation is consistent with extensive evidence from mammalian systems. In mice, Tregs represent a specialized CD4⁺ T-cell lineage indispensable for maintaining gut immune tolerance and homeostasis; and selective elimination of Tregs is sufficient to trigger severe and even lethal colitis [22, 23]. Thus, it is plausible that a similar imbalance—caused by the depletion of tilapia Tregs—underlies the uncontrolled inflammatory response we observed. However, due to the lack of antibodies for tilapia CD25 and Foxp3, we still cannot figure out the detail contribution of Treg cells in this fish species. Selective depletion of T cells also disrupted intestinal architecture, and impaired antibacterial defense, confirming their indispensable role in maintaining barrier integrity

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [Discussion] . Collectively, these findings indicate that intestinal T cells represent an ancient and conserved immune strategy, acting as central orchestrators of both antimicrobial defense and tissue homeostasis. Despite architectural divergence in mucosal immune systems, the essential functions of intestinal T cells appear to have been established early in vertebrate evolution and maintained across species, offering compelling evidence for the evolutionary continuity of mucosal immunity and the enduring significance of T cells in host adaptation.

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [Discussion] Teleost fish occupy a pivotal evolutionary position in the transition of jawed vertebrates from aquatic to terrestrial environments [24, 25], making them an ideal model for exploring ancestral modes of intestinal immune regulation. Using Nile tilapia, we investigated the interplay between intestinal T cells and the microbiota. T-cell depletion not only impaired pathogen clearance but also induced a distinct pattern of dysbiosis, characterized by abnormally elevated α-diversity and profound structural collapse of the microbial community. This response stands in sharp contrast to mammals, where T-cell deficiency typically associates with reduced α-diversity and TNF-α–driven inflammatory pathology [26]

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [Discussion] . This fundamental difference raises a profound question: does it reflect a more foundational role for T cells in maintaining barrier integrity within a “primitive” immune system that lacks sophisticated structures like Peyer’s patches? Our data confirmed this notion. We speculate that this divergence reflects severe epithelial barrier disruption in fish following T-cell loss. In tilapia that lacking Peyer’s patches, intestinal T cells are diffusely distributed. Upon T cell depletion, the gut’s physical barrier collapses, allowing massive influx of pathogens and exogenous antigens, which in turn drives catastrophic microbiota perturbation

text: [Discussion] . Furthermore, not only were there significant differences in intestinal microbiota diversity between gut regions in tilapia, but intestinal immune responses also displayed marked regional specialization. In both systemic and oral infection models, the hindgut mounted stronger T-cell responses, consistent with its enrichment of T cells, underscoring the central role of T cells in maintaining hindgut microbial stability. In addition, mammalian T cells help preserve epithelial integrity by producing cytokines such as IL-22, which promote barrier function and mucus secretion [27, 28]. Similarly, in the present study, we demonstrate that intestinal T cells in tilapia are capable of secreting IL-22

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [Discussion] . Similarly, in the present study, we demonstrate that intestinal T cells in tilapia are capable of secreting IL-22. This finding aligns with our previous study that activated spleen T cells in tilapia can produce IL-22 [29], further suggesting the potential role of tilapia T cells in regulating epithelial integrity via producing IL-22. Beyond T cells, innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) can also produce IL-22. Studies using single-cell RNA sequencing have identified ILC-like populations in teleost [30, 31], suggesting ILC-like cells may be another contribution for producing IL-22 and maintaining intestinal barrier integrity and homeostasis in tilapia

text: [Discussion] . In TNBS-induced enteritis, the foregut exhibited pronounced T-cell activation, indicating that foregut T cells, although typically quiescent, retain the capacity for robust responses under pathological conditions. This inducible activation likely reflects an evolutionary adaptation: as the primary entry point for food and pathogens [32], the foregut requires T cells with a “conditional” rather than “constitutive” activation mode, enabling efficient pathogen clearance while minimizing the metabolic cost of continuous activation. Such functional plasticity highlights a refined eco-immunological balance shaped during vertebrate evolution.

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [Discussion] The regionalized and diffusely organized intestinal immune strategy observed in tilapia stands in sharp contrast to the mammalian paradigm, which relies on Peyer’s patches to concentrate antigen sampling and orchestrate follicular responses [33]. From this comparison, we propose a stepwise evolutionary model of intestinal immunity in jawed vertebrates. In early vertebrates such as teleost fish, diffuse lymphocyte distribution coupled with regionally specialized immune microenvironments provided a primitive yet effective framework for infection defense. Correspondingly, the structure of its gut microbiota is relatively simple, yet core taxa such as the genus Cetobacterium play a critical role in coordinating immune and metabolic functions [34, 35]

text: [Discussion] . Amphibians represent the next stage, with intestines already showing nascent lymphoid aggregates, such as identifiable lymphoid follicles in frogs [36], indicating a transitional state from diffuse to organized structures. Birds and mammals then evolved highly developed secondary lymphoid structures, exemplified by Peyer’s patches [37], which enable efficient antigen surveillance and optimized adaptive immune responses [38]. Importantly, the microbiota-immune interaction network also exhibited increased complexity in mammals [39, 40]

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [Discussion] . Importantly, the microbiota-immune interaction network also exhibited increased complexity in mammals [39, 40]. For example, colonization of germ-free mice with the specific commensal bacterium segmented filamentous bacteria induces the activation of CD4+ T cells and the production of IgA [41]; while segmented filamentous bacteria can specifically induce Th17 cell differentiation, thereby finely modulating mucosal homeostasis and enhancing antimicrobial defense [39]. In contrast, Bacteroides fragilis can suppress intestinal inflammation through polysaccharide A-mediated activation of the TLR2/IL-10 pathway [42, 43]. Despite this structural progression, the central role of T cells in microbiota regulation looks remarkably conserved

text: [Discussion] . Despite this structural progression, the central role of T cells in microbiota regulation looks remarkably conserved. Because in both mice and tilapia, T-cell deficiency results in barrier disruption and microbial dysbiosis [44], including the loss of beneficial commensals such as Clostridium spp. and expansion of Enterobacteriaceae [45]. Moreover, the cooperative function of T and B cells consistently forms the cornerstone of mucosal immunity across vertebrate lineages [46]. At the immunoglobulin level, phylogenetic analyses reveal strong homology between the constant regions of teleost IgM and mammalian IgM, highlighting its early evolutionary establishment and conservation [10]

Thus, this stepwise model not only illustrates the gradual structural sophistication of intestinal immunity but also underscores how distinct vertebrate lineages achieve functional convergence in response to shared ecological challenges.

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [Discussion] The bidirectional interplay between intestinal microbiota and T cells represents a central axis of mucosal immune regulation [48, 49], yet its evolutionary origins remain poorly understood. Teleost fish, as early jawed vertebrates possessing primitive T cells, provide a critical model to dissect the emergence of microbe–T cell interactions. Our study reveals a reciprocal regulatory relationship between tilapia T cells and gut microbiota: disruption of microbial homeostasis triggers spontaneous T cell activation and proliferation, whereas T cell depletion induces microbial dysbiosis and expansion of opportunistic pathogens

text: [Discussion] . Notably, T cell deficiency markedly reduces the abundance of Cetobacterium, a dominant native gut commensal in freshwater fish, but is rare in mammals, contributing to diverse host benefits including carbohydrate metabolism [50], vitamin B12 synthesis [51], antiviral defense [52], and ammonia detoxification [53]. Feeding experiments further demonstrate that dietary supplementation with C. somerae SH518 enhances intestinal T cell activation, proliferation, and IL-2 and IFN-γ production, thereby reinforcing anti-infective immunity. Importantly, this immunomodulatory effect extends beyond the gut to peripheral organs such as the spleen, revealing systemic immune regulatory potential

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [Discussion] . These findings strongly suggest that T cells, from their earliest evolutionary emergence, actively collaborated with gut microbes to orchestrate host immunity, exhibiting remarkable plasticity and environmental adaptability. We propose that the bidirectional T cell–microbiota interaction is not an innovation unique to mammals but represents an ancient immune cooperation common to vertebrates. Compared with terrestrial probiotics, the interaction between aquatic-derived Cetobacterium and teleost T cells demonstrates a distinct mode of host–microbe crosstalk, reflecting habitat-specific evolution of intestinal immune symbiosis

text: [Discussion] . Based on these insights, we advance the “aquatic–terrestrial probiotic co-evolution” hypothesis, which provides a novel perspective on the evolutionary shaping of microbiota–immune interactions and informs the rational development of novel probiotics for aquaculture.

text: [Discussion] Given that previous studies revealed that Cetobacterium can produce some metabolites like vitamin B12 and short-chain fatty acids [51, 54–56], which are known to regulate T cell activation and function [57–59], we therefore speculate that C. somerae may promote T cell immunity in tilapia via the metabolites. However, further study is still needed to elucidate the exact mechanism by which Cetobacterium regulates T cell function in fish.

title: Gut T cell-microbiota crosstalk orchestrates antibacterial immunity and mucosal homeostasis in teleost
text: [Conclusions] Our study uncovers the conserved and indispensable roles of intestinal T cells in teleost fish, highlighting their dual function in pathogen defense and mucosal homeostasis, and their bidirectional partnership with commensal microbes, especially Cetobacterium (Fig. 10). These findings bridge fundamental gaps in our understanding of vertebrate immune evolution, revealing that core principles of T cell–microbiota crosstalk were established early and shaped by ecological pressures across habitats. Beyond evolutionary insight, the discovery of Cetobacterium–T cell cooperation provides a promising avenue for probiotic innovation in aquaculture, illustrating how ancient immune strategies can be harnessed for modern applications.Fig

text: [Introduction] Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies worldwide. In 2022, approximately 510, 992 new cases were reported globally, with 467, 409 associated deaths [1], A similar trend is observed in Taiwan, PDAC ranks as the 7th leading cause of cancer-related mortality [2]. Due to its asymptomatic nature in early stages, the 5-year survival rate remains a dismal 8% to 13% [3]. As traditional surgery and chemoradiotherapy frequently fail to achieve long-term remission, identifying novel therapeutic targets within the tumor’s complex signaling networks of PDAC remains an important clinical challenge. One such target is the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), which is commonly overexpressed in pancreatic cancer and associated with poor prognosis [4]

text: [Introduction] . However, the efficacy of EGFR-targeted therapies is often limited by the activation of compensatory escape pathways. Emerging evidence suggests that the cell surface receptor integrin αvβ3, which is highly overexpressed in pancreatic cancer cells and the tumor stroma [5], and proliferating endothelial cells, may facilitate this resistance. Beyond its structural role in cell adhesion, integrin αvβ3 functions as the primary membrane receptor for thyroid hormones including triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4) [6]. Binding of these hormones to αvβ3 triggers pro-angiogenic and pro-survival signaling pathways that drive tumor progression and may reduce the efficacy of existing anticancer therapies [7–11].

text: [Introduction] Critically, the therapeutic potential of targeting integrin αvβ3 is further underscored by its significant crosstalk with EGFR signaling. Previous studies have indicates that thyroid hormone-activated αvβ3 can increase EGFR expression and synergize with epidermal growth factor (EGF) to accelerate cancer cell proliferation [12]. Because both integrin αvβ3 and EGFR signaling converges on the Ras/Raf/ERK signal transduction pathway, they form a redundant survival network that allows tumor cells to bypass single-agent inhibition. Therefore, dual targeting of the thyroxine-αvβ3 axis and EGFR may provide a synergistic approach to disrupt these co-dependent pathways and overcome the therapeutic resistance characteristic of pancreatic cancer.

text: [Immunohistochemical and immunofluorescent validation of ITGAV and ITGB3 expression and their functional association with EGFR] Biologically, these findings confirm that integrin αvβ3 not only acts as a structural adhesion receptor but also functions as a co-receptor for EGFR, creating a signaling platform that amplifies downstream ERK1/2 and PI3K/AKT activation. This interaction may enhance anchorage-dependent growth, survival under stress, and migration, key hallmarks of pancreatic tumor aggressiveness. The A431-based IF model therefore provides crucial mechanistic evidence that αvβ3 can directly interface with EGFR to potentiate oncogenic signaling, supporting the concept that the αvβ3–EGFR complex serves as a driver of proliferative and immune-evasive phenotypes in PDAC.

text: [DL-N2 attenuates invasion- and angiogenesis-associated signaling through the integrin αvβ3-MMP axis] Furthermore, we evaluated the impact of DL-N2 on the expression of genes associated with matrix remodeling and angiogenesis. In BxPC-3 cells, DL-N2 treatment was associated with reduced expression of the metastasis-associated gene MMP9 and suppressed the pro-angiogenic factors bFGF2 and VEGF-α. In AsPC-1 cells, DL-N2 treatment also reduced MMP9 expression; monotherapy with either DL-N2 or gefitinib upregulated bFGF2 and VEGF-α. This suggests that blockade of αvβ3 not only restrains growth but also prevents compensatory activation of pro-angiogenic and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling pathways that typically emerge following EGFR inhibition.

text: [Discussion] Integrin αvβ3 is a structural plasma membrane protein that mediates extracellular matrix–cell interactions and has been repeatedly implicated in cancer pathogenesis. Previous studies have reported that integrin αvβ3 enhances pancreatic tumor progression and metastasis [46, 47]. Thyroxine, a thyroid hormone, can stimulate cancer cell proliferation through direct binding to the cell surface receptor integrin αvβ3, thereby activating downstream signal transduction cascades. The thyroxine–αvβ3 axis has been shown to play a crucial role in the progression of multiple malignancies, including pancreatic cancer [9–11].

text: [Discussion] Clinical transcriptomic datasets demonstrated that ITGAV and ITGB3, the subunits of αvβ3, are overexpressed in pancreatic cancer cells compared with normal pancreatic tissues. High ITGAV expression correlated with worse overall survival, while single-cell transcriptomic mapping localized both subunits to malignant ductal clusters and stromal fibroblasts, but not to normal acinar or endocrine cells. This tumor-specific induction suggests that αvβ3 is not a generic adhesion receptor but rather a malignancy-associated integrin that provides selective advantages in the tumor ecosystem. These findings are consistent with recent studies showing that αvβ3 is enriched in aggressive solid tumors and is associated with a poor prognosis [48, 49]

text: [abstract] Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is closely linked to cardiometabolic disorders, and cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death among affected individuals. Identifying simple biomarkers that capture metabolic–inflammatory burden and predict long-term mortality in MASLD remains a clinical priority. The C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index (CTI) integrates inflammation, dyslipidaemia, and glycaemic status, but its relevance to MASLD and long-term mortality has not been fully elucidated.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [abstract] Higher CTI levels were strongly and nonlinearly associated with the presence of MASLD in both cohorts. Among individuals with MASLD, elevated CTI was associated with significantly increased risks of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality. Each unit increase in CTI in NHANES was linked to a 57% increased risk of cardiovascular death (HR 1.57, 95% CI 1.24–1.99) and a 47% increased risk of all-cause death (hazard ratio [HR] 1.47, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.28–1.69) in fully adjusted models. A pronounced threshold effect was observed, with mortality risk rising sharply once CTI exceeded approximately 5.6. Consistent associations with all-cause mortality were observed in CHARLS

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Introduction] Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD), formerly known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, has become the most prevalent chronic liver disorder worldwide [1]. Its global burden continues to increase in parallel with the rising prevalence of obesity, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes [2]. Although MASLD is primarily a hepatic condition, accumulating evidence indicates that cardiovascular disease (CVD)—rather than liver-related complications—is the leading cause of death among individuals with MASLD [3]. The identification of reliable, easily obtainable biomarkers that capture the metabolic and inflammatory disturbances underlying MASLD and predict long-term mortality, therefore, represents a major clinical priority.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Introduction] Metabolic dysregulation and systemic inflammation metabolic dysregulation play central roles in both the progress of MASLD and its associated cardiometabolic complications [4]. High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP), triglycerides, and fasting glucose are well-established markers linked to insulin resistance, subclinical inflammation, atherogenesis, and adverse cardiovascular outcomes [5]. The C-reactive Protein–Triglyceride–Glucose index (CTI) combines these three components into a single composite marker, reflecting the combined metabolic–inflammatory burden [6]. Recent studies have shown that CTI is associated with metabolic syndrome, cardiometabolic risk, and all-cause mortality in general populations [7]

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Introduction] . Recent studies have shown that CTI is associated with metabolic syndrome, cardiometabolic risk, and all-cause mortality in general populations [7]. However, the relevance of CTI to MASLD and its long-term prognosis has not been fully elucidated.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Introduction] Two major knowledge gaps remain. First, it is unclear whether CTI is associated with the presence of MASLD at the population level. Second, and more importantly, no study has comprehensively evaluated whether CTI predicts long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality among individuals with MASLD, nor assessed the generalizability of such associations across diverse populations. Addressing these gaps would provide valuable insights into the metabolic–inflammatory pathways linking MASLD and cardiometabolic mortality.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Introduction] To fill these evidence gaps, we conducted a multi-stage investigation using two nationally representative, long-term prospective cohort studies from the United States and China. We first evaluated the cross-sectional association between CTI and the prevalence of MASLD in the U.S. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. We then examined the associations of CTI with long-term cardiovascular and all-cause mortality among individuals with MASLD in both the NHANES and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) cohorts. Together, these analyses aimed to determine whether CTI is a clinically meaningful biomarker for identifying MASLD and predicting its adverse long-term results.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Study design] This study integrated cross-sectional analyses and two prospective cohort analyses using two nationally representative datasets from the United States and China. The overall analytic framework consisted of three components: (1) cross-sectional assessment of the association between CTI and MASLD in NHANES and the baseline wave of CHARLS (2011); (2) prospective analysis of CTI and long-term fatality among participants with MASLD in NHANES; and (3) external validation of mortality associations in the CHARLS cohort. Figure 1 shows the flowcharts of participant selection for NHANES and CHARLS. Baseline characteristics of participants included in the analyses and those excluded due to missing data are presented in the Supplementary Materials (Table S1a).

text: [Data sources and study populations] To reflect the civilian population in the United States, NHANES uses a multistage probability sampling design [8]. Participants aged ≥ 20 years with available data on CRP, triglycerides, fasting glucose, MASLD indicators, mortality linkage, and covariates were included. Exclusion criteria included: excessive alcohol intake (≥ 14 drinks/week for men, ≥ 7 drinks/week for women), viral hepatitis (HBV/HCV positivity), pregnancy, implausible laboratory values, and missing covariates [9]. NHANES analytic procedures incorporated sampling weights, clusters, and strata per NCHS guidelines [10].

text: [Data sources and study populations] CHARLS is an ongoing nationally representative cohort of Chinese adults aged ≥ 45 years selected via multistage, stratified household sampling. Two components were utilised: the CHARLS 2011 baseline for cross-sectional analysis, and the CHARLS 2011–2018 follow-up for prospective mortality analysis [11]. Participants with available CRP, triglycerides, fasting glucose, anthropometric measures, covariates, and mortality follow-up were included. Individuals with viral hepatitis, excessive alcohol consumption, or missing data were excluded.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Exposure: C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index (CTI)] CRP (mg/L), triglycerides (mg/dL), and fasting glucose (mg/dL) were measured using standardised laboratory procedures in both cohorts [12]. CTI was modelled continuously and categorically (quartiles). Normal distribution assessments are shown in Fig. S1. CTI was not designed to replace existing TyG-based indices, but rather to extend the TyG framework by incorporating systemic inflammation, thereby capturing an integrated metabolic–inflammatory burden.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Exposure: C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index (CTI)] In NHANES, serum C-reactive protein was measured using standardised high-sensitivity assays under the supervision of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, with rigorous internal and external quality-control procedures. In CHARLS, CRP measurements were conducted in centralised laboratories following standardised protocols, including batch calibration and internal quality-control checks. Although laboratory platforms differed between cohorts, both studies employed validated assays and strict quality-control procedures to ensure measurement reliability.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Outcomes (MASLD)] In the CHARLS cohort, direct assessments of hepatic steatosis, such as liver imaging or histological data, were not available. Therefore, MASLD could not be defined using gold-standard diagnostic modalities. In line with previous large-scale epidemiological studies conducted in similar population settings, we operationalised MASLD using a validated non-invasive surrogate index [13–17].

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Outcomes (MASLD)] MASLD was operationally defined using the TyG-WC index, a metabolic surrogate that integrates fasting triglycerides, fasting glucose, and waist circumference, which are closely linked to hepatic fat accumulation and metabolic dysfunction [13]. We acknowledge that TyG-WC is not a liver-specific marker; however, in cohort studies where direct assessment of liver condition is unfeasible, this index has been employed in several pioneering articles as a surrogate indicator for fatty liver disease [18]. MASLD was defined using validated non-invasive indices: (1) NHANES: U.S. Fatty Liver Index (USFLI), excluding participants with viral hepatitis or alcohol overuse [19]. (2) CHARLS: TyG-WC index, excluding those with hepatitis or excess alcohol intake [17, 20].

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Outcomes (MASLD)] MASLD was identified in individuals with hepatic steatosis (FLI ≥ 60) and at least one of five cardiometabolic risk factors, as defined by expert panel consensus: overweight or obesity, insulin resistance, hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia and/or low high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels [21].

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Outcomes (MASLD)] According to previous validation studies in Chinese adults, MASLD was defined as: TyG-WC ≥ 750–800 in men, and TyG-WC ≥ 540–600 in women [16].

text: [Outcomes (MASLD)] To harmonise classification across sex, we applied sex-specific cutoffs and coded MASLD as a binary variable (yes/no). Participants with viral hepatitis or excessive alcohol consumption were excluded to avoid misclassification.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Prospective mortality outcomes] Mortality status in NHANES was obtained through linkage with the National Death Index (NDI) and was available through December 31, 2019. Both all-cause mortality and cause-specific mortality were identified. All-cause mortality: death from any cause. Cardiovascular mortality: deaths attributed to cardiovascular disease, defined using ICD-10 codes I00–I99 [22]. Time-to-event was calculated from the baseline examination date to the date of death or the end of follow-up, whichever occurred first. Participants who remained alive at the final NDI linkage were censored at the corresponding date.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Prospective mortality outcomes] In CHARLS, mortality information was collected during 2013, 2015, 2018, and 2020 follow-up waves through structured household interviews and verification by family members or local mortality registries [23]. Only all-cause mortality could be reliably ascertained in CHARLS, as cause-specific mortality information was not consistently available and therefore was not used in the main analysis. All-cause mortality: defined as death from any cause reported in follow-up waves. Survival time was calculated from the 2011 baseline to the final available follow-up in 2020 or the date of death. Participants without a death report were censored at their last contact date.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Covariates] Covariate selection was guided by both clinical knowledge and a directed acyclic graph (DAG) (Fig. S2), which identified variables with potential confounding influence on the relationship between CTI and mortality. The DAG indicated that demographic and socioeconomic factors—including age, sex, race/ethnicity (NHANES), educational attainment, and household income—could simultaneously affect CTI levels and mortality risk, and were therefore treated as key confounders [24–28]. Lifestyle behaviours (smoking status, alcohol consumption, and physical activity) were also contained because of their established affiliations with metabolic health and long-term outcomes [29–31].

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Covariates] Several cardiometabolic conditions, including BMI, hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia, were modelled as intermediate pathways or confounding factors depending on the specific analytic framework (e.g., mediation vs. multivariable adjustment), consistent with their positions in the DAG. Clinical laboratory markers such as ALT, AST, HDL-C, LDL-C, and HbA1c were incorporated to capture underlying metabolic and hepatic dysfunction. Additional comorbidities (e.g., cardiovascular disease, hypercholesterolemia, and hypertension) were included as confounders based on their direct links to mortality in the DAG. Together, these covariates represent all minimally sufficient adjustment sets derived from the causal structure.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Cross-sectional analyses (NHANES & CHARLS)] Multivariable logistic regression estimated odds ratios (ORs) and 95% CIs for MASLD across CTI levels. Three models were fitted: Model 1: A crude model with no covariates adjusted. Model 2: Model 1 + age, gender, race. Model 3: Model 2 + education, BMI, diabetes, hypertension, Hypercholesterolaemia, smoking, alcohol, and physical activity.

text: [Cross-sectional analyses (NHANES & CHARLS)] Restricted cubic splines (RCS) examined non-linear CTI–MASLD relationships. Subgroup analyses tested effect modification by age, BMI, diabetes, hypertension, and gender. Threshold effect analysis used two-piecewise logistic models.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Prospective analysis] In the prospective analysis, the relationships between CTI and mortality outcomes were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models. For NHANES, both all-cause and cardiovascular mortality were evaluated, whereas for CHARLS, only all-cause mortality was available. Three progressively adjusted models were constructed, incorporating demographic, lifestyle, and metabolic covariates. Survey-weighted Cox models were used in NHANES analyses to take the intricate sample design into consideration.

text: [Prospective analysis] For cardiovascular mortality in NHANES, competing risk analyses were additionally conducted using Fine–Grey subdistribution hazard models, treating non-CVD death as a competing event and assessing potential competing-suppression effects [32].

text: [Prospective analysis] Subgroup analyses examined potential effect modification by age, sex, BMI, diabetes, and hypertension using multiplicative interaction terms. Finally, threshold effect analyses were performed using Cox regression piecewise to identify possible non-linear inflexion points in the relationship between CTI and mortality outcomes.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Mediation analyses] Causal mediation analyses were performed exclusively within the MASLD population of the NHANES and CHARLS prospective cohorts. These analyses quantified the extent to which BMI, hypertension, and diabetes mediated the associations between CTI and mortality, specifically all-cause mortality in both cohorts and cardiovascular mortality in NHANES only. For each mediator, indirect, direct, and total effects were estimated using 5,000 bootstrap iterations. Mediation proportions were calculated, and suppression effects were reported when observed

text: [Mediation analyses] . Mediation proportions were calculated, and suppression effects were reported when observed. The mediation analyses were conducted under standard causal assumptions, including no unmeasured confounding of the exposure–mediator, mediator–outcome, and exposure–outcome relationships, as well as no time-varying confounding affected by prior exposure. Given the observational design and baseline assessment of variables, these assumptions cannot be formally tested and should be interpreted with caution.

text: [Sensitivity analyses] To address potential concerns regarding the biological specificity of MASLD definitions based on surrogate indices, we conducted extensive sensitivity analyses using alternative steatosis-related definitions. Sensitivity analyses also incorporated alternative MASLD definitions, using HSI in NHANES and applying lower TyG-WC cutoffs as well as VAI-based criteria in CHARLS [9, 33, 34]. In addition, sensitivity studies relevant to each cohort were carried out to evaluate the consistency of results between the two datasets.

text: [Baseline characteristics] Baseline characteristics for the cross-sectional analyses are presented in Table S1 (NHANES) and Table S2 (CHARLS), stratified by MASLD status. In both cohorts, participants with MASLD exhibited a substantially more adverse metabolic profile than those without MASLD, including higher BMI, waist circumference, triglycerides, fasting glucose, and a greater prevalence of hypertension and diabetes. CTI values were consistently higher among participants with MASLD, supporting the hypothesis that inflammatory–metabolic dysregulation is associated with steatotic liver disease.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Association between CTI and MASLD] In NHANES, CTI showed a strong positive association with MASLD in unadjusted and adjusted models (Tables S3 and S4). In the fully adjusted model, participants in the highest CTI quartile had significantly greater odds of MASLD compared with the lowest quartile (OR = 2.33, 95% 1.85–2.92).

text: [Association between CTI and MASLD] Smooth curve fitting using generalised additive models (GAM) revealed a clear non-linear increase in MASLD probability with rising CTI levels (Fig. S3). The fitted curve showed a modest slope at lower CTI values, followed by a progressively steeper rise at higher CTI levels, indicating that MASLD risk accelerated as the metabolic–inflammatory burden increased.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Association between CTI and MASLD] CTI and MASLD showed a strong non-linear association, according to restricted cubic spline analysis (Fig. 2, A: NHANES curve). MASLD prevalence rose steadily with increasing CTI. Subgroup analyses (Fig. S4) showed consistent results across subgroups defined by age, sex, BMI, hypertension, and diabetes, with no significant interactions (Table S5). ROC analysis (Fig. S5, Table S2) confirmed that CTI improved discriminatory ability for identifying MASLD. Compared with models incorporating TyG alone, CTI demonstrated modest but consistent improvements in discrimination for MASLD.

text: [Association between CTI and MASLD] In CHARLS, similar associations were observed using TyG-WC–defined MASLD (Tables S6 and S7). text: [Association between CTI and MASLD] Threshold-effect analysis further demonstrated a significant non-linear pattern (Table S8). A clear inflexion point was identified at CTI = 10.52. text: [Baseline characteristics] As shown in Table 1, participants with higher CTI levels were more likely to be older and female and showed significant racial/ethnic variation across quartiles. There were also notable differences in socioeconomic factors between CTI groups, such as marital status, education level, and poverty-income ratio.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Baseline characteristics] Clear cardiometabolic gradients were observed: higher CTI quartiles showed markedly increased frequency of obesity (BMI ≥ 30), hypertension, diabetes, and hypercholesterolemia. Unhealthy lifestyle factors, including smoking and lower levels of vigorous physical activity, were more common in higher CTI groups. Together, these patterns indicate that elevated CTI corresponds to an accumulation of adverse metabolic and lifestyle risk factors at baseline.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Baseline characteristics] Baseline characteristics for the CHARLS cohort are summarised in Table 2. Similar to NHANES, higher CTI quartiles were associated with a more unfavourable cardiometabolic profile. The prevalence of hypertension and diabetes increased sharply across quartiles, particularly diabetes, which rose from 4.47% in Q1 to 15.7% in Q4.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Baseline characteristics] Higher CTI was also significantly associated with greater BMI categories, with the proportion of obesity (BMI ≥ 28 kg/m²) increasing from 21.9% in Q1 to over 51% in Q4. Total cholesterol levels showed a comparable upward trend. Demographic and lifestyle factors—such as age, smoking, alcohol consumption, education, and household income—showed modest but non-significant or weak gradients across CTI quartiles.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Baseline characteristics] Overall, both NHANES and CHARLS cohorts demonstrated a consistent pattern: higher CTI quartiles were strongly linked to older age, poorer metabolic health, and a higher burden of cardiometabolic comorbidities, supporting CTI as a robust marker of systemic metabolic–inflammatory risk at baseline.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [All-cause mortality] During a median follow-up of 9.39 years, 688 all-cause deaths occurred across 48,162.58 person-years, corresponding to an overall mortality rate of 14.28 deaths per 1000 person-years. Chronic low-grade inflammation, reflected by elevated C-reactive protein, promotes endothelial dysfunction, vascular stiffness, and plaque instability through sustained activation of pro-inflammatory signalling pathways [35–37]. Inflammatory signalling exacerbates insulin resistance, while dysglycaemia and lipid abnormalities further fuel systemic inflammation, creating a self-reinforcing metabolic–inflammatory loop [49, 50]. CTI may therefore identify individuals in whom metabolic resilience has been lost, rendering them particularly vulnerable to adverse cardiovascular outcomes. This biological framework provides a plausible explanation for the strong and consistent associations observed between CTI and mortality across populations.

text: [Discussion] Although MASLD is defined by hepatic steatosis, it is increasingly recognised as a manifestation of systemic cardiometabolic dysfunction characterised by profound insulin resistance and chronic inflammation [58]. Our findings suggest that MASLD represents a high-risk cardiometabolic phenotype in which elevated CTI identifies individuals with particularly adverse metabolic–inflammatory profiles and heightened vulnerability to premature cardiovascular and all-cause mortality. In this context, MASLD may be viewed as a hepatic manifestation of a broader metabolic–inflammatory milieu rather than an isolated liver condition.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Discussion] The identification of a threshold effect in NHANES suggests a transition from compensated metabolic dysfunction to overt metabolic decompensation once CTI exceeds a critical level. Such a threshold may reflect the loss of metabolic resilience, beyond which escalating inflammation and worsening glycaemic dysregulation rapidly translate into accelerated vascular injury and excess mortality risk. The more gradual association observed in CHARLS may reflect differences in baseline metabolic profiles, lifestyle factors, or healthcare access; nevertheless, both cohorts demonstrated a consistent overall relationship between higher CTI and increased mortality risk, underscoring the generalisability of CTI as a cardiometabolic risk marker.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Discussion] From a clinical perspective, CTI is derived from routinely available laboratory parameters and does not require specialised testing or imaging, making it a pragmatic tool for cardiometabolic risk assessment. Elevated CTI may help identify individuals, particularly those with MASLD, who could benefit from earlier and more intensive interventions targeting glycaemic control, lipid management, and systemic inflammation, with the aim of mitigating long-term cardiovascular risk.

title: Association of the C-reactive protein–triglyceride–glucose index with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: evidence from two nationwide prospective cohort studies
text: [Discussion] This study has several strengths, including the use of two large, nationally representative cohorts, long-term prospective follow-up, and comprehensive analytic strategies incorporating non-linear, threshold, and mediation analyses. Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, due to the lack of direct hepatic imaging or histopathological measurements, MASLD in the CHARLS cohort was defined using noninvasive surrogate indices rather than gold-standard methods. Although this approach has been widely adopted in large population-based studies and supported by prior validation research, a certain degree of misclassification is inevitable

text: [Discussion] Another consideration is the partial overlap between the components of CTI and the variables included in the operational definition of MASLD. This overlap reflects shared metabolic pathways linking systemic metabolic–inflammatory burden and hepatic steatosis, rather than a circular reasoning inherent to the study design. Notably, CTI includes C-reactive protein, an inflammatory marker not incorporated into the MASLD definition, and the primary mortality analyses were conducted within the MASLD population, with mortality outcomes themselves being independent of MASLD classification. Furthermore, the consistency observed across multiple sensitivity analyses further indicates that the findings are not solely driven by component overlap
