Some respiratory diseases, such as COPD, can disrupt the niches of BCs, highlighting the potential of BC transplantation as a therapeutic strategy for these conditions [32]. Autologous BC transplantation offers the advantage of avoiding immune rejection; however, it has notable limitations. Given the absence of an effective method to purify normal BCs, this raises concerns regarding the therapeutic efficacy of autologous BC transplantation. Furthermore, the prolonged time required to cultivate autologous BCs may exceed the waiting period for patients in critical need. Therefore, hypoimmunogenic allogeneic BCs represent a viable alternative to address these challenges.

text: [Discussion] CRISPR/Cas9 is a novel, highly specific gene-editing technology that primarily influences the normal translational expression of proteins encoded by target genes, resulting in premature termination of the edited genes during subsequent protein translation [38]. To address the challenge of transfection efficiency in adult stem cells, we combined the sgRNA and the Cas9 protein extracellularly, and then transferred the combination into the BCs via the liposome transfection method, a technique reported in several studies [39, 40]. text: [Discussion] In the aspect of immune rejection, our study revealed the distinct responses between the tracheas and lungs after BC transplantation. In the tracheal epithelium, both WT BCs and B2m‾ BCs were capable of differentiating into the ciliated and secretory cells, surviving up to 28 days post-PDOC injury without evidence of immune cell infiltration. This finding aligns with the work of Farrow et al., who reported that human BCs could survive in nasal airways for at least 8 weeks after PDOC‐induced injury, suggesting that allogeneic BC transplantation in upper airways may not be easy to provoke rejection [42]

title: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated B2m knockout paves the way for allogeneic basal cell transplantation
text: [Discussion] . Conversely, the transplantation of WT BCs into the lungs resulted in pronounced immune rejection, evidenced by bronchial epithelium exfoliation and alveolar collapse, mirroring the pathological features observed in immune rejection after lung transplantation [29, 30]. Immunohistochemical staining for CD45 in lung sections further suggests that WT BCs may incite an immune response in the lungs, a phenomenon not observed with B2m‾ BCs. Additionally, H&E‐stained histological sections indicated that transplanted BCs are likely exposed to distinct microenvironments within the trachea, intrapulmonary airway, and alveolar regions post‐PDOC injury (Fig. S4B), indicating that BC–immune cell interactions may differ across different respiratory compartments.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated B2m knockout paves the way for allogeneic basal cell transplantation
text: [Discussion] Despite the promising findings, our study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. First, the PDOC-induced airway injury model, while providing a reproducible method to remove the airway epithelium and create space for transplanted cells, does not fully recapitulate the complex pathophysiological processes underlying human airway diseases such as COPD, cystic fibrosis, or idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Moreover, the advantage on transplantation efficiency of hypoimmunogenic BCs over wild-type BCs was not observed in the present study because of the lack of immune cells infiltration in the tracheas after PDOC injury (Fig. S6). As a result, the therapeutic potential of hypoimmunogenic BCs in clinically relevant disease contexts remains to be validated

text: [Discussion] . S6). As a result, the therapeutic potential of hypoimmunogenic BCs in clinically relevant disease contexts remains to be validated. Second, our evaluation of immune rejection was primarily based on histopathological assessment and pan-leukocyte (CD45) immunostaining. Although these approaches clearly demonstrated differences between WT and B2m‾ BCs transplantation, they do not allow for detailed characterization of the infiltrating immune cell subtypes, their activation states, or the specific molecular pathways involved. Technical challenges, including strong erythrocyte autofluorescence in the alveolar tissues and the inability to perform bronchoalveolar lavage without compromising epithelial integrity, limited our ability to conduct in-depth immune profiling

title: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated B2m knockout paves the way for allogeneic basal cell transplantation
text: [Discussion] . Third, the observation period in this study was restricted to 28 days post-transplantation. While this timeframe was sufficient to evaluate initial engraftment, differentiation, and acute immune responses, it does not address the long-term survival, functional integration, or potential delayed rejection of transplanted BCs. Finally, although we demonstrated the feasibility of generating hypoimmunogenic BCs through B2m KO, additional modifications, such as engineering of immune checkpoint molecules to achieve disease-specific immune evasion or design of kill-switch systems to provide extremely tight control over cell survival and/or proliferation, may be required in more stringent or clinically relevant settings [43].

title: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated B2m knockout paves the way for allogeneic basal cell transplantation
text: [Conclusions] In this study, we established a strategy to generate hypoimmunogenic BCs by disrupting the B2m gene with the CRISPR/Cas9 system. The resulting B2m‾ BCs preserved key BC characteristics, retained their capacity to differentiate into ciliated and secretory lineages, and demonstrated reduced immunogenicity following transplantation. Notably, these cells engrafted and contributed to epithelial repair in both proximal and distal regions of the respiratory tract without provoking overt immune rejection during the observation period. Together, these findings highlight hypoimmunogenic BCs as a promising candidate for universal airway regenerative therapy, while also underscoring the need for long-term studies and disease-relevant models to fully evaluate their clinical potential.

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [abstract] The Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II) builds on the landmark study Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study to develop real-world implementation strategies for preventing type 2 diabetes (T2DM). This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of digital and complex lifestyle intervention in reducing the incidence of T2DM among adults with increased risk of T2DM, compared to usual care over a 36-month period.

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [abstract] A three-arm, stratified, cluster-randomized controlled trial will be conducted in eight factories in Daqing, with clusters as the unit of randomization and individual participants as the unit of analysis. Fifty-seven clusters will be randomly allocated (1:1:1) to one of three groups: (1) Digital-based lifestyle intervention, (2) complex lifestyle intervention, or (3) usual care. Eligible participants will be adults aged 25–55 with increased risk of T2DM, defined by IFG, IGT, HbA1c 5.7–6.4%, and/or 1-h PG above 8.6 mmol/L, while not meeting the criteria for diabetes. Exclusion criteria include significant cardiovascular disease (CVD) within 6 months, impaired liver function, renal dysfunction, other significant medical or psychological conditions, or participation in similar studies

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [abstract] . The interventions will run for 3 years. The primary outcomes are the 3-year cumulative incidence of T2DM. The study will utilize the RE-AIM framework and Implementation Outcome Framework (IOF) to assess Reach, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance, Feasibility, Acceptability, and Appropriateness through process measures. Data collection will include plasma glucose (0, 1, and 2 h) and insulin levels (0, 1, and 2 h) based on the oral glucose tolerance test, laboratory tests, blood pressure, body mass index, waist circumference, and dietary and physical activity behaviors, diabetes knowledge, and quality of life. These measures will be assessed by trained doctors or nurses at baseline and at 6-,12-, 24-, and 36-month follow-ups.

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [abstract] The study will provide evidence on how population-level strategies of digital and complex lifestyle intervention can be implemented in real-world settings to prevent diabetes. If proven effective, these strategies could be integrated into Workplace Wellness Program in China and other countries to prevent diabetes and other noncommunicable diseases.

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [Background and rationale {6a}] In recent decades, China has seen a rapid increase in the disease burden of diabetes [1]. Globally, China has the largest number of individuals aged 20–79 years living with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), with 140.9 million cases in 2021. This number is projected to rise to 174.4 million by 2045 [2]. T2DM also imposes a significant economic burden on China, with the total cost of diabetes reaching US $250.2 billion in 2020 and increasing at an annual rate of 6.32%, exceeding the country’s overall economic growth rate [1]. With over 100 million people in China already living with T2DM, there is an urgent need to strengthen early detection, diagnosis, and treatment

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [Background and rationale {6a}] . With over 100 million people in China already living with T2DM, there is an urgent need to strengthen early detection, diagnosis, and treatment. However, a national survey conducted in 2018 found that more than half (63.3%) of individuals with diabetes remain undiagnosed, only one-third (32.9%) receive treatment, and, among those treated, only half (50.1%) had adequate glycemic control [3]. In light of these challenges, immediate action is essential to prevent T2DM.

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [Background and rationale {6a}] Prediabetes is characterized by impaired fasting glucose (IFG), impaired glucose tolerance (IGT), or elevated HbA1c (nondiabetic hyperglycemia — NDH) [4]. It represents an intermediate metabolic state that precedes T2DM. Although the progression rate varies across populations, on average, nearly 5–10% of individuals with prediabetes develop T2DM each year, and nearly 70% will eventually progress to T2DM unless effective intervention occurs [5]. For example, the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study in China reported that 93% of individuals with IGT in the control group developed diabetes over a 20-year follow-up period [6]

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [Background and rationale {6a}] . Even more concerning, 38.1% of adults aged 18 or older in China have prediabetes [3], which not only increases the risk of developing T2DM but also raises the risk of microvascular and macrovascular complications, as well as all-cause and cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality [7]. Given these risks, proactively addressing prediabetes should be a key priority in diabetes prevention efforts in China. Most diabetes prevention programs have focused on individuals with IGT, while evidence supporting the effectiveness of lifestyle interventions in individuals with isolated IFG (i-IFG) or NDH remains limited [8]

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [Background and rationale {6a}] . Recently, the International Diabetes Federation (IDF) defined prediabetes to include individuals with a 1-h post-load plasma glucose (1-h PG) value of 155 mg/dL (8.6 mmol/L) or higher, recommending lifestyle interventions and referral to diabetes prevention programs [9]. However, this approach requires rigorous evaluation, especially in real-world settings and resource-limited environments.

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [Background and rationale {6a}] Efficacy studies from many countries have consistently demonstrated that lifestyle modification is an effective intervention to prevent or delay the onset of diabetes in individuals with prediabetes [10]. However, the benefits depend on successful implementation in real-world settings [11]. The Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study, one of the most landmark randomized control trials for diabetes prevention [12], demonstrated that group-based, face-to-face lifestyle interventions delayed diabetes onset by a median of 4 years, with beneficial effects sustained for up to three decades [13]. Despite this, no implementation study in China has adopted the Daqing model

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [Background and rationale {6a}] . Despite this, no implementation study in China has adopted the Daqing model. In contrast, many studies conducted in Europe, the USA, and some Asian countries have primarily followed the US Diabetes Prevention Program (US-DPP) model [11]. Additionally, the limited effectiveness of lifestyle interventions that focus solely on diet and physical activity suggests that multifactorial lifestyle interventions should be implemented in at-risk populations [14, 15].Therefore, there is a pressing need for effective, scalable, and sustainable models to identify individuals with prediabetes and to deliver personalized, evidence-based lifestyle interventions.

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [Background and rationale {6a}] Strategies are urgently needed to prevent and manage both T2DM and prediabetes. The existing implementation studies have primarily focused on face-to-face counselling, delivered either individually or in groups [11]. However, limited face-to-face time with participants poses a challenge to deliver counselling effectively in real-world settings [16]. Future research should explore models for lower-intensity face-to-face and hybrid lifestyle interventions. Although digital interventions are generally more scalable than traditional face-to-face approaches [17–19], adherence remains a significant challenge

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [Background and rationale {6a}] . Evidence from developed countries suggests that digital-based lifestyle interventions can support weight control; [20, 21] however, there is limited evidence regarding their effectiveness in diabetes prevention [22, 23]. For instance, a study found that a combination of digital and face-to-face group lifestyle interventions, but not digital-only interventions, improved overall diet quality in real-world settings among individuals with prediabetes [12, 24]. Therefore, the impact of digital interventions on diabetes prevention remains unclear. Furthermore, the importance of a supportive environment should not be overlooked [25]

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [Background and rationale {6a}] . Furthermore, the importance of a supportive environment should not be overlooked [25]. Evidence suggests that support from family [26] and peers [27], which is typically present in group-based interventions, plays a crucial role in their effectiveness [28]. Additionally, the workplace environment plays a vital role in supporting employees’ health. For example, workplace cafeterias are key settings for providing access to healthy meals [29]. Hence, further studies are needed to develop and evaluate more feasible lifestyle intervention models for developing countries in real-world settings.

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [Background and rationale {6a}] To date, no large-scale RCTs in China have followed the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study while incorporating behavioral change techniques. The Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II) aims to adapt and implement the evidence-based lifestyle intervention from the original Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study in real-world settings. This paper outlines the protocol for identifying and recruiting individuals with prediabetes and conducting a randomized controlled trial to assess the effectiveness of digital and complex lifestyle intervention compared with usual care. Importantly, the risk identification and lifestyle intervention components will be fully integrated into the employees’ Wellness Program, facilitating long-term implementation.

text: [Sample size {14}] Assuming a 3-year cumulative incidence of T2DM of 29% [53] in the control group, an intra-cluster correlation of 0.05 [54], and a dropout rate of 20%, we calculated that 475 individuals in each arm would be needed to detect a 40% risk reduction [54, 55] in the intervention arm. The calculation was based on a significant level of 2.5% and type II error of 20% (i.e., power = 80%), allowing for 20% incomplete follow-up. To ensure feasibility and account for clustering effects, 19 clusters per arm, with approximately 25 participants per cluster, were included in the study design. The target sample size is 1425 participants across 57 clusters to assess the effectiveness of the digital-based lifestyle intervention and complex lifestyle intervention in reducing the incidence of T2DM over 3 years.

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [Sequence generation {16a}] The trial employs stratified cluster randomization with zuoyequ as clusters and individual participants as the unit of analysis. The randomization process will be stratified by factory and type of work. A total of 57 clusters will be randomly allocated in a 1:1:1 ratio to one of three groups: (1) digital-based lifestyle intervention, (2) complex lifestyle intervention, or (3) usual care. Each group will receive the corresponding intervention to evaluate the effectiveness on diabetes prevention. An independent statistician, not involved in participant recruitment, data collection, or intervention delivery, will generate the randomization schedule using a computer-based sequence with variable block sizes.

text: [Data management {19}] For paper-based questionnaires, a double data entry process is conducted by two independent staff members in the local implementation team. section: Statistical methods for primary and secondary outcomes {20a}
text: [Statistical methods for primary and secondary outcomes {20a}] All analyses will follow an intention-to-treat approach, meaning that individuals will be analyzed in the group to which they were originally assigned, regardless of their adherence to the intervention. The primary objective is to evaluate the effects of the digital-based lifestyle intervention, complex lifestyle intervention, on the prevention of T2DM, relative to a usual care arm, without directly comparing the two interventions to each other. Survival curves will be used to estimate the cumulative incidence of diabetes, with the difference in incidence of T2DM tested using a two-sided log-rank test as descriptive curves

section: Statistical methods for primary and secondary outcomes {20a}
text: [Statistical methods for primary and secondary outcomes {20a}] . The primary time-to-event analysis of incident diabetes will use a marginal Cox proportional hazards model to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) for each intervention arm versus the usual care arm. The link/scale is log hazard. Cluster-robust (sandwich) variance will account for the cluster randomized design. The time origin will be the date of randomization. The model will adjust for a pre-specified minimal adjustment set, including intervention arm, age, gender, glycemic status, and weight status. Stratification by factory or type of work will be applied if baseline hazards differ meaningfully across factories.

section: Statistical methods for primary and secondary outcomes {20a}
text: [Statistical methods for primary and secondary outcomes {20a}] The proportional hazards assumption will be assessed using scaled Schoenfeld residuals, global and covariate-specific tests, and graphical inspection of Schoenfeld residuals and log–log survival curves. If violations are detected, time-varying coefficients or stratified Cox model will be considered for the affected covariates, and alternative flexible parametric model may be explored if needed. Competing risk of death will be explored using Fine-Gray models. Since two primary comparisons will be made for primary outcome (each intervention arm vs. usual care), a Bonferroni correction will be applied to control for multiplicity, and p-values < 0.025 will be considered statistically significant

text: [Methods for additional analyses (e.g., subgroup analyses) {20b}] A per-protocol analysis set will be specified a priori, consisting of participants who satisfy the predefined adherence requirements, i.e., attendance at the initial intervention activity as in a previous study [57]. This set will be used for sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of the primary findings. We will explore whether the effects of the interventions on outcomes differ according to pre-specified variables, including prediabetes phenotype, baseline weight status, and gender. Twenty imputed datasets will be generated, with convergence checks to ensure stable imputation, and results will be combined using Rubin’s rules. Sensitivity analysis will be conducted to check the robustness of the findings and include the following: (1) Complete-case analysis; (2) analysis exploring departures from MAR using delta-adjusted and tipping-point approaches, in which imputed values are systematically adjusted to evaluate how violations of the MAR assumption could affect the intervention effect and identify tipping points where conclusions would change; and (3) per-protocol analysis with pre-specified criteria.

text: [Discussion] This cluster randomized controlled trial is the first large-scale trial conducted in a real-world setting to assess the effectiveness of digital-based lifestyle intervention and complex intervention in reducing incidence of T2DM and promoting the reversal to normoglycemia. Building on the foundation established by the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study, the trial aims to provide valuable insights into how the Daqing model can be integrated and scaled effectively. The successful implementation of this trial will contribute to the development of a sustainable and replicable model to identify at-risk individuals and deliver evidence-based lifestyle interventions

text: [Discussion] Prediabetes is a significant global public health concern, with its prevalence increasing, particularly among older adults and obese individuals [59]. Rising rates of obesity and prediabetes globally are increasing the burden of diabetes and other noncommunicable diseases. Early intervention is key, as evidence suggests that diabetes prevention strategies are most effective when implemented during the early stages of the disease [60]. However, the identification of prediabetes is complicated by the use of multiple definitions, each based on different thresholds for HbA1c, fasting glucose, and 2-h glucose levels [61]. Recently, 1-h post-load glucose has been proposed as a valuable metric for identifying prediabetes [9], though it has not yet been widely adopted in practice

title: A three-arm, parallel group, cluster randomized controlled trial to evaluate digital and complex lifestyle interventions as compared with usual care for type 2 diabetes prevention: protocol for the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II)
text: [Discussion] . The risk of progressing to diabetes varies depending on the definition of prediabetes used [59], and meeting one, two, or all glycemic criteria influences the degree of risk for developing diabetes [61]. As a result, there is a growing call for more precise risk stratification to target individuals at high or very high risk of diabetes. However, implementing evidence-based approaches to identify and intervene with individuals at increased risk of T2DM in real-world settings remains a challenge, underscoring the need for scalable and effective strategies.

text: [Discussion] The importance of early intervention in adults with prediabetes is strongly supported by findings from diabetes prevention trials [12, 62, 63]. Current guidelines recommend lifestyle modification as the primary approach for preventing diabetes in individuals with prediabetes in clinical practice, regardless of the specific definition used [4]. However, the risk of progression to diabetes varies based on how prediabetes is defined. text: [abstract] Diffuse midline glioma (DMG) is a rare and aggressive pediatric brain tumor, with a median survival of less than 12 months. Due to its location in the pons, surgical resection is impossible, leaving radiation therapy as the only palliative treatment option. Unfortunately, radiation therapy yields minimal improvement in survival. text: [Background] . In the brain, the blood-brain barrier (BBB) controls exchanges between the blood and the brain parenchyma to maintain brain homeostasis and represents the vascular component of the TME. The BBB restricts the access of neurotoxic compounds but also of xenobiotics and chemotherapeutics. In addition, the BBB allows the delivery of nutrients essential for nervous cells function. Located at the level of endothelial cells (ECs) of brain capillaries, the BBB forms a dynamic barrier, whose properties throughout life are finely regulated by communications at the level of the neurovascular unit (NVU) thanks to chemical mediators or extracellular vesicles [12]. The NVU is made up of ECs, brain pericytes (hBPs) (embedded in the ECs basement membrane), astrocytes, neurons and glial cells [13, 14]

text: [Background] . The NVU is made up of ECs, brain pericytes (hBPs) (embedded in the ECs basement membrane), astrocytes, neurons and glial cells [13, 14]. To ensure its barrier properties, the BBB ECs possess physical properties (presence of tight junctions between ECs) and metabolic properties (efflux pumps and drug metabolizing enzymes) to limit the passage of compounds [15, 16]. However, the BBB is permeable and selective, thanks to specific receptors and transporters, to support neuronal function [17, 18]. Renamed blood-brain tumor barrier (BBTB) in the vicinity of the tumor, the BBTB limits the access of therapeutics to tumor cells and is involved in the drug resistance mechanism [19, 20]. text: [RT-qPCR] The Reverse transcription (RT) step was performed using a thermocycler (MJ Research, Reno, USA) to obtain cDNA from 250ng of total RNA. The reaction mix contains a reverse transcriptase enzyme from the iScript™ Reverse Transcription Supermix kit (1708841, BioRad, Hercules, USA). The enzyme was used according to the manufacturer’s protocol. To detect possible contamination of samples with genomic DNA, enzyme-free negative controls were performed. The reverse transcription step (20 min at 46 °C) was preceded by a primer hybridization step (5 min at 25 °C) and followed by an enzyme inactivation step (1 min at 95 °C). Samples were stored at -20 °C.

text: [Western blot analysis] Western blot assays were performed using 20 µg of total protein mixed with Laemmli loading buffer (1610747, Bio-Rad) supplemented with β-mercaptoethanol (M-3148, Sigma Aldrich). Following electrophoresis, a wet transfer of proteins was performed on nitrocellulose blotting membranes (0.45 μm NC 10600003, Cytiva Amersham™ Protran). Membranes undergo a 90 min saturation step in a solution of Tris-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween 20 (TBST: 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 0.1% Tween 20; Bio-Rad) containing 5% milk and 3% of goat serum. Then the membranes were incubated with the primary antibody (Table 3) diluted in 1% milk TBS-Tween solution for 2 h at room temperature (RT) (20 min for anti- β-actin primary antibody), or overnight at 4 °C.

text: [Efflux pump activity] Efflux pump activity of P-gp/ BCRP in hBPs was assessed by real-time Rhodamine 123 pump out assay according to the method described by Sevin et al.,2019 [30]. To do so, hBPs were incubated for 2 h at 37 °C with R123 solution at 20µM. Then the cells were washed twice with RH solution at room temperature and incubated with or without Verapamil solution at 50µM a P-gp/ BCRP inhibitor. The efflux of R123 in the medium was directly monitored every 2 min during 90 min at 37 °C by fluorescent measurement at 501/538nm (BioTek Cytation C10 Confocal Imaging Reader, Agilent). The results in RFU/min/ng proteins were expressed as a percentage relative to the control.

text: [Mitochondrial activity assays] The MTT tetrazolium reduction assay was used to assess the mitochondrial activity of endothelial cells. Seven days after irradiation, the cell culture medium was changed with 0.5 ml of MTT solution (3-(4,5-Dimethyl-2-thiazolyl)-2,5-diphenyl-2 H-tetrazolium Bromide) (Sigma-Aldrich) at a concentration of 1 mg/ml, the cells were incubated at 37 °C until formation of purple crystals. Crystals formation results from the reduction of tetrazolium to formazan by mitochondrial succinate dehydrogenase of metabolically active cells. Pure DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide) was used to solubilize intracellular formazan crystals to measure the absorbance at 570 and 630 nm to determined cell activity rate and background subtraction. The results were expressed as a percentage to non-irradiated control.

text: [Induction of DNA double-strand breaks] To investigate how radiations, impact the BBB and BBTB properties, triple culture models consisting of ECs, hBPs and astrocytes for the BBB model or ECs, hBPs and DMG cells (HSJD-DIPG-007 or HSJD-DIPG-013) for the BBTB-007 and BBTB-013 models (Fig. 1A) were exposed to a single dose of radiation ranging from 2 Gγ to 6 Gγ. To ensure a uniform exposure of all cell types, DNA double-strand breaks were visualized at 2 h and 7 days post-irradiation using γ-H2AX staining. As shown in Fig. 1B (and in Additional file 1 A&B), representative images taken 2 h after single dose of 6 Gγ exposure, revealed a homogeneous distribution of γ-H2AX foci in the nuclei of all cell types

At 2 h post-irradiation, 100% of the ECs nuclei were positive (similar results were obtained for BBTB-007 ECs and BBTB-013 ECs, data not shown), 77.6% of hBPs nuclei, 79% of astrocytes and 89% of DMG nuclei. The non-individualization of γ-H2AX foci has rendered impossible the quantification of γ-H2AX foci per nucleus. However, the induction of DNA double-strand breaks seemed to increase with the dose. Even if after 7 days, the endothelium does not present a complete recovery of DSB after exposure to 6 Gγ, for the 44.3% positive cells, the number of γ-H2AX positive foci per cell which is between 1 and 6 (mostly 2), is reduced compared to 2 h and 24 h conditions.

section: Consequences of radiation on BBB & BBTB at the molecular level: focus on the metabolic properties
text: [Consequences of radiation on BBB & BBTB at the molecular level: focus on the metabolic properties] Metabolic properties were analysed at a molecular level to further understand the consequences of irradiation on the BBB/BBTB ECs. To do so, gene expression analysis was performed on ECs and hBPs and focused on selected efflux pumps and detoxification enzymes known to be involved in the chemoresistance mechanisms by modulating drug bioavailability. The analysed efflux pumps were P-gp, BCRP, MRP1, MRP2, MRP4 and MRP5 (respectively genes names ABCB1, ABCG2, ABCC1, ABCC2, ABCC4 and ABCC5) and the detoxification enzymes from the cytochrome P450 family (CYPs) were CYP1A1, CYP1B1, CYP2D6 and CYP2S1.

section: Consequences of radiation on BBB & BBTB at the molecular level: focus on the metabolic properties
text: [Consequences of radiation on BBB & BBTB at the molecular level: focus on the metabolic properties] As shown in Figs. 3A and 7 days after irradiation, no modulation of mRNA level was measured for ABCB1 and ABCC1 in BBB ECs. However, significant reductions of mRNA expression of ABCG2 and ABCC4 were quantified in BBB ECs, with a decrease of 58% and 41% respectively at 6 Gγ compared to the non-irradiated control. Hence, similarly to BBB ECs, the BBTB-007 ECs displayed a decrease in ABCG2 and ABCC4 with a decrease of 36% and 41% respectively induced by 6 Gγ irradiation. In addition, there was an increase in ABCC1 and ABCC5 mRNA levels (Fig. 3B). Similar results to BBB ECs were obtained for BBTB-013 ECs (Additional file 6 A).

text: [Discussion] Recent advances in the characterization of DMG, along with the integration of molecular features, have emerged since the new classification of brain tumors in 2016 [31]. These developments highlight the complexity of brain tumors and underscore the importance of studying each tumor type individually to enable the development of personalized therapies. Nevertheless, despite advances in understanding the mechanisms underlying treatment responses at the tumor cell level, treatment resistance remains challenging and represents a major obstacle [32]. This is why, radiotherapy still remains the only standard of care for DMG. Therefore, considering not only the tumor cells but also the complexity of the TME is prime of importance [33]

title: Consequences of irradiation on blood-brain tumor barrier model of Diffuse Midline Glioma: characterization of physical and metabolic properties
text: [Discussion] . Therefore, considering not only the tumor cells but also the complexity of the TME is prime of importance [33]. Indeed, while the role of the TME in tumor progression is now widely accepted, characterising the TME in treatment response remains to be explored as an actor in the modulation of the treatment efficiency. The TME of DMG is a complex environment that encompasses multiple cell types in addition to tumor cells, extracellular matrix as the acellular component but also the vasculature. The brain tumor vasculature is composed of brain capillaries responsible for nutrient and oxygen supply but, also limiting the treatment efficacy [34, 35]

title: Consequences of irradiation on blood-brain tumor barrier model of Diffuse Midline Glioma: characterization of physical and metabolic properties
text: [Discussion] . Indeed, the specific and restrictive properties of the brain capillaries include physical and metabolic properties that are regulated by communications among the NVU. Moreover, the presence of cancer cells interferes with these communications and plays a pivotal role in the regulation of the BBB properties which is then renamed BBTB. The physical and metabolic characteristics of the BBTB of DMG are still poorly understood. The development of relevant preclinical models that combine both tumor biology and the TME is prime of importance for understanding the treatment responses and also for advancing effective treatments. For this reason, we have previously developed a BBTB model specific to the DMG [21, 24].

title: Consequences of irradiation on blood-brain tumor barrier model of Diffuse Midline Glioma: characterization of physical and metabolic properties
text: [Discussion] Our experimental in vitro approach uses a syngeneic human BBB model consisting in ECs cultivated with hBPs and astrocytes [21, 24]. This triple culture model has been adapted from a patented co-culture model [25]. Moreover, in order to model specifically the vasculature of the DMG, a BBTB model has been developed by including DMG cells instead of astrocytes [21]. The setting of these models allowed to integrate the reciprocity of cell-cell communication in the induction of BBB phenotype but also following disease or treatment conditions and at the same time to separately collect each cellular component for further molecular analysis

title: Consequences of irradiation on blood-brain tumor barrier model of Diffuse Midline Glioma: characterization of physical and metabolic properties
text: [Discussion] . Our previous results have demonstrated that unlike other brain tumors, DMG cells don’t lead to physical disruption of the BBTB [21], as already suggested by clinical and in vivo results [20, 10]. Although DMG tumor displays a strong chemoresistance, our previous study has demonstrated that the metabolic BBTB properties were not strengthened [21]. Hence, in the present study using the BBTB model, we aimed at studying the impact of radiotherapy on the tumor vasculature by focusing on physical and metabolic properties involved in drug delivery.

text: [Discussion] The model has been exposed to a single dose of radiation, ranging from 2 Gy to 6 Gγ, using a contact device. According to the literature, doses used comprised a range of radiations commonly used in cell culture systems, starting at 2 Gγ, which represents the reference dose in clinic for patients that receive a fractionated radiotherapy protocol and allows to assess the consequences of radiation by inducing measurable effects without massive cell death occuring at early stage post-irradiation [36–38]

text: [Discussion] . In fact, the doses tested in an in vitro model do not correspond to the total doses received by patients during treatment protocol, but rather to a cumulative dose administered at the beginning of treatment after one (2 Gy), two (4 Gy), and three (6 Gy) radiotherapy sessions, in order to understand how BBTB can be modulated at the beginning of the therapeutic session. In addition, the dose of 6 Gγ is close to the estimated dose of healthy tissue exposed to a single exposure (7 Gγ) [39]. Anyhow, the different doses were all able to induce significant DNA damage in all cell types of the cell culture system since the nuclei of all cells had displayed a positive staining for the DSB

text: [Discussion] . In addition, even if the density of DSB foci in nuclei has rendered impossible the quantification, the quantity of DSB foci increased with the dose received. This effect, was also observed at 7 days since the foci were still detected in some nuclei for the dose 6 Gγ but not for the 2 Gγ. In addition, this dose response effect was also observed on endothelial cell count, since a significant decrease in endothelial cell number was measured after 6 Gγ in the BBB and the BBTB. These results are in line with a previous study using a primary bovine in vitro BBB model where the follow-up has been done until 7 days post-irradiation [37]

However, following radiation, cell usually undergoes cell death; our study showed that the decrease in cell number was not correlated with a loss of endothelium physical integrity whatever the dose of radiation. Nevertheless, a significant decrease in the metabolic activity of endothelial cells was observed 7 days after exposure to 6 Gy of radiation. The intercellular spaces between the endothelial cells of the BBB are sealed by tight junctions, which help maintain the physical integrity of the BBB. The permeability of the endothelium after irradiation remains similar to the non-irradiated control and correlates with the staining of VE-cadherin adherent junctions and ZO-1 tight junctions

Claudin-5 is one of the main tight junction proteins expressed by ECs, is responsible of the restriction of paracellular permeability to small molecules (< 800Da) as described in Claudin-5 knock-out mice [40]. In our study, Claudin-5 expression in ECs appears to be heterogeneous after irradiation. Our results were similar in the BBB and BBTB ECs, but do not fully correlate with other in vitro studies using animal models. In these studies, the BHE showed a significant increase in permeability one week after irradiation with 2 Gγ and 4 Gγ [37, 41, 42]. However, these models used ECs co-cultured with mixed glial cells and did not include hBP

text: [Discussion] . However, these models used ECs co-cultured with mixed glial cells and did not include hBP. In the literature, the question of BBB/BBTB dysfunction or leakage after irradiation is still debated [43, 44] The physical integrity of the BBB/BBTB depends on the radiation dose, follow-up kinetics, and experimental model used in preclinical studies. Nevertheless, radiation-induced damage to the BHE is often associated with inflammatory events [45].

title: Consequences of irradiation on blood-brain tumor barrier model of Diffuse Midline Glioma: characterization of physical and metabolic properties
text: [Discussion] In fact, radiotherapy is known to induce inflammation, which increases tissue damage severity [46, 47] Following radiotherapy, patients receive anti-inflammatory treatment with corticosteroids in order to limit oedema formation [10, 48]. Hence, in vitro studies, demonstrating radiation-induced BBB damages, have used cellular models containing microglial cells, known to be the resident immune cells in the central nervous system, alone or within a mix of glial cells population [37, 45, 47]. The absence of microglia cells in our cell culture model could explain the maintenance of the physical integrity. Astrocytes and DMG cells are not sufficient to create a pro-inflammatory condition following radiation in the time frame of our study

title: Consequences of irradiation on blood-brain tumor barrier model of Diffuse Midline Glioma: characterization of physical and metabolic properties
text: [Discussion] . Astrocytes and DMG cells are not sufficient to create a pro-inflammatory condition following radiation in the time frame of our study. Nevertheless, when the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines was mimicked by a TNFα treatment, a disruption of the BBB was measured and demonstrates that irradiation exacerbates by 8.6-fold the increase in the endothelial damages induced by inflammatory stress [49]. Interestingly, this effect was measured in a much lesser extent in the BBTB model, since after irradiation, TNFα treatment induced a 3.1-fold increase in permeability, revealing that the tumoral DMG environment trends to maintain the endothelium integrity

text: [Discussion] . This result is in correlation with the clinical situation since, contrary to other types of brain tumor such as glioblastoma, DMG is known to be a « cold » tumor, with a specific DMG TME where at any stage there is no major lymphocyte infiltration [50–52] and in line with a recent in vitro data where the DMG were demonstrated to maintain an immunosuppressive environment [53]. Indeed, irradiation does not provoke only DNA damages; its effects extend more broadly to the entire cell components, and can impact the plasma membrane [54, 55]. This could explain the potentiating effect of TNFα exposure after irradiation on the BBB ECs [55]. In our study, using TNFα allowed to mimic the neuro-inflammation stage following radiation

title: Consequences of irradiation on blood-brain tumor barrier model of Diffuse Midline Glioma: characterization of physical and metabolic properties
text: [Discussion] . In our study, using TNFα allowed to mimic the neuro-inflammation stage following radiation. This stage occurs as a consequence of radiation-induced pro-inflammatory cytokines release [56–58]. As one of the major pro-inflammatory cytokines released during the neuro-inflammation, TNFα is widely used in experimental setting in vitro [27, 59]. In addition, the permeation effect of TNFα is now tested as a therapeutic treatment for brain tumors. In fact, the combination of chemotherapeutic drug with TNFα derivatives is now developed to selectively increase the BBTB permeability to improve the drug delivery [60]. This approach is particularly useful because it allows for the permeabilization of the BBB/BBTB in tumors with an intact BBB physical integrity, as is the case with DMG

To further study radiation-induced neuro-inflammation in our BBTB model and also take into account intratumoral heterogeneity, DMG cells could be replaced by organoids derived from surgical resection [61, 62]. However, the complex location of DMG and the rarity of samples make it difficult to collect representative tumor samples that accurately reflect the intratumoral heterogeneity of this tumor.

title: Consequences of irradiation on blood-brain tumor barrier model of Diffuse Midline Glioma: characterization of physical and metabolic properties
text: [Discussion] Over the past few decades, clinical trials have been tested the combination of radiotherapy and chemotherapy against DMG to improve the therapeutic strategies However, the chemotherapeutic or immunotherapy agents tested are generally substrates of efflux pumps (P-gp, BCRP, MRP1) which limits their access to the tumor cells [19, 63]. Therefore, studying the effects of radiation on efflux pumps expression and activity is important.

title: Consequences of irradiation on blood-brain tumor barrier model of Diffuse Midline Glioma: characterization of physical and metabolic properties
text: [Discussion] At a molecular level, focusing on the metabolic properties of the BBB and the BBTB reveals that at 7 days post-irradiation, expression of numerous efflux pumps and detoxification enzymes was modulated. For ECs, the efflux pumps BCRP and MRP4 expression was decreased in the BBTB following radiation. Moreover, the impact of radiation was more important in the BBTB-ECs since significant decrease in expression and activity of P-gp/ BCRP were measured. Further analysis is needed to identify the mechanisms responsible for changes in BCRP expression and activity. It cannot be ruled out that these results are the consequence of post-translational modifications and/or an increase in degradation pathways

text: [Discussion] . It cannot be ruled out that these results are the consequence of post-translational modifications and/or an increase in degradation pathways. In addition, the BBTB ECs are distinguished from the BBB ECs by an upregulation of MRP1 and MRP5. These two multidrug resistance proteins are described in the resistance to treatment of numerous brain cancers [64] and their upregulation was found in ependymoma and glioma and can represent potential targets to overcome the BBTB [64].

text: [Discussion] Interestingly, hBPs showed a compensatory effect, while BCRP expression was decreased in the endothelium, it was conversely maintained in hBPs. However, even reduced following irradiation, the activity of efflux pump P-gp/BCRP in hBPs remained efficient and still represents a mechanism to overcome to improve the drug delivery. In addition, no differences were measured from hBPs in the BBB and in the BBTB after irradiation.

title: Consequences of irradiation on blood-brain tumor barrier model of Diffuse Midline Glioma: characterization of physical and metabolic properties
text: [Discussion] Concerning the detoxification enzymes, the CYPs are able to metabolize many endogenous and exogenous compounds (such as chemotherapeutic drugs). In addition, certain CYPs are active in cerebral microvessels, such as CYP1A1, CYP1B1, CYP2D6, and CYP2S1, which are located in the BBB ECs [65, 66]. While transporters tend to influence the distribution of drugs, CYPs also impact their effect through biotransformation.

title: Consequences of irradiation on blood-brain tumor barrier model of Diffuse Midline Glioma: characterization of physical and metabolic properties
text: [Discussion] Consistent with the analysis of efflux transporters, irradiation induced an increase of CYPs expression in hBPs. Nonetheless, no differences were detected between hBPs from the BBB model and those from the BBTB. However, the time window of analysis may need to be extended for protein analysis since, even if the higher modulation rate was measured at 7 days post-irradiation for mRNA, for the majority of molecular target candidates no increase or decrease in proteins expression were validated in the BBB and BBTB ECs at 7 days. MRP4 and BCRP were the only ones to demonstrate a correlation between mRNA and protein expression only in BBTB ECs. Member of the multidrug resistance family, further investigations are required to understand the role of MRP4 in BBTB ECs.

text: [Discussion] Interestingly, MFSD2A, a lipid transporter known to be a marker of BBB establishment, has exhibited an increase in expression of mRNA transcript following radiation in all cell types [67]. However, its expression at protein level has demonstrated a regulated mechanism where only the first isoform was decreased. While the BBB/BBTB ECs physical integrity was maintained the decrease in protein expression can be a preliminary event that precedes BBB/BBTB disruption.

title: Consequences of irradiation on blood-brain tumor barrier model of Diffuse Midline Glioma: characterization of physical and metabolic properties
text: [Discussion] According to the literature, the maintenance of ECs physical integrity following irradiation can be linked to CYP1B1 and MFSD2A upregulation. Indeed, the metabolic activity of CYP1B1 was demonstrated to be involved in the maintenance of junction integrity and P-gp function. Moreover, its inhibition is associated with BBB leakiness [68]. Concerning MFSD2A, known to mediate uptake of the essential fatty acid DHA across the BBB, this protein is associated with BBB establishment and is strongly regulated by hBPs [69, 70]. Notably, reduced MFSD2A expression has been linked to BBB disruption in brain cancer [71]

title: Consequences of irradiation on blood-brain tumor barrier model of Diffuse Midline Glioma: characterization of physical and metabolic properties
text: [Discussion] . Notably, reduced MFSD2A expression has been linked to BBB disruption in brain cancer [71]. Consequently, lipid metabolism emerges as a significant pathway warranting further investigation to enhance our understanding of the mechanisms underlying BBB/BBTB damages following radiation exposure. In addition, experimental data suggest also a link between MFSD2A and Claudin-5 expression [72, 73]. Additional experiments need to be conducted to decipher if a regulation pathway is existing.

title: Consequences of irradiation on blood-brain tumor barrier model of Diffuse Midline Glioma: characterization of physical and metabolic properties
text: [Discussion] Pericytes play a crucial role in the induction and regulation of the BBB ECs, but, at the molecular level, the characterization of pericytes is often overlooked in favour of ECs. Importantly, this regulatory mechanism highlights that regardless of the BBB’s physical integrity, pericytes contribute to treatment resistance, particularly in restricting the brain penetration of therapeutic agents, should not be underestimated. This may provide insight into the persistence of drug resistance in some cancer types even where structural integrity of the BBTB is compromised.

title: Consequences of irradiation on blood-brain tumor barrier model of Diffuse Midline Glioma: characterization of physical and metabolic properties
text: [Conclusions] In this study, we have demonstrated that in the absence of inflammatory stress, the physical integrity of the BBB and the BBTB was preserved but associated with heterogeneous distribution of Claudin-5 at the ECs borders and decreased of expression after irradiation. Moreover, the response to inflammation was one of the most relevant effect to distinguish the BBB from the BBTB. For metabolic properties, the compensatory effect observed with pericytes has clearly indicated the importance of pericytes in the regulation of BBB/BBTB properties. Additional molecular analyses are required to better characterize the consequences of irradiation on the BBTB ECs involving the fatty acid metabolism and transport, especially following inflammatory conditions

title: Development and cross-validation of a novel multi-omic assay to assess locoregional recurrence risk and adjuvant therapy benefit in early-stage hormone receptor positive invasive breast cancer patients
text: [abstract] Breast cancer management is shifting towards personalized treatment regimens, particularly for early-stage, hormone receptor positive (HR+) invasive breast cancer (IBC) patients following breast conserving surgery (BCS) where locoregional recurrence (LRR) rates are low. A critical unmet need is the development of tools that can both improve prognostic risk assessment and identify which patients are likely to benefit or not benefit from adjuvant radiation therapy (RT). Herein we developed and cross validated a novel multi-omic assay to assess LRR risk and expected RT benefit for early-stage HR+/HER2-negative IBCs.

title: Development and cross-validation of a novel multi-omic assay to assess locoregional recurrence risk and adjuvant therapy benefit in early-stage hormone receptor positive invasive breast cancer patients
text: [abstract] A retrospective multi-institutional cohort of 922 patients (T1-2, N0-1, HR+, HER2-) treated with definitive breast conserving surgery (BCS) with or without adjuvant treatment was used to develop and cross-validate a test to predict IBC LRR after BCS ± RT. Treatment assignment was not randomized. The test integrated NGS and proteomic assay data using two biosignatures to generate results: a Decision Score (DS) to predict 10-year LRR prognosis and a radiation resistance index (RRI) to predict differential RT effect on LRR. Associations between DS and RRI with LRR risk and RT interaction were tested using multivariable Cox models.

text: [abstract] In this large retrospective, non- randomized multi-institutional cohort, the novel multi-omic biosignature was associated with lower and higher LRR risk after BCS and associated with statistically significant differential RT effect for LRR risk reduction. Clinically meaningful risk groups that were associated with differential RT benefit were identified using the biosignature, supporting its potential utility in the assessment of the LRR risk in early-stage HR+/HER2-negative IBC. Further clinical validation studies are in process, and prospective validation studies are being planned to establish the role of the test in clinical practice.

text: [Discussion] For patients with early-stage HR+/HER2- IBC, radiation oncologists routinely address the role of RT after BCS to decrease the risk of breast cancer recurrence in consultation with their patients. title: The role of vaccination, underlying health conditions, and working in healthcare in the socioeconomic disparities in COVID-19 hospitalization: a mediation analysis using interventional effect models
text: [abstract] Shifting from moderate or high education to low education increased the probability of COVID-19 hospitalization by 0.694% points (95% CI 0.561–0.819) during the Delta period and 0.547% points (95% CI 0.491–0.603) during the Omicron period. Most of this increase was due to the direct effect of education, accounting for 84.6% of the total effect during Delta and 93.1% during Omicron. During the Delta period, education disparities in COVID-19 hospitalization were partially mediated by vaccination (10.1%) and underlying health conditions (6.3%). During the Omicron period, education disparities in COVID-19 hospitalization were partially mediated by underlying health conditions (4.8%), vaccination (1.4%), and working in healthcare (0.7%).

title: The role of vaccination, underlying health conditions, and working in healthcare in the socioeconomic disparities in COVID-19 hospitalization: a mediation analysis using interventional effect models
text: [abstract] This study demonstrates that socioeconomic disparities in COVID-19 hospitalization rates are partially mediated by vaccination and underlying health conditions. This suggests that public health interventions aimed at increasing vaccination rates and preventing underlying health conditions could mitigate some of the effects of socioeconomic disparities in COVID-19 hospitalization outcomes. However, future research is needed to investigate additional mediating factors of education in COVID-19 hospitalization, such as living and working conditions, to better elucidate the causal pathways of social inequalities in severe COVID-19.

title: The role of vaccination, underlying health conditions, and working in healthcare in the socioeconomic disparities in COVID-19 hospitalization: a mediation analysis using interventional effect models
text: [Introduction] Rapidly, a large body of literature highlighted a clear social gradient in both SARS-CoV-2 infection and the development of subsequent severe COVID-19 outcomes (e.g. hospitalization, ICU admission, death), disproportionately affecting individuals from lower socioeconomic (SE) groups (e.g. low levels of income or education, living in overcrowded households, poor housing conditions) [2–7]. As a result, the COVID-19 pandemic was very quickly described as a syndemic, emphasizing the interaction between the purely biological nature of the virus and the social determinants of health (e.g., education, housing, employment), exacerbating social inequalities already deeply rooted in our society [2, 8, 9].

title: The role of vaccination, underlying health conditions, and working in healthcare in the socioeconomic disparities in COVID-19 hospitalization: a mediation analysis using interventional effect models
text: [Introduction] Within the syndemic framework of the pandemic, four key pathways explain how the social determinants of health shape inequalities in COVID-19 health outcomes [10, 11]. First of all, unequal exposure indicates that disadvantaged SE groups are overrepresented in essential and in person occupations with limited opportunities for remote work [12, 13], and rely heavily on public transportation during the pandemic [14–17], increasing their risk of exposure. Secondly, unequal transmission, whereby disadvantaged SE groups are more likely to live in densely populated urban areas [18–20] or in overcrowded households [21–23], increasing the risk of viral transmission

Lastly, unequal treatment and preventive services with SE inequalities observed in access to preventive health behaviors during the COVID-19 pandemic, including vaccination [27–29]. Although vaccination effectively reduce the risk of severe COVID-19 [30–32], the spread of such preventive measures is accompanied by an increase in social health inequalities, particularly in its early stages [33]

text: [Mediators] In the causal inference framework for observational studies, an exposure can be associated with an outcome through both direct and indirect pathways [47]. text: [Statistical analyses] To assess the role of multiple mediators in the association between education and COVID-19 hospitalization, we applied causal mediation analysis within the interventional effects framework. Causal mediation analysis are usually applied within the potential outcomes framework, defining the causal effect for a given unit as the difference in its outcome under exposure versus control conditions, measured at the same time point [54–56]. However, this approach requires strong assumptions when multiple mediators are involved. Specifically, it assumes a known causal ordering of mediators and no unmeasured confounding, conditions that are rarely satisfied in practice [57].

Thanks to this method, each indirect effect passing through each distinct mediator can be assessed separately [61]. Interventional effects are perfectly suited to assess effects of non-manipulable exposures such as SE determinants and have to be interpreted on the population level rather than the individual level [61]

This approach offered a number of advantages. First, for binary outcomes, linear regression is often preferred for estimating causal effects of an exposure [62]. Indeed, when computing linear regression coefficients, the effects estimated are directly interpretable as probabilities and the decomposition of the total effect into direct and indirect effects is more straightforward [62, 63]. Linear models are also more robust when interaction terms are included [62]

In recent years, MP has shown widespread prevalence both domestically and internationally, accompanied by an increasing incidence of severe and critical cases. Among these, FMPP presents with an acute onset and poses a life-threatening risk, necessitating urgent attention. This study retrospectively analysed the clinical data of FMPP patients admitted to our hospital in 2023 to investigate their risk factors and clinical characteristics.

Inflammation activates the coagulation cascade, leading to increased consumption of fibrinogen and consequently lowering its levels

text: [Discussion] . As a soluble product derived from fibrin degradation, D-dimer is associated with thrombotic disorders. However, within this study cohort, only 30.3% (20/66) of the children in the FMPP group presented elevated D-dimer levels; notably, no significant correlation was found between these elevations and respiratory failure occurrence, with thrombosis reported infrequently (in only two cases). title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [abstract] The aim of the current analyses of a phase 3 randomized controlled trial conducted in Japan was to assess the long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant 75 mg, taken for up to 52 weeks, for the preventive treatment of migraine.

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [abstract] The study included adults in Japan with a history of 4–18 migraine attacks/month of moderate or severe pain intensity. After 12 weeks’ double-blind treatment with rimegepant 75 mg or placebo every other day, participants took open-label rimegepant 75 mg every other day and additionally as needed on nonscheduled dosing days (maximum one dose of rimegepant 75 mg per calendar day), for up to 40 weeks. Safety assessments included adverse events and hepatic function. Effectiveness endpoints included change in monthly migraine days, medication use, and changes in migraine-related quality of life and disability.

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [abstract] Of 496 participants who received double-blind treatment, 458 participants were treated with rimegepant in the open-label-extension phase (mean age 43.9 years, 90.8% female) for a mean of 37.5 weeks. During the open-label extension phase, the most common adverse events were nasopharyngitis (25.1%) and COVID-19 (13.1%); the rate of adverse events leading to rimegepant discontinuation was 1.3% and the rate of serious adverse events was 0.9%. Aminotransferases >3x the upper limit of normal occurred in four (0.9%) participants during the open-label extension phase; none of these participants had concurrent elevations with total bilirubin >2x upper limit of normal

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [abstract] . For the open-label extension phase overall, monthly migraine days of any pain intensity reduced by a mean (95% confidence interval [95% CI]) of –4.5 (95% CI –4.8, –4.2) days with 55.4% (95% CI 50.8, 59.9) of participants experiencing ≥50% reductions compared with the observation period. The use of acute treatments for migraine was low through the open-label extension phase. Improvements from baseline in Migraine-Specific Quality-of-Life Questionnaire v2.1, Migraine Disability Assessment (MIDAS), and EQ visual analog scale were observed through the 52-week study.

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [abstract] Sustained effectiveness, with a favorable safety profile, was observed in treatment with rimegepant 75 mg taken up to once daily for up to 52 weeks.

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [Background] The recurring headache, nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia associated with migraine [1] have a detrimental effect on all aspects of patients’ lives, including mental health, quality of life and work productivity [2]. Worldwide, migraine is a leading cause of disability [3]. The long-term prognosis is variable, but for many patients migraine requires management over many years [4–6] and both preventive and acute treatment options.

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [Background] There is a substantial unmet need for the preventive treatment of migraine [7, 8]. Many patients are not prescribed a preventive treatment [9] and traditional treatments (including beta-blockers, antidepressants, antiepileptics, and calcium channel blockers) can have limited efficacy and poor tolerability [10–12] resulting in high discontinuation rates [9, 13]. Injectable calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) monoclonal antibodies are recommended for migraine prophylaxis [10, 11, 14] but their long half lives mean immediate cessation is not possible [15], and patients may prefer oral treatments to injections [16].

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [Background] Rimegepant is an oral, small-molecule CGRP receptor antagonist that is effective for both the acute treatment of migraine [17–21] and the preventive treatment of migraine [22, 23]. The long-term effectiveness and safety of open-label rimegepant have been demonstrated in studies conducted in the United States [24, 25], but have not yet been reported elsewhere.

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [Background] A phase 3 study conducted in Japan was the first double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine to be conducted outside of the United States and the second globally [23]. It comprised a 12-week double-blind treatment (DBT) phase, during which participants took rimegepant 75 mg or placebo every other day (EOD), followed by a 40-week open-label extension (OLE) phase, during which participants took rimegepant 75 mg EOD on scheduled dosing days and as needed (PRN) when they had a migraine on nonscheduled dosing days. In the DBT phase, the efficacy of rimegepant was superior to placebo with a favorable safety profile [23], extending the evidence base for preventive treatment beyond the study conducted in the United States [22].

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [Background] There are currently few long-term data available for rimegepant, and these are exclusively from the USA [24, 25]. The aim of the current analyses of the phase 3 study conducted in Japan [23] was to evaluate long-term safety, as well as effectiveness, in participants in Japan treated with open-label rimegepant for up to 40 weeks, and in those who were randomized to rimegepant during the DBT phase and subsequently took rimegepant in the OLE phase for up to 52 weeks in total.

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [Study design] This prospective, phase 3, double-blind, randomized, multicenter trial (study number C4951021 or BHV3000-309; NCT05399485), conducted at 44 study sites in Japan, evaluated the effectiveness and safety of rimegepant 75 mg orally disintegrating tablet (ODT) compared with placebo for the preventive treatment of migraine. The study comprised a 28-day observation phase (OP), a 12-week DBT phase, and a 40-week OLE phase (Fig. 1). Full methodology and the primary findings for this study were reported previously [23]. The current analyses include both the 12-week randomized DBT phase and the 40-week OLE phase.

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [Study population] . Briefly, key eligibility criteria for the study were adults with a ≥ 1 year history of migraine (with or without aura) consistent with a diagnosis according to International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3) [1]; onset of migraine before 50 years of age; migraine attacks lasting, on average, 4–72 h if untreated; 4–18 migraine attacks/month (4 weeks) of moderate or severe pain intensity within the last 3 months prior to the screening visit; four or more migraine days during the OP; ≤18 headache days during the OP; and the ability to distinguish migraine attacks from tension-type or cluster headache

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [Study population] . Excluded were brainstem aura (basilar migraine), hemiplegic migraine, or retinal migraine; headache (migraine or non-migraine) occurring ≥ 19 days per month in any of the 3 months prior to screening; and history with current evidence of uncontrolled, unstable, or recently diagnosed cardiovascular disease (such as ischemic heart disease, coronary artery vasospasm, cerebral ischemia) or myocardial infarction, acute coronary syndrome, percutaneous coronary intervention, cardiac surgery, stroke or transient ischemic attack during the 6 months prior to screening.

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [Study population] Participants were allowed to remain on one background preventive migraine medication (other than CGRP antagonists) throughout the study, provided the dose was stable. Acute treatments (standard of care, including aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, baclofen, acetaminophen, antiemetics, and muscle relaxants) were allowed if needed. The use of triptans was prohibited during the OLE phase as participants used rimegepant as needed for acute treatment. Use of triptans in the OLE phase or ergotamine at any point during the study was recorded as a protocol deviation and counted as acute migraine-specific medication use if administered.

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [Intervention] After 12 weeks of DBT with rimegepant 75 mg or placebo EOD, eligible participants continued open-label treatment with rimegepant for up to 40 additional weeks. During the OLE phase, participants took one rimegepant 75 mg EOD, regardless of migraine status (i.e., scheduled dosing days). On nonscheduled dosing days, if participants experienced a migraine they could take one rimegepant 75 mg on that calendar day to treat the migraine. Therefore, during the OLE phase, participants could take a maximum of one rimegepant 75 mg ODT per calendar day for up to 40 weeks.

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [Procedures and assessments] Visits were at screening and baseline, then at Weeks 2, 4, 8, and 12 during the DBT phase and at Weeks 14 and 16, then every 4 weeks until Week 52/end of treatment, during the OLE phase. title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [Procedures and assessments] Participants used an eDiary every day during study to record migraine occurrence, migraine pain features and associated symptoms, and use of acute migraine medication (i.e., triptan, ergotamine, or other). text: [Statistical analyses] Efficacy and effectiveness were assessed in 3 analysis sets. The DBT efficacy analysis set comprised randomized participants taking ≥ 1 dose of DBT study drug. The OLE rimegepant migraine analysis set comprised randomized participants who took open-label rimegepant regardless of DBT treatment assignment, that is: randomized participants who took ≥ 1 dose of DBT study drug and ≥ 1 dose of rimegepant during the OLE phase, and who had ≥ 14 days of eDiary efficacy data (not necessarily consecutive) in both the OP and ≥ 1 month (4-week interval) in the OLE phase.

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study

text: [Statistical analyses] Effectiveness endpoints during the OLE phase were prespecified as exploratory endpoints; these data were observed and summarized descriptively. text: [Discussion] To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this was the first trial reporting the long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine conducted outside the United States. Sustained effectiveness, with a favorable safety profile, was observed in the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan. The data for the OLE phase were consistent with the DBT phase [23], the previous study of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine conducted in the United States [22], and longer-term open-label data [24, 25, 33]. The dosing regimen for the OLE phase (EOD plus PRN on nonscheduled dosing days) is consistent with the expected clinical use for rimegepant (up to one 75 mg-tablet per calendar day).

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [Discussion] Rimegepant is the only medication that is effective for both the acute [17–21] and preventive [22, 23] treatment of migraine, and therefore offers a comprehensive approach to long-term management. Japanese treatment guidelines recommend the traditional, oral preventive treatments for patients with more than two migraine attacks per month or a history of headache interfering with daily activities on more than three days a month, as well as for patients for whom acute treatments have not worked or are not suitable [14]. Elsewhere, migraine-specific and CGRP-targeted therapies are widely recommended first-line for migraine prophylaxis [35, 39]. Although the injectable CGRP monoclonal antibodies are available in Japan [14], the oral gepants are not yet available.

title: Long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: an open-label extension of a phase 3 study
text: [Discussion] Rimegepant had a favorable safety profile in the current OLE phase and was well tolerated. As seen in other studies [24, 25, 33], AEs were mostly mild to moderate, most commonly upper respiratory tract infection-related, and rates of hepatic AEs, AEs leading to discontinuation and serious AEs were low. Clinical laboratory tests were mostly unremarkable, and no participants had aminotransferases >3x ULN concurrent with elevations in TBL >2x ULN, replicating the lack of drug-induced liver injury as was confirmed in previous long-term studies with rimegepant [22, 24, 25, 33].

title: Feasibility of a school-based peer-led high-intensity interval training intervention: the Young Fitness Leaders project
text: [abstract] While school-based high-intensity interval training (HIIT) has demonstrated efficacy for improving adolescents’ physical and mental health, interventions have largely been researcher-led, which limits scalability. This could be resolved via peer-led programmes, whereby older pupils (i.e., peer-leaders) deliver HIIT to younger pupils (i.e., peer-recipients). We aimed to explore the feasibility of a school-based peer-led HIIT intervention.

Five Year 12–13 pupils (aged 17.3 ± 0.4 years) were recruited as peer-leaders and received training on school-based HIIT based on boxing and whole-body exercises. Peer-leaders then delivered twice weekly HIIT sessions during morning tutor time. Primary outcomes were recruitment, retention, attendance and acceptability (explored in post-intervention focus groups with peer-recipients, peer-leaders and teachers)
