text: [Discussion] The main limitations of this study include its small sample size, which is partly attributable to the current paucity of real-world data for patients with RVO-associated ME [20]. While stratification into CRVO and BRVO subgroups reduced statistical power for functional comparisons, it represents a methodological strength of this study by allowing a differentiated assessment of treatment response across RVO subtypes with distinct natural histories.

title: Short-term real-world outcomes of switching to faricimab in anti-VEGF-refractory retinal vein occlusion: a prospective study
text: [Discussion] Further limitations include, the lack of a control group, which limits comparative interpretation. Emerging agents, such as aflibercept 8 mg, have demonstrated sustained disease control in a substantial proportion of patients with nAMD (PULSAR) or DME (PHOTON) through 96 weeks with extended treatment intervals [33, 34]. While not approved for RVO-associated ME during our study period, aflibercept 8 mg may still be a promising option for RVO-associated ME. The mean follow-up period of our study group was relatively short and varied among patients, reflecting the typical challenges of real-world clinical practice. Many patients in our cohort had experienced a substantial treatment burden, with a median of 23 prior anti-VEGF injections before switching to faricimab

title: Short-term real-world outcomes of switching to faricimab in anti-VEGF-refractory retinal vein occlusion: a prospective study
text: [Discussion] . Inconsistent follow-up was likely influenced by reduced adherence due to chronic treatment fatigue. However, the strength in this study is our treatment protocol - initiating faricimab in a TAE regimen with an initial single loading dose - which allowed early extension of treatment intervals. Importantly, our study is among the first to prospectively evaluate short-term outcomes in a well-defined cohort of anti-VEGF refractory patients with RVO, managed using a TAE approach without the conventional loading phase. This approach supports personalized treatment approach, but contributed to the variability in follow-up.

title: Short-term real-world outcomes of switching to faricimab in anti-VEGF-refractory retinal vein occlusion: a prospective study
text: [Discussion] In conclusion, our prospective real-world data indicate that faricimab, administered within a modified TAE regimen with a single-injection loading phase, provides significant short-term anatomical improvement and enables early treatment interval extension in anti-VEGF–refractory RVO-associated ME. These effects were consistent across CRVO and BRVO subgroups, while functional improvements showed favorable numerical trends without reaching statistical significance after stratification. Larger studies with longer follow-up are warranted to confirm these findings and to further clarify functional outcomes across RVO subtypes.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [abstract] Stem cell donation (SCD) is essential to expanding donor pools for hematopoietic transplantation, yet the knowledge and educational needs of medical students remain insufficiently characterized. This study assessed medical students’ knowledge, attitudes, and behaviours regarding stem cell donation.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [abstract] This cross-sectional study was conducted during the 2024–2025 academic year at the Faculty of Medicine, Gaziantep University (Turkey). A questionnaire assessed sociodemographic characteristics and SCD-related knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [abstract] A total of 378 students (aged 18–34 years; 60.1% female) participated. Overall, 2.1% reported having donated stem cells and 38.9% intended to donate. 19% had received prior SCD training. The mean knowledge score was 14.67 ± 5.92 out of 27 (54.3%). Knowledge was higher among clinical-phase than preclinical students (p < 0.001), among those who had received training (p = 0.005), and among those willing to receive training (p = 0.009). Reluctance to donate was most often attributed to anticipated pain (20.6%) and concerns about adverse effects (13.8%); 47.9% would donate only to family members if needed.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [abstract] Medical students demonstrated low-to-moderate knowledge with clear, teachable gaps. Integrating targeted early-phase modules and awareness activities into the curriculum may improve knowledge and willingness to donate, supporting donor recruitment efforts.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Introduction] Clinical research indicates that hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be an effective option in the management of more than 70 hematologic and immunologic disorders of varying etiology [1]. These treatments include the management of many life-threatening conditions such as leukemia, lymphoma, aplastic anemia, and inherited blood disorders [2]. Stem cell–based therapy is a modern treatment approach that utilizes the unique proliferative capacity of these cells and their ability to differentiate into various cell types, with the aim of regenerating damaged tissues or replacing them with new, healthy, and functional cells [3, 4].

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Introduction] According to the Worldwide Network for Blood and Marrow Transplantation (WBMT), approximately 1.5 million hematopoietic cell transplants were performed globally between 1957 and 2019. In 2018 alone, 93,105 procedures were reported worldwide, of which 48,680 were autologous and 44,425 were allogeneic transplants [5]. Current transplant volumes appear insufficient to meet global demand; it is estimated that 110,000–120,000 patients require transplantation each year [6]. In Turkey, the Turkish Stem Cell Coordination Center (TÜRKÖK) reported that, as of 2025, the number of active unrelated volunteer hematopoietic stem cell donor candidates reached 1,181,208, with 29,791 matches achieved [7].

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Introduction] These data underscore the vital importance of stem cell donation (SCD). Insufficient or incorrect public information—as well as fears and concerns related to the process—are among the key barriers to recruiting adequate numbers of donors [8]. Consequently, assessing the public’s knowledge, attitudes, and practices about stem cell donation is critical for expanding donor pools and improving access to treatment. Medical students, as future physicians, serve as reliable sources of information for patients and families regarding stem cell donation, play an important role in correcting misconceptions, and contribute to shaping public trust in donation systems through their professional authority

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Introduction] . Although physicians do not routinely counsel healthy donors, their recommendations are known to significantly influence health-related decisions such as vaccination, blood donation, and organ donation. Therefore, evaluating medical students’ knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding stem cell donation is essential both to inform future clinical practice and to train health professionals who can play an active role in public education. This study aimed to determine medical students’ knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors concerning stem cell donation.

text: [Study design] This was a cross-sectional, descriptive study. Data were collected from students who volunteered and provided informed consent using a 39-item questionnaire administered either online or through face-to-face interviews.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Participants] The study population comprised students enrolled at the Faculty of Medicine, Gaziantep University, Turkey. Sample size (n = 325) was computed using a single-proportion formula with 95% confidence (Z = 1.96), expected proportion p = 0.50, margin of error d = 0.05, and a design effect of 1.0 (allowing for ~ 10% non-response). title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Discussion] In this study, 2.1% of medical students reported having donated stem cells, while 38.9% stated an intention to donate in the future. Among Saudi medical students, 1.6% reported bone marrow donation and 2.9% reported peripheral blood stem cell donation [8]. Additionally, the proportion of individuals registered as potential bone marrow donors was reported to be 9% in Saudi Arabia and 52.3% in Poland [8, 11]. In Turkey, 89.1% of midwifery and nursing students stated they planned to become hematopoietic stem cell donors [12]. These findings indicate that actual stem cell donation rates among medical students remain low across countries despite substantially higher levels of intention or donor registration, highlighting a persistent gap between willingness and actual donation behavior.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Discussion] In our study, 24.6% of participants were aware of the eligibility criteria for stem cell donors. Similarly, only 8% of first-year medical and law students reported having knowledge about transplantation procedures [13], and 19.2% of health sciences students stated that they knew what stem cell donation entails [14]. Consistent with our findings, these studies indicate insufficient knowledge levels among students, and multiple reports from different regions of Turkey highlight gaps in educational curricula regarding stem cell donation and transplantation.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Discussion] In our sample, 19.0% of participants had received education on stem cell donation, whereas 67.2% expressed a desire to receive such education. Similarly, in Saudi Arabia, 14% of medical students reported having received education on stem cells, while 72.1% indicated a willingness to pursue advanced training [15]. In Poland, 55% of medical students expressed interest in attending university courses on this topic [11]. Thus, both our study and prior work show limited training exposure but high demand for education.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Discussion] The leading information source in our cohort was medical school education (80.4%), followed by the internet (32.8%) and social media (30.7%). In Jordan, physicians most often cited the internet (52.9%), books (52.1%), and lectures (47.6%) [16]. Among health sciences students in Turkey, 60.6% of those informed about stem-cell donation cited online sources, and 53.8% cited school-based sources [14]. Unlike several reports, our students predominantly referenced formal medical education, which may reflect curricular content, cultural context, and access to digital resources. Strengthening curricula, updating course content, and integrating high-quality online materials may simultaneously raise knowledge and motivation to donate.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Discussion] Our students’ mean knowledge score was 14.67 ± 5.92 (54.3%). In Saudi medical students, overall stem-cell knowledge of 38.8% has been reported [15]; another Saudi study found 37.4% knowledge regarding donor compatibility and 23.6% regarding the donation process [8]. In Jordan, physicians’ overall knowledge averaged 51.3% [16], whereas Polish medical students showed 64.9% knowledge regarding HSCT [11]. In China, 79% of practitioners and medical students had low or moderate knowledge [17]. Collectively, our findings and prior research indicate low-to-moderate knowledge levels, supporting the need for targeted educational programs integrated into curricula and complemented by campaigns that promote active student engagement, which may also improve donation rates.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Discussion] We found no sex-based difference in knowledge (p = 0.314). Prior studies have reported higher knowledge in male physicians (Jordan) [16] or female medical students (Poland) [11]. Discrepancies likely reflect cultural, demographic, and educational factors.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Discussion] Knowledge was significantly lower in preclinical than clinical students (p < 0.001), mirroring a Saudi study in which clinical-phase students outperformed preclinical peers (p < 0.001) [8]. Given the emphasis on basic sciences in preclinical years and patient care/case-based learning in clinical years, an increase in knowledge with training progression is expected. Additionally, in its fourth year (clinical phase), HSCT is formally introduced as part of hematology and oncology rotations. Our results reinforce that curricular progression supports knowledge gains in this domain. It should not be overlooked that the disproportionate representation of certain academic years may have affected the overall information estimates.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Discussion] Knowledge did not differ between students who had and had not previously donated (p = 0.085), consistent with reports from Saudi Arabia [8]. This suggests that donation behavior is not solely knowledge-driven; personal motivation, social awareness, process accessibility, and individual attitudes likely play important roles. Hence, efforts to increase donation should couple education with motivational messaging and process facilitators.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Discussion] Students who had received training scored higher than those without training (p = 0.005), and those willing to receive training scored higher than those unwilling (p = 0.009). Controlled educational interventions—e.g., among nursing students in Korea—have demonstrated significant knowledge gains post-training [18], as have course-based interventions among first-year medical and law students in Turkey [13]. These findings support integrating structured educational modules, seminars, and campaigns to elevate knowledge and foster positive attitudes toward donation.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Discussion] Regarding barriers, 20.6% of students did not want to donate because of anticipated pain, and 13.8% cited concerns about adverse health effects (e.g., anemia, musculoskeletal problems, infection). Comparable concerns were reported among Polish university students (pain 21.5%, complications 16.6%) [11] and Saudi medical students (long-term side effects 48.7%, procedural pain 38.7%) [8]. While reasons are broadly similar across settings, their prevalence varies, likely due to cultural and educational contexts. These data highlight the importance of myth-targeted education and awareness campaigns, with clear information on safety, pain management, and potential side effects to reduce anxiety and improve participation.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Discussion] In our study, 38.9% planned to donate, yet 47.9% would donate only to family members. In Poland, 98% of medical students would donate to a sibling or parent if needed [11]; in the United States, 72% of medical students were willing to donate to any patient, while 98% would donate for a family member [19]. In Saudi Arabia, 47.2% of the public were willing to donate to both relatives and non-relatives, 32.6% to relatives only, and 20.2% were unwilling [20]. Our findings align with this pattern: willingness is higher for family members, suggesting donation motivation is closely tied to emotional bonds. Campaigns emphasizing solidarity and altruism may help extend willingness beyond the family circle.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Discussion] In our study, 57.9% of students stated that stem cell donation is a social responsibility that everyone should fulfill, while 54.8% reported that providing financial compensation to stem cell donors could increase donation rates. In contrast, a study conducted in Poland reported that 72.9% of participants believed that stem cell donation should not be encouraged through financial incentives [11]. Similarly, in the study by Switzer et al. [21], the intention to donate hematopoietic stem cells among potential donors was found to be positively associated with individuals’ perceived sense of social responsibility toward society

text: [Discussion] . In Turkey, hematopoietic stem cell donation is voluntary and unpaid for healthy individuals aged 18–50 years, and direct medical costs are covered by the healthcare system. However, indirect costs related to the donation process, such as lost workdays, transportation, or childcare expenses, may not always be fully reimbursed. This may partly explain participants’ views that providing financial support to donors could increase donation rates. Therefore, perceptions of financial neutrality may influence attitudes toward donation.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study

The literature notes frequent confusion between blood group and HLA matching in donor eligibility [8, 14, 25]. Authoritative sources emphasize that allo-HSCT matching is HLA-based and that ABO incompatibility is generally clinically manageable [26]. Incorporating brief case-based modules highlighting “HLA ≠ blood group” may reduce such misconceptions.

text: [Discussion] Finally, 27.2% correctly recognized that bone marrow vs. peripheral blood transplantation carries a similar risk of acute GVHD but a lower risk of chronic GVHD with bone marrow, and 29.9% correctly noted that GVHD does not occur in autologous transplants. title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Limitations] This study has several limitations. First, its cross-sectional, single-institution design limits causal inference and generalizability beyond similar settings. Second, data were self-reported and may be influenced by selection and social desirability biases. Third, although the questionnaire was developed from prior literature, external validation was limited, and item-level misclassification is possible. Fourth, we used convenience sampling during a defined time window; nonresponse bias cannot be excluded. Fifth, convenience sampling limits generalizability beyond similar educational contexts. title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Conclusions] These findings indicate a clear need for targeted educational interventions to increase awareness and participation in stem-cell donation among medical students. We recommend strengthening medical curricula with content that explicitly covers stem-cell donation, hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, and donor eligibility/processes; complementing this with student-led awareness campaigns, seminars, and volunteer donor information activities. In addition, experiential learning—for example, field placements and structured collaboration with bone marrow donor centers/registries—may foster students’ active engagement in the donation pathway.

title: Are tomorrow’s doctors ready to donate? Insights into medical students’ knowledge and attitudes on stem cell donation: a cross-sectional study
text: [Conclusions] Enhancing the knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors of medical students—tomorrow’s health professionals—will not only help raise donation rates but also counter misconceptions and increase public awareness around stem-cell donation. In the longer term, such initiatives are expected to expand the donor pool and thereby increase the life-saving potential of transplantation in hematologic diseases.

title: Effects of noise isolation using noise-canceling headphones during lymphedema liposuction on postoperative pain in patients undergoing general anesthesia: a protocol for a randomized controlled trial
text: [abstract] This randomized controlled trial will include 90 patients undergoing elective lymph liposuction under general anesthesia. The intervention group will wear noise-canceling headphones throughout surgery, while the control subjects will receive standard care. Primary outcomes include postoperative pain scores (NRS) at 6, 12, and 24 h. Secondary outcomes comprise intraoperative nociceptive threshold index (PTI) monitored via multifunctional electroencephalography (EEG), preoperative/postoperative sleep quality (PSQI), and anxiety levels (HADS). In addition, mediation analysis will be conducted to examine noise exposure duration/intensity as predictors of pain outcomes.

text: [abstract] This randomized controlled trial will assess the efficacy and safety of noise-canceling headphones for reducing postoperative pain after lymph liposuction under general anesthesia. Since non-pharmacological interventions play critical roles in multimodal pain management, intraoperative noise reduction may effectively mitigate postoperative pain while avoiding pharmacological masking of ischemic limb symptoms. By integrating real-time neurophysiological monitoring of pain threshold dynamics, this trial explored how auditory environmental factors modulate nociceptive processing during anesthesia

text: [Background and rationale {6a}] Noise, defined as undesirable and unpleasant sound that disrupts normal auditory perception, constitutes a stochastic and unstable acoustic mixture [1]. Beyond auditory damage, noise exposure correlates with diverse non-auditory health problems, including annoyance [3], sleep disturbance [4], cardiovascular diseases [5, 6], and cognitive impairment in children [7]. Since the 1970 s, intraoperative noise has been recognized as the third major type of contaminant in modern surgical practice [8].

section: Explanation for the choice of comparators {6b}
text: [Explanation for the choice of comparators {6b}] Standard perioperative pain management will be applied to patients undergoing liposuction for lymphedema. Standardized anesthesia protocols will be administered intraoperatively. During surgical wound dressing, flurbiprofen axetil (50 mg IV) and palonosetron hydrochloride (0.25 mg IV) will be administered as standardized perioperative prophylaxis. Postoperative analgesic strategies allow the use of opioids, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), paracetamol, tramadol, and other adjunctive analgesics when clinically needed. The standard protocol was employed as a control to investigate whether intraoperative use of noise-canceling headphones for noise isolation can provide better postoperative analgesia, reduce the dose of analgesics, and promote postoperative recovery.

text: [Intervention description {11a}] Participants will undergo routine preoperative assessments. Next, informed consent will be obtained, and the detailed protocol will be explained 24 h before surgery. Baseline assessments comprise multimodal electroencephalographic (EEG) monitoring, mechanical pain pressure threshold (PPT) measurements, and psychometric assessments using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS).

title: Effects of noise isolation using noise-canceling headphones during lymphedema liposuction on postoperative pain in patients undergoing general anesthesia: a protocol for a randomized controlled trial
text: [Intervention description {11a}] Standard intraoperative monitoring encompassing electrocardiography (ECG), pulse oximetry, hemodynamic parameters (heart rate and blood pressure), and bispectral index (BIS) will be implemented upon admission to the operating room. A standardized anesthetic protocol will be administered in both groups as follows: rapid sequence induction with midazolam (0.04 mg/kg IV), sufentanil (0.3–0.5 µg/kg IV), propofol (2–2.5 mg/kg IV), and rocuronium (0.6 mg/kg IV), followed by maintenance therapy combining remifentanil infusion (0.1–0.2 µg/kg/min), inhaled sevoflurane (1 MAC), and propofol infusion (1–4 mg/kg/h) titrated to maintain BIS at 40–60 with hemodynamic stability (± 20% baseline). Rocuronium redosing will be administered based on surgical needs.

title: Effects of noise isolation using noise-canceling headphones during lymphedema liposuction on postoperative pain in patients undergoing general anesthesia: a protocol for a randomized controlled trial
text: [Intervention description {11a}] Participants in the intervention group will wear noise-attenuating Peltor™ X5A earmuffs (3 M™, Poland; 37 dB signal-to-noise reduction) from anesthetic induction until surgical closure to isolate ambient noise. In contrast, participants in the control group will receive no acoustic intervention. Continuous A-weighted sound pressure levels (dBA) will be recorded at 1 Hz intervals using AVOS-K8 dosimeters (Wuhan Zhongce Measurement Instrument Co., China). Subsequent analysis will be conducted to calculate the mean dBA intensity and percentage time exceeding 70 dB. The pain threshold index (PTi) will be continuously monitored intraoperatively using a multiparametric EEG monitor.

section: Statistical methods for primary and secondary outcomes {20a}
text: [Statistical methods for primary and secondary outcomes {20a}] Baseline characteristics of the two groups will be presented with appropriate descriptive statistics. For primary outcomes, between-group comparisons of resting and movement-evoked pain scores (continuous variables) will be conducted using independent samples t-tests in the presence of normal distribution (expressed as mean ± standard deviation) or Mann-Whitney U tests in the absence of normal distribution (reported as median with interquartile range). Maximum pain intensity across postoperative intervals will be evaluated through linear mixed-effects models incorporating time-stratified covariance structures, with Bonferroni-adjusted p-values for multiple comparisons.

section: Statistical methods for primary and secondary outcomes {20a}
text: [Statistical methods for primary and secondary outcomes {20a}] Secondary outcomes will be compared using the following tests: χ2 tests or Fisher’s exact tests for categorical analgesic requirements (presented as frequencies/percentages); paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for pre-post comparisons of multimodal EEG parameters (continuous data); and two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Greenhouse-Geisser correction for mechanical pain threshold trajectories. Correlation analyses will be conducted using Pearson’s (normal data) or Spearman’s coefficients (non-normal), while multivariable linear regression with stepwise variable selection and adjustment for baseline covariates (entry: p < 0.05; removal: p > 0.10) will be conducted to assess intervention effects. All analyses will be conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics 27 (α = 0.05)

text: [Discussion] Epidemiological studies have reported that 40–65% of patients experience moderate-to-severe postoperative pain worldwide [23]. Suboptimal postoperative analgesia increases the risk of surgical complications and delays early mobilization and recovery [24]. However, pharmacological approaches, particularly opioid analgesics, can lead to adverse effects, including urinary retention, pruritus, nausea, vomiting, postoperative ileus, dizziness, and cognitive dysfunction [18]. These limitations have encouraged the use of non-pharmacological, non-invasive analgesic modalities, such as acupuncture and educational video interventions [21, 25].

text: [Discussion] In the operating room, noise pollution caused by medical equipment affects both patients and healthcare providers. Previous studies have reported that the auditory cortex remains active under general anesthesia and processes auditory information [9]. Recent studies have suggested that intraoperative exposure to positive auditory stimuli (e.g., music, white noise) can mitigate postoperative pain, indicating that auditory perception persists during general anesthesia and modulates response to surgical trauma [12, 26]. Although environmental noise isolation has been proposed as a potential strategy for analgesia [27], existing studies have reported heterogeneous noise parameters (intensity: 45–85 dB; duration: 20–180 min), limiting their clinical generalizability

text: [Discussion] . Lymphatic liposuction surgery presents a unique model for investigating noise-related analgesia since powered liposuction devices generate consistent noise levels of nearly 70 dB. The clinical necessity to monitor ischemic pain in the operated limb restricts the postoperative administration of analgesics, thereby increasing the significance of non-pharmacological analgesia. This underscores the critical need for the present randomized controlled trial to investigate the effects of noise isolation on postoperative pain intensity, analgesic consumption, perioperative neurophysiological states, and anxiety/sleep disturbances.

title: Effects of noise isolation using noise-canceling headphones during lymphedema liposuction on postoperative pain in patients undergoing general anesthesia: a protocol for a randomized controlled trial
text: [Discussion] In conclusion, this study represents the first randomized double-blind controlled trial investigating the effect of active noise cancelation under standardized noise conditions (70 dB) on postoperative pain and cerebral function in patients undergoing liposuction. By assessing postoperative pain trajectories, analgesic consumption, perioperative neurophysiological states, and anxiety/sleep quality, this study aims to establish a novel paradigm for non-pharmacological pain management. If efficacious, auditory environmental modulation can serve as a safe and cost-effective adjuvant to conventional analgesic regimens.

title: Evaluation of large language models in emergency medicine scenarios: a comparative analysis of ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-pro, and DeepSeek-R1
text: [abstract] This study evaluated the performance of four LLMs—ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and DeepSeek-R1—using 11 representative emergency simulation cases encompassing six core domains: triage, assessment and diagnosis, treatment decision-making, post-treatment management and follow-up, psychosocial support, and prognosis and rehabilitation. The responses generated by each model to domain-specific clinical queries were independently evaluated by a panel of 20 emergency physicians, all with more than eight years of clinical experience. Evaluations were based on response quality, relevance, and applicability. Misleading or inappropriate outputs were re-prompted to assess the models’ self-correction capabilities.

title: Evaluation of large language models in emergency medicine scenarios: a comparative analysis of ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-pro, and DeepSeek-R1
text: [abstract] All models demonstrated acceptable inter-rater reliability (ICC > 0.60), with an overall ICC of 0.897 indicating high consistency. ChatGPT-4o and Gemini 2.0-Pro outperformed the others in overall quality and relevance. Notably, Gemini 2.0-Pro achieved the highest relevance and applicability scores in the psychosocial support domain (P < 0.001). DeepSeek-R1 also showed strong applicability in psychosocial tasks, surpassing ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-o3mini (P < 0.05). Triage emerged as the most error-prone domain across all models. Following re-prompting, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and DeepSeek-R1 showed significant improvements in applicability, particularly in triage, psychosocial support, and follow-up management.

text: [Design, classification, and evaluation of simulated clinical scenarios] Clinical simulation scenarios were constructed on basis of six key domains of emergency medicine: triage, assessment and diagnosis, treatment decision-making, post-treatment management and follow-up, psychosocial support, and prognosis and rehabilitation. These domains were operationally defined by the research team through literature synthesis and consultation with two experienced emergency medicine specialists, rather than adopted from a single predefined framework. One expert with extensive clinical experience in triage and initial assessment ensured that the scenarios accurately reflected the evaluation and preliminary diagnostic processes of emergency patients

text: [Evaluation methods] The responses of ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and DeepSeek-R1 were evaluated on basis of three core dimensions: quality, relevance, and applicability. Predefined evaluation criteria were applied, with each dimension carefully defined and supported by a corresponding scoring mechanism to ensure scientific rigour and consistency in the assessment. text: [Scoring method] To ensure the objectivity of the evaluation, a double-blind approach was employed. In this study, ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and Deepseek-R1 were anonymized and designated as AI1, AI2, AI3, and AI4, respectively. Expert raters were unaware of the actual identity of the models. A total of 20 experts were invited to independently evaluate the responses generated by AI1 through AI4. To address possible inter-rater variability, we employed a “majority consensus” approach to determine the final score: when more than 50% of the experts (at least 11 out of 20) assigned the same score to a given response, that score was adopted as the final score

text: [Scoring method] . For example, if 12 out of 20 experts assigned a score of 2 to a response from AI1, while 6 assigned a score of 3 and 2 assigned a score of 4, the final score was recorded as 2. If a clear consensus was not reached—defined as no single score receiving 11 or more expert ratings—this indicated a substantial divergence in opinions. In such cases, we adopted a stricter evaluation standard: the lowest score among all ratings was used as the final score, reflecting a conservative worst-case aggregation strategy commonly employed in safety-critical clinical assessments [18]. Detailed scoring criteria are provided in Supplementary Table 1.

text: [Statistical methods] All the statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS version 25.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY) and GraphPad Prism version 8.0.1 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA). Scoring consistency across expert raters was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Dunn’s post hoc test was employed to compare mean scores of overall accuracy, relevance, and applicability. For responses generated by the four AI models across six specific domains, the Mann–Whitney U test was used to detect statistically significant differences between domains. When multiple hypothesis tests were performed, P-values were adjusted using the Bonferroni correction method. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

text: [Inter-rater reliability among evaluators for each LLM] The analysis of inter-rater consistency revealed that the ICC for ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and Deepseek-R1 were 0.693, 0.769, 0.856, and 0.887, respectively—all exceeding the commonly accepted threshold of 0.60. text: [Discussion] With the expanding application of LLMs in the medical field, their role in clinical decision support is gradually evolving—from simple“text generators” to more advanced“cognitive assistants” [20]. This shift is particularly pronounced in emergency medicine, a clinical setting characterised by high information density and urgent decision-making requirements. While interest in LLMs within this domain is increasing, comprehensive and systematic evaluations of their specific capabilities, applicability boundaries, and associated risks in real-world clinical scenarios remain insufficient. In particular, there is a lack of in-depth research on the performance of emerging open-source models such as DeepSeek-R1 in the medical domain

text: [Discussion] . In particular, there is a lack of in-depth research on the performance of emerging open-source models such as DeepSeek-R1 in the medical domain. In this study, we compare the performance of DeepSeek-R1 in core emergency tasks alongside other mainstream models to provide empirical evidence for its potential clinical application.

title: Evaluation of large language models in emergency medicine scenarios: a comparative analysis of ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-pro, and DeepSeek-R1
text: [Discussion] Our results reveal marked performance heterogeneity among the evaluated models. ChatGPT-4o and Gemini 2.0-Pro demonstrated excellent performance across multiple task dimensions. Specifically, ChatGPT-4o exhibited high stability in structured information organization and reasoning, whereas Gemini 2.0-Pro excelled in emotional support and unstructured scenarios. Although DeepSeek-R1 showed slightly lower overall performance, it demonstrated potential in psychological support, indicating heterogeneity in task adaptability across models. These findings support the principle of “model-task matching,” which advocates for the selective application of LLMs on the basis of the specific characteristics of emergency tasks, rather than attempting to use a one-size-fits-all approach [21–23].

text: [Discussion] The text analysis further revealed key risk points in current model outputs, mainly related to misclassification in triage, insufficient identification of warning signs, and failure to effectively integrate professional guidelines. An in-depth analysis of answers labelled as “potentially misleading” or “factually incorrect” revealed that all four LLMs showed varying degrees of systematic bias across the six core emergency domains. In the triage domain, most models tended to misclassify level II–III patients as level I, suggesting an overemphasis on isolated chief complaints at the expense of holistic clinical reasoning [19]

Moreover, when clinical information exhibited progressive features, models generally lacked a sense of “dynamic assessment” and were inclined to make static judgments on the basis of initial inputs, making it difficult to simulate the clinical reasoning pattern of “continuous observation and repeated validation” used by clinicians. text: [Discussion] Further analysis showed that LLMs also had deficiencies in post-treatment management, psychological support, and prognosis and rehabilitation. For example, in the management and follow-up of elderly patients after treatment, Gemini 2.0-Pro failed to identify the potential risks associated with the use of opioid analgesics and overlooked the high sensitivity of elderly individuals to adverse drug effects, such as falls and delirium [24]. In the psychological support domain, ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-o3mini inadequately applied psychological assessment tools and ignored factors that are critical to patients’ psychological recovery, such as family support systems, psychological resilience, and experiential avoidance [25]

text: [Discussion] . Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, all evaluations were conducted in simulated emergency scenarios, which, while ensuring standardization and expert comparability, cannot fully capture the complexity and uncertainty of real clinical settings. Certain model characteristics, such as structured reasoning and verbosity, may therefore be advantaged under controlled simulation conditions compared with real-world emergency department workflows. Future work will therefore involve prospective validation using real-world clinical data. title: Low muscle density on chest computed tomography is associated with early death in non–small cell lung cancer
text: [abstract] This retrospective study included patients with NSCLC who underwent curative resection and postoperative chest CT between March 2020 and April 2021. Cross-sectional area and density of the trunk muscles were measured on CT at the level of the first lumbar vertebra. Cox proportional-hazards models were used to predict worse posttreatment survival risk at different follow-up time intervals adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was calculated to evaluate the diagnostic performance.

text: [abstract] Among 263 patients, 181 died after a median follow-up of 4.1 years. The measured muscle properties were higher in patients who did not die compared with those in patients who died. An increase of one standard deviation in L1 muscle density was associated with a 28% lower risk of death after the second year (HR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.56, 0.93; P = 0.01). The AUC of L1 muscle density for predicting death within the first year was 0.735.

text: [Introduction] Lung cancer was the leading cause of cancer death globally in 2022; with an estimated 1.8 million deaths, it accounted for 18.7% of all cancer-related deaths that year [1]. Non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most prevalent histological type of lung cancer. Major improvements in NSCLC treatment have been made owing to advances in targeted therapies and immunotherapies [2]. Despite medical advances, patients often experience alterations in body composition, which may be further exacerbated by the disease and treatments [3, 4]. This wasting condition is known as “cachexia,” and it occurs in 50% of patients with lung cancer [5–7].

title: Low muscle density on chest computed tomography is associated with early death in non–small cell lung cancer
text: [Introduction] Cancer cachexia is a metabolic syndrome that causes ongoing voluntary weight loss, loss of skeletal muscle mass, and decreased muscle strength. It is associated with reduced physical function, poor treatment tolerability, and increased risk of death [7, 8]. Sarcopenia is a sign of cancer-induced cachexia in patients, and it refers to the presence of skeletal muscle depletion [8]. Recently, a meta-analysis reported that patients with sarcopenia have a 1.57-fold higher risk of death and poor overall survival [9, 10]. In addition, patients with sarcopenia exhibit twofold higher risk of death within 30 days after surgery [11]

With the increasing number of lung cancer surgeries, the loss of skeletal muscle has been regarded as an important postoperative prognostic factor beyond tumor-related characteristics [4, 12]. Although considered a well-established indicator of cachexia, weight loss cannot represent all aspects of cachexia and cannot discriminate between fat and muscle mass loss [8]. Thus, comprehensive assessment of skeletal muscle depletion is also needed, and diagnostic tools for cachexia should not only depend on body weight.

text: [Introduction] Skeletal muscle depletion in patients with cancer is related to both the shrinkage of mass and the decrease in density, the latter of which is characterized by myosteatosis resulting from inter- and intra-muscular fat deposition [4, 13]. Thus, muscle quality may better capture risk factors than the simple quantification of muscle mass. Accurate imaging techniques, such as computed tomography (CT), which are also performed for cancer diagnosis and follow-up, provide unique advantages for the assessment of the mass and density of skeletal muscles [14, 15]. While the level of the third lumbar vertebra is not included in chest CT, the level of the first lumbar vertebral body (L1) is included, and it has been investigated as an alternative level for muscle assessment [16].

text: [Assessment of trunk muscle properties] The cross-sectional area (cm2) and density (HU) of trunk muscles were measured on a single axial slice at the level of L1 (Fig. 2). Manual delineation of muscle boundaries was carried out with the “pencil” tool to outline muscle contours. Then, the two-dimensional/three-dimensional segmentation module was applied to semiautomatically select skeletal muscle regions within the predefined HU intensity thresholds (− 30 to 150 HU). The trunk muscle index (cm2/m2) was derived by dividing the trunk muscle area by the height squared.

text: [Discussion] In this study, we evaluated the diagnostic performance of trunk muscle properties for predicting worse posttreatment survival at different follow-up time intervals in patients with NSCLC. Our study demonstrated high diagnostic performance of L1 muscle density for the assessment of worse survival. There was a positive association between L1 muscle density and improved overall survival. No associations between the trunk muscle index and survival or trunk muscle area and survival were observed. In addition, patients with high L1 muscle density were more likely to have a lower risk of death within the first year. These findings suggest that low L1 muscle density is a poor prognostic factor for posttreatment survival, especially within the first year.

text: [Discussion] We found that low muscle density was associated with death, whereas an increase in L1 muscle density was associated with a decreased risk of early death. The receiver operating characteristic curves further confirmed a stronger discriminative power for mortality risk with the inclusion of L1 muscle density than either. Statistical comparisons confirmed that L1 muscle density exhibited superior diagnostic performance for predicting early death, with significant differences in AUC values compared to other muscle properties after adjustment for multiple testing. The superior predictive value of muscle density over muscle area or index can be mechanistically explained by its direct reflection of muscle quality, specifically the presence of myosteatosis

text: [Discussion] . These results are in line with previous studies, emphasizing the critical role of L1 muscle density in cancer [13, 19–21]. Xiao et al. found that low skeletal muscle density was associated with a substantially higher 30-day mortality risk [20]. According to Sjøblom et al., reduced muscle density reflects high muscle fat content, which is associated with altered metabolism and systemic inflammatory response [21]. Myosteatosis is not merely a marker of volume loss but indicates a pathophysiological state characterized by lipid infiltration within muscle fibers. This condition is closely linked to metabolic dysfunction, including insulin resistance and impaired mitochondrial function, which can exacerbate cancer-associated cachexia and systemic inflammation

text: [Discussion] . Metabolically healthy subjects tend to show a higher proportion of trunk muscles with normal muscle density [19]. Systemic inflammatory response—an independent prognostic marker in cancer in general—is linked to cachexia and may reduce body defense and stimulate growth of neoplasia [22, 23]. The interplay between myosteatosis and a pro-inflammatory state (e.g., elevated cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-α) can create a vicious cycle, further promoting muscle wasting, metabolic dysregulation, and tumor progression, thereby explaining the strong association with early mortality. Furthermore, time-dependent effect of covariates is usually not evaluated, contributing to bias in survival analyses in a previous study [24]; yet, this effect faded within the second year in our study

In contrast, muscle density specifically captures the radiodensity of muscle tissue, which decreases with fat accumulation. Therefore, in our cohort, the qualitative deterioration of muscle (myosteatosis) appeared to be a more critical determinant of survival than the quantitative loss of muscle mass alone

text: [Discussion] In conclusion, our study indicates that low L1 muscle density is an important poor prognostic factor for worse survival and that it is associated with death after treatment, especially within the first year. This emphasizes the role of a time-dependent effect of L1 muscle density on survival in patients with NSCLC. title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Background] Older adults are at a higher risk of developing CVD than younger individuals [8]. Globally, the number of people aged 60 years and older is projected to increase from 1.1 billion in 2023 to over 1.4 billion by 2030 [9]. Age as a factor in CVD development may be related to the opportunity for exposure to the modifiable factors that affect some individuals more than others [10], with increased CVD risk for individuals from the age of 55 years [4]. Given the established burden of CVD in this age group, effective and innovative approaches to secondary prevention and management are of particular importance in those with existing CVD.

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Background] For older adults the issues of social isolation and loneliness are pertinent, and amplify the modifiable CVD risk factors [11]. Older adults are particularly vulnerable to social isolation and loneliness due to transitions that occur later in life, including decline in mobility and cognition, changes in living situations and loss of quality and quantity of social connections [12]. Additionally, social isolation and loneliness in the older adult population has been amplified by the Covid-19 pandemic and its requirement for social distancing and quarantine measures, further highlighting the need for effective strategies to reduce social isolation and loneliness in this population group [13]

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Background] . Loneliness is an experience where a person perceives both the quantity and quality of their social interactions to be insufficient and has been described as a disconnect between desired and true social connections [8, 14]. Social isolation is defined as having few social relationships or roles or infrequent social contact [15]. Social isolation and loneliness are two interconnected but distinct concepts, whereby a person may be socially isolated, but not lonely or vice versa [15]. Social support is often defined as the perceived or actual availability of social contact, and those considered to be socially isolated or lonely tend to have lower levels of social support [16, 17]. Improving social support has been shown to reduce levels of social isolation and loneliness [18].

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Background] Compelling evidence links social isolation and loneliness to poorer cardiovascular and mental health outcomes [19] as well as an increased risk of early mortality [20] For patients with existing CVD, there are a variety of interventions available to manage disease burden and reduce risk of further disease. Interventions aimed at enhancing psychosocial wellbeing in patients with existing CVD [21–24] included pharmacological (e.g. anti-depressants) and non-pharmacological strategies such as environmental enrichment [21], peer-support [22, 23] and/or caregiver-oriented support [24]

text: [Selection process] Duplicates were removed. Pairs of researchers (KC, A.Blassey, CL, IP, JVW, SH, A.Brown and LB) independently screened all titles and abstracts in Covidence, an online tool for systematic review screening and data extraction [28]. The data extraction table included author and title information, intervention description, measures, outcomes (separated into domains of CVD, quality of life, psychological, and social isolation), findings, and conclusions. A second researcher (KC, A.Blassey, IP, SH, A.Brown, CL or JVW) reviewed data extraction for each paper to ensure there was consistency in what was being extracted.

text: [Bias and quality assessment] Included RCTs were assessed by pairs of researchers using Version 2 of the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (ROB2) [29] to appraise the risk of bias in randomised studies. The ROB2 tool is structured into different domains of bias with focus on several aspects of the study, such as design, conduct and reporting. The stratification of papers into ‘low risk’, ‘some concerns’ and ‘high risk’ of bias was completed in accordance with the supplied algorithm.

CASP checklists involve a series of questions examining the method by which trials are created, analysed and interpreted. Each question on the CASP tool is answered with “Yes”, “No” or “Can’t tell” by the appraiser [30]. title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Cardiovascular disease outcomes] Five studies reported on CVD outcomes [37, 38, 40–42, 44], of which, three reported changes from baseline [40] (see Tables 3 and 4). Cardiovascular disease outcomes included dyspnoea, fatigue, 6-minute walking tests (6MWT), cholesterol panels, time to readmission for cardiovascular causes/death from cardiovascular causes and systolic blood pressure. One study reported on dyspnoea, fatigue, and 6MWT [37, 42], another study reported on cholesterol panels [38], two studies reported on time to re-hospitalisation [40, 41] and one study reported on systolic blood pressure [44]. Hui (2006 and 2009) reported significant improvements in dyspnoea, fatigue and 6MWT. Kreikebaum et al. (2011) evaluated CVD outcomes using cholesterol panels taken throughout the duration of the intervention [38]

text: [Risk of bias] . Riegel et al. (2004) was also assessed to have a high-risk score for concerns in multiple domains [41]. Firstly, there were baseline differences in the intervention groups that suggested a problem with the randomisation process itself. Secondly, there was no explicit confirmation of blinding of participants in the trial. Thirdly, there was non-adherence to the assigned intervention that potentially affected participants’ outcomes. Lastly, there were inconsistencies in the data available for all randomised participants; 88 were randomised, 58 had data for self-care and 57 had data for social support. This missing data has a possibility of confounding the true value of the other data presented.

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Discussion] This systematic review of non pharmacological interventions targeting loneliness, social isolation and/or social support for older adults with CVD indicates that most types of interventions improved psychosocial wellbeing outcomes. However, changes in CVD outcomes could not be attributed to interventions that were focused on enhanced social support as these also included other lifestyle components (such as exercise). Programs focusing on group activities, incorporating exercise and education, were superior to or as effective as routine care in improving social support, QOL and psychological outcomes [36–41, 43, 47]

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Discussion] . Group messaging [36] was also found to be effective at improving social support and QOL, and peer-mentor programs [35, 41] produced similar outcomes to usual care across all domains. This review noted the impact of face-to-face group-based interventions on improving loneliness and social isolation in older patients with CVD. Studies with face-to-face interventions [37–40, 42, 43, 46] had statistically significant improvements in most outcomes assessed. Studies that used non-face-to-face interventions, including phone calls and online WeChat accounts, reported varied levels of effectiveness [35, 36, 41]. Hu et al. (2022) utilised a tailored discharge plan and online WeChat account to facilitate information and programs to patients [36]

text: [Discussion] . Hu et al. (2022) utilised a tailored discharge plan and online WeChat account to facilitate information and programs to patients [36]. Similar to the results reported in the Clayton 2019 review noting a positive change with use of a peer support app, Hu et al. (2022) reported significant improvements in both social and QOL outcomes [24]. Whilst the impact of the WeChat account on psychological and CVD outcomes was not assessed, this suggests that the use of online interventions to address social support issues in the future would be worthwhile. Multiple prior studies found no consequential improvement in social support with the use of a phone call-based intervention [24, 47, 48]. Comparably, Colella et al. (2018) and Riegel et al

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Discussion] . Comparably, Colella et al. (2018) and Riegel et al. (2004) both had phone calls as a component of their program however observed no positive change. The lack of improvement in these studies may be attributed to the overall type of intervention being peer support-based and may not solely be placed on the telephone communication aspect. While face-to-face group-based interventions show promise clinically, the critical appraisal of these papers indicated some areas of concern (particularly related to the blinding of participants and researchers). Future research into such interventions using robust methods is warranted.

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Discussion] Studies with group-based education and exercise programs demonstrated impact on both social and CVD outcomes as well as QOL and psychological outcomes [37, 38, 42, 46]. Notably, this contrasts the outcomes of the review by Clayton (2019) who reported that cardiac rehabilitation programs (CRP), containing similar elements, had no positive effect on social support. This difference in findings may be due to the CRPs focusing on individual development supported by a facilitator in a group, whereas studies in this current systematic review utilised the group environment as a component of their intervention. A decline in adherence to health behaviours following the conclusion of CRPs was noted by Clayton’s (2019) review

text: [Discussion] . A decline in adherence to health behaviours following the conclusion of CRPs was noted by Clayton’s (2019) review. This raises concerns regarding the long-term effectiveness of interventions described in this current systematic review, as effectiveness post-intervention was not assessed in many of the studies. Further research regarding the long-term impact is needed.

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Discussion] The two studies that demonstrated improvements in CVD outcomes, Hui et al. (2006 & 2009) and Kreikebaum et al. (2011), both utilised interventions that incorporated exercise, education, and encouraged a better dietary intake. Interventions involving exercise, education and dietary change have established evidence that demonstrates their effectiveness in the secondary prevention of CVD and they have been incorporated into standard cardiac rehabilitation practice [49]. Hence it would not be appropriate to attribute the improvement in CVD to solely the social aspects of these interventions. This is further supported by a lack of statistically significant changes reported by the remaining studies that did not include an exercise-based intervention

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Discussion] . The role of social aspects of these interventions cannot be clearly attributed to the resulting outcomes as papers did not report accounting for other confounders in their design or analysis. Hui et al. (2006 & 2009) and Yeh et al. (2016) both included qualitative aspects to their study; their key themes reported that the social aspect of these studies encouraged patient participation in the primarily exercise-based interventions.

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Discussion] In line with findings reported by the Clayton review (2019), none of the peer support interventions included in this review demonstrated a statistically significant increase in social support. Given this, peer mentor programs alone are unlikely to be beneficial in increasing social support in patients with CVD. It should be noted, however, Riegel et al. (2004) demonstrated statistically significant increases in readmission for heart failure and health care utilisation which the authors attributed to increased patient understanding of their disease. As the study did not measure patient understanding of their disease in its measures, further research with appropriate measures would be required to give further insights.

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Discussion] This review had several strengths in its methodology and approach. The review had a well-defined and specific research question that focused on assessing the impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness in older adults with CVD. The search strategy used in this review was thorough, as it involved searching across four different databases. To minimise errors in the search terms and enhance accuracy, the researchers sought assistance from an experienced librarian with expertise in academic searching. This collaboration helped refine the search process and reduce the risk of missing relevant studies

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Discussion] . This collaboration helped refine the search process and reduce the risk of missing relevant studies. The researchers employed recognized checklists such as CASP, MMAT, and ROB2 to assess the quality of the included papers, and TiDier and RE-AIM to assess reporting and reproducibility of interventions [29–32]. These checklists provided structured frameworks for evaluating various aspects of the research, including methodological transparency, study quality, and potential biases. Lastly, the involvement of multiple reviewers in screening, conflict resolution, data extraction, and quality assessment ensured reliability and consistency throughout the study.

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Discussion] Several limitations should be acknowledged in this review. There were challenges related to the lack of standardized measures for social support and difficulties in accurately measuring social support, as evidenced by Riegel’s work [41]. As a result, there was insufficient data to answer the research questions related to effectiveness categorically by means of a meta-analysis. Another limitation stems from the lack of complete data in some studies, as not all outcomes were assessed uniformly across all included studies. Similarly, the heterogeneity of the CVD conditions reported in each study and the severity of these limits the ability to make categorical recommendations

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Discussion] . The application of the ROB2 tool revealed that a considerable proportion of included studies exhibited a moderate to high risk of bias, which could potentially compromise the overall validity and reliability of the study’s findings [29]. However, this bias risk could be mostly attributed to an inability to blind, due to the nature of the interventions in these studies.

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Discussion] To examine the potential impact of this review’s findings on future practice, it is important to first explore the nature of current guidelines and compare them to the studies included in this systematic review. As reported by the Australian Cardiovascular Health and Rehabilitation Association [49] and the Australian Heart Foundation [50], there are certain components and domains that need to be addressed in cardiac rehabilitation. These are classically defined as; referral and access to services, assessment and short-term monitoring, recovery and long-term maintenance, lifestyle and behaviour modification, medication adherence, developing heart health knowledge, and psychosocial wellbeing

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Discussion] . While all domains typically have strict guidelines outlining how cardiovascular outcomes can be improved, often psychosocial wellbeing is approached in a vague manner. The Australian Heart Foundation states that while depression screening does not directly lead to improved outcomes in populations with CVD, it has been shown that patients with depression and CVD, have worse outcomes overall [51]. This further outlines the need for a more direct approach to interventions that target social isolation and psychosocial wellbeing of patients with CVD. The outcomes measured varied between studies ranging from minimally to substantially statistically significant

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Discussion] . The outcomes measured varied between studies ranging from minimally to substantially statistically significant. Hence, it would be useful to focus on the interventions provided by the five studies with positive outcomes in terms of applications to older CVD patients in the community. These interventions included group-based exercise and education, and group messaging programs. However, while these interventions all demonstrated a positive effect on participant outcomes, the papers yielded some limitations; namely recruitment of populations that may not have completely represented the wider community of CVD sufferers

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Discussion] . As a result, some papers had recruitment bias as it may have been possible that the participants were a subset of highly motivated individuals that were more inclined to pursue novel and social-focussed interventions. Hence, further research is required for the judicious implementation of social support interventions for older adults with CVD, with a focus on a wider range of individuals from all facets of society, to ensure an unbiased approach to improving patient outcomes.

title: Impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness for older adults with cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
text: [Conclusion] This systematic review identified that face-to-face group-based interventions with exercise components may provide a basis for reducing loneliness and social isolation among older adults with CVD. Improvements were noted across social support, psychological wellbeing and quality of life. While improvements in physical measures were also noted in a small group of studies, these may not be attributed to enhanced social support, as interventions included a variety of lifestyle components, including exercise. Due to the limited number of high quality studies and heterogeneity of outcome measures, results do need to be interpreted with caution, highlighting the need for further research.

title: Unlocking the potential of EphA2 with precision-guided cancer therapy: bicycle drug conjugates
text: [abstract] Therapeutic advances have improved cancer survival outcomes for an increasing number of patients, but novel approaches are still urgently needed for patients who cannot tolerate, or do not respond to current treatments. Erythropoietin-producing hepatocellular receptor A2 (EphA2) is highly expressed in a variety of solid tumors, which is associated with poor prognosis, especially in tumors considered difficult-to-treat, such as pancreatic and head and neck cancer.

title: Unlocking the potential of EphA2 with precision-guided cancer therapy: bicycle drug conjugates
text: [abstract] EphA2 has emerged as a promising therapeutic target for the treatment of solid tumors; however, efficacy and safety issues have halted clinical development of previous EphA2-targeting agents including MEDI-547, DS-8895a, MM-310, and dasatinib. Despite these setbacks, interest in targeting EphA2 in solid tumors remains, with ongoing development of investigational therapies such as antibodies, antibody drug conjugates, EphA2 antagonists, peptide drug conjugates, bicyclic peptide drug conjugates, and tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Among these, BT5528, a Bicycle® Drug Conjugate (BDC), has shown an emerging differentiated safety profile, in contrast to prior EphA2-targeting agents, and promising antitumor activity in patients with advanced solid tumors

title: Unlocking the potential of EphA2 with precision-guided cancer therapy: bicycle drug conjugates
text: [abstract] . BT5528 comprises an EphA2-targeting bicyclic (Bicycle) peptide, linked to the cytotoxin monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE) via a valine-citrulline cleavable linker. The high specificity of BT5528 to EphA2, combined with its high affinity, enables precision-guided delivery of MMAE, while its peptidic nature results in rapid distribution and retention of MMAE within the tumor, limited systemic exposure, and liver-sparing renal elimination.

title: Unlocking the potential of EphA2 with precision-guided cancer therapy: bicycle drug conjugates
text: [abstract] The preclinical and emerging clinical data for BT5528 suggest that novel approaches to targeting EphA2 can achieve efficacy without the safety issues that plagued earlier agents. Here, we review EphA2 as a target and the historical and current clinical development of EphA2-targeting therapeutic agents.

title: Unlocking the potential of EphA2 with precision-guided cancer therapy: bicycle drug conjugates
text: [Background] Despite significant therapeutic advances that have improved cancer survival outcomes for an increasing number of patients [1], novel approaches are still urgently needed for patients who cannot tolerate, or do not respond to current treatments, especially in tumors considered difficult to treat. Erythropoietin-producing hepatocellular receptor A2 (EphA2) is a member of the receptor tyrosine kinase family that is highly expressed in a variety of solid tumors and contributes to oncogenesis, tumor-associated angiogenesis, invasiveness, and metastasis [2–9]

title: Unlocking the potential of EphA2 with precision-guided cancer therapy: bicycle drug conjugates
text: [Background] . Although EphA2 has long been recognized as a promising therapeutic target, its full potential in solid-tumors has yet to be realized, largely due to efficacy and safety challenges encountered in early clinical trials for EphA2-targeting agents [10–13]. In this article we explore the novel next-generation agents that we believe are poised to unlock the potential of EphA2 using multiple precision-guided approaches.

title: Unlocking the potential of EphA2 with precision-guided cancer therapy: bicycle drug conjugates
section: EphA2: a high-value target in oncology
text: [EphA2: a high-value target in oncology] Erythropoietin-producing hepatocellular receptors are the largest group of receptor tyrosine kinases. EphA2 signaling has been shown to regulate cell proliferation, survival, and migration via activation of the AKT-mTORC1 and RAS-ERK oncogenic pathways and the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway [14–17]. EphA2 exhibits diverse biological functions [18], and while typically expressed at low levels in healthy tissues [19], immunohistochemistry studies of clinical tumor samples and preclinical cell lines have demonstrated that EphA2 is highly expressed in a variety of tumor types, with high EphA2 expression in clinical samples from bladder, brain, breast, head and neck, lung, prostate and pancreatic tumors [2–7, 20–34]

text: [EphA2: a high-value target in oncology] Substantial evidence indicates that high expression of EphA2 is significantly correlated with higher tumor grade, later stage, increased likelihood of metastasis, and worse prognosis across multiple solid tumors [2–9, 31, 34, 36–38]. For example, in a study from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database and the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) portal, a significant correlation between increasing pathological stage and EphA2 expression was reported among patients with PAAD; furthermore, those with high EphA2 expression had shorter overall survival and disease-free survival than those with low EphA2 expression [31]. Furthermore, immunohistochemical analysis of NSCLC tissue from patients revealed that high expression of EphA2 predicted disease relapse as well as the site of relapse [3]

Regarding metastasis, high EphA2 levels were associated with brain metastases in patients with NSCLC, whereas low EphA2 expression correlated with no relapse, or the subsequent development of contralateral lung metastasis [3]. A number of studies in breast cancer, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, colorectal carcinoma and HNSCC tissue suggest high EphA2 expression correlates closely with metastasis [4, 9, 38], providing further evidence for the role of EphA2 in tumor progression.

text: [MEDI-547 (MedImmune)] MEDI-547 is an antibody drug conjugate (ADC) comprising the EphA2-targeting monoclonal antibody (mAb) 1C1 conjugated to the cytotoxin maleimidocaproylmonomethyl auristatin phenylalanine (mcMMAF). In preclinical studies using nude mouse xenograft and rat syngeneic tumor models, MEDI-547 effectively inhibited the growth of EphA2-expressing tumors with no observable adverse effects in either model [39]. Similarly, MEDI-547 effectively inhibited endometrial cancer growth in mouse orthotopic xenograft tumor models without overt signs of toxicity, while also reducing metastatic spread [40].

title: Unlocking the potential of EphA2 with precision-guided cancer therapy: bicycle drug conjugates
text: [MEDI-547 (MedImmune)] Despite these promising preclinical findings, clotting abnormalities were reported in cynomolgus monkey, mouse, and rat models, and hematological toxicity was observed as a dose-limiting toxicity in human studies [50]. The first-in-human Phase 1 trial (NCT00796055) was terminated prior to enrollment of the second dose escalation cohort, due to bleeding and coagulation events in 5 of the 6 treated patients. As a result, further clinical investigation of MEDI-547 was discontinued [10, 50].

title: Unlocking the potential of EphA2 with precision-guided cancer therapy: bicycle drug conjugates
text: [DS-8895a (Daiichi Sankyo)] DS-8895a, an afucosylated anti-EphA2 mAb, demonstrated increased in vitro antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) and significantly inhibited tumor growth in EphA2-positive breast and gastric cancer xenograft mouse models [41]. In the first-in-human Phase 1 dose escalation/dose expansion study (NCT02004717), DS-8895a was generally well tolerated in patients with EphA2-positive esophageal and gastric cancers (dose expansion arm) when administered at 20 mg/kg. Infusion-related reactions were reported in 40% of patients, but these were low grade and considered manageable [11]. Despite evidence of enhanced ADCC activity, DS-8895a did not induce strong tumor shrinkage, and all enrolled patients ultimately discontinued the study [11]

title: Unlocking the potential of EphA2 with precision-guided cancer therapy: bicycle drug conjugates
text: [DS-8895a (Daiichi Sankyo)] . Subsequent investigation in a Phase 1 safety and bioimaging study of patients with advanced EphA2-positive cancers (NCT02252211) also failed to demonstrate adequate therapeutic efficacy of DS-8895a at 1 mg/kg and 3 mg/kg (as seen by 89Zr-DS-8895a imaging), likely due to low tumor uptake [42]. Biodistribution data from this trial were central in stopping further clinical development of DS-8895a; biodistribution was a secondary endpoint alongside tumor uptake [bioimaging] and pharmacokinetics [42].

title: Unlocking the potential of EphA2 with precision-guided cancer therapy: bicycle drug conjugates
text: [MM-310 (Merrimack Pharmaceuticals, Inc.)] MM-310 is a liposomal formulation of a docetaxel prodrug, conjugated to a high affinity single-chain variable fragment targeting EphA2, designed for sustained delivery of active drug to solid tumors [43, 44, 51]. Preclinical studies have demonstrated a strong correlation between EphA2 expression and the uptake or biodistribution of MM-310 [44, 45]. Multiple xenograft models have demonstrated that MM-310 has greater tumor penetration and overall antitumor activity compared to its non-targeted counterpart or to free docetaxel, while maintaining a favorable toxicity profile [7, 44]
