text: [NGS-based screening of phage display library clones] Through NGS analysis, phage display screening has evolved from a low-throughput, clone-by-clone validation process into a quantitative and comprehensive exploration of sequence–function relationships. This advancement enables the identification of rare, high-affinity, and developable antibody variants that would have been missed by conventional approaches, while also providing deeper insights into how sequence diversity governs binding specificity and functional performance.

title: Phage Display Technology: Design, Library Construction, and Panning Strategies for Antibody Development
section: AI-driven phage display library design and developability assessment
text: [AI-driven phage display library design and developability assessment] In recent years, considerable efforts have been devoted to designing antibody libraries in silico through artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning-based methodologies. Traditional Position-Specific Scoring Matrix (PSSM)-based design approaches are inherently limited by their treatment of each amino acid position as independent. However, the integration of language models with Bayesian optimization enables more sophisticated sequence space exploration by capturing inter-residue correlations and dependencies, facilitating the generation of scFv libraries that exhibit both improved binding affinity and greater sequence diversity (Li et al., 2023).

section: AI-driven phage display library design and developability assessment
text: [AI-driven phage display library design and developability assessment] Extending beyond binding optimization, a recent model integrates developability considerations directly into antibody library design. Trained on large-scale, high-quality antibody sequence datasets curated based on the physicochemical properties of marketed therapeutic antibodies, this model can generate novel and diverse sequences with medicine-like characteristics (Rajagopal et al., 2024). Antibodies produced through this AI-driven approach have demonstrated critical drug development properties, including high expression yields, enhanced thermal stability, minimal non-specific binding, and low propensity for self-aggregation

text: [AI-driven phage display library design and developability assessment] AI is also increasingly applied to evaluate and prioritize the developability of candidate sequences after they are generated. These early-stage assessments—covering attributes such as aggregation, solubility, and immunogenicity—represent a critical strategy for shortening development timelines and minimizing failure rates in downstream clinical trials. Given that traditional experimental approaches are costly and time-consuming, sequence-based AI prediction technologies have emerged as complementary tools.

text: [AI-driven phage display library design and developability assessment] Protein aggregation is a major factor that compromises the stability and safety of biopharmaceuticals. To predict aggregation propensity, a framework has been proposed that utilizes AlphaFold-predicted structures from protein sequences combined with molecular dynamics simulations (Knez et al., 2025). This methodology integrates local surface curvature with hydrophobicity mapping, enabling highly accurate predictions (r = 0.91) of protein aggregation rates at high concentrations using only simple linear machine learning models. Complementing this structural approach, the CamSol approach enables quantitative prediction of protein solubility across pH conditions based solely on sequence information (Oeller et al., 2023)

text: [AI-driven phage display library design and developability assessment] Similarly, Sweet-Jones and Martin (2025) developed a protein language model (PLM)-based triage pipeline for large-scale antibody candidates from phage display screening. Using AntiBERTy, an antibody-specific language model, candidate sequences were embedded and compared against distributions of clinically approved versus failed antibodies for early developability assessment. A linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier, a machine learning classifier that separates data into distinct groups, was trained on these datasets to determine whether new candidates resembled the approved or failed population, overcoming affinity-focused selection biases.

text: [CONCLUSIONS AND PERSPECTIVES] To date, most FDA-approved antibody therapeutics have been developed through animal immunization-based approaches, including hybridoma technology and transgenic animal systems. Animal-derived antibodies offer distinct advantages: they undergo natural affinity maturation in vivo, yielding antibodies with high binding affinity and specificity, while providing variable region sequences with pre-validated expression and stability profiles. Notably, the advent of humanization technologies and transgenic mouse platforms (e.g., XenoMouse, VelocImmune) has enabled the generation of fully human antibodies, establishing a robust track record of successful clinical translation and drug development.

title: Phage Display Technology: Design, Library Construction, and Panning Strategies for Antibody Development
text: [CONCLUSIONS AND PERSPECTIVES] In contrast, phage display technology enables direct in vitro selection of antibodies without animal immunization, offering rapid screening within several weeks at relatively lower costs. Importantly, this platform provides access to challenging targets that are unsuitable for or refractory to animal immunization, including toxic antigens, highly conserved proteins, and self-antigens. Building upon these advantages, phage display technology has emerged as a powerful in vitro platform for the efficient selection of antigen-specific antibodies, undergoing continuous advancement over the past three decades since its inception

text: [CONCLUSIONS AND PERSPECTIVES] . Extensive efforts have been directed toward improving library design by increasing diversity and expression efficiency while minimizing undesirable PTMs and sequence liabilities. These advances have contributed to the successful development and regulatory approval of 20 therapeutic antibodies to date.

text: [CONCLUSIONS AND PERSPECTIVES] Nevertheless, as an in vitro platform, phage display harbors several inherent limitations. First, the absence of in vivo affinity maturation may result in initially selected antibodies exhibiting relatively lower binding affinity or specificity. Second, antibodies selected under simplified in vitro conditions may display unpredictable developability characteristics—including solubility, aggregation propensity, viscosity, nonspecific binding, and immunogenicity—when exposed to the complex physiological environment. Additional challenges include library size constraints, discrepancies between prokaryotic and eukaryotic expression systems, and limitations in antigen presentation and structural integrity during panning. Finally, the bacteriophage-based nature of the platform necessitates rigorous control of trace contaminants, including residual phage proteins, bacterial endotoxins, and DNA fragments.

title: Phage Display Technology: Design, Library Construction, and Panning Strategies for Antibody Development
text: [CONCLUSIONS AND PERSPECTIVES] To address these limitations, various strategies have been actively pursued, including high-throughput screening, cell-based panning, structure-guided antibody engineering, and rational library design that balances sequence diversity with developability. Furthermore, NGS has enabled quantitative tracking of sequence evolution across panning rounds, facilitating the identification of rare, high-value clones that might otherwise be overlooked due to E. coli propagation bias, thereby yielding antibody candidates with superior binding and stability profiles.

title: Phage Display Technology: Design, Library Construction, and Panning Strategies for Antibody Development
text: [CONCLUSIONS AND PERSPECTIVES] Recently, AI and machine learning technologies have been increasingly integrated throughout the antibody discovery pipeline. When combined with NGS analysis, these computational approaches are being applied across multiple stages, including library design, biopanning process monitoring, and developability assessment of antibody candidates. Notably, AI-driven analysis enables precise selection of high-quality antibody candidates at early stages, thereby significantly reducing failure rates in clinical development and substantially enhancing the likelihood of regulatory approval.

title: Phage Display Technology: Design, Library Construction, and Panning Strategies for Antibody Development
text: [CONCLUSIONS AND PERSPECTIVES] Taken together, these technological advancements are progressively addressing the intrinsic limitations of phage display technology, positioning it as a pivotal platform for the development of next-generation, high-performance antibodies in the era of precision medicine.

text: [abstract] Cancer is one of the diseases with high incidence and mortality rates. As a result, many studies have led to the development of therapeutic agents such as immune checkpoint inhibitors. However, the research on cancer treatment is still essential because of problems including drug resistance, genetic variation among patients, and drug toxicity. To address these problems, several candidate chemicals, including phytochemicals, have been studied for cancer treatment. Phytochemicals exhibit a variety of biochemical and physiological functions in the body and have been studied as having lower toxicity than synthetic chemicals. These properties have led to research into their potential as anti-cancer agents as well as their therapeutic applications for a variety of other diseases

text: [abstract] . The structural diversity of phytochemicals leads to considerable variations in their mechanisms of action. Therefore, it is important to understand the mechanism of action of each phytochemical when studying phytochemicals. Tangeretin (TAN) is mainly extracted from citrus fruits and is characterized by the presence of a methyl group. The presence of a methyl group in TAN is thought to enhance its intracellular uptake and confer greater resistance to degradation compared with other phytochemicals. Previous studies on the use of TAN in cancer treatment have mainly focused on its ability to induce oxidative stress as the primary anti-cancer mechanism

Although various research and development efforts are conducted to treat cancer, cancer treatment remains challenging due to various problems, including immune evasion, autocrine action, and drug resistance of cancer cells. Immune evasion of cancer cells is mainly activated by immune checkpoint proteins (ICPs), such as programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) and programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), and has been targeted in various studies for cancer treatment (Wang et al., 2024)

text: [Lung cancer] In 2022, lung cancer was the most frequently diagnosed cancer globally and was the primary cause of cancer-related deaths (Inoue, 2024). Lung cancer is generally classified into two primary cancer types: non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small cell lung cancer (SCLC). NSCLC, which grows and spreads slowly compared to SCLC, is more common, with subtypes such as adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma. SCLC tends to grow and spread much faster than NSCLC. Due to this aggressive characteristic, SCLC is often diagnosed at an advanced metastatic stage (Li et al., 2024a; Taniguchi et al., 2024).

text: [Lung cancer] Excessive accumulation of reactive oxygen species induces oxidative stress, which can lead to cell death and inhibit cancer cell proliferation (Nakamura and Takada, 2021). To counteract this, cancer cells often activate the nuclear factor erythroid 2 related factor 2 (Nrf2) signaling pathway as a protective mechanism against oxidative damage (Zimta et al., 2019). TAN has been reported to exert anti-cancer effects in NSCLC A549 cells by suppressing the expression of Nrf2, a key regulator of antioxidant defense (Xie et al., 2022). Furthermore, Nrf2 upregulates the expression of P-glycoprotein (P-gp), a key protein involved in multidrug resistance. P-gp uses ATP to export anti-cancer drugs and other toxic substances from cells (Callaghan et al., 2014; Sadeghi et al., 2018)

Cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) is a key protein that binds to cyclin E to regulate the transition from G1 phase to S phase of the cell cycle (Zhang et al., 2022) and is regulated by the tumor suppressor protein p53, which is activated by various external stresses, including anti-cancer drugs (Rastogi et al., 2015)

text: [Esophageal squamous cancer] Anti-cancer effects of TAN were validated not only in vitro but also in an in vivo tumor model. text: [BIOAVAILABILITY AND METABOLISM OF TAN] TAN exhibits pronounced lipophilicity due to its multiple methoxy substitutions, a physicochemical property that markedly reduces its aqueous solubility and consequently limits its gastrointestinal absorption. In a pharmacokinetic study in rats, oral administration of TAN (50 mg/kg) yielded a Tmax of 340.0 ± 48.99 min and a Cmax of 0.87 ± 0.33 μg/mL, suggesting relatively slow absorption and limited systemic exposure following conventional oral dosing (Hung et al., 2018). These results indicate that a drug delivery system is needed to bring TAN into clinical application.

title: Molecular Mechanisms Underlying the Anti-Cancer Effects of Tangeretin, a Phytochemical from Citrus Extracts
text: [BIOAVAILABILITY AND METABOLISM OF TAN] TAN exhibits metabolic biotransformation in vivo, which substantially influences its systemic exposure and biological fate. The primary metabolic pathways of TAN include demethylation, demethoxylation, hydroxylation, and remethoxylation, followed by phase II conjugation reactions such as glucuronidation and sulfation. These metabolic reactions generate multiple structurally modified metabolites with altered physicochemical properties. Cytochrome P450 enzymes, particularly CYP1A1 and CYP1B1, play a central role in TAN metabolism in the liver and extrahepatic tissues, catalyzing hydroxylation and demethylation reactions that yield metabolites such as 5-demethyltangeretin (5-DT) and 4′-hydroxy tangeretin (4′-OH TAN)

section: Physiological and pathological contexts of hypoxia
text: [Physiological and pathological contexts of hypoxia] Oxygen concentration in peripheral tissues varies widely, ranging from approximately 0.1% to 8%, depending on the balance between vascular oxygen supply and cellular oxygen consumption. Profoundly hypoxic regions (0.1-1% O₂) are commonly observed in solid tumors as well as in specialized stem cell niches, indicating that hypoxia is not merely a pathological condition but also a physiologically relevant microenvironment (Mohyeldin et al., 2010; Sullivan et al., 2008). Within these contexts, hypoxia profoundly influences cellular fate decisions. In tumors hypoxic cancer cells frequently acquire resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, while stem cells exposed to low oxygen resist differentiation and preferentially maintain stemness

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Physiological and pathological contexts of hypoxia
text: [Physiological and pathological contexts of hypoxia] . Hypoxia supports a microenvironmental niche that favors quiescent survival under metabolic stress rather than directly inducing therapy-related dormancy. In this context, hypoxia-associated factors such as TGFβ2 and p27 contribute to the maintenance of quiescent survival within the hypoxic niche (Butturini et al., 2019). Although non-proliferative, these dormant cells remain viable after treatment and can persist for extended periods, ultimately serving as a reservoir for tumor recurrence. Thus, hypoxia not only compromises immediate therapeutic efficacy but also shapes long-term cellular trajectories that underlie cancer persistence and relapse (Triana-Martinez et al., 2020).

section: Hypoxia delays senescence and extends lifespan
text: [Hypoxia delays senescence and extends lifespan] Beyond cancer biology, hypoxic conditions have long been associated with delayed cellular senescence and lifespan extension across diverse organisms. When cultured under physiological oxygen levels (approximately 3%), mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) fail to undergo replicative senescence, whereas cells maintained under atmospheric oxygen (20-21%) accumulate substantially more DNA damage (Ezzati et al., 2012; Krivoruchko and Storey, 2010; Lutz et al., 2003; Otero-Albiol and Carnero, 2021; Parrinello et al., 2003; Rogers et al., 2023). Reduced oxygen tension similarly extends replicative lifespan in primary human lung fibroblast, primary human mesenchymal stem cell, and human natural killer cells (Leontieva et al., 2012; Lim et al., 2021; Tsai et al., 2011)

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Hypoxia delays senescence and extends lifespan
text: [Hypoxia delays senescence and extends lifespan] . The anti-senescent effects of hypoxia are conserved across species. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, hypoxia induced by limited aeration extends chronological lifespan, with even brief hypoxic exposure during early growth conferring long-term survival benefits (Bonawitz et al., 2007). In Caenorhabditis elegans, exposure to 0.5% oxygen during the L4 larval stage increases median lifespan in a manner dependent on hypoxia-responsive transcription (Leiser et al., 2013; Rogers and Mootha, 2025). The naked mole rat (Heterocephalus glaber), which inhabits crowded subterranean burrows with estimated oxygen levels of approximately 6%, exhibits an exceptionally long lifespan exceeding 30 years—nearly tenfold longer than that of common laboratory rats (Pamenter, 2022)

section: Hypoxia delays senescence and extends lifespan
text: [Hypoxia delays senescence and extends lifespan] . Likewise, human populations residing at high altitudes, such as those in Tibetan and Andean regions where ambient oxygen levels of approximately 11%, display increased longevity (Burtscher et al., 2025; Ezzati et al., 2012; Li et al., 2017; Wuren et al., 2014).

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Hypoxia delays senescence and extends lifespan
text: [Hypoxia delays senescence and extends lifespan] Direct experimental evidence that oxygen restriction, analogous to dietary restriction, can modulate mammalian aging comes from studies using the Ercc1Δ/− mouse model of accelerated aging (Rogers et al., 2023; Weeda et al., 1997). These mice harbor defects in nucleotide excision repair, leading to rapid accumulation of DNA damage, early onset of senescence-associated phenotypes, and a markedly shortened lifespan (Cagan et al., 2022; Lopez-Otin et al., 2013). Remarkably, exposure to continuous hypoxia (11% oxygen) beginning at 4 weeks of age extends lifespan by approximately 50% and delays neurological decline

section: Hypoxia delays senescence and extends lifespan
text: [Hypoxia delays senescence and extends lifespan] . Importantly, hypoxia does not significantly alter food intake or canonical markers of DNA damage and senescence, suggesting that oxygen restriction does not simply compensate for defective DNA repair but instead acts through downstream or parallel mechanisms (Rogers et al., 2023).

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
text: [O₂-SENSING EPIGENETIC REGULATORS UNDER HYPOXIA] Hypoxia influences a broad spectrum of cellular processes, including angiogenesis, erythropoiesis, glycolysis, tumor invasion, and metastasis, while simultaneously repressing differentiation, tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle activity, and cellular senescence (Lee et al., 2020; Semenza, 2012; Wicks and Semenza, 2022). Many of these hypoxia-driven responses are mediated by oxygen-sensitive regulators whose activities are directly constrained by oxygen availability. These include hypoxia-inducible transcription factors (HIFs) as well as a broader class of oxygen- and α-ketoglutarate (α-KG)–dependent dioxygenases that regulate histone, DNA, and RNA methylation (Fig

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Canonical oxygen sensing through HIF signaling
text: [Canonical oxygen sensing through HIF signaling] The best-characterized oxygen-sensing pathway involves activation of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF), a heterodimeric transcription factor composed of an oxygen-sensitive α subunit (HIF-1α or HIF-2α/EPAS1) and a constitutively expressed β subunit (HIF-1β/ARNT) (Ivan et al., 2001; Semenza, 2001; Wang et al., 1995). Under normoxic conditions, HIF-α is hydroxylated at conserved proline residues by prolyl hydroxylase domain proteins (PHDs), which require molecular oxygen and α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) as co-substrates. Hydroxylated HIF-α is recognized by the von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) E3 ubiquitin ligase and targeted for proteasomal degradation (Jaakkola et al., 2001)

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Canonical oxygen sensing through HIF signaling
text: [Canonical oxygen sensing through HIF signaling] . Hydroxylated HIF-α is recognized by the von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) E3 ubiquitin ligase and targeted for proteasomal degradation (Jaakkola et al., 2001). Hypoxia suppresses this hydroxylation, allowing HIF-α stabilization, heterodimerization with ARNT, and binding to hypoxia-responsive elements across hundreds of target genes (Fig. 2) (Lee et al., 2017).

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Canonical oxygen sensing through HIF signaling
text: [Canonical oxygen sensing through HIF signaling] HIF-α transcriptional activity is further regulated by asparagine hydroxylation mediated by factor inhibiting HIF (FIH), another oxygen- and α-KG–dependent dioxygenase (Mahon et al., 2001). Notably, FIH contains a Jumonji C (JmjC) domain, a motif later recognized as a defining feature of a large family of histone lysine demethylases. This shared catalytic architecture provided an early conceptual link between oxygen sensing and epigenetic regulation (Fig. 3) (Black et al., 2012).

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Oxygen-dependent histone demethylases as epigenetic sensors
text: [Oxygen-dependent histone demethylases as epigenetic sensors] Beyond HIF regulation, hypoxia directly impacts chromatin and epigenetic regulation through inhibition of oxygen-dependent demethylases. JmjC-domain–containing histone lysine demethylases (KDMs), as well as related dioxygenases that act on DNA (TET family) and RNA (ALKBH/FTO family), require molecular oxygen and α-KG for catalytic activity (Fig. 1, 3A, 3B) (Black et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2014). Although these enzymes share common co-substrates, their kinetic parameters, — particularly the Km values for oxygen and α-KG— differ substantially, rendering individual demethylases differentially sensitive to reduced oxygen availability (Table 1) (Chang et al., 2019; Diehl and Muir, 2020; Kooistra and Helin, 2012)

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Oxygen-dependent histone demethylases as epigenetic sensors
text: [Oxygen-dependent histone demethylases as epigenetic sensors] . To date, more than 20 JmjC-domain–containing KDMs have been identified, each with distinct substrate specificities and oxygen sensitivities. Under severe hypoxic conditions (typically <0.5% O₂), global levels of histone methylation increase, consistent with selective inhibition of oxygen-sensitive histone demethylase activities (Krieg et al., 2010; Laukka et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2013, 2017; Shi et al., 2004).

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Metabolic control of epigenetic regulation under hypoxia
text: [Metabolic control of epigenetic regulation under hypoxia] Histone modifications are dynamically regulated by three classes of proteins : writers, which deposit covalent marks; erasers, which remove them; and readers, which recognize modified histones and recruit transcriptional, replicative, repair or structural complexes (Hyun et al., 2017). Importantly, both writers and erasers depend on metabolic intermediates—such as S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), α-KG, reducing cofactors, and molecular oxygen—placing chromatin regulation at the intersection of metabolism and oxygen sensing (Chang et al., 2019; Diehl and Muir, 2020; Schvartzman et al., 2018). Hypoxia profoundly rewires cellular metabolism by promoting glycolysis and suppressing mitochondrial oxidative metabolism

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Metabolic control of epigenetic regulation under hypoxia
text: [Metabolic control of epigenetic regulation under hypoxia] . Hypoxia profoundly rewires cellular metabolism by promoting glycolysis and suppressing mitochondrial oxidative metabolism. This shift is driven by HIF-dependent induction of glycolytic enzymes and pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK), which inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase and limits acetyl-CoA production (Bell et al., 2007; Hamanaka et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2006). Hypoxia also enhances mitophagy via induction of BNIP3 and BNIP3L, facilitating the selective removal of damaged mitochondria (Bellot et al., 2009). Chronic hypoxia can reduce intracellular α-KG levels when glutamine- and glutamate-derived anaplerotic inputs are limited, and promotes the accumulation of L-2-hydroxyglutarate (L-2HG), an oncometabolite that competitively inhibits α-KG–dependent dioxygenases, including KDMs (Fig

section: Metabolic control of epigenetic regulation under hypoxia
text: [Metabolic control of epigenetic regulation under hypoxia] . 4) (Chang et al., 2019; Dang et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2011). By simultaneously rewiring metabolism and constraining oxygen-dependent epigenetic erasers, hypoxia promotes a hypermethylated chromatin landscape (Chowdhury et al., 2011; Intlekofer et al., 2015; Oldham et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2011).

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Transcriptional noise and loss of epigenetic constraint
text: [Transcriptional noise and loss of epigenetic constraint] Cellular senescence represents a stable cellular state characterized by irreversible cell-cycle arrest and progressive loss of cellular identity (Baker and Sedivy, 2013; Di Micco et al., 2006; Gorgoulis et al., 2019; Hernandez-Segura et al., 2018; Miwa et al., 2022; Moiseeva et al., 2009; Sen et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2016; Takasugi et al., 2023). Cellular identity is maintained by cell type–specific transcriptional programs, whose fidelity depends critically on epigenetic mechanisms that constrain chromatin accessibility and suppress inappropriate gene expression (Fig. 5)

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Transcriptional noise and loss of epigenetic constraint
text: [Transcriptional noise and loss of epigenetic constraint] . 5). Single-cell transcriptomic analyses of young and aged tissues have revealed that aging is accompanied by a marked increase in transcriptional variability at the level of individual cells (Enge et al., 2017; Goodell and Rando, 2015; Hong et al., 2023; Jia et al., 2023; Levy et al., 2020; Swisa et al., 2017; Xin et al., 2016). Landmark studies, including analyses of human pancreatic islet cells, demonstrated that aged cells exhibit elevated transcriptional noise and evidence of fate drift, indicating that aging proceeds as a stochastic and heterogeneous process rather than a uniform genetic program (Enge et al., 2017). Similar increases in transcriptional variability have also been reported across diverse tissues (Goodell and Rando, 2015; Hong et al., 2023)

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Transcriptional noise and loss of epigenetic constraint
text: [Transcriptional noise and loss of epigenetic constraint] At a mechanistic level, chromatin structure dictates the accessibility of promoters and regulatory elements, thereby shaping transcriptional output. (Klemm et al., 2019; Pollex et al., 2024; Uyehara and Apostolou, 2023). Combinatorial post-translational modifications of histones specify chromatin states and precisely constrain transcriptional programs. (Table 2) (Jenuwein and Allis, 2001; Millan-Zambrano et al., 2022; Su and Denu, 2016; Taverna et al., 2007; Tessarz et al., 2014)

section: Transcriptional noise and loss of epigenetic constraint
text: [Transcriptional noise and loss of epigenetic constraint] . (Table 2) (Jenuwein and Allis, 2001; Millan-Zambrano et al., 2022; Su and Denu, 2016; Taverna et al., 2007; Tessarz et al., 2014). Based on the diversity of histone modifications reported in the literature (Millan-Zambrano et al., 2022), epigenetic constraints are finely tuned by histone codes, which can theoretically generate up to ~1×10174 distinct combinatorial states on a single histone octamer, together with their corresponding reader proteins (Table 2).

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Transcriptional noise and loss of epigenetic constraint
text: [Transcriptional noise and loss of epigenetic constraint] During aging, the integrity of these histone code–based epigenetic constraints progressively weakens. As a consequence, increased transcriptional noise is not merely the result of random transcriptional errors but reflects an entropic drift arising from stochastic disorganization of histone modification patterns that collectively constitute the histone code across the genome (Fig. 5). A central unresolved question is why chromatin structure becomes progressively destabilized during aging, and whether specific environmental conditions—such as hypoxia—can reinforce epigenetic constraints to suppress transcriptional noise and stabilize chromatin architecture.

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
text: [Age-associated DNA methylation remodeling] In addition to transcriptional noise, aging is accompanied by highly reproducible changes in DNA methylation. Statistical analyses have identified specific CpG sites whose methylation status correlates strongly with chronological age, forming the basis of DNA methylation–based epigenetic clocks (Horvath, 2013; Maierhofer et al., 2017; Petkovich et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017). Although global DNA methylation levels generally decline with age, a defined subset of CpG sites consistently undergoes hyper- or hypomethylation across tissues and species. The methylation patterns at these age-associated CpG sites enable accurate prediction of biological age, which often diverges from chronological age (Unnikrishnan et al., 2019)

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
text: [Age-associated DNA methylation remodeling] . Defining how such ordered epigenetic patterns emerge and are maintained during aging remains a central challenge in aging biology.

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Oncogene-induced senescence and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci
text: [Oncogene-induced senescence and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci] Oncogene-induced senescence (OIS), triggered by enforced activation of oncogenes such as Ras, Raf, or Myc in primary cells, induces a rapid and stable senescent state through activation of the p53 and Rb tumor suppressor pathways (Baker and Sedivy, 2013; Di Micco et al., 2006). OIS is widely recognized as an intrinsic tumor-suppressive mechanism that constrains early tumorigenic progression (Wang et al., 2024). Although both replicative senescence and OIS culminate in irreversible cell-cycle arrest, they differ markedly in their effects on higher-order chromatin organization (Falk et al., 2019; Sen et al., 2016; Solovei et al., 2013). A defining cytological feature of OIS is large-scale spatial reorganization of heterochromatin

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Oncogene-induced senescence and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci
text: [Oncogene-induced senescence and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci] . A defining cytological feature of OIS is large-scale spatial reorganization of heterochromatin. In proliferating cells, heterochromatin is predominantly tethered to the nuclear periphery through interactions between lamins, HP1, and H3K9me3, whereas OIS cells frequently display redistribution of heterochromatic domains toward the nuclear interior (Fig. 5) (Chang et al., 2025). This reorganization, termed senescence-associated heterochromatin foci (SAHF), represents a striking and reproducible manifestation of senescence-associated chromatin remodeling.

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Oncogene-induced senescence and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci
text: [Oncogene-induced senescence and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci] Mechanistically, during OIS, reductions in both lamin B1 and H3K9me3 levels weaken lamina–heterochromatin interactions, facilitating detachment from the nuclear periphery (Sadaie et al., 2013). Polymer modeling and quantitative imaging analyses indicate that lamina detachment alone is insufficient to explain SAHF formation (Chiang et al., 2019; Sati et al., 2020). Instead, homotypic interactions among heterochromatic regions promote phase separation from euchromatin, enabling the emergence of discrete SAHF within the nuclear interior (Belaghzal et al., 2021; Falk et al., 2019)

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Oncogene-induced senescence and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci
text: [Oncogene-induced senescence and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci] . In addition to HP1–H3K9me3 interactions, other chromatin-associated factors, including H3K27me3-marked regions, HMGB family proteins, and DNMT1, contribute to intranuclear segregation of heterochromatin during OIS (Zirkel et al., 2018).

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Oncogene-induced senescence and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci
text: [Oncogene-induced senescence and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci] Population-based Hi-C studies, together with single-cell transcriptomic and imaging analyses, suggest that senescent cell populations exhibit substantial heterogeneity in chromatin organization, although direct single-cell Hi-C evidence in senescence remains limited. (Shaban and Gasser, 2025; Zirkel et al., 2018). Chromatin loops and compartmental segregation patterns vary substantially within senescent populations, indicating that oncogene-induced senescence is associated with a spectrum of chromatin states rather than a uniform architectural outcome

section: Oncogene-induced senescence and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci
text: [Oncogene-induced senescence and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci] . Consequently, senescence-associated chromatin reorganization, including SAHF, differentially alters nuclear architecture across individual cells, increasing the diversity of transcriptional states accessible to each cell and giving rise to the cell-to-cell heterogeneity and transcriptional variability observed during OIS (Fig. 5) (Olan et al., 2023).

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: Oncogene-induced senescence and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci
text: [Oncogene-induced senescence and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci] Beyond changes in histone modifications and nuclear architecture, OIS is also associated with proteolytic remodeling of chromatin (Chang et al., 2025). The lysosomal protease cathepsin L has been reported to translocate to the nucleus during senescence, where it cleaves histone N-terminal tails. This proteolytic processing introduces an additional layer of chromatin regulation that may further influence chromatin stability and higher-order organization during OIS (Table 2) (Duncan, 2025).

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: DNA damage, epigenetic disruption, and convergent senescence states
text: [DNA damage, epigenetic disruption, and convergent senescence states] Progeroid syndromes caused by inherited defects in diverse cellular systems including the nuclear lamina, mitochondrial function, and DNA repair pathways, converge on premature senescence and chromatin disorganization. Notably, diverse acquired cellular stresses can drive cells toward a remarkably similar senescence-associated state, underscoring convergence at the level of cellular state rather than a single linear initiating mechanism (Rieckher et al., 2021; Soto-Palma et al., 2022). Recently, in vivo evidence further supports the idea that aging phenotypes can arise from epigenetic disruption triggered by DNA damage

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: DNA damage, epigenetic disruption, and convergent senescence states
text: [DNA damage, epigenetic disruption, and convergent senescence states] . Recently, in vivo evidence further supports the idea that aging phenotypes can arise from epigenetic disruption triggered by DNA damage. Yang and colleagues demonstrated that inducible DNA double-strand breaks—referred to by the authors as ICE (Inducible Changes to the Epigenome)—are sufficient to accelerate biological aging in mice in a model designed to induce controlled DNA breaks with minimal detectable mutagenesis (Teefy and Benayoun, 2023; Yang et al., 2023b). This model provides compelling evidence that DNA double-strand breaks that primarily perturb the epigenome, even without overt cytotoxicity or loss of cellular function, can promote aging-associated phenotypes

section: DNA damage, epigenetic disruption, and convergent senescence states
text: [DNA damage, epigenetic disruption, and convergent senescence states] . Together, these findings support a state-centric model in which diverse insults converge on aging-associated phenotypes through perturbation of epigenetic constraints. How such perturbations are manifested at the level of epigenetic heterogeneity across individual cells remains to be determined.

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: DNA damage, epigenetic disruption, and convergent senescence states
text: [DNA damage, epigenetic disruption, and convergent senescence states] Unlike transcriptional regulation, which can be readily interrogated at defined genomic elements such as promoters and enhancers (Klemm et al., 2019), chromatin regulation in the context of DNA damage lacks fixed genomic coordinates. DNA lesions are transient, heterogeneous, and asynchronous across cell populations, rendering damage-associated histone modification signals difficult to capture using conventional genome-wide approaches such as ChIP-seq. Consequently, while histone modifications have been extensively mapped in transcriptional contexts, their roles in DNA repair and genome maintenance remain less systematically characterized (Soto-Palma et al., 2022)

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: DNA damage, epigenetic disruption, and convergent senescence states
text: [DNA damage, epigenetic disruption, and convergent senescence states] . This gap hinders efforts to integrate DNA damage–associated chromatin regulation into unified models of epigenetic aging and senescence. Nevertheless, despite the absence of system-level datasets, multiple lines of evidence indicate that histone lysine demethylases (KDMs) targeting H3K4, H3K36, H3K9, and H3K27 participate directly in DNA damage responses (Gong and Miller, 2019). Because these enzymes are oxygen- and α-KG–dependent, hypoxic conditions have the potential to modulate DNA repair–associated chromatin states by constraining KDM activity.

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS
text: [HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS] Oncogene-induced senescence (OIS) provides a powerful and experimentally tractable model for investigating histone methylation, nuclear lamina integrity, and higher-order chromatin organization during senescence. Induction of oncogenes for only 4-6 days is sufficient to elicit a robust senescent state, accompanied by canonical senescence markers, including SA-β-gal activity, senescence-associated secretory phenotypes (SASP), and induction of p16INK4a and p21CIP1. Importantly, OIS uniquely allows direct visualization of SAHF by microscopy, enabling direct assessment of large-scale chromatin reorganization during senescence onset (Chang et al., 2025).

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS
text: [HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS] Using top-down proteomic analyses, Chang et al. (2025) identified selective proteolytic cleavage of histones H3, H2B, and H4 during OIS, occurring at H3 A21/T22, H2B T19/K20, and H4 G11/K12, respectively (Table 2). In contrast, histone H2A remained intact, indicating a histone-specific cleavage process. These cleavage events were mediated by the lysosomal protease cathepsin L, revealing an additional and previously underappreciated layer of chromatin remodeling associated with senescence (Chang et al., 2025). The causal relationships among histone clipping, chromatin reorganization, and nuclear architecture during OIS have yet to be fully resolved

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS
text: [HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS] . The causal relationships among histone clipping, chromatin reorganization, and nuclear architecture during OIS have yet to be fully resolved. Notably, hypoxia suppresses histone clipping, SAHF formation, and nuclear lamina destabilization while preserving Rb and p53 pathway activity downstream of oncogene activation. Thus, hypoxia does not prevent OIS by blocking oncogene-induced cell-cycle arrest, but instead modulates chromatin-associated events that occur subsequent to senescence initiation.

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS
text: [HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS] Pharmacological inhibition of histone lysine demethylases (KDMs) using the pan-KDM inhibitor JIB-04 effectively blocks histone clipping, indicating that histone methylation status critically influences susceptibility to proteolytic processing. In vitro competitive enzyme kinetic assays further demonstrated that methylation at H3K23 and H3K18—residues flanking the cleavage site—reduces the susceptibility of histone H3 to cathepsin L, suggesting that methylation of cleavage-proximal residues directly protects histones from irreversible cleavage. One plausible mechanism is that H3K18/23 trimethylation facilitates the recruitment of reader proteins that shield histone H3 from cathepsin L access.

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS
text: [HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS] However, KDM inhibition alone is insufficient to prevent SAHF formation. While KDM inhibition does not prevent the OIS-associated reduction of nuclear lamins, hypoxia robustly preserves lamin integrity. These observations indicate that hypoxia exerts broader protective effects on nuclear architecture that extend beyond the maintenance of histone methylation. The nuclear envelope is mechanically supported by coordinated interactions among heterochromatin, nuclear lamina components, and the actin cytoskeleton (Ungricht and Kutay, 2017)

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS
text: [HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS] . Hypoxia is associated with enhanced perinuclear actin organization, suggesting that hypoxic potentiation of the cytoskeleton may contribute to the mechanical support and structural stability of nuclear architecture during senescence, although the mechanistic basis of this effect has yet to be fully elucidated (Stephens and Miroshnikova, 2024).

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS
text: [HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS] Histone clipping has been observed across diverse species and cellular contexts, including mouse intestinal villi, human monocytes, yeast sporulation, and neuronal differentiation of stem cells (Chang et al., 2025; Cheung et al., 2021; Duarte et al., 2014; Duncan, 2025; Duncan et al., 2008; Ferrari et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2023a) (Table 2). This rare but irreversible post-translational modification is typically associated with terminal differentiation or stable cell fate transitions, including oncogene-induced senescence (Corpet et al., 2014; O’Sullivan et al., 2010; Tagami et al., 2004)

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS
text: [HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS] . Unless counteracted by de novo histone synthesis, histone clipping represents a permanent alteration of chromatin structure, underscoring its potential significance in directing long-term cellular outcomes. Consistent with this notion, ChIP-seq analysis using an H3cs1 (H3 cleaved site 1)-specific antibody revealed enrichment of cleaved H3 at open chromatin regions and transcription start sites (TSS) of active genes in human monocytes (Cheung et al., 2021). Similarly, ATAC-seq analysis of OIS cells demonstrated preferential histone clipping within accessible euchromatin, rather than within condensed heterochromatin such as lamina-associated domains (LADs) (Chang et al., 2025)

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS
text: [HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS] . These findings raise the possibility that histone clipping occurs downstream of chromatin opening, rather than serving as its initiating event.

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS
text: [HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS] Together, these findings suggest that histone clipping selectively targets transcriptionally permissive chromatin and introduces irreversible chromatin alterations that constrain subsequent transcriptional plasticity whereas hypoxia limits this process by reinforcing histone methylation and overall chromatin stability, thereby preserving a chromatin state that remains amenable to dynamic histone modification in response to diverse signals.

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
section: HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS
text: [HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS] Collectively, these observations indicate that hypoxia suppresses aging and senescence not through a single dominant pathway, but by reshaping cellular environments toward low-damage, low-entropy states. Rather than reversing senescence programs, hypoxia limits the propagation of senescence-associated chromatin instability by modulating metabolism, redox balance, histone modification, and nuclear architecture. Through these coordinated effects, hypoxia slows the transition from transient stress responses to stable senescence-associated cellular states.

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
text: [HYPOXIC THERAPEUTICS] Ischemia, defined by an interruption of blood supply rather than reduced oxygen availability per se, has long been recognized as a potent trigger of cell death. In contrast, accumulating evidence that hypoxia can delay senescence and extend lifespan raises the possibility that hypoxia, or hypoxia-mimetic strategies, may be harnessed to modulate aging-associated cellular states and mitochondrial diseases in therapeutic contexts (Rogers and Mootha, 2025)

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
text: [HYPOXIC THERAPEUTICS] . Biochemical characterization of oxygen-sensing enzymes, including prolyl hydroxylase domain protein 2 (PHD2), factor inhibiting HIF-1 (FIH-1), KDM4 family histone demethylases (H3K9me3 demethylases), KDM5, and TET1, revealed Km values in the range of 30 to 250 µM, corresponding to oxygen concentrations near physiological levels in peripheral tissues (Table 1) (Chang et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2017; Mohyeldin et al., 2010). These findings suggest that basal levels of HIF-α activity and the methylated histones marks such as H3K9me3 are likely higher in vivo at around 3% oxygen than in standard cell culture conditions maintained at 20% oxygen

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
text: [HYPOXIC THERAPEUTICS] . In the setting of mitochondrial electron transport chain dysfunction, “unused” oxygen may accumulate to levels exceeding the Km values of oxygen-dependent enzymes. This can result in aberrant activation of PHDs, FIH, and KDMs, thereby suppressing HIF signaling and reducing levels of methylated histones and DNA. This observation raises the intriguing possibility that chronic continuous hypoxia (CCH) may restore the basal tone of hypoxia-sensing and epigenetic regulatory pathways in inherited or acquired mitochondrial disorders that are frequently observed in aged individuals (Fig. 3) (Table 1).

title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation
text: [HYPOXIC THERAPEUTICS] Consistent with this concept, preclinical studies have demonstrated that CCH at 10-11% oxygen confers substantial benefit in mouse models of mitochondrial disease, including Leigh syndrome (LS) (Jain et al., 2016) and Friedreich’s ataxia (Rogers and Mootha, 2025) all of which share impaired mitochondrial respiration. Paradoxically, CCH has also shown protective effects in mouse models of myocardial infarction and ischemic stroke (Nakada et al., 2017; Rogers and Mootha, 2025) echoing long-standing clinical observations of hypoxic preconditioning in ischemia–reperfusion injury, although the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood.

text: [Hypoxic conditioning: opportunities and limitations] Athletic training strategies such as “live high altitude (low-oxygen conditions), train low altitude,” in which individuals sleep in hypoxic tents with nitrogen-diluted air, are well established and commercially available (Wilber, 2007). An alternative strategy to reduce tissue oxygen tension is to increase the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen, thereby decreasing the pool of free, unbound oxygen. Drugs originally developed for sickle cell disease, including voxelotor (formerly GBT440) (Hutchaleelaha et al., 2019) and mitapivat, have been approved by the FDA based on this principle. text: [Hypoxic medicines] Collectively, these studies suggest that hypoxia represents a therapeutic strategy distinct from approaches that target individual molecular defects. By reducing oxygen availability, hypoxia reshapes the biochemical landscape sensed by oxygen-dependent enzymes and acts at the level of cellular state to restore epigenetic and metabolic balance in mitochondrial dysfunction and aging. Despite challenges for clinical translation, including safety and dosing, hypoxia-based interventions offer a compelling framework for reconsidering oxygen as a therapeutic variable in aging and age-associated disease.

text: [abstract] Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is increasingly recognized as a disorder with significant vascular involvement, with microvascular damage and thromboinflammation often preceding classical amyloid pathology by several years. Elevated levels of prothrombin and thrombin, along with aberrant platelet activation, have been reported in individuals with AD. We hypothesized that platelet hyperactivity in AD results from an exaggerated response to thrombin in the presence of elevated amyloid beta 1-40 (Aβ₁₋₄₀), a peptide that accumulates during the early stages of AD. text: [INTRODUCTION] A critical mediator of this vascular component is platelet activation (Zhang et al., 2013). Beyond their established roles in thrombosis and hemostasis, platelets actively participate in neuroinflammation and vascular endothelial interactions. Numerous studies have shown that Aβ₁₋₄₀ can induce platelet aggregation, upregulate procoagulant surface markers, and modulate platelet–endothelium adhesion. Mechanistically, Aβ₁₋₄₀ stimulates the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), including superoxide (O₂⁻) and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), primarily through activation of NADPH oxidase (NOX) (Donner et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2021). Among the NOX isoforms, NOX2 is abundantly expressed in platelets and constitutes a principal source of oxidative signaling during platelet activation

ROS contribute to the activation of integrin αIIbβ3, a critical receptor complex responsible for fibrinogen binding, platelet aggregation, and thrombus stabilization (Donner et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2021). text: [INTRODUCTION] Thrombin, a serine protease generated during the coagulation cascade, is among the most potent endogenous platelet activators. Acting via protease-activated receptors (PARs), thrombin initiates rapid integrin activation, cytoskeletal remodeling, and granule secretion. Elevated thrombin levels have been documented in conditions involving neuroinflammation, traumatic brain injury, and AD. Importantly, platelets from patients with AD demonstrate heightened responsiveness to thrombin, potentially reflecting a primed phenotype resulting from chronic exposure to circulating Aβ and oxidative stressors (Grammas et al., 2006; Gupta et al., 2005; Zipser et al., 2007)

title: Aβ₁₋₄₀ Enhances Platelet Sensitivity to Thrombin via NADPH Oxidase–ROS Signaling and Integrin αIIbβ3 Engagement
text: [INTRODUCTION] To address these gaps, we investigated whether Aβ₁₋₄₀ amplifies thrombin-induced platelet activation and explored the underlying molecular mechanisms. Specifically, we examined the roles of NOX-derived ROS and integrin αIIbβ3 activation using selective pharmacological inhibitors. We further evaluated downstream functional consequences, including cytoskeletal remodeling and adhesion to human brain microvascular endothelial cells (hBMECs). Through this mechanistic framework, we aim to elucidate how amyloid and coagulation pathways intersect to drive cerebrovascular inflammation in AD.

text: [Preparation of washed platelets] Human whole blood was collected from healthy volunteers following ethical approval by the Ajou University Ethics Committee (202211-HM-EX-001). Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) samples were also obtained from healthy donors through the Korean Red Cross Center. PRP was centrifuged at 1,000×g for 10 min at 23°C, avoiding disruption of the platelet pellet. The resulting pellet was washed twice with Tyrode buffer (pH 7.4) and resuspended to a final concentration of 2×10⁸ cells/mL for use in optical aggregometry, flow cytometry, ROS assays, immunoblotting, and adhesion studies.

text: [Platelet aggregation] Light transmission aggregometry was performed using a Chronolog aggregometer (Chrono-Log Corporation). PRP samples were preincubated with or without Aβ₁₋₄₀ for 5 min, followed by stimulation with thrombin at concentrations of 0.03, 0.05, 0.075, and 0.1 U/mL. Platelets were pretreated with Aβ₁₋₄₀ (0.1, 1, or 10 μg/mL), trolox (100 μM), VAS2870 (10 μM), or eptifibatide (50 μM) for 5 min before agonist addition. Aggregation was recorded at 37°C for 6 min. Additional measurements were performed using a 490D coagulometer (Chrono-Log Corporation) for 5 min at 37°C. Maximum aggregation within 8 min post-stimulation was recorded as mean ± SEM. The EC₅₀ was calculated from dose-response curves for each donor, and average EC₅₀ values were determined across donors.

text: [Platelet adhesion to fibrinogen] Glass-bottom dishes were coated with fibrinogen (10 μg/mL) at 37°C for 30 min. Following washing with BSA-containing buffer, CMFDA-labeled platelets (10 μM) were incubated on the coated surface at 37°C for 30 min. Non-adherent cells were removed by gentle washing with PBS. Images from randomly selected fields were acquired using a confocal microscope (Nikon, Japan). Adhesion was quantified by calculating the area occupied by adherent platelets as a percentage of the total imaged area. Experiments were repeated independently three to five times.

text: [Measurement of NADPH oxidase activity] NOX activity in intact platelets was measured using a lucigenin-enhanced chemiluminescence assay (Hur et al., 2025). Lucigenin reacts with superoxide anions to produce luminescence, which was quantified using a luminometer. The reaction mixture contained 1 mM EGTA and 5 μM lucigenin in phosphate buffer (pH 7.0). The reaction was initiated by adding 50 μM NADPH immediately prior to measurement. Luminescence was detected using a tabletop luminometer (BD Systems), and values were averaged per sample.

text: [Measurement of ROS] Intracellular ROS production was evaluated using a single-cell fluorescence assay with H₂DCFDA and DHE (Ji et al., 2021). To evaluate platelet–endothelial interactions, immunofluorescence microscopy was used to quantify platelet adhesion to hBMECs. In control samples, platelet adhesion was minimal; however, Aβ₁₋₄₀-potentiated thrombin treatment significantly increased platelet attachment to hBMECs (Fig. 6B). This effect was substantially suppressed by VAS2870, Trolox, and eptifibatide, suggesting that the combined action of Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin is mediated through ROS generation and integrin αIIbβ3 signaling, leading to platelet structural activation and increased cerebrovascular adhesion. These findings suggest that platelet-endothelial interactions could potentially contribute to AD-related vascular dysfunction.

text: [DISCUSSION] Physiological hemostasis is maintained by the coordinated actions of endothelial cells, coagulation factors, and platelets, which together form localized clots at sites of vascular injury (McRae, 2011; Scridon, 2022). Upon activation by stimuli such as collagen, thromboxane A₂ (TXA₂), adenosine diphosphate (ADP), and thrombin, platelets adhere to damaged endothelium and aggregate to form hemostatic plugs (Tomaiuolo et al., 2017). These processes are tightly regulated under normal conditions to prevent either hemorrhage or pathological thrombosis (McRae, 2011). However, dysregulation of these pathways can result in pathological platelet activation, contributing to vascular dysfunction and thrombotic complications (Koupenova et al., 2017; Massberg et al., 2003)

Circulating platelets from individuals with AD exhibit heightened reactivity and an increased propensity to form thrombi, a phenomenon correlated with elevated levels of Aβ peptides, particularly Aβ₁₋₄₀ (Stellos et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2018). title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [abstract] Arterial thrombosis remains a leading cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality despite widespread use of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin and P2Y12 inhibitors. Although these agents reduce ischemic events, their efficacy is counterbalanced by dose-dependent bleeding and their inability to distinguish pathological platelet activation from physiological hemostasis. Recent advances in platelet biology have shifted therapeutic development toward hemostasis-sparing antiplatelet strategies—approaches designed to selectively inhibit thrombosis while preserving baseline hemostatic function

Early-phase clinical and translational studies of such agents demonstrate antithrombotic efficacy with minimal impact on bleeding time, supporting their mechanistic selectivity. In parallel, contemporary clinical practice increasingly utilizes individualized risk assessment, platelet function testing, and genetic profiling to tailor treatment intensity

text: [INTRODUCTION] Arterial thrombosis remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. According to the World Health Organization, 19.8 million people died from cardiovascular disease (CVD) in 2022, accounting for approximately 32% of all global deaths, with nearly 85% attributable to myocardial infarction and stroke—canonical atherothrombotic events driven by platelet-rich arterial thrombosis. This burden is unevenly distributed, with more than three-quarters of CVD deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries, underscoring an urgent need for safer and more deployable antithrombotic strategies worldwide (World Health Organization, 2025)

Although DAPT has substantially reduced recurrent ischemic events, its clinical utility is constrained by the inevitable trade-off between antithrombotic efficacy and bleeding liability (Capodanno and Greco, 2023). Bleeding complications are associated with increased mortality and often necessitate early therapy discontinuation, undermining the net clinical benefit—particularly in high-bleeding-risk (HBR) populations such as the elderly, those with renal impairment, or patients with prior hemorrhagic events

The emerging objective is hemostasis-sparing antiplatelet therapy—that is, the selective inhibition of pathologic platelet activation and thrombus formation while preserving baseline hemostatic function. This concept centers on two interrelated mechanistic axes:

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Adhesion under arterial shear] Arterial thrombosis unfolds on a damaged or inflamed arterial wall under high shear. The initiating step is tethering/adhesion of circulating platelets to exposed collagen/vWF, followed by activation and aggregation into a platelet-rich thrombus (Rana et al., 2019). First, GPIb–IX–V on platelets catches multimeric vWF strings exposed on subendothelium; this shear-dependent bond allows rolling and translocation across the surface and positions platelets over collagen-rich niches. Second, GPVI, an Ig-superfamily receptor that constitutively associates with Fc receptor γ-chain (FcRγ), binds fibrillar collagen

text: [Adhesion under arterial shear] . Second, GPVI, an Ig-superfamily receptor that constitutively associates with Fc receptor γ-chain (FcRγ), binds fibrillar collagen. These encounters provide the spatial and mechanical context in which signaling begins and define the arterial (high-shear) selectivity of ensuing thrombus formation (Bye et al., 2016; Li et al., 2010) (Fig. 1).

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [ITAM signaling and Ca2+ mobilization] Collagen engagement is mediated predominantly by GPVI, a member of the immunoglobulin superfamily that constitutively associates with the FcRγ. Collagen binding clusters GPVI–FcRγ complexes and triggers immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif (ITAM) phosphorylation, recruitment/activation of SYK, and propagation to PLCγ2. PLCγ2 hydrolyzes phosphatidylinositol 4,5-biphosphate (PIP₂), generating inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate (IP₃) and diacylglycerol (DAG) to drive Ca²⁺ release, granule secretion, and inside-out activation of integrin αIIbβ3—the final common aggregator by stabilizing platelet-platelet cohesion. Multiple canonical studies and reviews have mapped this pathway and its crosstalk with Src-family kinases and G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling (Estevez and Du, 2017).

text: [Amplification loops] Activated platelets amplify the response via secretion of ADP and synthesis of TXA₂, which stimulate P2Y12 (Gi-coupled) and thromboxane-prostanoid (TP) receptors, respectively, reinforcing integrin activation and thrombus growth. Thrombin generated on the platelet surface further augments platelet activation via protease-activated receptor 1/4 (PAR1/PAR4). These amplification loops are the historical targets of aspirin (COX-1) and P2Y12 antagonists (Bye et al., 2016) (Fig. 1).

text: [Thrombo-inflammation and leukocyte crosstalk] Beyond hemostasis, platelets orchestrate thrombo-inflammatory circuits: they bind leukocytes by expressing P-selectin that ligates P-selectin glycoprotein ligand-1 (PSGL-1) on leukocytes (Kling et al., 2013), stabilize inflamed microvasculature and foster Neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation (Colicchia et al., 2023). NETs interlace with vWF and fibrin, stiffen clots, and propagate microvascular occlusion. These processes couple immunity and thrombosis (immunothrombosis), amplifying injury in ACS, stroke, infection, and ischemic/reperfusion settings

These axes extend therapeutic reach beyond classical agonists to adhesion receptors (GPVI, GPIb), hemITAM CLEC-2 (via podoplanin in inflamed/tumor endothelium), and signaling nodes (SYK/BTK/PI3Kβ) as hemostasis-sparing opportunities because they are preferentially engaged under high shear or strong stimulus (Mack et al., 2024; Muller et al., 2015).

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [CURRENT ANTIPLATELET AGENTS AND LIMITATIONS] Current antiplatelet regimens predominantly target amplification and effector pathways. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX-1, blocking TXA₂ production, and thus reduces platelet aggregation through the TXA₂ axis. P2Y12 receptor inhibitors (clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor) suppress ADP-mediated platelet activation and reinforce the antithrombotic effect of aspirin. In certain high-risk settings, GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors, which block final common fibrinogen binding, and PAR1 antagonists have also been utilized (Jourdi et al., 2021).

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Mechanisms of current agents] Aspirin (COX-1 inhibitor): Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) remains the cornerstone of antiplatelet therapy and the most widely prescribed drug in cardiovascular medicine. It acts through irreversible acetylation of the serine 530 residue in platelet COX-1, thereby blocking the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandin H₂, the precursor of TXA₂ (Cyrus et al., 2002). By preventing TXA₂ generation, aspirin reduces platelet recruitment and aggregation at sites of vascular injury, curtailing the self-amplifying wave of activation that drives arterial thrombosis

text: [Mechanisms of current agents] . Low-dose regimens (75-100 mg daily) selectively suppress platelet COX-1 while minimizing inhibition of endothelial COX-2–derived prostacyclin, which exerts vasodilatory and antithrombotic effects (Cyrus et al., 2002; Jiang et al., 2020; Xian et al., 2015). Large-scale randomized trials established aspirin as the foundation of secondary prevention in myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, and peripheral artery disease, reducing serious vascular events by ≈25% (Frelinger et al., 2006). It is equally indispensable in combination with P2Y₁₂ inhibitors after PCI (which is called DAPT). Its strengths include once-daily dosing, low cost, and proven reduction of MI/stroke in secondary prevention

text: [Mechanisms of current agents] . Its strengths include once-daily dosing, low cost, and proven reduction of MI/stroke in secondary prevention. Limitations are dose-independent GI and intracranial bleeding, and non-selective suppression of thromboxane signaling that does not discriminate pathological from physiological activation (Hirsch, 2021; Hopkins, 2012).

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Mechanisms of current agents] P2Y12 inhibitors (clopidogrel → prasugrel, ticagrelor): The platelet P2Y₁₂ receptor is a Gᵢ-coupled purinergic receptor that responds to ADP released from dense granules of activated platelets (Dorsam and Kunapuli, 2004). ADP binding suppresses adenylate cyclase (AC), decreases cyclic AMP (cAMP), and stabilizes integrin αIIbβ3 activation, thereby amplifying and sustaining platelet aggregation (André et al., 2003; Li et al., 2023). Pharmacologic antagonism of P2Y₁₂ prevents this positive-feedback loop and represents the key synergistic partner to aspirin in DAPT. Clopidogrel (Savi et al., 1998), prasugrel (Jakubowski et al., 2007), and ticagrelor (Husted and Van Giezen, 2009) underpin DAPT after PCI/ACS (Bhatt et al., 2006; Jacob et al., 2012; Mehran et al., 2019)

text: [Mechanisms of current agents] PAR-1 antagonism (vorapaxar) and thrombin pathways: Thrombin-mediated platelet activation represents one of the most potent amplifiers of arterial thrombosis. Thrombin exerts its effects through PARs, primarily PAR1 and PAR4, which are expressed on the platelet surface (Brito and Tricoci, 2013). Upon proteolytic cleavage by thrombin, the N-terminal ectodomain of these receptors exposes a tethered ligand that binds intramolecularly to activate intracellular signaling cascades. This self-activation mechanism triggers G-protein–coupled signaling pathways, leading to Ca²⁺ mobilization, granule secretion, and integrin αIIbβ3 activation, thereby reinforcing platelet aggregation and thrombus stability (Negrescu et al., 1995)

text: [Mechanisms of current agents] PAR1 is a high-affinity, rapidly activated receptor that responds to low nanomolar thrombin concentrations and mediates the early, essential phase of hemostatic platelet activation. In contrast, PAR4 has lower thrombin affinity and exhibits slower but more sustained Ca²⁺ signaling, driving dense-granule release, cytoskeletal contraction, thrombus consolidation, and fibrin-rich clot maturation—processes that disproportionately contribute to pathological thrombus propagation, particularly under high-shear arterial flow (Liu et al., 2021). This division of labor implies that inhibiting PAR1 disrupts primary hemostasis, whereas selectively modulating PAR4 may primarily blunt the amplification and stabilization phases of thrombosis.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Mechanisms of current agents] Among pharmacologic modulators of this pathway, vorapaxar is the first and only PAR1 antagonist approved for clinical use (Tricoci et al., 2012). It is indicated in the United States for patients with a history of myocardial infarction (MI) or peripheral artery disease (PAD), where it acts as an irreversible inhibitor of PAR1, blocking thrombin-mediated platelet activation (Cavender et al., 2015; Morrow et al., 2013; Tricoci et al., 2012). Vorapaxar has a rapid onset (1-2 h) but a prolonged half-life (effective ~3-4 days, terminal ~8 days), resulting in sustained platelet inhibition even after drug discontinuation

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Mechanisms of current agents] . The efficacy of vorapaxar has been evaluated in large randomized controlled trials, including TRACER and TRA 2°P–TIMI 50, which enrolled patients with prior MI, stroke, and/or PAD. When added to standard antiplatelet therapy—either single (SAPT) or dual (DAPT)—vorapaxar reduced composite ischemic endpoints such as cardiovascular death, MI, and stroke compared with standard therapy alone. However, these gains were offset by a substantial increase in moderate and severe bleeding, particularly intracranial hemorrhage in patients with prior stroke or advanced age and low body weight (Morrow et al., 2013). Consequently, such populations were excluded from the FDA-approved indication
