text: [Mechanisms of current agents] . Consequently, such populations were excluded from the FDA-approved indication. Overall, vorapaxar demonstrates that targeting PAR1 can provide incremental ischemic benefit, but its narrow therapeutic window and irreversible inhibition limit broader applicability.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Mechanisms of current agents] These limitations have shifted therapeutic development toward reversible and PAR4-selective antagonists that preserve the early PAR1-dependent hemostatic response while attenuating the PAR4-mediated propagation phase of thrombosis. Small-molecule PAR4 antagonists such as BMS-986120 demonstrate potent and selective inhibition of PAR4-driven platelet activation, markedly reducing arterial thrombus formation in preclinical models without significantly prolonging bleeding time (Merali et al., 2022; Rwibasira Rudinga et al., 2018; Wilson et al., 2018). Mechanistically, PAR4 blockade suppresses sustained Ca²⁺ signaling, granule secretion, and clot stabilization while maintaining the initial platelet plug formation required for vascular sealing

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Mechanisms of current agents] . This mechanistic selectivity supports the concept that PAR4 antagonism may achieve true hemostasis-sparing antithrombotic activity, directly addressing the safety limitations that hindered PAR1-directed therapy. Ongoing research is thus directed toward developing reversible or PAR4-selective antagonists, which may attenuate thrombin-driven platelet activation while minimizing bleeding liability.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Limitations of current strategies] (1) Bleeding liability: The major adverse effect of all current antiplatelet agents is bleeding, which may lead to morbidity, transfusion, or therapy discontinuation (Park, 2022). Current agents broadly inhibit platelet activation, affecting both pathologic and physiologic responses. This indiscriminate suppression is the root of bleeding complications. In many trials, the net clinical benefit is weighed carefully against bleeding risk, especially in elderly or comorbid populations. (2) Residual thrombotic risk: Even under optimal DAPT (Hara et al., 2021), a significant proportion of patients experience ischemic events, suggesting incomplete control of upstream adhesion/signaling or non-platelet thrombotic drivers

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Limitations of current strategies] . Many antiplatelet agents primarily target amplification and effector steps, including TXA₂ generation, ADP-mediated signaling, and integrin binding. Upstream adhesion events, receptor clustering, signal initiation, or conversion to procoagulant platelets are less well addressed by current therapy. (3) Inter-individual variability (genetics, pharmacokinetics, comorbidity) yields high residual platelet reactivity in a meaningful subset. (4) Therapeutic strategies are often static, while patient risk evolves over time—fueling interest in shortened DAPT/monotherapy approaches.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
section: Evidence for de-escalation and abbreviated DAPT
text: [Evidence for de-escalation and abbreviated DAPT] Contemporary randomized trials demonstrate that risk-adapted approaches can lower bleeding without excess ischemia in PCI populations. In TWILIGHT, high-risk patients on 3-month DAPT who continued ticagrelor alone had significantly less BARC 2-5 bleeding vs. continued DAPT, with noninferior ischemic outcomes (Mehran et al., 2019). Additional data-notably studies evaluating early aspirin discontinuation with ticagrelor monotherapy-similarly support shorter DAPT horizons in selected cohorts (Hong et al., 2024; Tarantini et al., 2025); newer updates continue to report noninferiority or superiority for bleeding while maintaining ischemic protection, although generalizability across all risk states remains an area of active research.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Rationale for next-generation (“hemostasis-sparing”) targets] Given these gaps, there is a compelling rationale to explore targeted inhibition of surface receptors and intracellular kinase pathways that lie upstream of broad platelet activation. By intervening at these nodal points, one may attenuate pathological thrombosis while potentially preserving basal platelet function under low-stimulus conditions.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Rationale for next-generation (“hemostasis-sparing”) targets] Because legacy drugs broadly suppress amplification pathways (TXA₂/ADP) or final aggregation, they inevitably attenuate physiologic hemostasis. Upstream interventions—adhesion receptors (GPVI, GPIb–vWF, CLEC-2) and signal-initiation/propagation nodes (SYK, BTK, PI3Kβ, PLCγ2)—promise context-dependent selectivity and therefore a lower bleeding penalty.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [EMERGING TARGETS IN ANTIPLATELET THERAPY] Key molecular targets and their corresponding novel antiplatelet agents are illustrated in Fig. 2 and summarized in Table 1.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Surface receptor & Adhesion receptor] Glycoprotein VI (GPVI): GPVI is the principal platelet collagen receptor that initiates platelet adhesion and activation following vascular injury. Upon collagen engagement, GPVI forms a complex with the FcRγ chain, leading to ITAM phosphorylation and downstream activation of SYK and PLCγ2, culminating in Ca²⁺ mobilization, granule secretion, and integrin αIIbβ3 activation (Massberg et al., 2003; Nieswandt and Watson, 2003). Genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of GPVI reduces arterial thrombosis in animal models while largely sparing physiological bleeding time (Lockyer et al., 2006). Revacept, a soluble dimeric GPVI-Fc fusion protein that blocks platelet–collagen interaction, has been evaluated in clinical trials (Ungerer et al., 2011)

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Surface receptor & Adhesion receptor] . The ISAR-PLASTER study (NCT01946854) and phase II REVACEPT–Carotid trial demonstrated safety and a reduction in microembolic signals without an increase in bleeding (Mayer et al., 2021). More recently, glenzocimab (ACT017), a humanized Fab targeting GPVI, showed favorable pharmacokinetics and safety in phase II trials in stroke and myocardial infarction patients (Mazighi et al., 2024; Renaud et al., 2020; Wichaiyo et al., 2022). These data collectively support GPVI as a promising hemostasis-sparing target for arterial thrombosis.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Surface receptor & Adhesion receptor] GPIb–vWF axis: The GPIb–IX–V complex mediates platelet tethering to vWF under high-shear conditions, such as in stenotic arteries (Ruggeri, 2007). Inhibition of this interaction attenuates shear-dependent thrombosis while minimally affecting tail-bleeding time in preclinical models (Koltsova et al., 2014; Prasannan and Scully, 2021). Anfibatide, a GPIbα-binding snake-venom-derived peptide, has completed phase I evaluation in healthy volunteers, showing a dose-dependent prolongation of platelet adhesion without serious bleeding (Lei et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2021). Caplacizumab, a humanized nanobody targeting the A1 domain of vWF, provides clinical proof-of-concept for therapeutic inhibition of GP1b-vWF axis (Peyvandi et al., 2016; Scully et al., 2019)

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Surface receptor & Adhesion receptor] . In patients with immune-mediated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (iTTP), clinical trials demonstrated faster platelet count recovery and reduced ischemic complications without marked increase in life-threatening bleeding (Albanell-Fernandez et al., 2023; Volker et al., 2020). However, real-world studies have reported higher rates of clinically relevant non-major bleeding-particularly mucocutaneous and gastrointestinal events-highlighting the need for careful patient selection (Neupane et al., 2024; Volker et al., 2023). Targeting this axis may be particularly valuable in diseases characterized by high-shear thrombosis, including ACS, stroke, and thrombosis associated with mechanical circulatory support devices.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Surface receptor & Adhesion receptor] GPIIb/IIIa (integrin αIIbβIII): The integrin αIIbβ3 (also known as GPIIb/IIIa) is the most abundant adhesion receptor on the platelet surface, mediating the final step of platelet aggregation. Upon platelet activation by various agonists—such as ADP, thrombin, or collagen—inside-out signaling converts αIIbβ3 from a low-affinity to high-affinity conformation, enabling binding to soluble ligands including fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, and fibronectin (Buitrago et al., 2020; Lefkovits et al., 1995).

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Surface receptor & Adhesion receptor] Pharmacologic inhibition of the GPIIb/IIIa receptor produces immediate and near-complete suppression of platelet aggregation, making this drug class among the most potent antiplatelet interventions developed (Rosove, 2004; Scarborough et al., 1993; Zavalloniand Rossi, 2004). Intravenous GPIIb/IIIa antagonists—abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban—have demonstrated efficacy in PCI, particularly in patients with high thrombus burden or no-reflow phenomena (Berkowitz, 2000). These agents act by blocking the ligand-binding pocket of αIIbβ3, thereby preventing fibrinogen cross-linking and subsequent platelet aggregation

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Surface receptor & Adhesion receptor] . These agents act by blocking the ligand-binding pocket of αIIbβ3, thereby preventing fibrinogen cross-linking and subsequent platelet aggregation. However, their clinical use has declined due to a high incidence of bleeding and immune-mediated thrombocytopenia, which limit application to bail-out or rescue scenarios rather than routine use.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Surface receptor & Adhesion receptor] Contemporary research aims to redefine this pharmacologic class through the development of short-acting, reversible, and subcutaneous formulations intended for prehospital or early ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) care. Molecules such as RUC-4 and zalunfiban provide rapid, transient inhibition of αIIbβ3, enabling early reperfusion therapy while reducing prolonged bleeding risk (Bor et al., 2021; Mattheij et al., 2013). This next-generation approach seeks to retain the potency of classic GPIIb/IIIa blockade but reframe it within a hemostasis-sparing, time-limited therapeutic window, aligning with modern goals of precision and safety in acute arterial thrombosis management.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Surface receptor & Adhesion receptor] CLEC-2–podoplanin signaling: CLEC-2 is a platelet hemITAM receptor whose primary physiological role lies not in classical hemostasis, but in vascular–lymphatic separation and lymphatic endothelial integrity. Its endogenous ligand, podoplanin, is minimally expressed on blood vascular endothelium and instead localized to lymphatic endothelium, stromal fibroblasts, and specialized tissue-resident cells. CLEC-2 contributes primarily to lymphatics-associated signaling and tumor-induced platelet activation, not to GPVI- or thrombin-driven physiological hemostasis (Lowe et al., 2012; Suzuki-Inoue, 2019; Suzuki-Inoue et al., 2011).

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Surface receptor & Adhesion receptor] Pathologically, CLEC-2–podoplanin interactions become prominent in tumor-induced platelet activation and thrombo-inflammation. Many podoplanin-expressing tumors—such as squamous cell carcinoma, glioblastoma, and certain hematologic cancers—activate CLEC-2 to promote platelet–tumor aggregation, metastatic dissemination, and microvascular thrombosis (Suzuki-Inoue et al., 2007).

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Surface receptor & Adhesion receptor] Because CLEC-2 contributes minimally to physiological hemostasis, its inhibition appears hemostasis-sparing in several preclinical models. Platelet-specific CLEC-2 deficiency produces normal bleeding times yet attenuates tumor-associated platelet activation and inflammatory thrombus formation (Hughes et al., 2010; Meng et al., 2021). Nonetheless, antibody-mediated CLEC-2 depletion has produced variable bleeding effects depending on model and method, indicating the need for translational caution.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Surface receptor & Adhesion receptor] Although no clinical CLEC-2–targeted agents exist, this pathway represents a promising non-hemostatic platelet activation mechanism disproportionately engaged in cancer and inflammation. Pharmacologic inhibition of CLEC-2 may therefore offer a hemostasis-preserving approach to mitigating tumor-associated thrombosis and thrombo-inflammation without the bleeding liabilities of conventional antiplatelet therapies.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Intracellular signaling axes] NADPH oxidase (NOX): Reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated by NADPH oxidase (NOX) enzymes act as key secondary messengers downstream of platelet adhesion receptors such as GPVI and GPIb (Violi and Pignatelli, 2014). Among the NOX isoforms, NOX1 and NOX2 are predominant in platelets, catalyzing superoxide (O₂•⁻) formation in response to collagen or shear stress (Walsh et al., 2014). This redox signaling amplifies intracellular Ca²⁺ mobilization, granule secretion, and integrin αIIbβ₃ activation, thereby reinforcing platelet aggregation and thrombus formation.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Intracellular signaling axes] Pharmacologic inhibition or genetic deletion of NOX isoforms markedly attenuates platelet activation and arterial thrombosis without significantly affecting primary hemostasis (Altenhofer et al., 2015; Chocry and Leloup, 2020). The pan-NOX inhibitor APX-115, developed as an orally bioavailable redox-modulatory compound, was among the earliest next-generation inhibitors shown to potently suppress ROS-dependent platelet activation and FeCl₃-induced thrombosis in preclinical models (Chocry and Leloup, 2020; Jang et al., 2025). Subsequently, setanaxib (GKT137831), a dual NOX1/4 inhibitor, further confirmed these findings by reducing collagen-induced platelet aggregation and arterial thrombosis while preserving hemostasis (Oh et al., 2024)

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Intracellular signaling axes] . More recently, GSK2795039, a selective NOX2 inhibitor from GlaxoSmithKline, demonstrated robust suppression of ROS production and platelet aggregation ex vivo, validating the key role of NOX2-derived ROS in thrombus amplification (Chocry and Leloup, 2020; Oh et al., 2025). Collectively, these studies support the concept that NOX-derived ROS act as amplifiers rather than initiators of platelet activation. Thus, selective inhibition of NOX1/2 represents a promising hemostasis-sparing antithrombotic strategy with translational potential.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Intracellular signaling axes] SYK–BTK–PLCγ2 cascade: Signal propagation from ITAM-bearing receptors (GPVI, CLEC-2) is mediated by SYK and its downstream effector BTK, leading to PLCγ2 activation and Ca²⁺ release (Senis et al., 2014). Selective inhibition of SYK or BTK reduces thrombus formation in vivo while leaving primary hemostasis largely intact (Berton et al., 2005; Quek et al., 1998).

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Intracellular signaling axes] SYK inhibitors such as fostamatinib (approved for immune thrombocytopenia) and next-generation compounds (cevidoplenib, lanraplenib) exhibit on-target platelet suppression at low micromolar concentrations (Gonzalez-Lopez et al., 2024; Newland and McDonald, 2020). BTK inhibitors, originally developed for B-cell malignancies, have revealed unexpected antiplatelet effects; however, first-generation covalent inhibitors (ibrutinib) were associated with bleeding due to off-target tyrosine kinase expressed in hepatocellular carcinoma (TEC) inhibition (Bye et al., 2015; Mendez-Ruiz et al., 2023). Second-generation reversible BTK inhibitors (acalabrutinib, pirtobrutinib) show reduced bleeding incidence (Frustaci et al., 2023; Series et al., 2019)

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Intracellular signaling axes] PI3Kβ and downstream kinases: PI3Kβ integrates signals from both GPCR and ITAM receptors, regulating integrin activation and thrombus stabilization (Garcia et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2009). Mice lacking PI3Kβ display reduced arterial thrombosis with normal bleeding times (Laurent et al., 2015). The isoform-selective inhibitor TGX-221 and its clinical analog AZD6482 demonstrated potent antithrombotic activity in human studies, lowering platelet aggregation without prolonging bleeding (Chen et al., 2019; Nylander et al., 2012). Although development was discontinued for non-efficacy reasons, the concept of isoform-selective PI3Kβ inhibition remains compelling.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [Intracellular signaling axes] Additional intracellular modulators: Other intracellular targets include 12-LOX, involved in oxylipin signaling and integrin activation; its inhibitor ML355 decreases thrombosis without affecting hemostasis (Yeung and Holinstat, 2011; Yeung et al., 2020). PDI participates in platelet aggregation and thrombin generation, and small-molecule PDI inhibitors such as quercetin-3-rutinoside suppress thrombosis in vivo (Flaumenhaft, 2013; Jasuja et al., 2012; Zwicker et al., 2019). These findings suggest that finely tuned inhibition of platelet intracellular enzymes may yield safer antiplatelet profiles.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [TRANSLATIONAL PERSPECTIVES AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS] A consistent theme across these mechanistic innovations is the pursuit of selectivity—targeting pathological thrombosis while preserving primary hemostasis. Several translational directions have emerged: (i) Hemostasis-sparing design: Upstream targets such as GPVI, GPIb–vWF, and PI3Kβ regulate thrombus formation only under high-shear or strong stimulation, sparing baseline haemostatic responses. This provides a physiological “selectivity filter” (Rana et al., 2019). (ii) Combination and de-escalation strategies: new agents may complement low-intensity P2Y12 inhibition or short-course DAPT, mitigating ischemic risk without bleeding penalty. The TWILIGHT and STOPDAPT-2 trials have already validated such de-escalation paradigms (Mehran et al., 2019; Watanabe et al., 2019)

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [TRANSLATIONAL PERSPECTIVES AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS] . The TWILIGHT and STOPDAPT-2 trials have already validated such de-escalation paradigms (Mehran et al., 2019; Watanabe et al., 2019). (iii) Patient stratification and precision therapy: Integration of platelet function testing, genetic polymorphism data, and bleeding risk scores such as PRECISE-DAPT and ARC-HBR allows tailoring of therapy intensity (Kadiyala et al., 2023; Marschall et al., 2024). (iv) Novel biomarkers and imaging: Flow-based microfluidic assays and intravital microscopy are increasingly used to quantify thrombus formation dynamics and evaluate target engagement for emerging agents (Mihalko et al., 2024)

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [TRANSLATIONAL PERSPECTIVES AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS] . (v) Emerging clinical evidence: The ACTIMIS and ACTISAVE phase II trials for glenzocimab have confirmed safety and a trend toward improved ischemic outcomes in stroke (Mazighi et al., 2024; Wichaiyo et al., 2022). Similarly, reversible BTK inhibitors (pirtobrutinib, fenebrutinib) have shown reduced bleeding rates compared with ibrutinib in pooled analyses (Frustaci et al., 2023). (vi) Outstanding challenge: Translating preclinical selectivity into clinical safety remains difficult, as platelet–coagulation cross-talk and off-target kinase inhibition can reintroduce bleeding risk. Large-scale randomized studies are required to validate the “hemostasis-sparing” hypothesis.

title: Hemostasis-Sparing Antiplatelet Therapy: Current Concepts and Emerging Targets in Arterial Thrombosis
text: [TRANSLATIONAL PERSPECTIVES AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS] In conclusion, the landscape of antiplatelet therapy is shifting from non-selective blockade of amplification pathways toward mechanism-guided, hemostasis-preserving strategies. Targeting adhesion receptors and intracellular signaling kinases holds significant promise for safer thrombosis prevention, bridging the gap between efficacy and safety in cardiovascular and thrombo-inflammatory disease.

title: Pluviatolide Attenuates Type I Hypersensitivity through Regulation of Mast Cell Activation
text: [abstract] This study examined the inhibitory effects of pluviatolide, a lignan derived from Podophyllum hexandrum, on mast cell activation and IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity, focusing on FcεRI-dependent and calcium-mediated pathways. Using bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs) and rat basophilic leukemia (RBL)-2H3 cells, we found that pluviatolide significantly decreased β-hexosaminidase release and suppressed the expression and secretion of TNF-α and IL-6 in a concentration-dependent manner, without causing cytotoxicity

title: Pluviatolide Attenuates Type I Hypersensitivity through Regulation of Mast Cell Activation
text: [abstract] . While we initially hypothesized that it would selectively modulate antigen-specific FcεRI signaling, pluviatolide also inhibited degranulation induced by calcium ionophore and thapsigargin, indicating its effects extend to receptor-independent, Ca2+-dependent activation mechanisms. Immunoblot analyses revealed decreased phosphorylation of proximal kinases (Lyn, Syk), adaptor proteins (LAT, PLCγ1), MAPKs (ERK1/2, JNK, p38), and NF-κB p65. In a passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) mouse model, oral administration of pluviatolide significantly reduced Evans blue extravasation and mast cell degranulation in ear tissues

title: Pluviatolide Attenuates Type I Hypersensitivity through Regulation of Mast Cell Activation
text: [abstract] . These findings demonstrate that pluviatolide suppresses both early and late-phase mast cell responses through multi-nodal inhibition of activation pathways, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic candidate for both IgE-mediated and non-IgE-mediated allergic disorders.

title: Pluviatolide Attenuates Type I Hypersensitivity through Regulation of Mast Cell Activation
text: [INTRODUCTION] Immediate-type hypersensitivity, also known as type I hypersensitivity, refers to a rapid immune response triggered by exposure to specific allergens (Abbas et al., 2025; Galli et al., 2008; Hamilton, 2010). Mast cells play a central role in this process by becoming activated when allergens cross-link immunoglobulin E (IgE) that is bound to high-affinity FcεRI receptors on their surface (Galli and Tsai, 2012; Gurish and Austen, 2012; Kinet, 1999). This activation triggers the rapid release of preformed mediators, including histamine, proteases, and pro-inflammatory cytokines. These substances contribute to hallmark allergic manifestations such as increased vascular permeability, smooth muscle constriction, and localized inflammation (Mukai et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2023)

title: Pluviatolide Attenuates Type I Hypersensitivity through Regulation of Mast Cell Activation
text: [INTRODUCTION] . These physiological outcomes are closely linked to allergic diseases, including asthma, anaphylaxis, and atopic dermatitis (Theoharides and Kalogeromitros, 2006). The prevalence of allergic disorders is rising worldwide, and many current treatment options are limited by suboptimal efficacy or adverse effects. This situation has prompted the search for novel agents with improved safety profiles. (Dierick et al., 2020; Ogulur et al., 2021). Naturally derived compounds, especially lignans, have garnered attention for their anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties (Jang et al., 2022). Lignans are plant-derived polyphenolic compounds that modulate immune responses and alleviate allergic symptoms by inhibiting mast cell activation and the release of mediators. (Farhan et al., 2024).

title: Pluviatolide Attenuates Type I Hypersensitivity through Regulation of Mast Cell Activation
text: [INTRODUCTION] Pluviatolide is a lignan compound originally isolated from the roots of Podophyllum hexandrum. It has been reported to exhibit anti-inflammatory, antitumor, cytotoxic, and antispasmodic activities (Decembrino et al., 2020; Grigore, 2017; Hazra and Chattopadhyay, 2016). However, its effects on mast cell–mediated allergic responses have not been explored. Mast cells, located at mucosal and dermal surfaces, act as immune sentinels and play a crucial role in initiating and amplifying type I hypersensitivity reactions (Zhang and Kurashima, 2021). Modulating mast cell activation is a logical strategy for controlling both the immediate and late phases of allergic inflammation (Katsoulis-Dimitriou et al., 2020).

title: Pluviatolide Attenuates Type I Hypersensitivity through Regulation of Mast Cell Activation
text: [INTRODUCTION] This study aimed to evaluate the anti-allergic potential of pluviatolide by examining its effects on mast cell degranulation, cytokine secretion, and intracellular signaling pathways. We utilized both in vitro and in vivo models to assess the compound’s ability to suppress FcεRI-mediated responses and to investigate the underlying mechanisms. Specifically, we explored whether the inhibitory effects of pluviatolide were limited to antigen-specific, receptor-dependent pathways or if they also extended to calcium-dependent, receptor-independent activation. The findings offer new insights into the pharmacological potential of pluviatolide as a promising therapeutic agent for allergic diseases linked to mast cell hyperactivation.

text: [Animals] Male BALB/c mice (5–6-weeks-old) were purchased from Orient Bio (Gyeonggi-do, Korea). The mice were housed in a specific pathogen-free environment at 22 ± 1°C with 55 ± 10% humidity, with ad libitum access to food and water. All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of Dong-A University (Approval No. DIACUC-21-11) and conducted in accordance with institutional guidelines.

title: Pluviatolide Attenuates Type I Hypersensitivity through Regulation of Mast Cell Activation
text: [Mast cell culture] Bone marrow cells were harvested from the femurs and tibiae of BALB/c mice and cultured in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% FBS, 100 µg/mL penicillin-streptomycin, 4 mM L-glutamine, 25 mM HEPES, 0.05 mM β-mercaptoethanol, and 10 ng/mL interleukin-3 (PeproTech, Cranbury, NJ, USA) for 4 weeks. Mature bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs) were identified by flow cytometric analysis using anti-c-Kit and anti-FcεRI antibodies (eBioscience, San Diego, CA, USA) and showed >95% purity. Rat basophilic leukemia (RBL)-2H3 cells (ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA) were cultured in MEM supplemented with 15% FBS, 100 U/mL penicillin-streptomycin, and 4 mM L-glutamine in a 5% CO2 humidified incubator at 37°C.

title: Pluviatolide Attenuates Type I Hypersensitivity through Regulation of Mast Cell Activation
text: [Cell viability assay] BMMCs (5×104 cells/well) were seeded in 96-well plates and treated with various concentrations of pluviatolide for 4 h. Cell viability was measured using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (Dojindo Laboratories, Kumamoto, Japan) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

title: Pluviatolide Attenuates Type I Hypersensitivity through Regulation of Mast Cell Activation
text: [β-Hexosaminidase release assay] BMMCs (2.5×105 cells/well) were sensitized with 100 ng/mL DNP-IgE for 4 h, washed, and resuspended in Tyrode’s buffer. Cells were pretreated with pluviatolide for 30 min, then stimulated with 50 ng/mL DNP-HSA for 15 min. Supernatants and cell lysates (0.1% Triton X-100) were incubated with p-NAG for 1 h at 37°C, and the reaction was stopped with carbonate buffer. Absorbance was measured at 405 nm, and degranulation was calculated as the percentage of β-hexosaminidase released into the supernatant relative to the total. text: [Inhibition of TNF-α and IL-6 production by pluviatolide] Given the central role of TNF-α and IL-6 in amplifying and sustaining allergic inflammation, we evaluated the impact of pluviatolide on cytokine expression and secretion. text: [DISCUSSION] Allergic diseases, such as atopic dermatitis, asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food allergies, affect a significant portion of the global population and are becoming increasingly prevalent (Alska et al., 2025; Dierick et al., 2020; Ogulur et al., 2021; Shin et al., 2023). Despite advances in understanding their immunopathogenesis, treatment strategies primarily focus on symptomatic relief and allergen avoidance. However, complete avoidance is often impractical due to the widespread presence and variability of allergens. Mast cells are key effector cells in IgE-mediated allergic reactions, and their activation triggers the rapid release of inflammatory mediators that contribute to both the acute and chronic phases of allergic inflammation (Abassi et al., 2004).

Pluviatolide significantly reduced antigen-induced degranulation in both murine bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs) and RBL-2H3 cells, demonstrating no cytotoxicity at effective concentrations (Fig. 1B, 1D, 1E). The IC50 for β-hexosaminidase inhibition in BMMCs was approximately 35 µM (Fig. 1C), indicating moderate potency with a favorable safety margin. Since β-hexosaminidase release is a well-established marker of mast cell degranulation (Fukuishi et al., 2014; Moon et al., 2014; Staats et al., 2013), these findings suggest that pluviatolide has a direct inhibitory effect on one of the earliest effector events in IgE-mediated hypersensitivity

text: [DISCUSSION] To our knowledge, this is the first report demonstrating that pluviatolide, a naturally derived lignan, suppresses IgE-mediated mast cell activation through both receptor-dependent and calcium-mediated pathways in multiple experimental systems. Although its anti-inflammatory and anti-tumor activities have been previously described (Decembrino et al., 2020; Grigore, 2017; Hazra and Chattopadhyay, 2016), its role in allergic regulation has not been addressed. Our findings support the further development of pluviatolide and its structurally related derivatives as potential treatments for mast cell-driven allergic diseases

Additionally, studies should assess its effectiveness in systemic anaphylaxis and chronic allergy models to determine its translational potential. Overall, pluviatolide effectively suppresses mast cell-mediated allergic responses by inhibiting both early-phase degranulation and late-phase cytokine production through the blockade of key FcεRI-associated signaling pathways (Fig. 6). title: Skin Organoids in Proteostasis Research: Early Insights into Aging
text: [abstract] The decline of proteostasis is a central hallmark of aging, the earliest manifestations of which have remained difficult to capture in human tissues with conventional model systems. The skin is a continuously renewing and environmentally exposed organ offering a uniquely accessible window into aging biology. Skin organoid technologies allow for long-term culturing of human epidermal and full-thickness skin-like tissues that accurately recapitulate important aspects of cellular heterogeneity, spatial organization, and stem cell dynamics

title: Skin Organoids in Proteostasis Research: Early Insights into Aging
text: [abstract] . In this perspective, we discuss how skin organoids are beginning to reveal early proteostasis alterations-encompassing impaired protein folding, reduced proteasomal activity, and autophagy dysfunction-that precede overt structural and functional hallmarks of skin aging, with particular emphasis on underexplored regulators- sebaceous gland and sebocyte-specific proteostasis, autophagy, and inflammaging. We also highlight emerging insights, conceptual challenges, and experimental limitations, and outline future directions for integrating skin organoids with skin-on-a-chip, single-cell proteomics, and stress-reporting approaches to advance proteostasis-targeted interventions in skin aging.

text: [INTRODUCTION] Proteostasis, defined as the maintenance of protein homeostasis, is essential for cellular function and organismal health. It encompasses an integrated network of pathways that regulate protein synthesis, folding, trafficking, and degradation, including molecular chaperones, the ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS), and autophagy–lysosomal pathways (ALP). A progressive decline in proteostasis capacity is now recognized as a core hallmark of aging, contributing to the accumulation of damaged and misfolded proteins, loss of cellular resilience, and functional deterioration across tissues (Hipp et al., 2019; López-Otín et al., 2023)

text: [INTRODUCTION] The skin represents a particularly attractive model for studying human aging and proteostasis. As a continuously renewing organ with well-defined stem cell compartments, the skin integrates intrinsic aging processes with chronic exposure to extrinsic stressors such as ultraviolet radiation, pollution, and mechanical injury (Böhm et al., 2025). These features make skin aging both experimentally accessible and biologically informative, while also placing exceptional demands on proteostasis networks to maintain tissue integrity over time. Despite these advantages, existing human aging models have significant limitations

text: [INTRODUCTION] . Despite these advantages, existing human aging models have significant limitations. Two-dimensional cell cultures lack tissue architecture and long-term proteostasis dynamics, while animal models often fail to recapitulate human-specific aging trajectories and stress responses (Hossain et al., 2024). Ex vivo human skin explants, although physiologically relevant, are limited by short viability and experimental flexibility (Lebonvallet et al., 2010). As a result, early, cell-type–specific proteostasis alterations during human aging remain poorly understood.

text: [INTRODUCTION] Recent advances in skin organoid technologies offer a conceptual breakthrough in this context. By recapitulating key aspects of three-dimensional organization, stem cell niches, and long-term tissue maintenance, skin organoids provide a human-specific platform to interrogate how proteostasis networks deteriorate during aging. As highlighted by emerging work on proteostasis regulation and stress responses (Hipp et al., 2019), such systems hold promise for uncovering early, mechanistic drivers of aging that have thus far remained experimentally inaccessible

Given the rapid advancement of organoid technologies and their increasing adoption in aging research, skin organoids offer a timely and powerful approach to unravel the molecular underpinnings of proteostasis breakdown, model age-related tissue decline, and evaluate potential therapeutic interventions. This perspective aims to highlight the scientific emergence of skin organoids as a platform for proteostasis studies, discuss their relevance for aging research, and explore future directions for leveraging these models in translational and therapeutic discovery.

title: Skin Organoids in Proteostasis Research: Early Insights into Aging
text: [PROTEOSTASIS DECLINE IN SKIN AGING] Aging is associated with a progressive decline in the proteostasis network, leading to reduced capacity to maintain protein quality and cellular homeostasis. In the skin, this decline has particularly strong consequences because epidermal renewal, barrier maintenance, and continuous exposure to environmental stressors place exceptionally high demands on protein quality control (Bulteau and Friguet, 2021). As a result, even subtle impairments in proteostasis can have outsized effects on tissue integrity and function. Multiple arms of the proteostasis network are affected with age, including the heat shock response, the ubiquitin–proteasome system, and autophagy–lysosomal pathways (Frankowska et al., 2022; Watanabe et al., 2023)

title: Skin Organoids in Proteostasis Research: Early Insights into Aging
text: [PROTEOSTASIS DECLINE IN SKIN AGING] . The heat shock response, largely regulated by heat shock factor 1 (HSF1) and molecular chaperones, serves as a first line of defense against proteotoxic stress by promoting proper protein folding and preventing aggregation (Dai, 2018; Kmiecik and Mayer, 2022). With progressing age, both the inducibility and robustness of this response decline. This attenuation leads to reduced chaperone expression and compromises the ability of skin cells to buffer misfolded or damaged o intrinsic metabolic stress and extrinsic insults such as ultraviolet radiation (Zhang et al., 2025).

title: Skin Organoids in Proteostasis Research: Early Insights into Aging
text: [PROTEOSTASIS DECLINE IN SKIN AGING] Parallel defects emerge in protein degradation systems. Proteasomal activity decreases with age, in part due to reduced expression and assembly of proteasome subunits, impairing the clearance of damaged or short-lived proteins. In addition, ALP, which are essential for the turnover of long-lived proteins and organelles, become progressively less efficient (Smith and Carroll, 2025). Defects in autophagosome formation, lysosomal function, and cargo recognition contribute to the accumulation of protein aggregates and dysfunctional organelles in aged cells (Liu et al., 2025; Palmer et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b). The age-associated decline in proteostasis in skin cells is depicted in Fig. 1. The consequences of proteostasis failure are highly cell-type specific within the skin

title: Skin Organoids in Proteostasis Research: Early Insights into Aging
text: [PROTEOSTASIS DECLINE IN SKIN AGING] . 1. The consequences of proteostasis failure are highly cell-type specific within the skin. Epidermal stem cells show reduced self-renewal capacity and altered differentiation trajectories. Dermal fibroblasts exhibit impaired extracellular matrix (ECM) maintenance and increased cellular senescence, while melanocytes display heightened sensitivity to oxidative and proteotoxic stress (Miny et al., 2025; Nan et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025). Collectively, these changes contribute to hallmark features of skin aging, including epidermal thinning, reduced elasticity, pigmentation abnormalities, and delayed wound healing.

title: Skin Organoids in Proteostasis Research: Early Insights into Aging
text: [PROTEOSTASIS DECLINE IN SKIN AGING] Despite their significance, early proteostasis defects are difficult to detect in vivo. Compensatory mechanisms often mask subtle declines, and aging-related changes accumulate asynchronously across cells and niches. Moreover, human skin aging unfolds over decades, limiting access to early transitional states. Collectively, these findings position proteostasis decline as an early, coordinated, and cell-type–specific hallmark of skin aging rather than a passive downstream consequence of tissue deterioration. The asynchronous emergence of proteostasis defects across epidermal stem cells, fibroblasts, and melanocytes, together with strong compensatory buffering in vivo, obscures early transitional states in human skin

text: [SKIN ORGANOIDS: A NEW EXPERIMENTAL PARADIGM] Three-dimensional skin organoid models composed of fibroblasts and keratinocytes have emerged as valuable platforms for investigating the mechanisms underlying skin aging. Skin organoids preserve the spatial organization, cell–cell interactions, and niche signaling required for coordinated protein quality control across multiple lineages. This architecture is particularly relevant for aging research, as proteostasis collapse unfolds in a tissue-context–dependent manner rather than within isolated cell types.

title: Skin Organoids in Proteostasis Research: Early Insights into Aging
section: SKIN ORGANOIDS: A NEW EXPERIMENTAL PARADIGM
text: [SKIN ORGANOIDS: A NEW EXPERIMENTAL PARADIGM] Skin aging phenotypes can be modeled in organoids through prolonged culture, induction of cellular senescence, or derivation from aged donors. These approaches reproduce hallmark characteristics of aged skin, including reduced ECM production, loss of cellularity, and thinning of the epidermal layer (Diekmann et al., 2016). Importantly, these phenotypes emerge alongside gradual deterioration of proteostasis pathways, allowing direct linkage between molecular mechanisms and tissue-level outcomes.

text: [SKIN ORGANOIDS: A NEW EXPERIMENTAL PARADIGM] Recent advances in skin organoids encompass a spectrum of models that differ in cellular composition, complexity, and developmental origin. Epidermal-only organoids, derived from keratinocyte stem cells recapitulate stratification, differentiation, and barrier formation, providing a tractable system to study proteostasis dynamics within the epidermal lineage (Kardeh et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Ramovs et al., 2022). However, full-thickness skin organoids that incorporate both epidermal and dermal compartments, offer a distinct mechanistic advantage by enabling investigation of interlayer communication, ECM remodeling, and stromal influences on proteostasis (Baek et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025a; Smith et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024). section: SKIN ORGANOIDS: A NEW EXPERIMENTAL PARADIGM
text: [SKIN ORGANOIDS: A NEW EXPERIMENTAL PARADIGM] For proteostasis research, skin organoids offer several key advantages. Their capacity for long-term culture allows progressive proteostasis changes to emerge over time, capturing gradual declines that are difficult to observe in short-lived systems. Organoids also preserve human-specific stress responses, avoiding interspecies differences that complicate interpretation of aging mechanisms in animal models (Zwi-Dantsis et al., 2025). Importantly, the three-dimensional organization of organoids supports cell–cell interactions and niche signaling, which are essential for coordinated proteostasis regulation across stem cells, differentiated cells, and supporting populations

text: [SKIN ORGANOIDS: A NEW EXPERIMENTAL PARADIGM] . Skin organoids have also provided insight into how age-related changes in the tissue microenvironment contribute to skin degeneration. In particular, fragmentation of collagen within the ECM has been identified as a critical driver of aging. Fibroblast proteostasis decline leads to collagen fragmentation and weakened cell–matrix attachment, resulting in altered TGF-β signaling and diminished ECM synthesis (Fisher et al., 2016; Quan et al., 2013), thereby exacerbating tissue fragility. In full-thickness organoids, these stromal changes propagate to the epidermal compartment, where they can induce keratinocyte stress responses, altered differentiation trajectories, and senescence phenotypes

text: [SKIN ORGANOIDS: A NEW EXPERIMENTAL PARADIGM] Skin organoids can further be classified by their cellular source. iPSC-derived skin organoids recapitulate aspects of skin development and allow modeling of genetic diversity, patient-specific mutations, and rejuvenation-associated epigenetic resetting (Yu et al., 2025). In contrast, adult stem cell–derived organoids retain age-associated features and epigenetic memory, making them particularly valuable for studying aging-related proteostasis decline (Zhao et al., 2025). These complementary approaches enable interrogation of both developmental and aging-associated trajectories of protein quality control

text: [SKIN ORGANOIDS: A NEW EXPERIMENTAL PARADIGM] Compared with traditional human skin explants, organoids provide greater experimental flexibility, genetic manipulability, and longevity (Huang et al., 2025b; Zeng et al., 2025). Unlike reconstructed skin equivalents, which rely on artificial assembly and limited self-organization, organoids more faithfully recapitulate endogenous tissue dynamics. Seminal studies demonstrating the self-organization and functional maturation of human skin organoids (Li et al., 2025a) and recent refinements in stem cell–derived skin models (Garriga-Cerda et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025a) underscore their potential as a next-generation platform to interrogate proteostasis decline during human skin aging

Collectively, skin organoids represent a conceptual shift from static or endpoint-driven skin aging models to dynamic, self-organizing human systems that preserve tissue architecture, cell–cell interactions, and human-specific stress responses. Their experimental longevity, genetic tractability, and capacity to retain age-associated epigenetic features uniquely position skin organoids to interrogate proteostasis decline as a progressive and mechanistically tractable process during human skin aging.

section: EARLY PROTEOSTASIS INSIGHTS EMERGING FROM SKIN ORGANOIDS
text: [EARLY PROTEOSTASIS INSIGHTS EMERGING FROM SKIN ORGANOIDS] Skin organoids are beginning to yield important early insights into how proteostasis deteriorates during human aging. One recurring observation across organoid systems is the emergence of age-like proteostasis drift during prolonged culture, even in the absence of overt genetic or environmental insults. Extended maintenance of skin organoids is associated with a gradual accumulation of misfolded or damaged proteins, reduced stress resilience, and altered responsiveness to proteotoxic challenges—features reminiscent of early aging phenotypes observed in vivo

Such temporal changes support the concept that proteostasis decline can arise intrinsically from sustained cellular activity and replication, consistent with theoretical frameworks of aging as a progressive loss of protein quality control (Bell and Tower, 2021; Tower, 2015). At the molecular level, skin organoids exhibit altered expression of key proteostasis components, including molecular chaperones, proteasome subunits, and autophagy-related genes (Eckhart et al., 2024; Jie et al., 2025). Reductions in heat shock protein expression and diminished induction of stress-responsive pathways suggest a blunted capacity to buffer proteotoxic stress over time

These alterations parallel age-associated proteostasis defects observed in multiple tissues, reinforcing the relevance of organoids as aging models.

text: [EARLY PROTEOSTASIS INSIGHTS EMERGING FROM SKIN ORGANOIDS] Importantly, skin organoids enable resolution of cell-type–specific vulnerability within a shared tissue context (Bock et al., 2021; Stabell et al., 2023). Epidermal stem and progenitor cells often display heightened sensitivity to proteostasis imbalance, with early stress signatures emerging before comparable changes in differentiated keratinocytes (Blanpain and Fuchs, 2009; Noormohammadi et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2024). In parallel, dermal fibroblasts within full-thickness organoids may exhibit distinct proteostasis trajectories, reflecting differences in metabolic demand and stress exposure (Cavallero et al., 2020; Sutterby et al., 2022). Such heterogeneity underscores the notion that aging does not proceed uniformly across cell types, even within the same organ

Notably, emerging evidence suggests that proteostasis disruption precedes overt differentiation and structural defects in skin organoids (Wang et al., 2023). Perturbations in protein quality control often manifest before detectable changes in stratification, barrier formation, or lineage commitment, positioning proteostasis decline as an early, potentially causal driver of tissue aging. Recent work linking proteostasis regulation to organismal aging trajectories (Ghosh et al., 2025) further supports the idea that skin organoids can capture initial molecular events that set the stage for later functional decline.

However, investigation of sebaceous gland proteostasis has been constrained by reductionist 2D cultures of immortalized sebocytes and short-lived ex vivo gland preparations, which fail to capture long-term proteostasis dynamics at the tissue level. hiPSC–based 3D skin models provide a powerful opportunity to overcome these limitations by enabling sustained, human-relevant interrogation of autophagy–proteostasis coupling in sebocytes

text: [EARLY PROTEOSTASIS INSIGHTS EMERGING FROM SKIN ORGANOIDS] In summary, insights from skin organoid models indicate that proteostasis imbalance arises early during aging and precedes detectable defects in tissue organization, differentiation, and barrier integrity. These observations support a causal framework in which impaired protein quality control initiates cellular vulnerability and shapes subsequent tissue-level aging trajectories. By resolving early proteostasis imbalance within a physiologically relevant tissue context, skin organoids provide a critical experimental bridge between molecular aging mechanisms and late-stage skin pathology, addressing a longstanding limitation in human skin aging research.

title: Skin Organoids in Proteostasis Research: Early Insights into Aging
section: DISSECTING INTRINSIC AND EXTRINSIC AGING USING SKIN ORGANOIDS
text: [DISSECTING INTRINSIC AND EXTRINSIC AGING USING SKIN ORGANOIDS] Skin organoids provide a uniquely tractable platform to disentangle intrinsic and extrinsic drivers of human aging under tightly controlled conditions. Intrinsic aging can be modeled through prolonged organoid culture and serial passaging, which recapitulate replicative stress, telomere attrition, and persistent DNA damage responses characteristic of cellular senescence (Gorgoulis et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2024). Within this framework, organoids enable investigation of mitochondrial–proteostasis crosstalk, whereby age-associated mitochondrial dysfunction exacerbates proteostatic collapse and tissue decline, processes that are difficult to resolve in vivo (Martic et al., 2023; Velarde et al., 2015)

text: [DISSECTING INTRINSIC AND EXTRINSIC AGING USING SKIN ORGANOIDS] In parallel, extrinsic aging mechanisms can be experimentally imposed through defined environmental insults, including ultraviolet radiation, oxidative stress, or chemical exposures. Skin and epithelial organoids subjected to UV irradiation reproduce key features of photoaging, such as proteotoxic stress, ECM remodeling, and impaired regenerative capacity, closely mirroring human extrinsic aging phenotypes (Cavallero et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2024b; Miyake et al., 2019; Olivatti et al., 2020; Sutterby et al., 2022). For example, UV-B irradiation has been reported to increase oxidative protein damage, promote accumulation of autophagy adaptor proteins such as p62, and disrupt proteasome activity in stratified epidermal models, particularly within basal keratinocyte layers

Importantly, while these studies demonstrate the feasibility of modeling extrinsic aging in organoid-based systems, comprehensive and systematic profiling of proteostasis markers—such as carbonylated proteins, chaperone expression dynamics, proteasome activity, and autophagic flux—remains sparse in skin organoids. This gap highlights a critical opportunity for future research to leverage advanced skin organoid platforms, in combination with single-cell proteomics and spatial analyses, to more precisely map how intrinsic and extrinsic stressors converge on proteostasis decline

text: [DISSECTING INTRINSIC AND EXTRINSIC AGING USING SKIN ORGANOIDS] By decoupling genetic background from environmental exposure, organoids offer unparalleled experimental control over dose, timing, and cellular context, allowing direct comparison of intrinsic versus extrinsic aging trajectories. This level of experimental control is difficult to achieve in vivo and unattainable in simpler in vitro systems. As a result, the ability of skin organoids to integrate intrinsic and extrinsic aging cues through proteostasis-centered mechanisms provides a foundation for predictive aging models and targeted interventions

section: LIMITATIONS OF CURRENT SKIN ORGANOID AGING MODELS
text: [LIMITATIONS OF CURRENT SKIN ORGANOID AGING MODELS] Despite promise, organoid models have some conceptual and technical limitations that must be acknowledged in aging research. Most organoid systems lack key non-epithelial components such as immune cells, vasculature, and innervation (Lee and Koehler, 2021; Lee et al., 2020; Sutterby et al., 2022), all of which play critical roles in tissue homeostasis and age-related decline. The absence of these elements constrains the ability to model complex intercellular interactions that shape proteostasis and inflammatory aging responses

While prolonged culture of skin organoids has been associated with proteostasis drift and increased expression of senescence markers such as p16NK4a, it is essential to distinguish authentic biological aging signatures from artifacts induced by in vitro stress conditions

text: [LIMITATIONS OF CURRENT SKIN ORGANOID AGING MODELS] Moreover, methodological variability across differentiation protocols, culture conditions, and handling practices introduces additional noise, making it difficult to compare results across laboratories or to establish universally accepted aging signatures. These inconsistencies are compounded by the lack of standardized, quantitative readouts for proteostasis in organoid systems, inhibiting robust assessment of interventions targeting protein quality control pathways. section: TOWARD PREDICTIVE HUMAN SKIN AGING MODEL AND PROTEOSTASIS-TARGETED INTERVENTIONS
text: [TOWARD PREDICTIVE HUMAN SKIN AGING MODEL AND PROTEOSTASIS-TARGETED INTERVENTIONS] Emerging technologies are reshaping how human skin aging can be modeled and predicted. The convergence of skin organoid models with high-resolution single-cell proteomics (Elias et al., 2019; Stabell et al., 2023), biological aging clocks, and organ-on-chip platforms offers new opportunities to quantify proteostasis dynamics in a human-relevant context. Single-cell proteomic technologies enable detailed mapping of protein quality control pathways within individual cell types, revealing aging trajectories that are obscured in bulk analyses. While human skin–equivalent (HSE) organoid systems capture key aspects of epidermal differentiation and cellular diversity, they should not be viewed as fully faithful surrogates of in vivo human skin

Partial phenotypic rescue following xenograft transplantation underscores the importance of the native microenvironment, while simultaneously revealing new lineage biases imposed by factors such as hypoxia (Stabell et al., 2023). These observations argue that future innovation in skin organoid platforms must move beyond structural mimicry toward dynamic integration of microenvironmental, metabolic, and spatial cues to achieve true physiological relevance

Such clocks have demonstrated robust age prediction across tissues and strong associations with disease risk. When applied to skin organoids, they offer objective metrics to assess aging trajectories and proteostasis decline under controlled experimental conditions.

text: [TOWARD PREDICTIVE HUMAN SKIN AGING MODEL AND PROTEOSTASIS-TARGETED INTERVENTIONS] Further physiological relevance can be achieved by embedding skin organoids within microfluidic organ-on-chip platforms. These systems enable controlled fluid flow, mechanical forces, and inter-tissue crosstalk, thereby better approximating systemic aging environments. Integrated platforms may function as early-warning systems, detecting subtle shifts in proteostasis or aging clock readouts in response to genetic, environmental, or pharmacological perturbations long before overt phenotypes emerge. This approach aligns with recent efforts to unify multi-scale biomarkers of aging into predictive frameworks (Fernandez et al., 2023; Pusparum et al., 2025; Theodorakis et al., 2024) and suggests a path toward actionable models that forecast individual aging trajectories and therapeutic responses

Natural compounds are being actively studied for their potential to delay cellular senescence and protect vascular health. text: [INTRODUCTION] Endothelial cells (ECs), which line blood vessels and maintain vascular tone and hemostasis, are highly susceptible to senescence (Sandoo et al., 2010). Cellular senescence is characterized by irreversible cell cycle arrest along with cell enlargement, increased granularity, vacuolization and increased senescence-associated beta galactosidase (SA-β gal) activity (Bode-Boger et al., 2005; Erusalimsky, 2009). However, these cells remain viable and metabolically active (Schafer et al., 2017). It can be induced in vitro by repeated passaging (replicative senescence) or be triggered prematurely by oxidative stress, angiotensin II, high glucose, radiation, and DNA damage (premature senescence) (Kim et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2011; Maeda et al., 2015)

text: [RBE delayed replicative senescence of PCAECs] Previous studies have indicated that serial passaging of PCAECs (P1-P3) resulted in the induction of senescence (Khemais-Benkhiat et al., 2016). To investigate whether RBE delays replicative ECs senescence, serial passaging of ECs from P1 to P3 was conducted in presence of RBE. Compared with P1 ECs, P3 cells exhibited a marked increase in the proportion of SA-β-gal–positive (senescent) cells. section: γ-Orz, a bioactive component of RBE, delayed replicative senescence and inhibited oxidative stress
text: [γ-Orz, a bioactive component of RBE, delayed replicative senescence and inhibited oxidative stress] γ-Orz, a phenolic compound abundantly present in RBE, has been widely reported as a potent antioxidant (Minatel et al., 2016). To evaluate whether γ-Orz reduces oxidative stress in senescent ECs, P1 ECs were cultured with different concentrations of γ-Orz followed by serial passaging until P3. Intracellular ROS levels were then assessed using DHE staining. P3 ECs showed increased oxidative stress compared to P1 ECs, as indicated by increased DHE fluorescence. Treatment with γ-Orz decreased ROS overproduction in a concentration dependent manner in P3 ECs (Fig. 3D, 3E). This suggests that γ-Orz has potent antioxidant effect and may prevent oxidative stress- induced replicative senescence in ECs.

section: RBE and γ-Orz prevented senescence-associated upregulation of cell cycle regulatory proteins
text: [RBE and γ-Orz prevented senescence-associated upregulation of cell cycle regulatory proteins] During replicative senescence, ECs undergoes cell cycle arrest by upregulating expression of cell cycle regulatory proteins such as p53, p16 and p21 (Matthaei et al., 2012; Mirzayans et al., 2012; Rosso et al., 2006). Consistent with this, P3 ECs exhibited markedly elevated levels of p53, p16, and p21 compared to P1 ECs, confirming their role in senescence-associated growth arrest. Treatment with RBE significantly suppressed the expression of these cell cycle regulators in P3 ECs (Fig. 4A-4D), thereby enhancing their proliferative potential. Similarly, γ-Orz treatment also led to a marked reduction in p53, p16, and p21 expression (Fig. 5A-5D), further supporting its ability to counteract senescence-associated cell cycle arrest

title: γ-Oryzanol Ameliorates Endothelial Replicative Senescence via Downregulation of SGLT2 Expression to Attenuate NADPH-Driven Oxidative Stress
text: [DISCUSSION] The present study investigated the role of RBE and its major component, γ-Orz in replicative senescence in vitro. The results demonstrated that both RBE and γ-Orz significantly delayed replicative endothelial senescence, as indicated by decreased SA-β- gal activity as well as reduced cell cycle regulatory proteins, such as p53, p21 and p16 expression. In addition, γ-Orz suppressed the progressive upregulation of SGLT2, NADPH oxidase subunits p22phox and NOX2, reduced ROS levels, and restored eNOS expression. Overall, these findings suggest that γ-Orz could be promising candidate against endothelial aging, capable of preserving vascular function and delaying the onset of cellular senescence.

text: [DISCUSSION] This study showed that RBE and γ-Orz delayed EC senescence as evidenced by the reduction of SA-β-gal activity in P3 ECs. SA-β-gal activity reflects aging of ECs and serves as a marker for senescence (Debacq-Chainiaux et al., 2009). During replicative senescence, ECs undergo cell cycle arrest which ultimately lead to limited number of cell divisions and the decrease in proliferation (Ben-Porath and Weinberg, 2005; Burger et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2015). In our study, RBE and γ-Orz promoted EC proliferation in P3 senescent cells which suggests that RBE and γ-Orz might prevent senescence- associated cell cycle arrest. These effects were accompanied by marked reduction in the expression of cell cycle regulatory proteins including p53, p21, and p16

text: [DISCUSSION] . These effects were accompanied by marked reduction in the expression of cell cycle regulatory proteins including p53, p21, and p16. p53 is activated by DNA damage, telomere dysfunction, and senescence. It activates the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor, p21 which inhibits cell proliferation (Rosso et al., 2006). Similarly, p16 is a member of the inhibitors of CDK4 protein family that acts through the Rb pathway to cause cell cycle arrest and lead to cellular senescence (Bhayadia et al., 2016). Reduced expression of these proteins suggests that RBE and γ-Orz delay endothelial senescence by suppressing the p53-p21 and p16-Rb pathways, which helps preserve proliferative capacity and maintain normal cell cycle progression.

text: [DISCUSSION] Recent studies have increasingly linked SGLT2 inhibition to the attenuation of oxidative stress associated with cellular senescence, highlighting its therapeutic potential beyond glycemic control (Yesilyurt-Dirican et al., 2025). For instance, Katsuumi et al. demonstrated that SGLT2 inhibition significantly reduces oxidative stress in senescent cells (Katsuumi et al., 2024). Mechanistically, SGLT2 inhibitors mitigate senescence-associated oxidative stress through multiple pathways, including inhibition of NADPH oxidase, activation of the NRF2/SIRT1 axis, and enhanced clearance of senescent cells (Dhakal et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2021). These mechanisms collectively preserve vascular and renal function, highlighting their role in aging-related pathologies

text: [Principal findings] Among the 2.7 million children born in Sweden between 1985 and 2020, the rate of ASD diagnoses increased about 10-fold over the study period (follow-up to 2022). For example, from 56.5 to 564.1 cases per 100 000 person years between 2000 and 2022, in people aged 10-14 years. The well known high MFR for ASD declined steadily for those with a diagnosis of ASD after 10 years of age, and for people with a more recent diagnosis (after 2010). A model based projection found a cMFR (sex difference in cumulative ASD incidence) close to 1 in Sweden for the 2022 calendar period, suggesting a similar lifetime rate of ASD diagnosis in both sexes.

title: Time trends in the male to female ratio for autism incidence: population based, prospectively collected, birth cohort study
text: [Principal findings] Our analyses of the MFR showed a substantial catch-up effect for ASD in the female cohort relative to the male cohort, over time and especially as age increased. This effect began at age 10 years, when the cMFR was about 3, and plateaued at age 20 years, after a rapid decline in the age specific MFR to <1 during adolescence.

text: [Comparison with other studies] Earlier studies have linked changes in ASD incidence to period effects (eg, the broadening of diagnostic criteria). ASD is diagnosed based on the fulfilment of descriptive criteria,15 thus the ASD rate and the MFR may have been affected by changes in the diagnostic manuals.12 While in post hoc analysis, we did not observe any abrupt alterations in either rates of ASD diagnosis or the MFR after the introduction of DSM-V in Sweden in 2013, new criteria can take several years to be implemented in a nuanced and consistent way. In addition, DSM-V was implemented at a time of growing awareness of ASD and formalised ASD as a spectrum

A Danish study found greatest increases in ASD diagnosis rates between the ages of 4 and 20 years, which the authors linked to increased diagnosis of autism spectrum after the introduction of ICD-10.27 A Norwegian population based register study of people born from 1967 to 2011 similarly found a higher MFR in children (3.7) than in adults (2.6).28

text: [Comparison with other studies] The high MFR may be linked to the so-called female protective effect,6 whereby female groups show greater genetic resilience, enabling them to carry more alleles contributing to ASD before reaching the threshold for an ASD diagnosis.6 8 However, compelling evidence for this theory is mixed. Greater heritability (ie, higher genetic contribution) was also identified as contributing to greater prevalence of ASD in males.21 The greater heritability in these individuals may have been observed because non-genetic factors contribute more to ASD in females, including diagnostic ascertainment and differences in clinical presentation.21

text: [Comparison with other studies] Lower rates of ASD diagnosis in female groups have also been attributed to a sex bias in both case ascertainment and clinical diagnosis, potentially resulting from differences in clinical presentation by sex and assessments and criteria favouring detection in male groups.4 9 28 For example, recent increases in rates of ASD diagnoses in females have been linked to the widening of diagnostic criteria.33 Camouflaging of traits associated with ASD (ie, taking behavioural cues from peers, including mimicking speech or expressions9) may also be more common in this group.33 In such cases, ASD-like behaviours may only become detectable during adolescence

text: [Comparison with other studies] . Earlier data suggest that women are more likely to seek general healthcare,34 suggesting more complex social and cultural factors also lead to the increase in diagnosis in young female adults. The clear increase in ASD diagnoses received by female adolescents documented in our study could thus be interpreted in several ways. Firstly, differences in presentation or application of diagnostic criteria by sex and age, or some relatively later manifestation of biological traits in female groups (ie, a sex-by-age interaction on the impact of biological traits). section: Strengths and limitations of this study
text: [Strengths and limitations of this study] A major strength of this study is the size and availability of clinically ascertained ASD. Clinical ascertainment of ASD using internationally recognised diagnostic criteria (DSM-V) allows outcomes to be generalised to similar populations. The ability to link data for a whole population to childhood medical and developmental assessment records in a publicly funded and operated healthcare system almost eliminated selection bias. Longer term studies allowed us to disentangle the effects of different time scales. However, using register data restricted our assessment of ASD type to specific ICD-10 coded categories, meaning we had less information about specific traits or clinical details, which could have enhanced the granularity of the study and provided a clinical perspective

title: Time trends in the male to female ratio for autism incidence: population based, prospectively collected, birth cohort study
text: [Conclusions] The findings, involving analysis of the Swedish population over a period of more than 35 years, indicate that the MFR for ASD has decreased over time, and that diagnosis of ASD has increased. This suggests that the MFR for ASD may be significantly lower than previously thought—to the extent that, in Sweden, it may no longer be distinguishable by adulthood. The decreasing MFR over time highlights the need to investigate why girls and women receive a diagnosis of ASD later than boys and men. Further research should focus on phenotypic differences in how ASD manifests by sex and the implications for screening and diagnostic practices.

text: [Introduction] Robotic surgery may improve short‐term outcomes and oncological efficacy compared with laparoscopic surgery [1]. However, robot‐specific intraoperative complications, including accidental organ injury and mechanical malfunction, have been reported [2], highlighting the need to improve the robot–human interface, instrument robustness, and surgeon training.

title: Robot‐Assisted Ileocecal Resection Using the Saroa Surgical System
text: [Introduction] Excessive force from robotic arms can cause tissue injury, a risk exacerbated by the lack of haptic feedback [3], which may partly explain limited improvement in surgical outcomes despite increased accuracy and dexterity [4]. Although robotic arms reduced pancreatic compression time during gastrectomy, a risk factor for leakage, complication rates did not decrease, and excessive instrument force was implicated [5].

title: Robot‐Assisted Ileocecal Resection Using the Saroa Surgical System
text: [Introduction] Saroa (RIVERFIELD Inc., Tokyo, Japan) is a novel robotic surgical system available in Japan for gastrointestinal, urological, thoracic (excluding cardiovascular), and gynecological procedures. It provides grip‐force feedback, and brief training improves force‐controlled grasping [6], potentially enabling gentler tissue handling. Furthermore, Saroa has three arms and requires no port docking; however, its fewer arms relative to the da Vinci system necessitate close assistant cooperation. Although Saroa has been clinically applied in urologic and thoracic surgery, its use in gastrointestinal cancer remains limited. Herein, we report a case of ileocecal resection using Saroa.

title: Robot‐Assisted Ileocecal Resection Using the Saroa Surgical System
text: [Case Presentation] A man in his late 70s with a history of appendectomy presented with hematochezia. Colonoscopy identified multiple polyps, which were resected endoscopically. Histopathologic examination revealed submucosal and vascular invasion in a lesion adjacent to the Bauhin valve (0‐Ip, Tub1, submucosal invasion of 4000 μm, v1). The patient and his family were counseled regarding the risk of lymph node metastasis and offered two management options: additional surgical resection or surveillance. The patient elected robot‐assisted surgery. Preoperative contrast‐enhanced computed tomography showed no lymphadenopathy or distant metastases, and tumor marker levels were within normal limits. Ileocecal resection with D2 lymph node dissection was planned

title: Robot‐Assisted Ileocecal Resection Using the Saroa Surgical System
text: [Case Presentation] . Ileocecal resection with D2 lymph node dissection was planned. Robotic surgery was performed following the 2024 Japanese Society for Cancer of the Colon and Rectum guidelines [7], relevant academic society guidelines, and institutional regulations. Under the general consent policy, the patient agreed to the anonymous use of clinical data for academic purposes.

title: Robot‐Assisted Ileocecal Resection Using the Saroa Surgical System
text: [Port Placement Plan and Devices] Saroa was used for robotic surgery. Optimal forceps manipulation was achieved within a 16 × 9 cm2 area extending approximately 9 cm anterior to the camera port (Figure S1). Therefore, the robotic setup was repositioned twice intraoperatively. Five ports were placed at the umbilicus and left upper, left lateral, left lower, and right lower abdomen (Figure S2). The left lateral abdominal port (initial camera port) was positioned approximately 4.5 cm lateral and slightly caudal to the umbilicus. The left upper, left lateral, and left lower abdominal ports were used to access the cecum and mid‐ascending colon (Figure 1A), whereas the right lower abdominal, umbilical, and left upper abdominal ports were used to access the hepatic flexure (Figure 1B)

text: [Port Placement Plan and Devices] . A 3D flexible scope with enabled sensory feedback and a 5:1 motion scale was used. Pneumoperitoneum was maintained using the AirSeal system with a 12‐mm access port (CONMED, Largo, FL) in the right lower abdomen. A Kii balloon blunt‐tip access system (Applied Medical, Rancho Santa Margarita, CA) was used at the umbilical port, and VersaOne 12‐mm trocars (Medtronic plc, Dublin, Ireland) were used at the remaining sites to facilitate smooth robotic arm movement.

title: Robot‐Assisted Ileocecal Resection Using the Saroa Surgical System
text: [First Setting of Saroa Arms] An assistant was positioned caudally to the patient's right side. The ileocolic artery (ICA) and vein (ICV) were retracted ventrally with fenestrated grasping forceps, and the mesentery was incised. Central serosal incision over the vessels exposed the anterior surface of the superior mesenteric vein and the ICV root (Figure 2A), which were clipped and divided. After exposure of the duodenum and anterior pancreatic surface, the ICA root was clipped and divided (Figure 2B).

text: [First Setting of Saroa Arms] Subsequently, the assistant applied ventral and outward traction to the peripheral ICA, while a second assistant retracted the central mesentery ventrally. The surgeon grasped the dorsal membrane to mobilize the ascending colon. During the lateral peritoneal incision, the first assistant introduced fenestrated forceps from the right lower abdomen to grasp and retract the adipose tissue of the ascending colon medially. The second assistant retracted the ileocolic folds from the umbilical port, while the left Saroa arm retracted the peritoneum laterally to the ascending colon.

title: Robot‐Assisted Ileocecal Resection Using the Saroa Surgical System
text: [Second Setting of Saroa Arms] To mobilize the hepatic flexure, the camera arm was inserted through the umbilical port, the right Saroa arm through the left upper abdominal port, and the left Saroa arm through the right lower abdominal port. To minimize instrument interference, the right arm was occasionally repositioned to the left lateral abdominal port. The assistant primarily retracted the colon toward the own port, while the surgeon's left hand provided lateral countertraction to facilitate incision and dissection. After mobilization, the colon containing the lesion was exteriorized through a mini‐laparotomy, resected, and reconstructed with a functional end‐to‐end anastomosis.

title: Robot‐Assisted Ileocecal Resection Using the Saroa Surgical System
text: [Second Setting of Saroa Arms] The total operative time was 351 min, including a console time of 182 min, with an estimated blood loss of 60 mL. The first bowel movement occurred on postoperative Day (POD) 5. However, paralytic ileus developed, as confirmed by physical examination and computed tomography. The ileus resolved with conservative management, oral intake resumed on POD 11, and the patient was discharged on POD 14. Pathologic examination demonstrated no residual tumor or lymph node metastasis among 11 retrieved lymph nodes.

title: Robot‐Assisted Ileocecal Resection Using the Saroa Surgical System
text: [Discussion] The Saroa surgical system provides haptic (grip) feedback, enabling delicate tissue manipulation. A preclinical study evaluated whether sensory feedback improves material stiffness estimation and grip force regulation [6]. Although force feedback did not significantly improve stiffness estimation, brief training to calibrate a 3‐N grip force resulted in superior force control under feedback‐enabled conditions [6]. In the present case, the surgeon's extensive experience with other robotic platforms may explain the lack of apparent benefit of sensory feedback. However, with more cases, Saroa's haptic feedback may reduce the risk of mesenteric injury from excessive grasping force and help shorten the learning curve for less experienced robotic surgeons.

title: Robot‐Assisted Ileocecal Resection Using the Saroa Surgical System
text: [Discussion] Because Saroa is limited to three arms, the assistant plays a critical role. In contrast, da Vinci systems utilize a fourth arm (e.g., a Tip‐Up Fenestrated Grasper) for operative field stabilization. Therefore, with Saroa, effective assistant traction and close surgeon‐assistant coordination are essential. In addition to technical skill and anatomical knowledge, surgeons must account for the limited range of motion of assistant forceps and potential collisions with robotic arms. Thus, future improvements may include optimized port placement, addition of a robotic arm, or effective use of an internal organ retractor [8]. text: [Discussion] Through this surgery, several areas requiring improvement in the Saroa system were identified. Limited availability of energy devices necessitates precise dissection with an electric scalpel, potentially prolonging surgical time and hemostasis. text: [Introduction] Research on the application of beetroot in poultry nutrition represents a promising but still developing area. Available studies indicate improvements in growth rate, feed efficiency, lipid metabolism, hematological indices, and egg quality at moderate inclusion levels.
