text: [Anti-inflammatory properties] Beetroot has gained considerable attention for its potential anti-inflammatory properties, which have been widely explored in different animals. Oral administration of fresh beetroot extract (0.25–0.5 g/kg/day) in rats markedly reduced inflammatory indices such as IL-6, TNF-α, myeloperoxidase (MPO), and NF-κB, while simultaneously enhancing non-protein sulfhydryl (NP-SH) groups and CAT activity, reflecting attenuation of inflammatory stress (El Gamal et al., 2014). Likewise, red beet juice supplementation (0.15–0.3 g/kg) significantly downregulated pro-apoptotic and inflammatory markers, including caspase-3, Bax, matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9), TNF-α, and NF-κB, further supporting the anti-inflammatory effects of beetroot-derived bioactive compounds (Raish et al., 2019).

Evidence from human studies corroborates these findings. Supplementation with beetroot extract capsules (70–200 mg/day) significantly lowered circulating inflammatory and oxidative stress markers, including TNF-α, IL-6, regulated upon activation normal T-cell expressed and secreted (RANTES), growth-regulated oncogene-α (GRO-α), and advanced oxidation protein products (AOPP), highlighting the systemic anti-inflammatory and antioxidant potential of beetroot bioactives (Pietrzkowski et al., 2010).

text: [Immunomodulatory properties] . Beetroot extract has demonstrated strong immunomodulatory activity in irradiated animal models. In γ-ray–exposed mice, oral supplementation with beetroot extract significantly enhanced splenocyte proliferation, increased hematopoietic stem cell differentiation, and restored peripheral blood cell counts. The treatment also elevated interleukin-3 (IL-3) levels and improved survival rates, indicating recovery of immune and hematopoietic functions following radiation-induced immunosuppression (Cho et al., 2017).

text: [Gastrointestinal protective properties] Consumption of red beet preparations has a substantial impact on almost every digestive tract organ, including the liver, colon, and pancreas. Red beetroot has a slight laxative effect and is widely recognized as an "internal cleansing" ingredient (Babarykin et al., 2019b). The cellulose in beets facilitates stool passage and peristalsis, which helps alleviate constipation and promotes stability for a healthy digestive system (Chaudhari & Nikam, 2015).The discernible substantial effect of red beetroot is to strengthen the stomach and intestinal system, facilitate digestion, and regulate intestinal activity (Şengül, 2021).

text: [Gastrointestinal protective properties] Celiac disease, colitis, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and Crohn's disease are important gastrointestinal illnesses that cause inflammation and damage to the intestinal lining. Research suggests that betalains may protect the stomach and intestine from disease-related inflammation and damage (Nirmal et al., 2024). Having more cellulose and fiber in the beetroot substantially decreased the occurrence of precancerous lesions, like aberrant crypt foci in the colon (Babarykin et al., 2019b; Tunnessen et al., 1969)

text: [Beetroot as a feed additive in poultry nutrition] Research on the use of beetroot in poultry feeding is steadily increasing, with emerging studies reporting potential benefits for productivity, physiological status, and product quality across poultry species. Beetroot’s rich composition of betalains, polyphenols, nitrates, and minerals provides a biochemical basis for its functional properties. Available poultry studies indicate improvements in antioxidant status, gut health-related indices, and selected performance traits following beetroot supplementation. text: [Blood biochemical and physiological responses] A study of the incorporation of beetroot juice in broiler chicks’ drinking water (30 ml/L) significantly improved hematological parameters such as PCV, RBC count, and Hb levels. Additionally, it lowered blood glucose, cholesterol, and triglyceride levels, highlighting its role in enhancing metabolic health (Grace et al., 2020). Similarly, dietary inclusion of beetroot powder and beetroot juice in broilers resulted in significant reductions in serum cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), reflecting improved lipid metabolism and liver function (Murad and Beski, 2025)

title: Beetroot (Beta vulgaris L.) as a functional feed additive in poultry nutrition: Implications for sustainable poultry production
text: [Blood biochemical and physiological responses] . In a study on Kadaknath chickens, supplementation with 25 mL of beetroot juice per liter of drinking water significantly reduced blood glucose, cholesterol, and triglyceride levels, while simultaneously improving hematological parameters such as packed cell volume (PCV) and hemoglobin (Hb), suggesting improved hematological and physiological status (Hina, 2023). Similar hypolipidemic effects of beetroot supplementation have been documented in laying hens. Dietary inclusion of beetroot powder at 0.5 % and 1 % significantly reduced serum total cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations in ISA-Brown hens, supporting its role in modulating lipid metabolism and maintaining physiological homeostasis (Ahmed et al., 2026)

text: [Blood biochemical and physiological responses] . Consistently, supplementation with red beetroot pulp and peel powder at inclusion levels ranging from 0.5 % to 1.5 % in ISA-Brown laying hens resulted in a marked reduction in serum total cholesterol levels, further reinforcing the potential of beetroot-derived products as functional feed additives for improving metabolic health in poultry (Prasetyo et al., 2024). The hypocholesterolemic effect of beetroot is attributed to the high concentration of bioactive compounds such as betalains, polyphenols, and dietary fiber, which enhance hepatic lipid metabolism, strengthen antioxidant defenses, and suppress lipid peroxidation

text: [Antioxidant and immune prospects] Beetroot contains a variety of bioactive compounds, including betalains, phenolics, and flavonoids, which exhibit potent antioxidant and immunomodulatory properties. In poultry, these compounds can scavenge free radicals, enhance endogenous antioxidant enzyme activity, and support immune system function, thereby improving overall health and resilience against oxidative stress and disease challenges (Table 8). Though direct measurements of classical antioxidant enzymes (SOD, CAT, GPx) or cytokine gene expression after beetroot supplementation are scarce in poultry, a small number of avian studies provide preliminary, supportive evidence, highlighting its potential role in scavenging free radicals and immunomodulatory impacts.

text: [Antioxidant and immune prospects] Supplementation of beetroot powder at 0.8 % to the basal diet resulted in decreased DPPH value in quils, explicating the better antioxidant capacity (Sarmiento-García et al., 2023). Likewise, incorporation of beetroot powder and juice at different dose levels in broilers and lohman brown chicken revealed enhanced total antioxidant capacity, as reflected by elevated activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD), glutathione peroxidase (GPx), and catalase (CAT). In addition, beetroot supplementation was associated with enhanced immunomodulatory responses in the supplemented groups, as evidenced by increased immunoglobulin levels and improved immune-related parameters (Murad and Beski, 2025; Vasiljeva et al., 2018)

section: Prospects of beetroot in sustainable poultry production
text: [Prospects of beetroot in sustainable poultry production] Enteric inflammatory diseases such as coccidiosis and necrotic enteritis (NE) remain among the most significant challenges to global poultry production, contributing to reduced feed efficiency, impaired growth performance, and high economic losses (Mathis et al., 2024; Shamshirgaran and Golchin, 2024). Similarly, oxidative stress in poultry reduces feed intake and growth rate, while worsening the feed conversion ratio (FCR), ultimately impairing production efficiency (Oke et al., 2024). It also damages gastrointestinal epithelial cells and tight junctions, resulting in compromised intestinal integrity, or “leaky gut,” which facilitates pathogen translocation and induces immunosuppression (Mishra and Jha, 2019)

title: Beetroot (Beta vulgaris L.) as a functional feed additive in poultry nutrition: Implications for sustainable poultry production
text: [Research gaps and recommendations] Despite promising evidence of beetroot’s antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and other health-protective effects in rodents and mammals, studies on its use in poultry remain limited. Most available work has focused mainly on growth and production performance, including serum biochemistry, rather than underlying mechanistic pathways. Information on dose response relationships, optimal inclusion levels, and possible antinutritional effects under commercial rearing conditions is also scarce. In addition, practical constraints such as variability in bioactive composition among beetroot sources, stability of bioactive compounds during processing, cost-effectiveness, and potential nitrate-related safety concerns remain insufficiently addressed in poultry nutrition research

title: Beetroot (Beta vulgaris L.) as a functional feed additive in poultry nutrition: Implications for sustainable poultry production
text: [Research gaps and recommendations] . To address these gaps, future research should prioritize: (1) dose–response studies to establish optimal inclusion levels of different beetroot forms (e.g., powder, extract, juice) for poultry; (2) long-term feeding trials under commercial production systems to evaluate performance, health status, and product quality; (3) assessment of potential antinutritional or nitrate-related effects, particularly at higher inclusion rates; (4) evaluation under environmental stress conditions, particularly heat stress, which is highly relevant to modern poultry production in tropical and subtropical regions

text: [Conclusion] This review synthesizes current mechanistic and applied evidence to demonstrate that beetroot represents a promising functional feed additive in poultry nutrition, with potential benefits for growth performance, health, and product quality. Its rich composition of bioactive compounds, betalains, polyphenols, nitrates, and dietary fibre collectively confers antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, hypolipidemic, and gut-protective effects. While most mechanistic evidence originates from mammalian and laboratory models, these conserved biological pathways suggest potential relevance to poultry

title: Beetroot (Beta vulgaris L.) as a functional feed additive in poultry nutrition: Implications for sustainable poultry production
text: [Conclusion] . By integrating phytochemical composition with physiological and productive responses, this review advances current understanding beyond individual studies and provides a structured framework for evaluating beetroot supplementation in poultry. To facilitate practical application under commercial rearing conditions, future research should focus on dose-response relationships, bioavailability, long-term safety, specific environmental evaluation, and production-scale validation. A systems-level approach integrating biochemical, molecular, and sustainability assessments will be crucial to establishing beetroot as a viable, eco-friendly feed ingredient that supports resilient and sustainable poultry production.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [abstract] Substantial oxidative stress during myocardial ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury precipitates cell death and heart failure, for which translatable redox therapies remain scarce. Here, we show that nicotinamide riboside kinase 2 (NMRK2) is rapidly upregulated after reperfusion and exerts redox protection by a previously unrecognized mechanism. We established myocardial I/R injury in mice and hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R) injury in cardiomyocytes. By elevating NADPH, restoring NAD+/NADH, increasing GSH/GSSG and activating Trx1, NMRK2 overexpression enhanced cellular antioxidant capacity and reduced oxidative damage during both myocardial I/R and cellular H/R injury. Knockdown of NAD kinase (NADK) abolished these protective effects

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [abstract] . Knockdown of NAD kinase (NADK) abolished these protective effects. Mechanistically, nucleocytoplasmic fractionation and immunofluorescence confirmed robust Yes-associated protein (YAP) nuclear entry in NMRK2-overexpressing cells; Co-IP revealed NMRK2-induced disruption of the integrin β–YAP interaction; knockdown of integrin β reduced NADK expression and increased YAP phosphorylation at Ser127; and ChIP-qPCR and luciferase assays demonstrated that YAP directly binds the NADK promoter (−1500 to −1000 bp) for its transcriptional activation. In conclusion, NMRK2 sustains redox protection by disrupting the integrin β–YAP complex and driving YAP-dependent NADK transcription, providing a readily translatable therapy against myocardial I/R injury.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Introduction] Myocardial ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury remains the foremost complication of reperfusion therapy for acute myocardial infarction [[1], [2], [3]]. While restoration of coronary blood flow limits infarct size, it simultaneously triggers an oxidative burst that depletes NADPH, overwhelms the glutathione (GSH) and thioredoxin (Trx) antioxidant systems, and precipitates cardiomyocyte death [[4], [5], [6], [7]]. Effective redox-targeted interventions applicable to this acute reperfusion window remain an urgent unmet clinical need.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Introduction] NADPH regeneration depends on NAD kinase (NADK)-mediated phosphorylation of NAD+ to NADP+ [8]; making NADK an attractive target for restoring redox balance during early reperfusion. Nicotinamide riboside kinase 2 (NMRK2), the rate-limiting enzyme of the NAD+ salvage pathway, is markedly upregulated within 24 h of reperfusion [9,10]. However, whether it governs NADK transcription or merely supports NAD+ synthesis is unknown. Consequently, the signaling cascades that acutely upregulate NADK during myocardial I/R injury remain undefined.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Introduction] Here, we demonstrate that NMRK2 mobilizes the Yes-associated protein (YAP)–NADK pathway to replenish NADPH during early reperfusion, thereby restoring the GSH and Trx antioxidant systems and attenuating injury following myocardial I/R in mice and hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R) in cardiomyocytes. We present a previously unrecognized NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis positions NADK as a signal-responsive redox node and offer a translatable strategy for acute cardioprotection against myocardial I/R injury.

text: [Evans blue/2,3,5-triphenyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) double staining] At the end of reperfusion, the LAD was re-ligated and a 1% Evans blue solution (Cat No. E2129, Sigma) was injected into the inferior vena cava to delineate the perfused myocardium. The hearts were subsequently excised, rinsed with ice-cold saline, frozen at −80 °C for 15 min, and sliced into 2-mm transverse sections. Slices were incubated in a phosphate buffer solution (pH 7.4) containing 1% TTC (Sigma, T8877) in phosphate buffer (pH 7.4, 37 °C, 30 min), fixed in 4 % paraformaldehyde (Cat No. BL539A, Biosharp, China), and photographed. Infarct size (IS) and area-at-risk (AAR) were quantified with ImageJ software (National Institutes of Health). The extent of myocardial infarction was evaluated by calculating the ratio of IS to AAR (IS/AAR).

section: NMRK2, NADK and integrin β knockdown with siRNA
text: [NMRK2, NADK and integrin β knockdown with siRNA] All small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) were synthesized by GenePharma Co., Ltd. (Suzhou, China). Cells were seeded into 6-well plates, cultured in antibiotic-free medium for 24 h, washed with PBS, and transfected with 25 nM siRNA using GP-transfect-Mate reagent. Cells were subsequently incubated at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2 for 48 h for gene expression analysis or 72 h for protein analysis and functional assays. All integrin β antibodies and siRNAs used in this study specifically targeted integrin β1.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP)] Protein–protein interactions between Integrin β and YAP were examined by Co-IP assays. Cardiomyocytes were lysed in ice-cold IP lysis buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. After centrifugation at 12,000×g for 15 min at 4 °C, equal amounts of total protein were incubated overnight at 4 °C with anti-integrin β1 antibody or control IgG, followed by incubation with protein A/G agarose beads for 2 h. The beads were then washed extensively with lysis buffer, and bound proteins were eluted by boiling in SDS sample buffer. Immunoprecipitated proteins and input lysates were analyzed by western blotting using antibodies against YAP and Integrin β.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-qPCR] ChIP assays were performed using a commercial ChIP kit (CST 9005S) to assess the binding of YAP to the NADK promoter. Cardiomyocytes were cross-linked with 1% formaldehyde at room temperature for 10 min and quenched with glycine. Cells were then lysed, and chromatin was sheared by sonication to obtain DNA fragments of approximately 200–500 bp. The fragmented chromatin was incubated overnight at 4 °C with an anti-YAP antibody or normal IgG as a negative control. Immunocomplexes were captured using protein A/G magnetic beads, washed extensively, and eluted. Cross-links were reversed, and DNA was purified and analyzed by qPCR using primers targeting the NADK promoter. Results were normalized to input DNA and presented as fold enrichment over IgG controls.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Luciferase reporter assay] To evaluate YAP-dependent transcriptional activation of the NADK promoter, truncated NADK promoter fragments (−2000/0, −1500/0, −1000/0, and −500/0 relative to the transcription start site) were cloned into a firefly luciferase reporter vector. Cardiomyocytes were co-transfected with these constructs and a YAP expression plasmid or control vector, along with a Renilla luciferase plasmid as an internal control. Luciferase activity was measured 24–48 h later using a dual-luciferase assay system. Firefly luciferase activity was normalized to Renilla luciferase activity and expressed as relative luciferase activity.

text: [Statistical analysis] Data from the GSE160516 dataset were processed using R software and various online bioinformatic tools. Experimental data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism 8 software. Continuous variables are expressed as mean ± standard error of mean (SEM). For the comparison between two groups, a two-sided unpaired Student's t-test was conducted, while differences among multiple groups were examined using either one-way or two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey's multiple comparisons test. A P value < 0.05 was deemed statistically significant.

text: [NMRK2 attenuates myocardial I/R injury by inhibiting apoptosis and oxidative stress] Successful transfection was observed 3 weeks after tail-vein delivery of AAV9-cTnT-NMRK2 (Fig. 2A, Supplement Fig. 1). Western blotting showed significantly increased NMRK2 protein expression in mouse cardiac tissue (Fig. 2B and C). Evans blue/TTC double staining demonstrated a pronounced reduction in infarct size relative to area-at-risk in NMRK2-overexpressing hearts following I/R injury (Fig. 2D–F), and H&E sections exhibited less histopathological damage of myocardium (Fig. 2G and H). title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] Earlier studies have established NMRK2 as a key enzyme in NAD+ salvage pathway and documented its metabolic importance in in heart and skeletal muscle [9,18]. NMRK2 is markedly upregulated in ischemic and hypertensive conditions, and confers protection by suppressing pro-apoptotic/fibrotic gene expression, enhancing mitochondrial function, and maintaining ATP production [19,20]. Conversely, NMRK2 deletion activates p38 MAPK, impairs metabolic adaptation, and exacerbates cardiac dysfunction [21]. These data underscore the critical role of NMRK2 in preserving energy homeostasis and redox balance under stress conditions.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] NADPH acts as a critical electron donor for major antioxidant systems and is regenerated via NADK-mediated phosphorylation of NAD+ to NADP+ [[22], [23], [24]]. While NADK is indispensable for redox homeostasis, it has traditionally been viewed as a constitutive housekeeping enzyme with no described transcriptional control in the heart [[25], [26], [27]]. Given that NMRK2 is an integrin-binding protein known to interact with the YAP pathway [15,28], it is plausible that NMRK2 modulates NADK expression through YAP signaling. YAP is increasingly recognized for its critical roles in regulating cellular metabolism, oxidative stress responses, and myocardial regeneration and remodeling. Activation of YAP stimulates cardiomyocyte proliferation and enhances cardioprotective gene expression [29,30]

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] . Activation of YAP stimulates cardiomyocyte proliferation and enhances cardioprotective gene expression [29,30]. Additionally, epigenetic modifications of the Hippo-YAP pathway promote YAP translation, support myocardial regeneration, reduce infarct severity, and improve cardiac function [31,32]. However, the signaling cascades related to NMRK2 and NADK during myocardial I/R injury remain unclear.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] Here, we performed bioinformatic analysis of the GSE160516 dataset and identified NMRK2 as one of the most prominently upregulated genes within 24 h of reperfusion, a finding corroborated in our murine I/R model. Gain-of-function experiments showed that NMRK2 overexpression reduced infarct size, preserved myocardial architecture, and attenuated oxidative damage during myocardial I/R injury. NMRK2 overexpression also lowered cleaved-caspase 3 and cleaved-PARP while increasing SOD1, SOD2, Trx1 and Prdx1 expression. In cardiomyocytes subjected to H/R, NMRK2 improved cell viability, decreased apoptosis, and curtailed ROS generation. Quantitative metabolite analysis showed that NMRK2 restored NAD+/NADH and NADPH/NADP+ ratios, elevated GSH/GSSG, and enhanced Trx1 activity

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] . Quantitative metabolite analysis showed that NMRK2 restored NAD+/NADH and NADPH/NADP+ ratios, elevated GSH/GSSG, and enhanced Trx1 activity. These protective effects are completely abolished by NADK knockdown, establishing that NMRK2-mediated antioxidant defense is NADK-dependent.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] Previous studies have reported the cardioprotective role of NMRK2 in ischemic cardiac injury and other cardiac diseases [9,10,18,21], but they primarily focused on the metabolic functions of NMRK2. Our work, however, reveals its dual role as both a metabolic and redox regulator. Our data provide the first evidence that NMRK2 rapidly upregulates NADK at the transcriptional level through a YAP-dependent mechanism., providing novel insight into NMRK2-mediated redox protection during myocardial I/R injury. As outlined in Fig. 14, NMRK2 acts as an early sensor of reperfusion stress and disrupts integrin β–YAP tethering at the cytosolic membrane, thereby releasing YAP for nuclear import. Inside the nucleus, YAP binds the NADK promoter (−1500 to −1000 bp) and trans-activates NADK transcription

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] . Inside the nucleus, YAP binds the NADK promoter (−1500 to −1000 bp) and trans-activates NADK transcription. Concomitantly, NMRK2-driven NAD+ salvage sustains NAD+/NADH balance and supplies substrate for the newly induced NADK. The resulting surge in NADP+/NADPH recharges the GSH and Trx systems, which in turn neutralize ROS and limit oxidative injury. Thus, by linking integrin-mediated mechanical signaling to YAP-dependent transcriptional control of NADPH regeneration, the NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis provides a coherent and translatable strategy for acute cardioprotection against myocardial I/R injury.Fig. 14Schematic of NMRK2-mediated cardioprotection against myocardial I/R injury

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] . 14Schematic of NMRK2-mediated cardioprotection against myocardial I/R injury. Under myocardial I/R conditions, NMRK2 reduces the integrin β–YAP interaction and facilitates YAP nuclear translocation. After entering the nucleus, YAP directly binds to the NADK promoter region (−1500 to −1000 bp) to promote NADK transcription. In parallel, NMRK2, as a key enzyme in NAD+ metabolism, contributes to maintain intracellular NAD+/NADH homeostasis and provide metabolic support for redox regulation. Upregulation of NADK enhances NADP+/NADPH production, activates the GSH and Trx antioxidant systems, and suppresses ROS accumulation and oxidative stress

text: [Discussion] There are several limitations. First, due to cellular heterogeneity of cardiac tissue and the dynamic regulation of Hippo–YAP signaling in vivo, mechanistic analyses were primarily conducted in cardiomyocyte models; validation of the NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis in primary cardiomyocytes will therefore be important to strengthen translational relevance. In addition, as this study predominantly relies on gain-of-function approaches, future in vivo loss-of-function models will be required to establish the necessity of NMRK2 in myocardial I/R injury

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] . Second, although our data support a model in which NMRK2 modulates YAP activity via integrin-associated signaling, the precise molecular interactions and signaling hierarchy linking NMRK2, integrin complexes, MST1 activity, and YAP regulation remain to be fully defined. Whether MST1 inhibition represents a direct consequence of integrin-dependent signaling or an independent regulatory input into YAP activation warrants further investigation. Moreover, as YAP functions as a transcriptional co-activator, future studies dissecting relevant TEAD isoforms and potential integrin β subtype specificity will further refine the transcriptional control of NADK expression

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] . Finally, beyond redox regulation and apoptosis, the roles of NMRK2 in mitochondrial energetics, inflammation, and long-term cardiac remodeling remain to be explored. Consistent with the temporal scope of the present study, functional analyses were limited to the early post-I/R phase, and effects on chronic remodeling and progression to heart failure will require longer-term investigation.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Conclusion] We uncover the NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis underlying myocardial I/R injury, in which NMRK2 senses reperfusion stress, disengages YAP from integrin β, and mobilizes YAP-dependent NADK transcription to replenish NADPH and restore antioxidant capacity. These findings offer a readily translatable therapeutic strategy for reducing myocardial I/R injury in high-risk patients.

title: Plasma metabolomic profiles and risk of hip fracture among US individuals: a nested case–control and prospective cohort study
text: [abstract] Hip fracture is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in ageing populations. Although emerging evidence suggests a role of metabolomic profiles in osteoporosis, their association with hip fracture risk has not been well established. We aimed to investigate plasma metabolomic profiles associated with risk of hip fracture.

title: Plasma metabolomic profiles and risk of hip fracture among US individuals: a nested case–control and prospective cohort study
text: [abstract] We conducted a nested case–control analysis (N = 1234) including 617 hip fracture cases and 617 matched controls (discovery data set) and a prospective cohort analysis including 10,031 participants (replication data set; 475 incident hip fractures) within the Nurses’ Health Study and the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study. Conditional logistic regression was applied in the case–control analysis to estimate odds ratios (ORs) per 1 SD increase in metabolite levels, and Cox proportional hazards models were used in the cohort analysis. A total of 653 plasma metabolites were examined, with false discovery rate (FDR) correction applied to control for multiple testing.

title: Plasma metabolomic profiles and risk of hip fracture among US individuals: a nested case–control and prospective cohort study
text: [abstract] In the nested–case control analysis, six metabolites related to phospholipid metabolism were consistently associated with hip fracture risk (P < 0.05), with five showing inverse associations. After FDR correction, 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC, a phosphatidylcholine metabolite, remained significantly associated with lower hip fracture risk (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.67–0.87, FDR = 0.02), and this association was replicated in the cohort analysis. At the class level, phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine were associated with reduced hip fracture risk (FDR = 0.01 and 0.05, respectively), with similar patterns in the replication cohort.

title: Plasma metabolomic profiles and risk of hip fracture among US individuals: a nested case–control and prospective cohort study
text: [abstract] Plasma metabolomic profiles, particularly phospholipid metabolism pathways and phosphatidylcholine, are associated with hip fracture risk. These findings suggest altered phospholipid metabolism may contribute to the development of hip fracture and highlight potential metabolic targets for prevention.

title: Plasma metabolomic profiles and risk of hip fracture among US individuals: a nested case–control and prospective cohort study
text: [Introduction] Hip fractures are among the most severe complications of osteoporosis and are a major cause of morbidity, long-term disability, and mortality in older adults.1, 2, 3 According to the Global Burden of Disease (2019), the prevalence of hip fractures in adults aged 55 years and older was 1191 per 100,000 people, contributing to 131 years lived with disability per 100,000 population.4 Despite advances in osteoporosis prevention and treatment strategies,5, 6, 7, 8 hip fractures continue to pose significant clinical and economic challenges, with their annual incidence is expected to double by 2050 as the population ages.1

title: Plasma metabolomic profiles and risk of hip fracture among US individuals: a nested case–control and prospective cohort study
text: [Introduction] Given the metabolic underpinnings of osteoporosis, metabolomic profiling offers a promising avenue for identifying biomarkers associated with bone health. However, single biomarkers, such as beta-C-terminal telopeptide, have shown limited ability to improve fracture prediction.9 In contrast, circulating metabolites may provide a more comprehensive assessment of bone metabolism and health, reflecting the cumulative effects of genetic and environmental influences.10

title: Plasma metabolomic profiles and risk of hip fracture among US individuals: a nested case–control and prospective cohort study
text: [Introduction] Previous studies have explored associations between plasma metabolites and bone mineral density (BMD) or osteoporosis, but most have been cross-sectional in design.9,11, 12, 13, 14 A systematic review highlighted the potential of metabolomics for clinical applications in osteoporosis; however, findings on metabolite associations with BMD remain inconsistent.15 Moreover, prospective studies investigating metabolomic profiles in relation to hip fracture risk—one of the most severe consequences of osteoporosis—are limited. While a recent study identified metabolites associated with BMD and overall osteoporotic fracture risk,16 it did not specifically examine their associations with hip fractures

text: [Introduction] To address this gap, we conducted a comprehensive investigation of plasma metabolomic profiles and hip fracture risk in a nested case–control analysis, followed by replication in a prospective cohort study within two well-established U.S. cohorts of females and males. We aimed to explore associations of individual metabolites and metabolomic classes with subsequent risk of hip fracture.

text: [Data source: nurses’ Health Study (NHS) and Health Professionals Follow-Up study (HPFS)] This study was conducted within the Nurses’ Health Study (NHS) and Health Professionals Follow-up Study (HPFS), two large prospective cohorts with ongoing biennial follow-up. The NHS was initiated in 1976 with 121,700 female registered nurses aged 30–55 years,17 and HPFS began in 1986 with 51,529 male health professionals aged 40–75 years.18 Participants have provided lifestyle and medical data through self-reported questionnaires with a follow-up rate exceeding 90% of the eligible person-time.

Chan School of Public Health (IRB24-0407; 1999P011114). At enrolment, participants received a letter being informed about the intent of the research and the IRBs allowed participants' completion of the self-administered questionnaire to be considered as implied consent. This research adheres to the 2024 Declaration of Helsinki ethical principles.

title: Plasma metabolomic profiles and risk of hip fracture among US individuals: a nested case–control and prospective cohort study
text: [Blood collection] Blood samples were collected between 1989 and 1990 from 32,826 NHS participants, with a subset of 18,743 providing a second sample between 2000 and 2001. In HPFS, blood samples were collected between 1993 and 1995 from 18,159 participants. Participants arranged for blood draws and shipped their samples via overnight courier, with 95% of samples arriving within 24 h.19 Plasma aliquots were stored in liquid nitrogen freezers at ≤−130 °C. For NHS participants, blood samples from the second collection were used. Hip fractures occurring after blood collection were identified through June 1, 2016, in NHS and January 1, 2016, in HPFS.

title: Plasma metabolomic profiles and risk of hip fracture among US individuals: a nested case–control and prospective cohort study
text: [Blood collection] A nested case–control study (N = 1234) was conducted, including 617 incident hip fracture cases (321 from NHS and 296 from HPFS), with blood samples collected prior to diagnosis. Each hip fracture case was individually matched to one control remained free of hip fracture by the end of follow-up (cumulative sampling) and controls were selected without replacement. Cases were matched 1:1 with controls based on age at blood collection (within 25 months, 90% matched within 12 months), cohort/sex, month and year of blood collection, time of day of blood draw (morning vs. other), fasting status, and ancestry (although both cohorts are >90% non-Hispanic White). For females, menopausal status and hormone therapy use at blood draw were also considered as matching factors

text: [Blood collection] A replication cohort analysis included 10,031 participants (7577 from NHS and 2454 from HPFS) from 14 prior metabolomics sub-studies for other health outcomes (Table S1).20 To avoid hip fracture case overlap, individuals with prior hip fractures at blood draw or those included in the nested case–control study were excluded from the replication analysis. The workflow for participant inclusion in the nested case–control and replication cohort studies is shown in Figure S1.

title: Plasma metabolomic profiles and risk of hip fracture among US individuals: a nested case–control and prospective cohort study
text: [Ascertainment of hip fracture] Hip fractures were identified through self-reported biennial questionnaires, with validation studies demonstrating high reliability that all reported hip fractures in a random subsample of the cohort were confirmed upon review of medical records.21 Supplemental questionnaires confirmed fracture details, including bone site, date, and trauma circumstances. High-trauma fractures (e.g., motor vehicle accidents, horseback riding, skiing) were excluded to focus on osteoporotic fractures. Only fractures of the proximal femur were classified as hip fractures.

title: Plasma metabolomic profiles and risk of hip fracture among US individuals: a nested case–control and prospective cohort study
text: [Metabolomics assays] Metabolomic profiling for the nested case–control study was conducted at Metabolon (Morrisville, NC, USA) using ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC/MS).22 All paired case and control samples were handled identically with the case–control status blinded to the assay lab and were processed in the same analytical run in random order

title: Plasma metabolomic profiles and risk of hip fracture among US individuals: a nested case–control and prospective cohort study
text: [Metabolomics assays] . Briefly, after sample accession and preparation, each sample was divided into one backup aliquot and four aliquots for the different measurement methods: 1) acidic positive ion conditions optimised for more hydrophilic compounds, 2) acidic positive ion conditions optimised for more hydrophobic compounds, 3) basic negative ion optimised conditions using a separate dedicated C18 column, and 4) negative ionisation following elution from a hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC) column. A total of 653 unique known metabolites (518 metabolites measured in NHS, and 360 metabolites measured in HPFS) were analysed after excluding those affected by delayed blood processing or with >70% missing data (Figure S2)

text: [Metabolomics assays] . In the cohort analysis, plasma metabolites were measured using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC/MS) at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard.23 After similar exclusion criteria, 45 overlapped metabolites, including 29 metabolites from the phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine classes, were included for replication. Our previous study showed that, on average, the intrapersonal stability of plasma metabolomic measurements over 10 years is similar to that of cholesterol, the most commonly used risk biomarker for cardiovascular disease.24

text: [Covariates] Covariates included demographic and anthropometric data such as date of birth, height, weight, and self-reported sex and ancestry. text: [Statistics] Statistical analyses were conducted using log-transformed and standardised metabolite data (z-scores) to enhance interpretability and comparability across metabolites. In the nested case–control analysis using cumulative sampling strategy, odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for incident hip fracture were estimated per one standard deviation increase in metabolite levels using multivariable-adjusted conditional logistic regression. To test for linearity, we modelled the association between plasma metabolites and hip fracture risk using restricted cubic splines and a Wald test P < 0.05 for the restricted cubic spline terms were considered a departure from linearity

title: Plasma metabolomic profiles and risk of hip fracture among US individuals: a nested case–control and prospective cohort study
text: [Discussion] Our study investigated the relationship between plasma metabolomic profiles and hip fracture risk in females and males. We identified an inverse association between several metabolites in the phosphatidylcholine (PC) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) classes and the risk of hip fracture in the nested case–control analysis and in the replication cohort analysis. Additionally, 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC, a specific phosphatidylcholine metabolite, was consistently associated with reduced fracture risk in the nested case–control study and was replicated in the cohort replication analysis. These findings support the hypothesis that dysregulated phospholipid metabolism contributes to fracture susceptibility.

text: [Discussion] Our study specifically focuses on prospective associations between plasma metabolites and hip fracture. A prior systematic review identified 16 studies linking metabolomic alterations to BMD and osteoporosis, many of which implicated amino acids (e.g., valine, leucine, glycine) in bone metabolism.15 These studies collectively assessed ∼400 unique metabolites in blood that were shown to be cross-sectionally associated with BMD

text: [Discussion] . However, only one study examined metabolite associations with osteoporotic fractures, and it was limited by a small sample size and a lack of specificity for hip fracture.16 Previous studies also indicate that hip fracture risk is associated with a relatively limited set of metabolites, primarily amino acids,32 tryptophan-related metabolites,33 non-esterified fatty acids,34 and lipoproteins.35 By focussing on hip fracture, a major and most severe clinical outcome associated with osteoporosis, our study advances the field by identifying phospholipid metabolism as a key pathway. A prior systematic review36 also highlighted certain pathways, such as amino acids and fatty acid metabolism, that are potentially involved in the development of osteoporosis, which are supported by the our results

text: [Discussion] The metabolites identified in our study differ in part from those previously reported in studies focused on BMD, such as the Framingham Osteoporosis Study and Hong Kong Osteoporosis Study.16 This divergence likely reflects the broader biological pathways underlying hip fracture risk, which extend beyond bone density to include factors such as falls, injury, muscle function, and cognition.37, 38, 39 In the NHS participants, we consistently found that 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC was inversely associated with fall history (Table S5). Although BMD remains a key determinant of fracture risk, it does not fully capture individual susceptibility, and certain metabolites may indicate fracture risk through BMD-independent mechanisms

text: [Discussion] . The partial overlap we observed, including phosphatidylcholine, glycine, and sulphate metabolites associated with both BMD and hip fracture, supports shared but distinct metabolic pathways.16,40 Methodological differences, such as the use of the Metabolon platform analysing over 600 metabolites in this current study compared with ∼200 in earlier studies, may also contribute to variability in findings. Collectively, these results underscore the potential translational value of metabolomic profiling for uncovering biological mechanisms and identifying complementary biomarkers that could, with further validation, enhance risk stratification for hip fracture.

text: [Discussion] Emerging evidence suggests that alterations in lipid metabolism may play a critical role in bone fragility.41,42 Phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine, the two most abundant phospholipids in mammalian cells, are synthesised via the Kennedy pathway and are integral to cell membrane integrity and signalling.43 Our findings align with prior studies showing that phosphatidylcholine levels are linked to BMD and osteoporosis based on cross-sectional designs. A lipidomic study revealed that the most significantly dysregulated class associated with low BMD was phosphatidylcholines, accounting for 25.2% of the dysregulated lipid metabolites.44 Zhang et al

text: [Discussion] In terms of individual metabolites, the identification of 1-stearoyl-2-dihomolinolenoyl-GPC (18:0/20:3n3 or 6), discovered in our nested case‒control analysis and replicated in the cohort analysis as a key metabolite, might be a biomarker and potential intervention target to prevent hip fracture. A prior study revealed associations between 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC, physical activity, and body mass index, which may play a role in mediating the health effects of physical activity and muscle strength on hip fractures.59 Using multimodal data, Shomorony et al. reported that 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC is also involved in metabolic health, which is closely correlated with bone and muscle health.60,61 More data on this specific metabolite and health profiles are needed.

We replicated our findings using two large, well-characterised cohorts with long-term follow-up, coupled with the integration of high-throughput metabolomics.

text: [Discussion] Even though this is a prospective analysis, we cannot fully exclude the role of residual or unmeasured confounding. Residual confounding due to measurement error in self-reported covariates, such as alcohol intake and other lifestyle factors, cannot be excluded. More mechanistic studies are needed to further shed light on mechanisms underlying our findings. While our results were partially replicated in the cohort analysis, future studies should aim to replicate these findings in other populations and investigate whether incorporating metabolite measures, alongside established risk factors such as BMD and FRAX scores, can improve fracture risk assessment

text: [Discussion] . As these clinical prediction scores and BMD data were not routinely available in the NHS and HPFS cohorts, our study primarily focused on identifying metabolites associated with hip fracture risk. Future studies are needed to elucidate the roles of BMD in the association between identified metabolites and risk of hip fracture. Moreover, further data are required to evaluate and compare the hip fracture prediction capacity of plasma metabolomics with other omics technologies, including polygenic risk scores and proteomics.70 Additionally, the availability of plasma metabolite measurements at a single timepoint limits our ability to assess how changes in specific metabolite classes and individual metabolite concentrations over time may affect the outcome of hip fracture

Further studies are needed to explore the underlying mechanisms and evaluate the effect of phosphatidylcholine as an intervention to prevent hip fractures.

title: Plasma metabolomic profiles and risk of hip fracture among US individuals: a nested case–control and prospective cohort study
text: [Discussion] In conclusion, this study provides the prospective evidence that altered phospholipid metabolism, particularly phosphatidylcholine, is associated with reduced hip fracture risk in both females and males. Our identification of 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC as a key protective metabolite implicates specific metabolic pathways in hip fracture risk. These findings highlight the potential of plasma metabolomics in identifying novel risk factors for hip fractures and may inform the development of metabolite-based interventions for fracture prevention in ageing populations.

title: TNF-alpha: Roles in pathogenesis and therapeutics in cancer
text: [abstract] Tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) is a pleiotropic cytokine that can both facilitate tumor progression and directly mediate tumor cell killing. This dual role creates a conundrum in which TNF can be either beneficial or detrimental for a tumor, depending on the context. Herein, we describe the history of the cytokine, the cases in which TNF-α has been considered as a cancer immunotherapy, and the toxicities that can manifest from its use. We also add context to its activity, particularly in T cells (via the engagement of TNF receptors) as well as the epigenetic and immunoregulatory pathways that are elicited

title: TNF-alpha: Roles in pathogenesis and therapeutics in cancer
text: [abstract] . Furthermore, we highlight the fundamental differences in the transcriptional and translational regulation of this cytokine, which plays a significant role in the context of malignancy and potential success of immunotherapies. This review aims to provide insight and background on molecular switches, cellular context, and TNF receptor dynamics that determine the role of TNF-α as both tumor suppressor and promoter in different models, which is essential for deriving maximal benefit from TNF therapies.

section: History of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and establishment of tumor necrosis factor superfamily
text: [History of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and establishment of tumor necrosis factor superfamily] Inflammation has been considered not only a hallmark of cancer, characterized by the release of proinflammatory cytokines from the tumor and its microenvironment, but has also been implicated in the progression of cancer itself (1). One proinflammatory cytokine implicated in this phenomenon is tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), a multifaceted cytokine originally termed as an endotoxin upon its discovery in the 1960s. Formerly known as “Coley’s mixed toxins,” TNF-α was hypothesized to be a bacterial byproduct that had the ability to regress tumors. Later, it was demonstrated that the tumor regression was independent of bacterial influence and was actually a result of a signaling molecule produced by immune cells as a response to the bacterial insult that led to tumor necrosis (2, 3, 4, 5)

title: TNF-alpha: Roles in pathogenesis and therapeutics in cancer
section: History of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and establishment of tumor necrosis factor superfamily
text: [History of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and establishment of tumor necrosis factor superfamily] . Finding the cellular source of TNF-α was of importance, as this could provide insight into its regulation and how it could be harnessed as a therapeutic. Groups eventually determined that one cellular source of TNF-α was macrophages, which was consistent within the context of previous research showing that bacterial infection triggered TNF-α production (3). However, it was subsequently shown that TNF could also be produced by B cells. Although the two factors originating from different cell sources were considered to be effectively synonymous, subsequent studies demonstrated only 30% amino acid homology between the two molecules from the macrophages and B cells (6, 7). The existence of a common surface receptor led to their renaming as TNF-α and TNF-β, respectively

text: [History of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and establishment of tumor necrosis factor superfamily] . The existence of a common surface receptor led to their renaming as TNF-α and TNF-β, respectively. These are distinguished by their cellular source (TNF-α commonly being produced by macrophages and monocytes, whereas TNF-β is commonly produced by activated T and B lymphocytes and NK cells) as well as their overall purpose and regulation (8, 9). Previous research determined that malignant cell lines had the ability to produce both cytokines. However, cell lines that produced TNF-β mRNA were able to secrete the cytokine. Conversely, cell lines producing TNF-α mRNA did not necessarily release it, suggesting that TNF-α gene expression may be controlled predominantly at the post-transcriptional level (9, 10, 11)

Subsequent work has gone into understanding how both cytokines differ, and how they both play a role in cancer progression and regression considering their cytotoxic abilities. TNF-α plays a dual role in cancer progression and regression, whereas the activity of TNF-β in cancer has mostly been associated with influencing growth, such as promoting proliferation and mediating antiproliferative effects in different tumor cell lines (9). While both cytokines play an important role in the context of cancer, the scope of this review will focus on TNF-α activity in particular. Research on these cytokines revolutionized the field of cancer immunology research and provided hope for the use of this cytokine as a therapeutic

Research on these cytokines revolutionized the field of cancer immunology research and provided hope for the use of this cytokine as a therapeutic. However, the decades since its discovery were spent unraveling the multiple ways in which TNF-α plays a role in cellular processes, and the intricacies in which TNF-α can act as both a protumor and antitumor agent, with multifaceted roles in mediating apoptosis, proliferation, survival, hematopoiesis, and cell differentiation (12).

section: History of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and establishment of tumor necrosis factor superfamily
text: [History of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and establishment of tumor necrosis factor superfamily] TNF-α was subsequently shown to be a multifunctional cytokine normally expressed as a type II transmembrane protein, proteolytically cleaved into its soluble form by TNF-α converting enzyme with the ability to signal through two different receptors, which are differentially expressed on many cell types. Tumor necrosis factor receptor 1 (TNFR1) is expressed on virtually all nucleated cells, whereas TNFR2 is present on specific subsets of cell types, including immune cell subsets, such as regulatory T cells (Tregs), CD8+ T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), as well as endothelial cells and fibroblasts (13). TNFR1 contains a prodeath signaling domain, whereas TNFR2 is mostly associated with preventing apoptosis and a survival gene/protein expression profile (14, 15, 16)

section: History of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and establishment of tumor necrosis factor superfamily
text: [History of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and establishment of tumor necrosis factor superfamily] . Depending on the form that TNF-α is in, it can trigger different cellular processes. For example, while both receptors have the ability to be activated by both soluble and membrane-bound TNF-α, TNFR1 demonstrates a preference for the soluble form of TNF-α, whereas TNFR2 is only fully activated by the membrane-found form of the cytokine (17, 18). One cellular process that is exclusive to TNF-α is its ability to be directly cytolytic (19, 20, 21). Cellular apoptosis can be triggered by a variety of pathways, including cellular damage, the subsequent activation of procaspases and caspases that lead to collapse of the cytoskeleton, disassembly of the nuclear envelope, and fragmentation of DNA (22).

title: TNF-alpha: Roles in pathogenesis and therapeutics in cancer
section: History of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and establishment of tumor necrosis factor superfamily
text: [History of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and establishment of tumor necrosis factor superfamily] TNF-α can trigger apoptosis by binding to receptors belonging to the TNF superfamily, most notably TNFR1, DR3, FAS-R (CD95), TNF-related apoptosis–inducing ligand receptor 1 (TRAIL-R1, also known as DR4), and TRAIL-R2 (also known as DR5) (23). These receptors can bind TNF-α directly (e.g., TNFR1) or can bind another member of the TNF superfamily, such as Fas ligand or TRAIL. Fas ligand is predominantly found on activated T cells, B cells, and NK cells, and to a much lesser extent on dendritic cells and tumor cells. Its expression is tightly regulated and transcriptionally controlled by factors, such as NF-κB and AP-1, as well as post-transcriptional regulation by microRNAs (24)

text: [History of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and establishment of tumor necrosis factor superfamily] . TRAIL is commonly found on various immune cells, such as NK cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, and T cells, mostly in the context of activation and significantly enhanced after exposure to interferon-gamma (25). Apoptosis, in the context of these receptors, is triggered by the presence of death domains. TNF-associated death domain, along with Fas-associated death domain and receptor-interacting protein (RIP), are intracellular, cytoplasmic components that form a complex and trigger caspase activation (26). Caspase activation is a tightly regulated process that requires the building of a death signaling complex and requires multiple forms of activation; otherwise, the process is aborted through the induction of cellular inhibitor of apoptosis proteins (cIAPs) (27, 28)

section: History of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and establishment of tumor necrosis factor superfamily
text: [History of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and establishment of tumor necrosis factor superfamily] . In addition to caspase activation, signaling through any of these proapoptotic receptors leads to transcription factor activation. The cellular response to TNF-α binding to TNFR1 (or any of the death receptors) is to modulate cellular activity by activating canonical NF-κB pathways. However, unsuccessful NF-κB transcription subsequently leads to the development of the death signaling complex, composed of TNF receptor–associated factor (TRAF2), TNF-associated death domain, and RIP proteins, followed by cytoplasmic apoptotic complex II leading to caspase activation (29). In other contexts, when the steps leading to apoptotic cell death are interrupted or not successful, the cell can undergo cellular necrosis (termed necroptosis) following TNF-α exposure

In this case, necroptosis is commonly associated with the rapid lysis of cells and the release of danger-associated molecular patterns, causing an augmentation of the inflammatory response taking place. However, in the context of TNF-α exposure (which already implies a highly inflammatory setting), necroptosis acts as a fast-acting way to get rid of these highly transcriptionally regulated inflammatory cells and therefore, diminish the robust inflammatory reaction (30). TNF-α can also lead to necrosis directly, which is a more unregulated process by virtue of the loss of cell membrane integrity

TNF-α can also lead to necrosis directly, which is a more unregulated process by virtue of the loss of cell membrane integrity. In these cases, TNF-α can lead to necrosis through the induction of NOX1 (a nonmitochondrial NADPH oxidase), which leads to the production of reactive oxygen species that can cause necrotic cell death (31).

section: History of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and establishment of tumor necrosis factor superfamily
text: [History of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and establishment of tumor necrosis factor superfamily] TNFR2 signaling is most associated with protective and anti-inflammatory functionalities. However, its activity is more complex. For example, TNFR2 has been suggested to activate TNFR1 pathways by sequestering TRAF2–cIAP1/2 complexes that induce canonical NF-κB activation, therefore antagonizing TNFR1 activation in the process and leading to cell death (32, 33). Furthermore, TNFR2 can trigger pathways involved in survival and cell migration directly through its activation of noncanonical NF-κB signaling. In addition, TNFR2 has been suggested to play a role in CD8+ T-cell activation, influencing costimulation, cell viability, and enhancing T-cell receptor (TCR)–induced apoptosis (34).

title: TNF-alpha: Roles in pathogenesis and therapeutics in cancer
section: TNF-α as an immunotherapy and toxicities
text: [TNF-α as an immunotherapy and toxicities] Research heavily focused on the mechanistic intricacies of TNF-α signaling and its therapeutic potential, particularly after the observed necrosis it caused in tumors. In vitro studies demonstrated its ability to inhibit growth and induce cytotoxicity in multiple malignant cell lines. In addition, in vivo studies showed that delivery of this cytokine decreased tumor progression and promoted tumor clearance (35, 36, 37, 38). This suggested that TNF-α could be a promising therapeutic candidate alone or in combination with other agents to improve clinical outcomes. Indeed, preclinical studies showed that systemic TNF-α was able to improve certain conventional chemotherapeutic efficacy in vitro and in vivo (39, 40).

title: TNF-alpha: Roles in pathogenesis and therapeutics in cancer
section: TNF-α as an immunotherapy and toxicities
text: [TNF-α as an immunotherapy and toxicities] The initial enthusiasm surrounding TNF-α as a therapeutic was subsequently subdued because of the significant toxicities that occurred after systemic delivery in human subjects. Not only did systemic TNF-α administration cause significant adverse effects, but also it was shown to be largely ineffective at reducing tumor progression

title: TNF-alpha: Roles in pathogenesis and therapeutics in cancer
section: TNF-α as an immunotherapy and toxicities
text: [TNF-α as an immunotherapy and toxicities] . Clinical trials performed in the 1980s and 1990s used TNF-α as both monotherapy and in combination with conventional chemotherapy such as alkylating agents (BCNU, carboplatin) (41) and antineoplastic or antitumor antibiotics (actinomycin D, doxorubicin) (42, 43, 44, 45); however, neither of these trials was able to reach their clinical endpoints since considerable toxicities were observed immediately after delivery, necessitating cessation of its administration (46, 47, 48). Even in trials where administered quantities of TNF-α in the periphery were low and approximated endogenous levels, significant adverse effects were observed, including hypotension, metabolic acidosis, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, neurotoxicity, respiratory arrest, hyperglycemia, and hyperkalemia (46)

section: TNF-α as an immunotherapy and toxicities
text: [TNF-α as an immunotherapy and toxicities] . TNF-α was also shown to cause cachexia, a metabolic condition characterized by loss and wasting of skeletal muscle, anemia, reduced caloric intake, and altered/decreased immune function (49), leading to TNF-α acquiring the nickname of “cachexin.” At this time, there are no drugs approved for the prevention or treatment of cachexia, only supportive care in terms of dietary modifications, physical therapy, and, in extreme cases, the use of systemic corticosteroids (50). Phase II clinical studies of TNF-α as monotherapy for the treatment of cancer were similarly disappointing. While these focused on advanced and metastatic cases of disease, no complete responses were observed, partial responses were rare, and significant adverse events were also common

text: [TNF-α as an immunotherapy and toxicities] . Given the lack of efficacy and the substantial toxicities that subjects experienced, these studies significantly dampened previous enthusiasm for TNF-α as a means of tumor control (38, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 57).

title: TNF-alpha: Roles in pathogenesis and therapeutics in cancer
section: TNF-α as an immunotherapy and toxicities
text: [TNF-α as an immunotherapy and toxicities] To circumvent the immune-related adverse events observed following TNF-α therapy, different attempts were made to decrease its toxicity by genetically modifying the cytokine or by localizing the delivery in order to prevent systemic effects. Some groups turned to isolated limb perfusion to localize and concentrate the effects of TNF-α in patients with melanoma or sarcoma (58, 59). In addition, other groups turned to oncolytic viruses encoding transgenic TNF-α to localize its delivery (35, 60). Despite efforts to localize the cytokine to achieve maximum efficacy with minimal toxicity, studies still showed no significant impact on tumor growth, along with significant adverse events, raising the question of whether TNF-α is a viable anticancer agent

text: [TNF-α as an immunotherapy and toxicities] . Much research has been done in this regard, which demonstrated certain scenarios where TNF-α can act as both a pro- or antitumor agent, depending not only on the timing of administration but also on the context of the malignancy.

section: TNF-α as a pro- and antitumor agent
text: [TNF-α as a pro- and antitumor agent] Despite the initial evidence that TNF-α, as it was aptly named, would primarily cause necrosis of tumors, preclinical and clinical studies observed more of a double-edged sword in which TNF-α could both promote tumor clearance and advance tumor progression (Fig. 1). Primarily, by virtue of TNF-α being a potent proinflammatory cytokine, chronic release of TNF-α can contribute to tumorigenesis. In addition, more aggressive forms of malignancy, particularly breast cancer, have been characterized by having higher levels of TNF-α, and individuals with lower levels of systemic TNF-α responded better to therapy (61, 62)

title: TNF-alpha: Roles in pathogenesis and therapeutics in cancer
section: TNF-α as a pro- and antitumor agent
text: [TNF-α as a pro- and antitumor agent] As previously discussed, the anticancer qualities of TNF-α are primarily its direct cytotoxicity. TNF-α can trigger cell death by triggering signaling cascades after engaging with TNFR1. However, TNF-α can also induce necrotic cell death via activation of NADPH oxidase, leading to the generation of reactive oxygen species. Despite this cytokine having the ability to trigger cell death directly, subsequent research has shown that the main mechanism by which TNF-α achieves any antitumor efficacy is by recruiting and activating other cell types.

title: TNF-alpha: Roles in pathogenesis and therapeutics in cancer
section: TNF-α as a pro- and antitumor agent
text: [TNF-α as a pro- and antitumor agent] Differential expression of the two TNF-α receptors present within the tumor can affect what role TNF-α plays in terms of being protumor or antitumor. High TNFR1 expression on tumor cells is most commonly associated with a “tumor suppressor” environment where TNF-α binding to TNFR1 can lead to cell death directly. However, when there is high expression of TNFR2 on tumor cells, as is the case for certain types of malignancy, including glioblastoma, kidney renal clear cell carcinoma, lower grade brain glioma, pancreatic adenocarcinoma, stomach adenocarcinoma, and testicular germ cell tumors, this environment is more suggestive of being “tumor promoter” since abundant TNFR2 signaling can enhance survival and proliferative pathways (65).

title: TNF-alpha: Roles in pathogenesis and therapeutics in cancer
section: TNF-α and its modulation of T cells
text: [TNF-α and its modulation of T cells] TNF-α plays a vital role in enhancing T-cell responses, particularly within the TME. TNF-α has been shown to promote CD8+ T-cell infiltration of tumors, commonly correlated with improved outcomes and responses to therapy since these cells are directly cytotoxic (66). However, TNF-α has also been shown to promote the clonal expansion of activated effector T cells and enhance activation of naive T cells, potentially by virtue of both canonical (survival and function) and noncanonical NF-κB activation (enhances T-cell activation and expansion) (67, 68)

section: TNF-α and its modulation of T cells
text: [TNF-α and its modulation of T cells] . Since antigen-mediated TCR activation only weakly activates NF-κB activation, TNF-α has been suggested to also act as a costimulatory signal to not only enhance TCR activation directly but also to lower the threshold necessary to initiate TCR signaling (69, 70). Altogether, evidence has shown that this potent proinflammatory signal not only improves T-cell infiltration into the tumor but also significantly enhances T-cell function. This is in comparison to the dual role it plays in Tregs, as it can both downregulate their immunosuppressive qualities, while also facilitating Treg accumulation within the tumor. While TNF-α plays this role on Tregs directly, it also has been reported to have the ability to increase resistance to Treg-mediated suppression (71).

text: [TNF-α and its modulation of T cells] In terms of survival, TNF-α also plays a dual role when it comes to T-cell activity. While TNFR1 signaling can trigger cell death directly, and T cells containing TNFR1 can die from its engagement of TNF-α, they also contain TNFR2, which is a prosurvival receptor capable of mediating not only survival but also enhancing proliferation (Fig. 2). However, the interplay between both receptors in T cells specifically is highly complex

title: TNF-alpha: Roles in pathogenesis and therapeutics in cancer
section: Transcriptional and translational regulation of TNF-α in the context of malignancy
text: [Transcriptional and translational regulation of TNF-α in the context of malignancy] While a main investigational focus is TNF-α production and secretion from immune cells as a response to malignancy, TNF-α production and release is also severely impacted in a variety of malignant cell types. For example, T-cell–based malignancies often have overexpression or mutations in signaling molecules affecting the NF-κB pathway, which inevitably affect TNF-α production and secretion. Similarly, TNF-α promoter regions can be modified or hypomethylated in some cancers and hematologic malignancies, as well as superenhanced in some T-cell lymphomas, driving high expression of TNF-α and other cytokines (75, 76).

section: Transcriptional and translational regulation of TNF-α in the context of malignancy
text: [Transcriptional and translational regulation of TNF-α in the context of malignancy] TNF-α mRNA contains AU-rich elements (AREs) in the 3′ untranslated region that target it for rapid degradation; this is what prevents it from accumulating inside of the cell and what allows for TNF-α to lack mRNA stability. Normally, transacting proteins that bind AREs stabilize or destabilize the transcript depending on the context. Three different ARE-binding proteins have been identified specifically for TNF-α ARE: tristetraprolin, a lipopolysaccharide-inducible protein that destabilizes the TNF-α mRNA, TIAR, and related protein TIA-1, which also bind the ARE, and are related with acting as a translational silencer (77, 78)

These ARE-binding proteins are always active, except in the context of activation, which leads to ARE repression and allows the TNF-α mRNA to stabilize in order to be translated and subsequently secreted from the cell (Fig. 3) (79). This pathway, however, has been observed to be dysregulated by affecting specific ARE-binding proteins, which stabilizes TNF-α mRNA and increases protein expression. While this would seem to be detrimental in the context of this malignancy because of the antitumor effects, the hypothesis is that increased TNF-α production leads to NF-κB activation, which facilitates growth and survival

text: [Transcriptional and translational regulation of TNF-α in the context of malignancy] In the context of T cells, transcriptional and translational control of TNF-α production is also tightly regulated and significantly affects the cellular responses that are triggered. For example, CD8+ T cells, in particular, employ several mechanisms by which they drive cytokine production upon T-cell activation. Studies have found large amounts of preformed TNF-α mRNA in resting CD8+ T cells, which can drive rapid translation upon activation by phosphorylation of eukaryotic initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) by mechanistic target of rapamycin, leading to its binding to TNF-α mRNA 5′ structures, which facilitates formation of the preinitiation complex, allowing it to be translated by ribosomes (81, 82)

This effect was observed exclusively in activated T cells, whereas in resting T cells without antigenic challenge, eIF4E was primarily expressed in its unphosphorylated isoform, repressing translation of the TNF-α mRNA (83). This means that to mount a potent TNF-α response, activated T cells need incredible post-translational aid in order to translate the preformed TNF-α mRNA both by destabilizing the formed mRNA through its ARE region, and by using PKC-mediated mechanistic target of rapamycin phosphorylation of eIF4E to drive the formation of the ribosome complex (82). This is particularly impactful when we consider the timing of these events and the transient presence of the RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) in mediating cytokine release

text: [TNF-α sensitization in the context of immunotherapies] The capacity of TNF as a protumor and antitumor agent could rely on the timing of its activity. Tumor cells can become resistant to TNF-α cytotoxicity through NF-κB transcription leading to increased cell survival or NF-κB–driven resistance to apoptosis. This could also be the reason why anti-TNF-α agents have gained popularity at not only decreasing TNF-α-mediated toxicities but also eliciting prolonged disease stabilization since they bypass this triggering of prosurvival NF-κB signaling (64, 87, 88, 89). section: TNF-α sensitization in the context of immunotherapies
text: [TNF-α sensitization in the context of immunotherapies] . Anti-TNF-α therapies (e.g., infliximab, etanercept) sequester soluble TNF-α, thus preventing signaling cascades that promote survival. Alternatively, cancer cells with prolonged exposure to TNF-α are sensitized and require another mechanism to trigger apoptosis independent of TNF-α signaling. Another hallmark of chronic TNF-α signaling within the tumor that sensitizes tumor cells is increased recruitment of macrophages, which can increase PD-L1 expression on tumor cells, leading to increased T-cell exhaustion and a decrease in their efficacy (90, 91).

text: [TNF-α sensitization in the context of immunotherapies] In addition, chronic TNF-α secretion within the tumor leads to the induction of inhibitory cell types, such as MDSCs and Tregs, both of which contribute to dampening antitumor immune responses (92, 93). This could imply that the tumor cells themselves are not being sensitized by the presence of the cytokine, but rather that chronic TNF-α signaling leads to an immunosuppressive TME that inhibits the natural mechanisms of TNF-α-mediated killing. Last, a characteristic of TNF-α that influences the sensitivity of cancer cells to immunotherapy is that prolonged exposure to the cytokine could make cancer cells dependent on TNF signaling for survival, therefore negating benefit from TNF-α secretion by immune cells into the tumor and bypassing TNF-α-mediated cell killing (94)

title: TNF-alpha: Roles in pathogenesis and therapeutics in cancer
section: TNF-α sensitization in the context of immunotherapies
text: [TNF-α sensitization in the context of immunotherapies] What becomes more evident is the pattern of balance when it comes to TNF-α. Early secretion of TNF-α sensitizes tumor cells to TNF-α-mediated killing by binding to TNFR1, killing them directly. TNF-α can also cause necroptosis through the RIP kinase pathway (95). However, too much TNF-α within the tumor leads to NF-κB resistance to apoptosis (96). Similarly, localized TNF-α within the tumor sensitizes tumor cells to immune attacks and chemotherapy. However, too much TNF-α (as occurs in chronic inflammation) can lead to tumorigenesis and promote restructuring of the TME to promote metastasis (64). This suggests that acute exposure to TNF-α, in early phase immune response to cancer, generally promotes immune cell activation and tumor cell death

This suggests that acute exposure to TNF-α, in early phase immune response to cancer, generally promotes immune cell activation and tumor cell death. However, chronic exposure to TNF-α, particularly in established tumors, normally leads to exhaustion, immune suppression, and enhances resistance mechanisms (97). This might be difficult to exploit therapeutically, considering that TNF-α′s systemic responses build with time. Therefore, high levels of TNF-α within the TME could create a vicious cycle, whereby tumor cells die, eventually evade immune attack, and lead to eventual dampening of the immune response by prolonged TNF-α exposure. One way to circumvent this is to block the NF-κB pathway to prevent sensitization of cells to the effects of TNF-α prior to immune activation

text: [TNF-α sensitization in the context of immunotherapies] In a therapeutic setting, TNF-α blockers are used for treatment of a wide variety of inflammatory disorders, although much more work is necessary to understand the role these inhibitors play in cancer progression. Whether these TNF-α blocking agents can synergize with conventional immunotherapies or be complementary to the standard of care remains an open question. These therapies, however, come with many unexplored phenomena. While they might be helpful in alleviating chronic TNF-α exposure, while retaining the initial benefit of acute TNF-α release within the tumor, little is known about the effects of long-term use of TNF-α inhibitors

There are a variety of Food and Drug Administration–approved TNF-α blockers, ranging from monoclonal antibodies, secreted forms of TNF-α receptors, and even PEGylated anti-TNF-α agents. However, the question remains on whether administering these TNF-α blockers could enhance tumor progression long term, or if they themselves would promote cancer initiation. Recent studies measuring cancer risk in adults with rheumatoid arthritis taking TNF-α inhibitors showed that TNF-α inhibition was significantly associated with increased risk for certain malignancies, such as follicular lymphoma, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, and nonmelanoma skin cancer (98, 99)

section: Molecular switches and cellular context that influence TNF as a tumor suppressor/promoter
text: [Molecular switches and cellular context that influence TNF as a tumor suppressor/promoter] Understanding when TNF-α can act as a tumor suppressor versus a tumor promoter is important, but of equal importance is to assess what types of therapies can synergize with TNF-α activity or instances in which we can differentiate TNF-α accumulation as being beneficial from detrimental. Early on, when TNF-α is acting as a tumor suppressor and initiating cancer cell killing, it would be appropriate to combine it with sensitizers, such as SMAC (second mitochondrial-derived activator of caspases) mimetics inhibitors and inhibitors of apoptosis protein (IAPs) to maximize cell killing (107). In addition, permissive enhancement of TNF-α signaling during initial T-cell immunotherapy, such as checkpoint blockade, could boost immune killing (108)

Comparatively, in the context of large amounts of TNF-α already present in the tumor and in a chronic exposure setting, inhibitors of NF-κB signaling would ensure cells stay vulnerable to TNF-α-mediated killing, and in other cases, stopping TNF-α altogether would be more appropriate, in which case, anti–TNF-α therapies can be used (109). In this context, lowering TNF-α concentrations can also be impactful if patients experience immune-related adverse events during checkpoint therapy or other forms of immunotherapy suggestive of damaging amounts of TNF-α within the tumor leading to systemic toxicities.
