text: [Molecular switches and cellular context that influence TNF as a tumor suppressor/promoter] Predictive factors for TNF-α activity as a tumor promoter or a suppressor include post-translational modification of key factors that affect the TNF-α signaling pathways, such as ubiquitination of RIPK1, which inherently activates the NF-κB prosurvival pathway (Fig. 4) (110). The presence of IAPs can also be a good negative predictor for efficacy, since they will innately promote cell survival by preventing apoptosis (111). Predictive factors for TNF-α being a tumor suppressor include having higher expression of TNFR1 present on tumor cells, which can lead to higher levels of TNF-mediated cytotoxicity, although some studies have shown that increased TNFR1 presence has been correlated to negative prognosis for some cancer models (64)

These might be good indicators by which one can categorize which patients would benefit from certain immunotherapies that inherently produce large amounts of TNF-α, and in which cases these therapies might cause toxicities or would be detrimental. title: TNF-alpha: Roles in pathogenesis and therapeutics in cancer
text: [Conclusion] TNF-α is a well-studied pleiotropic cytokine with influence in cellular processes that extend to everything from growth and survival to cell death. This review has summarized the cellular processes and molecular switches that influence whether tumors are more or less susceptible to TNF-α–mediated killing. There are several biomarkers that one can consider whenever determining if a patient would respond to TNF-α–based therapies, mainly surrounding controlling the activation of NF-κB, cIAPs, and the endogenous immune infiltration present in the tumor. Comparatively, there are ways to infer whether a patient with cancer would not benefit from TNF-α therapy and would be at higher risk for immune-related adverse events

title: TNF-alpha: Roles in pathogenesis and therapeutics in cancer
text: [Conclusion] We also explored topics centralized on whether the timing of TNF-α delivery would enhance or diminish immune activity. Previous studies show that acute TNF-α activation is significant in enhancing cell-based immunotherapy activity and synergizes with immune checkpoint blockade, two therapies routinely used in patients today. However, chronic exposure to TNF-α, which would happen after prolonged immune activation within the tumor or because of an endogenous amount of TNF-α within the tumor already, would prove to be detrimental to these therapies. Moreover, TNF-α in this context would be harmful and would potentially act as a tumor promoter, driving survival, angiogenesis, and metastatic phenotypes.

title: TNF-alpha: Roles in pathogenesis and therapeutics in cancer
text: [Conclusion] Overall, while TNF-α remains a double-edged sword in its role in cancer progression and regression, previous and ongoing research has helped refine the instances in which one can understand the nuances of TNF-α–based cancer therapies, particularly in the context of localized delivery with new and emerging technology.

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: [abstract] Targeted protein degradation (TPD) has emerged as a powerful approach for eliminating disease-associated proteins by harnessing the ubiquitin–proteasome system. Biologic degraders are modular protein chimeras that recruit ubiquitin machinery to target proteins. They offer high specificity, modular design, and the ability to access targets traditionally considered challenging for small-molecule ligands. This review surveys the expanding landscape of biologic TPD modalities, highlighting E3 ligase– and E2 enzyme–based degraders, TRIM-Away and TRIMbody-Away systems, and diverse biologics-based ligands that serve as target-binding components. We also discuss emerging peptide-based strategies, which bridge biologic and synthetic approaches

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: The ubiquitin–proteasome system is responsible for degrading approximately 80% of intracellular proteins and plays a critical role in maintaining proteostasis (1). In this pathway, a cascade of enzymes, including the E1-activating enzyme, E2-conjugating enzyme, and E3 ubiquitin ligase, mediates the activation and conjugation of ubiquitin to target proteins. Following ubiquitination, these proteins are directed to the proteasome, where they are cleaved into short peptides. E3 ubiquitin ligases confer substrate specificity either through dedicated substrate-binding proteins within multisubunit complexes or, in the case of single-unit E3 ligases, by directly recognizing and recruiting protein targets (2, 3)

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: . The growing field of intracellular targeted protein degradation (TPD) leverages this system through small molecules or protein-based approaches to induce the degradation of proteins of interest (POIs) (3, 4). An alternative degradation mechanism involves engaging cell surface receptors to direct POIs to the lysosome. This approach has been recently reviewed elsewhere and will not be discussed further in this review (5, 6).

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: TPD was first described by Crews and Deshaies in 2001 (7). In this seminal study, the authors synthesized a chimeric molecule composed of an IκBα phosphopeptide, recognized by the Skp1–Cullin–F box E3 ligase complex, and ovalicin, a methionine aminopeptidase-2 inhibitor. This molecule, dubbed “proteolysis-targeting chimera” (PROTAC), induced the degradation of methionine aminopeptidase-2 via the ubiquitin–proteasome system (7). This work demonstrated that induced proximity to an E3 ligase could effectively promote target protein degradation. Over the following 2 decades, PROTAC research shifted heavily toward small-molecule PROTACs (smPROTACs), which are heterobifunctional compounds composed of an E3 ligase–binding ligand, a POI-binding ligand, and a linker

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: . smPROTACs targeting the androgen receptor and estrogen receptor entered clinical trials around 2019 as cancer therapeutics (3). Similarly, molecular glues, which are small molecules that stabilize weak or transient interactions between E3 ligases and their targets, have also been successful in promoting POI degradation (8, 9). Despite their promise, smPROTACs and molecular glues face several challenges, including the potential for off-target and toxic effects driven by polypharmacology, the need for both the E3 ligase and POI to be ligandable in the case of smPROTACs, and the lack of well-defined design principles for molecular glues (4)

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: [Biologics-based heterobifunctional degraders] Biologics-based heterobifunctional degraders are modular protein chimeras designed to induce TPD. Like their small-molecule counterparts, biologic degraders harness the ubiquitin–proteasome system by recruiting E3 ligases to degrade POIs. A number of E3 ligases have been shown to support TPD, with smPROTACs commonly engaging cereblon and von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) (10). Nonetheless, a potential limitation of smPROTACs that engage these E3 ligases is the emergence of resistance because of genomic alterations or deletions that impair the endogenous E3 ligase machinery (11). Conversely, biologic degraders can introduce an exogenous E3 ligase or its functional domain, potentially bypassing this loss and overcoming acquired resistance.

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: [Biologics-based heterobifunctional degraders] Several formats of these biologic modalities have been developed, including ubiquibodies (12), chimeric F-box fusion proteins (13), affinity-directed protein missile (AdPROM) (14), antibody RING-mediated destruction (ARMeD) (15), and biological PROTACs (bioPROTACs) (16, 17) (Table 1). Although these strategies share the common principle of bringing a target protein into proximity with an engineered E3 ligase to trigger ubiquitination, they differ in their molecular design and choice of E3 machinery. Ubiquibodies and bioPROTACs use modular fusion of an E3 ligase or substrate adaptor (e.g., CHIP, SPOP, or RNF4) to an engineered target-binding domain, such as a nanobody or designed ankyrin repeat protein (DARPin) (12, 16, 17)

text: [Biologics-based heterobifunctional degraders] . F-box fusion proteins exploit the endogenous Skp1–Cullin–F box complex, in which the substrate-recognition domain of the F-box protein β-TrCP (also known as FBXW1) is replaced by a heterologous binder (e.g., nanobody or protein domain) (13). AdPROM uses an anti-GFP nanobody fused to the VHL adaptor, enabling degradation of GFP-tagged proteins (14), whereas ARMeD relies on the RING domain of RNF4 fused to a nanobody to mediate ubiquitination directly (15)

text: [E3 ubiquitin ligase for biologic degraders] To date, multiple E3 ligase families, including Cullin-RING ligases (e.g., SPOP), single-subunit RING ligases (e.g., tripartite motif [TRIM]21), HECT ligases (e.g., NEDD4), and U-box ligases (e.g., CHIP), have been shown to function effectively in biologic degrader constructs (12, 16, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24) (Fig. 2, A and B). The Partridge group used a system in which GFP was fused to histone 2B or KRAS and demonstrated that an anti-GFP nanobody (vhhGFP4) fused to five different E3 ligases, including FBXW1, SKP2, VHL, SPOP, and CHIP, achieved over 70% degradation of cellular GFP (16, 18). Moreover, both prokaryotic and nonhuman eukaryotic E3 ligases have been incorporated into biologic degrader designs, underscoring the versatility of this approach (25, 26)

text: [E3 ubiquitin ligase for biologic degraders] A key advantage of the diverse range of E3 ligases capable of mediating target degradation via biologic degraders is their ability to tailor constructs to specific cellular contexts and targets, such as exploiting the endogenous subcellular localization of E3 ligases to promote degradation within specific compartments. The Cullin-RING ligase substrate adaptor SPOP, for instance, is predominantly nuclear and has been harnessed in bioPROTAC systems to degrade nuclear proteins, such as proliferating cell nuclear antigen, thereby suppressing tumor growth (16, 23, 28, 29). Furthermore, E3 ligases or their functional domains used in biologic degraders can be redirected to desired organelles by incorporating localization sequences (23)

text: [E3 ubiquitin ligase for biologic degraders] . Continued development of biologic degraders that harness these E3 ligases offers a promising strategy for achieving highly specific degradation in subcellular environments that often present challenges for small-molecule degraders.

section: Exploiting TRIM E3 ligases for the development of biologic degraders
text: [Exploiting TRIM E3 ligases for the development of biologic degraders] TRIM E3 ligases comprise a family of approximately 80 proteins in humans that share a conserved RING domain (30). TRIM21 is unique for its high affinity toward the Fc domain of immunoglobulins (31). Endogenously, TRIM21 recognizes antibody-bound pathogens during infection (32). TRIM-Away is a method that exploits this pathway for TPD applications (Fig. 3A, Table 1). In the initial study, Clift et al. (33) microinjected or electroporated immunoglobulin G against nine targets and observed TRIM21-mediated degradation, achieving near-complete elimination. Notably, TRIM21 is expressed at relatively high endogenous levels, which are sufficient to support efficient degradation and enable the TRIM-Away system to function robustly across different cellular contexts

text: [Exploiting TRIM E3 ligases for the development of biologic degraders] To further reduce the size of biologic constructs used for TRIM-Away, Chen et al. (20) described a modified strategy termed TRIMbody-Away, in which a truncated TRIM21 lacking the Fc recognition domain is directly fused to nanobodies targeting a POI (Fig. 3B, Table 1). Using this approach, they successfully induced degradation of intracellular enhanced GFP. Notably, treatment with either a proteasome inhibitor or an autophagy-lysosome inhibitor suppressed degradation, indicating that both proteasome- and lysosome-mediated pathways are potentially involved. While TRIM-Away requires only antibody or nanobody microinjection in cells with sufficient endogenous TRIM21, cells with low TRIM21 expression need to receive both the ligase and the antibody to achieve efficient target degradation

Both TRIM-Away and TRIMbody-Away represent versatile technologies for biological research and potential therapeutic applications (34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39).

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
section: Exploiting TRIM E3 ligases for the development of biologic degraders
text: [Exploiting TRIM E3 ligases for the development of biologic degraders] In a recent study investigating the therapeutic effects of TRIM-Away–mediated protein degradation in breast cancer, Dey et al. (40) employed electroporation and antibody transfection to degrade HER2, HER3, and STAT3. As a result, degradation of these targets inhibited downstream signaling pathways for up to 8 days. This work demonstrated that direct removal of oncogenic proteins can reduce tumor growth without activating compensatory pathways. Moreover, this work demonstrated that TRIM-Away can target specific post-translational modifications, offering an additional layer of specificity and expanding the scope of this technology. For instance, phospho-activated forms of STAT3 were selectively degraded without affecting the total protein pool.

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: [E2 enzymes for biologic degraders] E2 ubiquitin–conjugating enzyme-based biologic degraders function similarly to E3 ligase–based degraders by engaging an upstream component of the ubiquitin–proteasome system. Work by Hunt and Taylor (42) demonstrated that chimeric E2 enzymes, including UBE2B and UBE2D1, could recognize and degrade targets, such as SHP2 and KRAS. This complementary approach has the potential to recognize a wide range of protein substrates and promote their degradation, owning to the promiscuity and abundance of E2 enzymes. Future research on E2-based biologic degraders should aim to identify additional E2 enzymes capable of promoting TPD and to assess whether they possess broader or distinct substrate specificities compared with UBE2B and UBE2D1

Another important direction is the development of methods to tune the activity of these E2 enzymes, enabling target degradation without disrupting their native functions or regulated degradation pathways. Overall, E2-based biologic degraders represent a promising new avenue for expanding TPD beyond traditional E3 ligase–centric approaches.

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: [Target-binding ligands for biologic degraders] Small-molecule degraders generally require highly specific chemical ligands that bind to a surface pocket of the target protein. Many proteins, however, lack suitable pockets for developing high-affinity chemical ligands, creating a significant barrier to targeting a broader range of proteins. As a result, the scope of small-molecule degraders is largely limited to conventionally druggable proteins, such as enzymes and receptors, which constitute only about 15% of the proteome (43). One advantage of biologic degraders over small-molecule degraders is the wide variety of target-recruiting elements that can be employed in their design. title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: [Target-binding ligands for biologic degraders] . Biologic-based ligands, such as antibodies, monobodies, and DARPins, bind target proteins through one or more complementary peptide sequences (Fig. 2, C–F), thereby providing high-affinity ligands for challenging targets that are often considered chemically inaccessible. To identify these ligands, display technologies, such as phage display and yeast display, enable the selection of peptide or protein binders to POIs from large combinatorial libraries (44). Moreover, these biologic ligands can be selected or further tuned to minimize crossreactivity with homologous proteins and isoforms or to act as broad recruiters of a protein family.

text: [Target-binding ligands for biologic degraders] KRAS is a well-studied oncogene with a high mutation rate in a variety of cancers and is associated with poor prognosis (45). Historically, KRAS has been difficult to target with small molecules. Although recent advances in small molecule development have partially overcome this limitation, these efforts remain largely restricted to specific KRAS mutations, such as G12C (45) and G12D (46). In contrast, biologic ligands that can target a broader panel of KRAS mutants have the potential to selectively engage oncogenic KRAS in cancer cells while sparing normal cells expressing wildtype KRAS. Their reduced size facilitates efficient transport between cellular compartments and allows for scalable production and optimization via directed evolution platforms (47). text: [Target-binding ligands for biologic degraders] . Work by Bery et al. identified a monobody that selectively recognizes active GTP–bound RHOB but not GDP-bound RHOB or either RHOA or RHOC (27). title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: [Target-binding ligands for biologic degraders] Nanobodies are camelid-derived single-domain antibodies (∼15 kDa), also known as variable domains of heavy chain–only antibodies (VHHs) (Fig. 2E). Owing to their high stability, small size, and ease of production, nanobodies have rapidly emerged as a versatile platform for both research and therapeutic applications (50). Several nanobody-based degrader systems have been developed. In the ARMeD approach, a nanobody is fused to the RING domain of RNF4 to recruit and degrade specific targets (15). Similarly, the AdPROM system employs an anti-GFP nanobody fused to VHL to direct the degradation of GFP-tagged proteins (14)

text: [Target-binding ligands for biologic degraders] DARPins are small (∼15 kDa), single-domain proteins that can be selected to bind targets with high specificity and affinity (51) (Fig. 2F). Bery et al. (52) screened for anti-KRAS DARPins and identified two, K13 and K19, which selectively bound and inhibited KRAS mutants in the colorectal cancer cell line HCT116. Although these DARPins could bind wildtype KRAS, they did not inhibit its function (52). In a follow-up study, the authors used the KRAS-specific DARPin K19 to generate a KRAS mutant degrader (24). Notably, comparison with pan-RAS degraders revealed that the KRAS-specific degrader selectively inhibited the proliferation of tumors harboring mutant KRAS without affecting cells expressing wildtype KRAS, whereas the pan-RAS degraders suppressed proliferation of all cell types tested

section: Peptide-based degraders: strategies and emerging modalities
text: [Peptide-based degraders: strategies and emerging modalities] Peptide-based degraders use peptides to engage E3 ligases, target proteins, or both, promoting POI degradation via induced proximity to the ubiquitination machinery. Depending on their design, peptides can serve distinct functional roles. In one format, peptides act as E3 ligase recruiters by mimicking endogenous degron motifs or E3-binding sequences to recruit the ligase (Fig. 4A). Alternatively, peptides can function as POI warheads, binding directly to the target protein to facilitate its ubiquitination when coupled to a suitable E3-binding module (Fig. 4B). A third strategy employs bivalent peptide recruiters that incorporate two distinct peptide ligands, one for the E3 ligase and one for the POI, thereby eliminating the need for small-molecule components (Fig. 4C)

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
section: Peptide-based degraders: strategies and emerging modalities
text: [Peptide-based degraders: strategies and emerging modalities] Another class of peptide-based degraders is based on degron-tagged POI ligands. Degrons are short peptide sequences recognized by E3 ligases that promote protein degradation (59). By fusing degrons to biologic ligands for specific targets, these degron-mediated pathways can be harnessed for efficient target degradation (Fig. 4D). For example, degron sequences can recruit ubiquitin ligases via an N-terminal arginine residue or a C-terminal PEST sequence (rich in proline, glutamic acid, serine, and threonine) (60, 61). Work by Tamaki et al. (62) demonstrated that a single-chain variable fragment targeting TAR DNA–binding protein 43 aggregates, a key driver of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, fused to a PEST-like sequence, effectively eliminated TAR DNA–binding protein 43 aggregation

Notably, studies have shown that adding a membrane-permeating sequence can efficiently promote cellular uptake of peptide-based degraders (63). text: [Peptide-based degraders: strategies and emerging modalities] Recently, a new peptide-based modality, termed HYbrid DegRAding Copolymer (HYDRAC), was reported to utilize polymer-conjugated peptides to promote TPD (68) (Fig. 4E). By linking multiple peptide units through a polymer backbone, HYDRAC enhances binding avidity and stability compared with conventional peptide–based degraders. This approach has been shown to degrade the transcription factor MYC and suppress tumor growth, demonstrating both effective target engagement and therapeutic potential

This design thereby expands the potential applicability of peptide-based degraders.

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: [Limitations of biologic degraders] Despite significant advances in biologics-based degrader technologies, several limitations remain to be addressed. A primary challenge is their poor cell permeability, which restricts their cellular uptake and limits in vivo efficacy. Many biologic degraders are large, multidomain protein constructs with limited ability to penetrate the plasma membrane. Consequently, alternative delivery strategies, such as lipid nanoparticle encapsulation or viral vector delivery, are typically required. Of promise, Shen et al. developed a cell-permeable bioPROTAC composed of an anti-BCL11A nanobody, a cell-penetrating miniature protein (ZF5.3) engineered with a cationic and amphipathic surface to facilitate membrane translocation, and a truncated E3 ligase (SPOP or RNF4)

text: [Limitations of biologic degraders] . This construct accumulated in the nucleus following extracellular incubation and reduced BCL11A levels by 70% after 12 h (17). This study highlights that limited cell permeability of biologic degraders can be overcome through protein engineering and/or delivery optimization.

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: [Limitations of biologic degraders] Another important consideration for biologics-based degraders is their potential immunogenicity. The use of nonhuman scaffolds, such as camelid-derived nanobodies, bacterial ligases, or Drosophila F-box domains, may increase the likelihood of antidrug antibody formation upon repeated administration. Even human or humanized proteins can expose novel epitopes when fused to engineered domains or linkers. Strategies to mitigate these risks include deimmunization of nonhuman sequences through epitope prediction and mutagenesis, the incorporation of human-derived or humanized scaffolds, and careful evaluation of immune responses during preclinical development. Establishing low-immunogenicity designs will therefore be crucial for advancing biologic degraders toward clinical translation.

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: [Limitations of biologic degraders] Beyond cellular uptake and immunogenicity, additional challenges include achieving tissue-specific distribution, minimizing off-target degradation, and ensuring sufficient expression of the recruited E3 ligase within the target cell type. These issues can be addressed through careful selection of ligases with compatible subcellular localization and expression profiles, the design of high-affinity and/or isoform-specific target ligands, and the use of delivery systems engineered for tissue- or cell-type specificity. Such design considerations will be essential for translating biologic degraders into clinically effective therapeutics.

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: [Summary and outlook] TPD has rapidly evolved from its conceptual origins in the early 2000s to an expanding set of therapeutic modalities. smPROTACs and molecular glue degraders have demonstrated the feasibility of redirecting the ubiquitin–proteasome system for protein elimination and are progressing in clinical trials. Nevertheless, these approaches face challenges, including dependence on ligandable surfaces, the emergence of resistance mechanisms, and limited design principles. Biologic degraders have emerged as a complementary class of TPD strategies that overcome some of these barriers by expanding the repertoire of ligases and ligands that can be harnessed for targeted degradation

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: [Summary and outlook] . Leveraging diverse E3 ubiquitin ligases, E2-conjugating enzymes, and peptide- or antibody-based binders, biologic degraders provide modularity, high specificity, and the ability to target proteins traditionally considered inaccessible. Recent work highlights their potential in addressing challenging oncogenic proteins, such as KRAS mutants, in selectively targeting conformational or specific states, and in developing versatile degrader platforms such as TRIM-Away and TRIMbody-Away. Together, these advances underscore the unique promise of biologics in expanding the landscape of TPD.

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: [Summary and outlook] Looking forward, recombinant protein technologies are poised to push the boundaries of proteome manipulation, with emerging strategies offering both degradative and stabilizing capabilities. For example, novel constructs, such as ligand-ubiquitin fusion proteins, may overcome orientation and engagement limitations inherent to degrader design (69), whereas biologic DUBTACs could stabilize proteins by removing ubiquitin chains, offering a direct counterpoint to degradation (70, 71, 72, 73)

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: [Summary and outlook] . Beyond proteasome-mediated degradation, lysosomal- and autophagy-based strategies, together with induced proximity platforms for other post-translational modifications (such as phosphorylation-targeting chimeras, acetylation-targeting chimeras, and phosphorylation-inducing chimeras) (74), will further expand the scope of proteome editing to include extracellular proteins, aggregates, organelles, and nucleic acids.

title: Emerging biologic modalities for targeted protein degradation
text: [Summary and outlook] The next phase of biologic degraders will require both technical advances and conceptual innovation: improving delivery systems for large biologics, optimizing degrader formats for specific subcellular environments, and integrating strategies to minimize off-target effects. Equally important will be translating these tools into clinically viable therapeutics and demonstration of efficacy in complex disease models. Biologic degraders, by virtue of their modularity and specificity, are positioned to diversify therapeutic strategies and expand our ability to reprogram proteostasis. As the field advances, these modalities are expected to play a crucial role in both fundamental biology and next-generation precision medicines.

title: Comparison of Signal‐ and Volume‐Based Ventilation‐Weighted Assessment Using 3D FLORET UTE MRI in Patients With Various Pulmonary Disease
text: [abstract] 3D free‐breathing, proton, contrast‐agent‐free MR methods are increasingly used for pulmonary ventilation‐weighted measurements. The methods are split between: (1) signal‐based, which rely on lung parenchyma signal changes during respiration, and (2) volume‐based that utilize the Jacobian determinant of deformation fields from the image registration. This study compares both proton methods using respiratory‐resolved images acquired using fermat‐looped orthogonally encoded trajectories (FLORET) acquisition.

title: Comparison of Signal‐ and Volume‐Based Ventilation‐Weighted Assessment Using 3D FLORET UTE MRI in Patients With Various Pulmonary Disease
text: [abstract] Free‐breathing FLORET data were acquired from participants with various pulmonary conditions (N = 29) and healthy controls (N = 7), and reconstructed into respiratory phase‐resolved images. Signal‐based regional ventilation (RVent) was quantified using the 3D phase‐resolved functional lung algorithm, and volume‐based Jacobian ventilation (JVent) was derived as the Jacobian of the deformation field from the direct image registration of the end‐expiratory image to the end‐inspiratory image. Differences between the means, coefficients of variation (CoVs), and their ventilation defect percent (VDP) were quantified by Bland–Altman plots. The spatial overlap of the defect maps was determined by multi‐class Sørensen–Dice coefficient, and Spearman correlations to 129Xe MRI were assessed.

text: [Discussion] Understanding regional lung ventilation is critical to detect and monitor pulmonary abnormalities. Among respiratory‐resolved proton UTE MRI approaches, both Jacobian‐based ventilation (JVent) derived from image registration and signal‐based ventilation (RVent) derived from dynamic signal changes offer complementary pathways to estimate ventilation. In theory, RVent and JVent should yield similar results, as both quantify regional lung volume changes during respiration. While JVent captures geometric expansion derived from image registration, RVent reflects the corresponding change in air content

title: Comparison of Signal‐ and Volume‐Based Ventilation‐Weighted Assessment Using 3D FLORET UTE MRI in Patients With Various Pulmonary Disease
text: [Discussion] . While JVent captures geometric expansion derived from image registration, RVent reflects the corresponding change in air content. Ideally, these measures should align closely; however, discrepancies can arise due to physiological differences and technical factors such as registration accuracy, signal‐to‐noise ratio, and susceptibility effects. Despite their shared goal, differences in their underlying assumptions, sensitivity to noise, and image processing demands can lead to varying results and require careful interpretation. Therefore, a direct comparison of these methods is essential to assess their relative accuracy, reliability, and clinical utility, particularly in relation to established benchmarks like hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI

title: Comparison of Signal‐ and Volume‐Based Ventilation‐Weighted Assessment Using 3D FLORET UTE MRI in Patients With Various Pulmonary Disease
text: [Discussion] The results indicate significant differences between the RVent and JVent methods for assessing lung ventilation via 3D proton FLORET UTE MRI. VDPRVent demonstrated a stronger correlation with 129Xe MRI and PFTs, likely due to inferior image quality of the JVent maps. Volume‐based JVent ventilation displayed a blurrier appearance, as previously reported [29], and showed a weaker correlation with 129Xe MRI. In the development of the JVent VDP calculation in this study, it was necessary to additionally apply a median filter of 7 × 7 × 7 to derive meaningful VDP values in the expected range while also maintaining correlation to 129Xe MRI. We also performed threshold analysis on unfiltered JVent maps as well as those processed with 3 × 3 × 3 and 5 × 5 × 5 median filters

However, the 7 × 7 × 7 filter yielded superior AUC values and produced VDP measurements within the expected healthy range for the control group in our study. This filter may have contributed to the observed blurring as well as higher SNR of the JVent maps.

text: [Introduction] The intertidal zone in coastal habitats can be a dynamic and stressful environment because it is subject to cyclical changes based on the daily tides. This includes rapid swings in oxygen content of the water, where during the night, the fauna and flora within pools deplete oxygen via aerobic respiration without the benefit of oxygen replacement from photosynthesis. While pools close to the water line may be refilled with oxygen-rich seawater as the tides rise, splash pools above the water line may experience longer and more intense fluctuations in oxygen content. Any organism that inhabits these pools must be tolerant of extremely low oxygen content and reoxygenation when the sun rises (Legrand et al. 2018; Powers et al. 2025)

Levels of coastal hypoxia have recently become more intense and widespread, causing mass mortality across several taxa (Whitney 2022), prompting the need to better understand evolutionary mechanisms that allow some taxa to thrive in extreme conditions.

text: [Introduction] Broadly, animals have evolved two cellular strategies for dealing with hypoxic stress. These are (i) enhanced oxygen delivery to hypoxic tissues by production of new red blood cells (erythropoiesis), increased respiratory proteins, new blood vessels (angiogenesis), and vasodilation and (ii) enhanced energy production via anaerobic pathways, such as glycolysis, while depressing O2-dependent OXPHOS (Fuhrmann and Brüne 2017). While both strategies may be used simultaneously in some species, the former occurs primarily in vertebrates and during moderate hypoxia, while the latter is common in invertebrates undergoing periods of prolonged hypoxia or anoxia (Gorr et al. 2006)

The formation of the functional HIF-1 heterodimer only occurs when oxygen levels within the cell become critical, and it is controlled by oxygen-sensing enzymes called prolyl hydroxylases (PHDs), primarily PHD2 (or EGLN). Once HIF-1 is active, it works by recognizing and attaching to DNA regions called HREs (hypoxia response elements) located upstream of target genes, thus manipulating their expression patterns (Kaluz et al. 2008).

text: [Sugar Metabolism and Exoskeletal Modification] Why T. californicus may be modifying its exoskeleton to deal with hypoxic stress has yet to be explained. We hypothesize that this copepod may modify its cuticle and chitin content to increase density and decrease porousness to prevent loss of residual intracellular oxygen. This species lacks a circulatory system, respiratory pigments, or gills and passively diffuses oxygen across its cuticle to respire. Rearrangement of the cuticle and the buildup of chitin (to reinforce the exoskeleton or produce chitosan in response to oxidative stress) may allow T. californicus to sequester what little oxygen remains when DO in the environment becomes scarce

This strategy would contrast with that of plants, which increase cuticle permeability to facilitate greater gas exchange during hypoxia (Kim et al. 2017). While modification of the exoskeleton has yet to be fully confirmed experimentally via microscopy and advanced imaging, we did observe changes in gene regulation that suggest this process is occurring. While physiological evidence is needed to confirm our hypotheses, we suggest that this is accomplished with minimal adjustment to the expression of genes coding components of mitochondrial OXPHOS complexes except for a possible priming strategy involving the assembly of cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV). text: [Conclusions] . Rather than suppressing OXPHOS activity in the face of oxidative stress, T. californicus mounts a transient antioxidant response using the glutathione system and the alternative oxidase AOX to buffer against ROS and stabilize mitochondrial membranes. These responses are likely bolstered by antioxidant activity of carotenoid pigments, whose cleavage was downregulated steadily through hypoxia and into reoxygenation. While T. californicus does not appear to slow its respiration via OXPHOS, the species does transiently increase its usage of anaerobic glycolysis at even the early stages of hypoxia exposure but abandons this strategy quickly during recovery

text: [Hypoxia Exposure] We exposed groups of copepods to five treatment levels along a course of hypoxia exposure: normoxia, mild hypoxia, severe hypoxia at Pcrit (critical oxygen tension), anoxia, and recovery (Fig. 1). title: Mechanistic studies on HNRNPA2B1 suggest binding but not selective recognition of m6A
text: [abstract] HNRNPA2B1 contains two RRM domains and has been investigated for its possible role as an m6A reader protein. The targetome of HNRNPA2B1 was shown to overlap with the m6A methylation motif, but further investigations of its binding affinity for m6A-containing RNAs have been less clear on the relative selectivity of HNRNPA2B1 for methylated transcripts. Our computational and experimental studies depict that when an m6A modification is positioned in between the two RRM domains, and in the context of the GGACU motif that can be written by methyltransferases, the binding affinity is nearly identical and slightly less favourable to the unmodified sequence. Our study suggests that HNRNPA2B1 is not a (selective) reader but has high affinity for m6A in a sequence-dependent manner

title: Mechanistic studies on HNRNPA2B1 suggest binding but not selective recognition of m6A
text: [abstract] . Our study suggests that HNRNPA2B1 is not a (selective) reader but has high affinity for m6A in a sequence-dependent manner. This can be attributed to the strong interactions conferred by AGG and UAG motifs rather than adenine or m6A in the GGACU motif which are predicted to interact weakly, intercalating between the two RRMs or positioned outwards. Overall, our findings highlight the higher complexity of HNRNPA2B1 and RRM recognition properties compared to well-studied YTH domains in the recognition of m6A, as well as modified and unmodified sequences.

text: [Introduction] The heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein (HNRNP) family consists of 33 proteins which contain one or more RNA-binding domains (RBDs) [1]. Of these RBDs, the RNA recognition motif (RRM) is the most common and is present in a majority of HNRNPs [1]. HNRNPs have been demonstrated to play critical roles in important cellular processes, including post-transcriptional modifications, transcription, and translation. Heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein A2B1 (HNRNPA2B1) is one such protein which contains two RRMs (RRM1 and RRM2) in the N-terminus and is associated with transcription, RNA transport, and alternative splicing of pre-mRNA [2–6]

text: [Introduction] . In addition to testing unmodified RNA sequence variation, HNRNPA2B1 binding was also investigated in the context of the m6A modification. Given previous work suggesting that this protein could recognize m6A bearing transcripts, in vitro binding assays were conducted with an m6A modified 10-mer (5’-AAGG-m6A-CUAGC-3’) [5], combining AGG and UAG, as well as m6A within the DRACH motif. Methyltransferases, known as writer proteins, catalyse m6A modification within the consensus sequence DRACH (D = A, G, or U; R = A or G; H = A, C, or U; A = m6A), in which GGACH is a favoured insertion context [27,28], while GGACU comprises a pronounced consensus motif according to higher precision tools [29]

title: Mechanistic studies on HNRNPA2B1 suggest binding but not selective recognition of m6A
text: [Introduction] . Experiments showed a significant decrease in affinity for the m6A-modified RNA in comparison to unmodified RNA in the context of 5’-AAGG-m6A-CUAGC-3’ [5]. Interestingly, when binding assays were conducted with an RNA pentamer corresponding to the m6A methylation motif (5’-GGACU-3’), HNRNPA2B1 showed a lower affinity for unmodified RNA compared to m6A modified RNA, but at the same order of magnitude [5]. These results, in conjunction with previous research linking HNRNPA2B1 to m6A-dependent processes [30,31] raise significant interest in further understanding the mechanisms of protein-RNA binding, both in the context of the preferred binding motifs of this protein and m6A modification.

title: Mechanistic studies on HNRNPA2B1 suggest binding but not selective recognition of m6A
text: [Introduction] To investigate HNRNPA2B1–RNA binding in these contexts, we used a combination of state-of-the-art computational and experimental tools and additionally employed computational affinity screens to predict putative RNA modifications that may be accommodated by HNRNPA2B1. Our studies agree with previous experimental studies on the affinity of several RNAs with canonical substitutions [5] and we provide an atomistic explanation for these findings. Notably, our computational and experimental studies depict that when the m6A modification is positioned in between the two RRM domains, in the context of the GGACU methylation motif, the binding affinity is nearly identical and slightly less favourable to the unmodified sequence

title: Mechanistic studies on HNRNPA2B1 suggest binding but not selective recognition of m6A
text: [Introduction] . Our study suggests that HNRNPA2B1 is not a (selective) reader but has high affinity for m6A in a sequence-dependent manner. This can be attributed to the strong interactions conferred by AGG and UAG motifs rather than the presence of adenine or m6A in the GGACU motif which are predicted to interact weakly, intercalating between the two RRMs or positioned outwards

When m6A was solvent exposed, guanine at position 4 formed stronger polar interaction with K22 and D49 in the first homodimer (RRM1) compared to when m6A was placed between the two RRMs. This was due to the repulsion between positively charged K22 and the hydrophobic methyl group of m6A, pushing the base away from guanine at position 4. Therefore, the solvent exposure of m6A facilitated stronger interactions between guanine at position 4 and K22 and D49, perhaps due to additional space available in the pocket.

text: [Simulation of 5’-AAGG-m6A-CUAGC-3’ in complex with HNRNPA2B1 reveals that m6A binding between the RRM1 and RRM2 domains has minimal effect on RNA binding affinity] Overall, in our simulations of 5’-AAGGACUAGC-3’ and 5’-AAGG-m6A-CUAGC-3’ in complex with HNRNPA2B1, the binding was primarily attributed to AGG and UAG motifs in complex with RRM1 and RRM2, respectively, while either adenine or m6A at the fifth position, regardless of their conformations with respect to HNRNPA2B1, do not contribute much to the binding. In this context, HNRNPA2B1 seems to favourably bind GGXCU motifs, such that they are positioned in between RRM1 and RRM2, and most presumably because GG and U are part of the preferred motifs AGG and UAG recognized by RRM1 and RRM2, respectively, participating in favourable interactions with the protein.

This modification is catalysed by the METTL3/METTL14 methyltransferase complex, which recognizes the GGACH sequence motif [27,28]. Of the proteins implicated in m6A-dependent regulation, HNRNPA2B1 represents a complex case. Some previous work has shown direct binding to m6A-bearing transcripts and an overlap of HNRNPA2B1 binding sites with the RGAC motif [6]. Other work, however, has shown that HNRNPA2B1 binds to methylated RNA at lower affinities in the context of an HNRNPA2B1 preferred binding motif, which varies depending on whether the entire protein was included versus RRM domains only [5]

Our simulations and experiments depict for the first time that both adenine and m6A can be favourably accommodated at position 5 within the 5’-AAGGACUAGC-3’ sequence (Figure 6). We demonstrate computationally that this position, sandwiched between the two RRM domains, minimally affects the overall RNA binding affinity. For both the modified and unmodified forms of this sequence, the flanking AGG and UAG preferred RNA motifs serve as the main drivers of binding affinity

text: [Discussion] It is known that other HNRNPs besides HNRNPA2B1 can bind other RNA modifications. HNRNPD, for example, has been shown to interact with 8-oxoG [75–78], and different HNRNP binding sites overlap with intronic pseudouridines [79]. Considering these findings, it is possible that HNRNPA2B1 might interact with other RNA modifications. To investigate if HNRNPA2B1 can interact with other modified nucleobases outside of the m6A context, we performed a screening-based search of modified RNAs at different binding pockets of HNRNPA2B1 with reference to 5’-AAGGACUAGC-3’. We find that i6A, m6A, m62A modifications can be accommodated at positions 2, pseudouridine and m5U modifications at position 7, and Am modification at position 8, and represent possible novel modified targets for HNRNPA2B1 recognition

text: [Discussion] Our findings highlight the delicate balance between sequence context, RNA modifications, and RRM recognition, and they provide a framework to speculate in disease context on how amyloidogenic proteins, like Tau, may further influence this regulatory layer [80]. Tau binds RNA through low-complexity domains and has been shown to interact with HNRNP proteins, including HNRNPA2B1, within stress granules [7]. Importantly, previous studies showed that oligomeric Tau and HNRNPA2B1 to both co-localize with cytoplasmic m6A granules and that HNRNPA2B1 is required for co-localization of oligomeric Tau with m6A, further suggesting that HNRNPA2B1 tethers oligomeric Tau to m6A and enables a translational stress response mediated by oligomeric Tau [7]

text: [Discussion] . While m6A involvement in oncology is well studied, its association to tauopathy and AD was more recently uncovered [7]. Under basal conditions, m6A is confined mostly to the nucleus, and with stress, m6A can translocate into the cytoplasm [81,82]. Similar cytoplasmic accumulation of m6A was evident in vivo for P301S tau mice as well as in AD-affected human brain tissue [7]. A recent study showed that m6A abundance is elevated in the hippocampus in 6-month-old APP/PS1 mice, an AD mouse model, and comparative analysis of mRNA m6A modification profiles revealed substantial variation in m6A modifications between APP/PS1 mouse model and control mice [83]

While m6A modification of RNA is found to be relatively high in neurons, it is noticeably low in glial cells, and as ageing occurs, the general level of m6A modification tends to decrease in the brain from 5xFAD and control mice [83]. Given the importance of dynamics of m6A during AD development, and the potential role for m6A modification in the onset of the disease [84], high levels of m6A within GGACU-containing transcripts can lead to high-affinity interactions with HNRNPA2B1. An analogous HNRNP, i.e. HNRNPDL2, was proposed to possess RNA recognition properties along with its fibrillar forming properties in its C-terminal domain, and its functionality to bind RNA was suggested to be attributed to its RRM domains [85]

It is also important to note that our study does not necessarily preclude the possibility of additional indirect binding, potentially via a mechanism shown for HNRNPC [31]. However, given the fact that HNRNPC contains a single RRM domain which recognizes poly-(U) sequences [86], the mechanism of recognition for m6A-containing transcripts by the two RRM domains of HNRNPA2B1 could be more complex. Furthermore, HNRNPA2B1 has been found to denature stem loop structures, such as the one present in the CDK6 3’UTR [87]

text: [Discussion] . Furthermore, HNRNPA2B1 has been found to denature stem loop structures, such as the one present in the CDK6 3’UTR [87]. This further obfuscates the hypothesis that HNRNPA2B1 binds with a similar mechanism to HNRNPC, as the latter relies on an increase in accessibility of a single-stranded region of the MALAT1 transcript upon m6A methylation [30]. title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [abstract] Chronic pain often involves abnormalities in central pain processing. Two commonly used experimental methods for central pain modulation are conditioned pain modulation (CPM) and offset analgesia (OA). However, it is uncertain how similar the underlying processes they measure are. Here, we applied CPM and OA in patients with fibromyalgia, a model disease of central sensitization, to explore these questions further.

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [abstract] Fifty‐four female participants (27 fibromyalgia patients and 27 healthy participants) completed the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ) and the McGill questionnaire and underwent CPM and OA in a randomised order.

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [abstract] CPM and OA were positively correlated in healthy participants (R s = 0.40, p = 0.03) but negatively correlated in patients (R s = −0.47, p = 0.01). Additionally, we divided patients into responders and nonresponders for CPM and found that a significant negative correlation existed exclusively in nonresponders (R s = −0.64, p = 0.02), whereas no correlation existed in responders. Furthermore, CPM in patients was positively correlated with FIQ (R s = 0.4, p = 0.04) and McGill (R s = 0.65, p = 0.003), whereas OA was negatively correlated with both FIQ (R s = −0.445, p = 0.02) and McGill (R s = −0.47, p = 0.03).

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [abstract] This study is the first to show that OA, not just CPM, is correlated with clinical features in fibromyalgia patients and that these two paradigms are inversely correlated and differentially related to disease symptomatology in fibromyalgia patients.

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [abstract] This study is the first to demonstrate that conditioned pain modulation (CPM) and offset analgesia (OA) are inversely correlated in patients with fibromyalgia compared with healthy controls and show distinct associations with symptom severity. These findings reveal divergent mechanisms of central pain inhibition in chronic pain, highlighting the potential of both OA and CPM as novel markers for disease characterisation.

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Introduction] Fibromyalgia syndrome (FMS) is a chronic pain disorder characterised by widespread musculoskeletal pain and systematic symptoms (Clauw 2009). Although a peripheral pain generator has not been conclusively identified, FMS has been associated with marked alterations in central nervous system (CNS) pain processing (Woolf 2011). These features have led to its classification under the emerging category of nociplastic pain—a mechanism‐based designation describing dysfunctional modulation of nociceptive signalling at multiple CNS levels rather than tissue injury—which is increasingly recognised as a core component of several primary centralised pain syndromes (Fitzcharles et al. 2021).

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Introduction] Among the defining neurophysiological characteristics of nociplastic pain are reduced efficacy of endogenous pain inhibition and increased facilitation of nociceptive input (Arendt‐Nielsen 2015). Experimental paradigms such as conditioned pain modulation (CPM) and offset analgesia (OA) have been developed to probe these processes (Hermans et al. 2016).

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Introduction] The CPM is a widely used proxy for descending inhibitory control, reflecting the capacity of a noxious conditioning stimulus to suppress the perception of a separate test stimulus (Nir and Yarnitsky 2015). This mechanism is believed to involve many brain areas, especially brainstem structures, particularly the periaqueductal grey (PAG) and rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM) (Nahman‐Averbuch and Timmers 2023). OA, by contrast, refers to a disproportionately large reduction in perceived pain following a minor decrease in stimulus intensity (Julien et al. 2005) and is thought to reflect cortically mediated temporal filtering, engaging regions such as the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and insula (Li et al. 2022).

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Introduction] Unsurprisingly, impairments in both CPM and OA have been widely reported in FMS, which is consistent with dysregulated central pain modulation (Potvin and Marchand 2016; Oudejans et al. 2015). However, most studies have investigated these mechanisms in isolation, and only a few have assessed them concurrently in the same cohort (Honigman et al. 2013; Nahman‐Averbuch et al. 2014). Although CPM and OA are generally believed to rely on distinct mechanisms, each reflecting different aspects of endogenous pain modulation, the exact nature of the relationship between these two paradigms remains unclear and incompletely understood

Importantly, from a clinical standpoint, it is still uncertain what it means to exhibit an intact CPM response in relation to OA and vice versa in healthy individuals; that is, whether individuals who show effective descending pain inhibition through CPM also demonstrate efficient temporal filtering of nociceptive input, as captured by OA

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Introduction] The aim of this study was to examine the relationship between CPM and OA in individuals with FMS and in healthy controls, as both paradigms are widely used experimental measures of endogenous pain modulation. We tested two primary hypotheses. First, we hypothesized that the association between CPM and OA would differ between healthy individuals and patients with FMS, reflecting altered integration of pain modulatory mechanisms in FMS. Second, we hypothesized that CPM and OA abnormalities in FMS would be differentially related to clinical and disease‐specific symptoms, with each paradigm showing distinct associations with specific aspects of the FMS symptom profile

text: [Study Procedure] On arrival, a rheumatologist or a pain specialist evaluated the FMS patients and healthy participants, selected as previously outlined. text: [Conditioned Pain Modulation] . This is particularly relevant in FMS, where descending inhibition is often impaired (Julien et al. 2005) and where dynamic, concurrent stimulation may better reveal individual differences in pain modulation capacity. Additionally, the parallel design has been validated in multiple CPM studies involving both healthy individuals and patients with chronic pain, including FMS (Yarnitsky et al. 2008). The baseline temperature was set to 32°C, with rates of increase and decrease of 2°C per second. text: [Conditioned Pain Modulation] . Following a 15‐min break, the nondominant hand was immersed in a cold‐water bath (up to the wrist) for 60 s. During the final 30 s of immersion, the ‘test stimulus’ was reapplied, and the participants rated their pain intensity again at three time points (0, 15 and 30 s after the reapplication of the test stimulus). The CPM magnitude was determined by subtracting the average pain ratings obtained from the test stimulus alone (Ts_alone) from the average rating obtained when the test stimulus was applied simultaneously with the conditioned stimulus (Ts_conditioned). title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Offset Analgesia] The OA was implemented via a three‐temperature paradigm for the volar aspect of the dominant arm (Ligato et al. 2018; Szikszay et al. 2019). The temperature of the heat probe was increased at a rate of 2°C per second from a baseline of 32°C to the individual's test temperature (VAS60 temperature), which was held constant for 5 s. The temperature was then raised to 1°C for another 5 s before the samples were returned to the individual's test temperature (a decrease of 1°C). This temperature was maintained for 20 s, followed by a rapid return to the baseline temperature at a rate of 5°C per second. We defined the initial temperature increase reaching VAS 60 as T1, the 1°C increase maintained for 5 s as T2 and the phase of returning to the VAS 60 temperature, held for 20 s, as T3.

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Offset Analgesia] The participants sequentially rated the intensity of the perceived pain via a computerised visual analog scale (CoVAS) device. The magnitude of OA was computed by subtracting the peak CoVAS score at T2 from the minimum CoVAS score within the initial 10 s of T3 (Kobinata et al. 2017). A negative OA magnitude indicates efficient OA.

text: [Offset Analgesia] OA was conducted over three trials, with each trial separated by an interstimulus interval of at least 5 min. The thermode was slightly moved to reduce habituation between trials. The final OA magnitude was calculated by averaging the results from all three trials, with outliers excluded. Outliers were identified via Z scores, and values greater than 3 or less than −3 were excluded from the analysis (Ligato et al. 2018; Oudejans et al. 2015; Szikszay et al. 2021).

text: [Statistical Analysis] The sample size calculation was conducted via a power analysis with G*Power software (version 3.1.9.7). The analysis aimed to ensure sufficient statistical power to detect significant differences and correlations between both test groups. In accordance with previous studies (Lewis et al. 2012; Nuwailati et al. 2022; Szikszay et al. 2019), we set the effect size at 0.8, an alpha level of 0.05% and 80% power. A two‐tailed independent t‐test was used to determine that a minimum of 26 participants per group would be needed for the OA test. In addition, our results indicate that these two indices of supraspinal pain modulation are inversely related in patients with FMS, in contrast to the pattern observed in healthy controls

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Discussion] Studies investigating endogenous pain modulation in chronic pain patients have revealed diminished pain‐related activity within inhibitory pathways, explicitly involving the rostral anterior cingulate cortex (rACC), the PAG and the RVM (Harper et al. 2018; Zhang et al. 2018). Both CPM and OA serve as experimental measures used to assess endogenous pain modulation, but they are not identical. In addition to their different psychophysical properties, where CPM relies on a secondary painful stimulus (Nir and Yarnitsky 2015) and OA responds to changes in the intensity of a single painful stimulus (Ligato et al. 2018), a variance in the central mechanisms involved in each paradigm has been suggested (Nahman‐Averbuch et al. 2014).

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Discussion] CPM refers to the reduction in perceived pain of an ongoing painful stimulus following the application of a separate conditioning noxious stimulus. This process heavily involves descending inhibitory pathways originating in the PAG and RVM, which release endogenous opioids and serotonin to dampen spinal‐level pain signalling (Sprenger et al. 2011). Although CPM engages higher‐order regions such as the ACC and PFC, its primary mechanism for inhibiting pain relies predominantly on brainstem‐driven descending modulation. Cortical areas contribute by providing some attentional and emotional modulation (Nahman‐Averbuch and Timmers 2023). However, these cortical influences are less critical to the main inhibitory effect of CPM (Ossipov et al. 2010)

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Discussion] . However, these cortical influences are less critical to the main inhibitory effect of CPM (Ossipov et al. 2010). Accordingly, CPM provides more sustained modulation in the presence of the conditioning stimulus. This gradual effect persists with the secondary stimulus, reflecting the slower, steady nature of descending inhibition.

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Discussion] OA, in contrast, is triggered by a minor decrease in the intensity of a single painful stimulus, leading to a disproportionately large reduction in perceived pain. Although this response engages brainstem regions such as the PAG and RVM, it is particularly sensitive to dynamic changes in pain intensity. This process relies more strongly on cortical regions, including the ACC, PFC and insula, which rapidly detect subtle stimulus changes and recalibrate pain perception through a combination of top‐down and sensory mechanisms (Nahman‐Averbuch et al. 2014; Yelle et al. 2008). Thus, OA produces a rapid and short‐lived analgesic effect that occurs almost immediately after a reduction in stimulus intensity

text: [Discussion] Various pharmacological studies have indicated differences between the two paradigms. For example, in patients with diabetic polyneuropathy, opioid agonists increase CPM effectiveness (Niesters et al. 2014). In contrast, neither opioid agonists nor antagonists had any effect on OA in individuals experiencing opioid‐induced hyperalgesia (Martucci et al. 2012). Furthermore, administering an SNRI enhances CPM in patients with diabetic neuropathies (Yarnitsky et al. 2012), whereas a drug from the same class does not affect OA in healthy individuals (Olesen et al. 2018)

Moreover, a recent study from our group revealed that the psychoactive cannabinoid component Δ9‐tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) exerts differential effects on these two pain modulation paradigms in FMS, as it enhanced OA but did not significantly alter CPM, further supporting the interpretation that OA and CPM could rely on partially distinct underlying mechanisms (Agbaria et al. 2025). These variations may help to further clarify the distinctions between the paradigms, although the research remains inconclusive (France et al. 2016; Okkerse et al. 2017).

text: [Discussion] Importantly, the short‐term discontinuation of centrally acting medications before testing may have influenced CPM and OA in this study. On one hand, medication withdrawal may have reduced any direct pharmacological enhancement or suppression of descending pain modulation. On the other hand, early discontinuation or rebound effects may have transiently altered pain sensitivity, arousal, mood and sleep‐related factors. These changes could, in turn, affect psychophysical pain paradigms and increase between‐subject variability.

text: [Discussion] This issue is particularly relevant for SNRIs, as discontinuation symptoms can emerge within days of cessation. Accordingly, a 48‐h washout may not fully eliminate pharmacologic exposure for all compounds and may, in some individuals, bias CPM and OA estimates toward reduced apparent inhibitory capacity and/or greater variability. However, because only six FMS patients discontinued such medications (four of whom used SNRIs), any impact on group‐level conclusions is likely limited. Future studies should consider longer, compound‐specific washout periods or fully medication‐free cohorts when feasible.

text: [Discussion] We observed a significant positive association between CPM and OA in the healthy cohort, indicating that participants who exhibited stronger CPM inhibition also tended to show a greater OA effect (i.e., greater pain reduction following offset). This pattern is consistent with the notion that while CPM and OA reflect partially distinct dimensions of endogenous modulation (spatial vs. temporal filtering), they may still share overlapping inhibitory components at the individual‐differences level (Honigman et al. 2013; Nahman‐Averbuch et al. 2014).

text: [Discussion] Taken together, our findings, along with broader evidence demonstrating that OA and CPM can be differentially modulated across chronic pain conditions and experimental contexts, support the view that OA and CPM provide complementary information about pain modulation. These paradigms may therefore aid in stratifying patients into subgroups with distinct dominant alterations. For example, some patients may show impaired spatial inhibitory control, whereas others may exhibit altered temporal contrast processing. This approach is consistent with the increasing emphasis on mechanism‐informed patient stratification, rather than presuming a uniform deficit in descending inhibitory function across all chronic pain populations (Hermans et al. 2016).

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Discussion] The findings of this study underscore the potential clinical significance of CPM and OA measures in chronic pain patients, as their divergent patterns in FMS may help identify subgroups of patients with different modulatory profiles. Such distinctions could be clinically valuable for patient phenotyping and classification and may guide the development of personalised treatment strategies targeting specific deficits in central pain modulation. For example, patients with impaired CPM but preserved OA may benefit from therapies aimed at restoring tonic descending inhibition (e.g., certain antidepressants or exercise‐based interventions), whereas others may require broader neuromodulatory approaches.

text: [Discussion] Future studies should integrate both OA and CPM within the same experimental framework to investigate whether individual differences in these pain modulation processes predict treatment response over time. These findings may provide deeper insights into the distinct roles of CPM and OA in FMS and other chronic pain conditions. Moreover, future studies involving pharmacological manipulations of both CPM and OA could be highly valuable for advancing our understanding of the mechanisms underlying these paradigms.

For example, Tran and colleagues (2011) found that adults who stutter exhibited higher depressive mood than 200 age‐ and sex‐matched peers, whereas Tudor and colleagues (2013), using the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI; Beck et al. 1996) with 21 adults who stutter and 21 matched peers, found no group differences in self‐reported depression scores. text: [Mindfulness] Research concerning mindfulness in adults who stutter has expanded in recent years (Beilby et al. 2012; Israel et al. 2023; Medina et al. 2023). For example, Israel and colleagues (2023) used an online survey to investigate the levels of mindfulness, self‐compassion, decentralization capacity and impact of stuttering with 150 adults who stutter. text: [Coping Styles] Coping refers to intentional efforts to manage stressful occurrences or situations (Compas et al. 2001). Coping styles have a significant impact on physiological well‐being (Farley et al. 2005). Various coping styles (Skinner et al. 2003) are often grouped into active or passive styles (Nielsen and Knardahl 2014). Active coping styles (e.g., seeking social support, positive reframing, problem‐solving) are typically adaptive, whereas passive strategies (e.g., avoidance, withdrawal, substance use) are generally maladaptive (Wood and Bhatnagar 2015). Coping strategies may vary depending on the situation or the person who uses them. In some cases, taking action may help to solve a perceived problem, while in others, regulating emotions and thoughts may be useful for active coping.

title: Predictive Value of Mindfulness and Coping With Stress Styles on Depression, Anxiety and Stress Levels of Adults Who Stutter
text: [Discussion] This study primarily aimed to examine the predictive value of mindfulness and coping styles on depression, anxiety and stress levels and the relationships between these variables in 47 adults who stutter. Secondarily, the differences in these variables among stuttering severity groups were explored. Findings revealed a significant positive relationship between depression, anxiety and stress levels; mindfulness was found to be a significant predictor of depression, anxiety and stress levels; and helpless and submissive coping styles were found to be significant predictors of depression, and anxiety levels; no significant differences were observed among stuttering severity groups. The findings and clinical implications of this study will be discussed in detail below.

title: Predictive Value of Mindfulness and Coping With Stress Styles on Depression, Anxiety and Stress Levels of Adults Who Stutter
section: Predictive Effects of Mindfulness and Coping Styles on Depression, Anxiety and Stress
text: [Predictive Effects of Mindfulness and Coping Styles on Depression, Anxiety and Stress] The findings of this study revealed that lower levels of mindfulness and higher use of helpless and submissive coping styles (i.e., passive coping styles) were associated with higher reported scores of depression, anxiety and stress. In other words, lower mindfulness levels, along with more frequent use of passive coping styles, were found in this study to be predictors of depression, anxiety and stress. The active coping styles (i.e., self‐confident, optimistic and social support) investigated in this study did not contribute significantly to the model as predictors of depression, anxiety and stress levels. In interpreting these results, it is important to note that the seeking social support subscale demonstrated relatively low internal consistency (α = 0.47)

section: Predictive Effects of Mindfulness and Coping Styles on Depression, Anxiety and Stress
text: [Predictive Effects of Mindfulness and Coping Styles on Depression, Anxiety and Stress] Comparisons among adults who stutter, grouped by stuttering severity, revealed no significant differences in depression, anxiety, stress levels, mindfulness, or coping styles scores, which is consistent with recent literature on this topic (Blumgart et al. 2012; Manning and Gayle Beck 2013). The overall well‐being of individuals is influenced by the complex interplay of personal, environmental and social factors. These findings, together with previous research, suggest that psychological outcomes in adults who stutter do not appear to stem directly from the observable severity of their stuttering, but instead may arise from broader personal and environmental factors.

title: Predictive Value of Mindfulness and Coping With Stress Styles on Depression, Anxiety and Stress Levels of Adults Who Stutter
text: [Clinical Implications] Lower mindfulness and greater reliance on passive coping styles have been associated with elevated levels of depression, anxiety and stress, which may consequently have negative individual, social and environmental outcomes. These findings highlight the potential value of incorporating strategies that enhance mindfulness and promote active coping within stuttering interventions. Mindfulness practices may improve individuals’ ability to attend to the present moment, observe experiences nonjudgmentally, and regulate negative thoughts and emotions more adaptively, while fostering functional coping strategies and reducing reliance on dysfunctional approaches can support adaptive stress responses, engagement in daily activities, and social connectedness

text: [Conclusions] In conclusion, lower mindfulness levels and more frequent use of passive coping styles appeared to be predictors of higher levels of depression, anxiety and stress. Therefore, mindfulness levels and the frequency of engaging in passive coping strategies appear to be important considerations in decision‐making processes for effectively managing stuttering and its adverse impacts in adults who stutter.

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [abstract] Scientific research on the mental health effects of disasters has primarily focused on short-term consequences. This review aims to provide a long-term perspective, examining multiple contributing factors simultaneously. We registered this review (PROSPERO 2020, CRD42020108528), and searched Medline, PsycInfo, PTSDpubs, Web of Science, and SocINDEX from inception to July 2024. After screening 33,205 titles and abstracts, we extracted epidemiological longitudinal data from 71 studies, with up to six waves and a total of 137,004 participants

Despite high heterogeneity, the mental health burden in exposed populations decreased from month 1 to 300 after an initial peak in the first months, followed by a second peak after approximately a decade, before declining again (p<0.001). Mental health burdens post-disaster may be more universally distributed than previously believed. Earlier studies identifying gradual post-disaster recovery may have underestimated the long-term effects. The analysis revealed a shortage of high-quality studies with measurements beyond four years. The topic requires further investigation with consistently repeated measurements at standard intervals to confirm the presence and early predictors of both larger and smaller peaks.

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [INTRODUCTION] Populations have been confronted with disasters and major devastating events for as long as people have populated Earth. Although the exact number of natural and human-induced disasters, coupled with future prevalence, remains a topic of debate, societies varyingly confront floods, fires, earthquakes, technological disasters, terrorism, and mass violence.1–3 A combination of climate change, population growth, humanitarian crises, conflict, and war can potentially exacerbate the effects of such events.2 Although precise developments remain uncertain, new events involving loss of life, damage, and destruction are highly probable, and such events entail detrimental consequences for societies as a whole

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [INTRODUCTION] . The mental health effects of disaster exposure have been examined systematically for decades, resulting in a variety of overview studies. For example, there are studies that focus specifically on changes in occurrence of a particular mental health outcome (e.g., posttraumatic stress disorder [PTSD], depression, or suicide),4–9 type of disaster (natural or human-made),10 or disaster event category (e.g., earthquake, flood, terrorist attack, shooting).8–11 Some reviews have synthesized findings on multiple aspects.12–16

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [INTRODUCTION] Review of this literature reveals certain patterns. First, disaster exposure may have a substantial influence on mental health and psychopathology,4,5,9,12–15 with the number of human casualties playing a relevant role (i.e., effect size is strongly related to death rate or injury).4,12 Prevalence has been established as higher after the disaster compared to before,9,10 and higher in exposed versus unexposed comparison groups.7,10

Labels like “resilient,” “recovery,” “delayed onset,” or “chronic” have been assigned to such patterns or trajectories. The first two labels are most prevalent. text: [INTRODUCTION] Sixth, and most critically, there is a dearth of long-term and longitudinal research, a shortcoming consistently mentioned in available systematic reviews.4–6,8,11,13,19 Length of follow-up is also limited among studies that include some durational findings. In two recent meta-analyses, by Bonde and colleagues7 and Beaglehole and colleagues,10 timelines were primarily restricted to 24 and 48 months, respectively; they did not examine long-term effects. While highly informative in many respects, the systematic review by Newnham and colleagues,16 which compares mental health trajectories across different disaster categories, considers the long-term as just one time frame: longer than 24 months.

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [INTRODUCTION] We conducted a search in Medline (Ovid), PsycInfo (Ovid), PTSDpubs (formerly PILOTS: Published International Literature on Traumatic Stress), ProQuest, Web of Science, and SocINDEX (EBSCOhost) in August 2024 using the search terms: review OR meta-analysis OR systematic review AND disasters AND long-term OR long term OR lasting OR longitudinal. Based on the reviews mentioned and this search, we conclude that no systematic review or meta-analysis has assessed the long-term effects of disaster exposure across different time periods while controlling for multiple characteristics that potentially affect mental health risks.

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [INTRODUCTION] In summary, available reviews consistently highlight the serious mental health effects of disasters and related trajectories. They also frequently highlight factors that determine risk and vulnerability for affected populations across diverse disaster categories, both natural and human-made. At the same time, they point toward a major lacuna regarding long-term influence. This multilevel meta-analytic review aims to shed light on disaster-related long-term mental health effects and progression, taking into account relevant contextual predictors and control variables. The focus is on a broad range of mental (not physical) health outcomes (e.g., PTSD, depression, anxiety, suicidality, substance abuse, panic disorder) measured repeatedly along the post-disaster timeline
