title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Guidelines and registration] This systematic review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. We conducted our search in Covidence, and pre-registered the review in Prospero (2020, CRD42020108528).

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria] We included articles published in English-language peer-reviewed journals that contained full-text reports of quantitative studies assessing disaster effects. As what constitutes a disaster is not always clear, we defined the term specifically to denote acute, collectively experienced events with sudden onset.13 (See also Supplemental Data File 1, https://links.lww.com/HRP/A254.) Following categorization of search terms, we formulated inclusion and exclusion criteria.

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Population] Population-level inclusion criteria encompassed exposed adults, children, and adolescents (<18) of nonclinical populations who were directly (e.g., survivors of an accident or earthquake) or indirectly (e.g., living in disaster region) affected by a disaster. Exclusion criteria included professionals or responders and those not living in the vicinity of a disaster, as well as victims of war and armed conflict.

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Exposure] Exposure inclusion criteria comprised disaster exposure that affected a group and had an external cause (e.g., not mass suicide) and disasters that occurred at a workplace where the event happened to occur (e.g., terrorist attack, school shooting). Exclusion criteria included studies assessing the effects of multiple disasters within one sample or measurements from long-term single-disaster studies since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic (to avoid contamination of findings by pandemic-related threats, losses, and stressors).

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Outcome] Inclusion criteria encompassed studies containing mental health outcomes as measured via questionnaire, interview, or medical records regarding individual prevalence of mental health disorder (e.g., depression, anxiety, distress, PTSD, anxiety disorder, substance abuse, or suicidality). Exclusion criteria involved studies reporting health effects (stress-related) limited to physical symptoms (e.g., brain injury, medically unexplained symptoms), post-disaster interventions, mental health utilization, positive outcomes (e.g., posttraumatic growth), and psychotic disorders (e.g., schizophrenia).

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Method] Inclusion criteria entailed longitudinally designed studies with two or more post-disaster assessments of the same sample: measurement durations not longer than three months, with measurement intervals of at least three months. The last measurement had to be at least 12 months post-event and outcome measures had to be comparable across assessments. Studies needed to encompass at least 30 participants at baseline who experienced the disaster. The design excluded studies that developed a methodology or instrument or that contained an intervention, as well as studies that did not use the same methodology or instrument across all measurements. Studies with outcomes reported by an ancillary, unprofessional person (e.g., a parent or caregiver) were also excluded

text: [Screening Procedure] Titles and abstracts were divided and independently screened by two authors. Disagreements were discussed until we reached consensus. If necessary, a third person was consulted. When in doubt about a title/abstract, the article was retained for the full text stage. For manuscripts based on the same dataset, we included the first published article unless a subsequent paper measured more relevant mental health variables or included more assessment waves. If the more recent paper did not measure all variables assessed in the first published paper, we included both. We only used mental health variables from the initial paper, however, that were not measured in the later one

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Quality Assessment] We conducted an assessment of study quality using an adapted version of the Quality Assessment Tool for Quantitative Studies from the Effective Public Health Practice Project.21 This assessment included criteria such as selection bias, study design, data collection methods, withdrawal, and dropout. Additionally, one item from the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort studies was incorporated to assess outcome quality.22 A study with no poor scores was considered strong, while those with up to two poor scores were deemed moderate. We excluded studies with three or more poor scores. (Supplemental Data File 3, https://links.lww.com/HRP/A255 contains more information on quality assessment per study.)

text: [Data Extraction] From the included papers, we extracted available information on: disaster type and category, year, country, and region of disaster occurrence, population age (i.e., adult, children and adolescents, or all ages), relevant mental health outcomes observed (e.g., PTSD, depression, suicidality), number of assessments conducted (measurement waves), month of measurement (in cases with multiple measurement months, the last month was taken), type of instrument used, total sample size per wave (denominator), and number of participants with a mental health problem per wave (numerator). We calculated prevalence based on the numerator and denominator. The distinction between disorders and symptoms was not always consistent among different authors

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Statistical Analyses] We used a multilevel (meta-analysis) logit-logistic regression model to generate pooled estimates of mental health problems in the disaster timeline.23–25 This type of analysis enabled us to distinguish between fixed and random effects. Fixed effects capture specific characteristics that remain constant across outcomes, while random effects account for variability and differences among clustered outcomes. Clustering applies to hierarchical levels (observations, measurement waves, studies, and countries), as well as mental health problems and disaster categories. (Figure 1 displays the data’s multilevel structure.)

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Statistical Analyses] Multilevel data structure. Note: In the dataset, six hierarchical levels can be distinguished. Level 1 (“observations”) captures the prevalence of a specific mental health outcome for a distinct sample at a specific post-disaster time point. Observations are grouped into Level 2 (“measurement waves”), representing each follow-up time within a study. Multiple waves belong to the same study (Level 3). Studies are further grouped by country (Level 4), disaster category (Level 5), and outcome type (Level 6). The data therefore follow a cross-classified structure.

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Statistical Analyses] As a first step, we estimated the effect of several factors on the overall average prevalence of mental health problems (similar to the overall rate in other forms of meta-analysis). As a second step, we estimated average prevalence of mental health problems per disaster category (e.g., earthquake, flood, shooting), disaster type (natural or human-made), country income group (low to high), population type (children/adolescents, adults, all ages), study quality (moderate or high), outcome category (type of mental health issue), and month.

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Fixed effects] We included month (time since disaster; modeled with linear, quadratic, and cubic components; see also Norris and colleagues13), disaster year, population type (children/adolescents, adults, all ages), disaster type (natural or human-made), study quality (moderate or high), and country income group (low to high) as fixed effects in the model.

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Random effects] The model consisted of six levels. Level 1 denoted individual prevalence per outcome from each observed population; at this level, we modeled binomial error variance (constrained to 1). Level 2 modeled variance between measurement waves within studies. Level 3 accounted for variance among studies, and Level 4 among countries. We included variance among disaster categories and outcome types as cross-classified Levels 5 and 6, respectively (Figure 1).

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Random effects] All fixed effects (months since disaster, disaster year, population type, disaster type, study quality, and country income) and random effects (six levels) were estimated simultaneously in a single model. Thus, we controlled effect estimates for the other effects in the model.

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Random effects] All models were estimated in MLwiN version 3.01 using restricted iterative generalized least squares with first-order penalized quasi-likelihood (PQL). The overall pooled prevalence of mental health problems was equally weighted for the fixed effects factors and categories within a factor (indicator scoring [0,1] minus 1/N[cat], N[cat] = number of categories in factor). No weight was added for sample size differences (often implemented in meta-analyses), primarily because heterogeneity among individual observations and studies was so large that weighting for sample size would make the different model estimates significantly more difficult to interpret.

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [DISCUSSION] We conducted this review with the objective of better understanding the long-term mental health effects of disasters, a lacuna identified in the international disaster mental health literature. By conducting a multilevel meta-analysis, controlling for multiple factors simultaneously, we estimated the pooled prevalence of current or recent mental health problems at 22.1% (95% CI [10.95–39.57]). Although our analysis revealed extensive heterogeneity across and within studies, we clearly found that a substantial proportion of people affected by disasters experiences mental health problems of one type or another. We verified the well-established effects disasters have in the first months and years on the mental health of affected populations

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [DISCUSSION] . We verified the well-established effects disasters have in the first months and years on the mental health of affected populations. In large part, other disaster mental health reviews and meta-analyses confined their investigations to a relatively short time frame, typically spanning two to four years,7,10,16 or compared post-disaster measurements with predisaster or control groups.9,10 The broad time frame of our analysis, spanning 1–300 months, distinguishes our review. Our controlled evaluation demonstrates significant fluctuations over time. We found that, after initial improvement, a gradual increase in mental health problems generally follows, potentially peaking again years after a disaster.

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [DISCUSSION] Another noteworthy finding concerns the differences among event types. Arguably, the classic, conceptual dichotomy between natural and human-made disasters and their inherent causes is becoming less clear. Natural disasters such as floods and storms can have a human cause (climate change) or be exacerbated by human interference (pollution, communities near rivers and coastlines), further complicating reflections on whether events were preventable and/or caused by negligence or even malign intent

text: [DISCUSSION] . We found no significant differences in mental health outcome between natural and human-made disasters, contrary to the conclusions of other authors.12,13 Similarly, we did not find significant distinctions in effects among disaster categories, such as earthquakes, mass violence, and industrial disasters.12,13,16

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [DISCUSSION] One underexplored issue is how cultural and socioeconomic contexts influence mental health outcomes of disasters. Norris and colleagues13,14 found higher prevalence of deleterious mental health post-disaster in developing countries. They speculated that how disasters are assessed in different socioeconomic contexts may have influenced their findings; less severe disasters are more often studied in developed countries, while studies from developing countries may be limited to more severe disasters. Unfortunately, the absence of low-income countries and the small number of lower-middle-income countries in our reviewed studies did not allow us to thoroughly explore this theme

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [DISCUSSION] . More research is needed to understand how cultural and socioeconomic contexts influence the mental health effects of disasters, both in manifestation and assessment. Although lower prevalence of poor mental health in lower-income contexts aligns with country-level studies showing a positive relationship between wealth and mental impairment,97–101 the predictive value of context is unlikely to eclipse the importance of disaster exposure level and other potentially traumatic events.97,98

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [DISCUSSION] When considering directions for further research, it is important to emphasize Norris and colleagues’14 warning not to unnecessarily burden study participants and waste scarce resources on redundant investigations: “We will state our opinion unequivocally that we do not need more research that establishes only that severely exposed disaster victims develop psychological disorders or, worse, that barely exposed disaster victims do not. We need carefully conceived and theory-driven studies of basic process that are longitudinal in design.” Based on our preliminary results, we concur and reemphasize the importance of long-term over short-term research.

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [DISCUSSION] The current study has several strengths worth noting. We conducted research using an extensive predefined search strategy and applied stringent inclusion criteria and comparability standards. By integrating data from a wide range of studies with a sizable number of participants, we were able to conduct the first multilevel meta-analytic review on the mental health effects of disasters, controlling for multiple factors simultaneously. We also excluded measurements potentially contaminated by the global COVID-19 pandemic. Only one study by Hikichi and colleagues50 included a final follow-up measurement during the pandemic; we excluded this measurement from the meta-analysis.

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Limitations] Notable study limitations include restriction to English-language studies, the possibility of missing relevant studies (despite identifying a vast number of records through the search), and exclusion of continuous outcomes from our analysis. Additionally, though our range of mental health problems is similar to earlier reviews,12,13,15,16 it is not exhaustive (for instance, psychotic disorders are excluded), and certain mental health outcomes, particularly PTSD, may be overrepresented. Moreover, not all assessments constitute clinical diagnoses

text: [Limitations] . Moreover, not all assessments constitute clinical diagnoses. It is likely that a portion of study participants already had mental health problems before experiencing respective disasters.15 The selective nature of outcomes—ranging from clinical diagnoses and probable disorders to trauma-related symptoms and subjective experiences of distress—further complicates the longitudinal comparability of mental health outcomes, even though we found no significant differences among outcome types. In addition, cross-cultural differences and variations in data collection methods, diagnostic criteria, assessment instruments, and assessment timeframes pose potential biases

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Limitations] Each measured mental health outcome reflects a unique combination of characteristics linked to, among other things, the disaster, affected population, point in time, methodology used, and cultural and socioeconomic context, all contributing to heterogeneity. Our analysis is a first effort in considering multiple factors simultaneously. Nevertheless, we can extend and optimize our approach. Unfortunately, we were unable to include more risk and protective factors in the meta-analysis. In an attempt to include female sex, a confirmed risk factor for post-disaster mental health,12,13,15 the baseline female sex proportion was not a reliable proxy for follow-up measurements.

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Limitations] Perhaps the most significant limitation, given our objective, was the limited availability of post-disaster measurements exceeding 48 months (6.95% of observations; 16 of 71 studies). Thus, we need to exercise caution in drawing firm conclusions about the shape of long-term trends. In the data on which Figure 3 is based, there are 11 measurements between 72 and 144 months (six to twelve years). In 8 of these, prevalence is higher than before 72 months, producing the second peak. All 8 measurements are from the last wave of their respective measurement series—the studies end at that point, with no follow-up measurements. Beyond 144 months, and up to 300 months (13–25 years), we found 9 observations. Each was preceded by at least 1 measurement before, but not in, the 72–144-month period

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Limitations] . Each was preceded by at least 1 measurement before, but not in, the 72–144-month period. In every case, prevalence decreased during this time frame. These particularities are relevant for two reasons. First, we cannot determine how the trend continued in populations contributing to the second peak, since measurement stopped at that point. Second, the few studies with the longest follow-up (up to 300 months) do not sufficiently unpack the prevalence changes in the large middle area of the timeline. Longer-duration measurements with periodic follow-ups are essential to fill gaps and improve the accuracy of estimates. Such longer durations are also necessary to determine more detailed trajectories or response courses, as repeatedly recommended in the literature.4,8,16,19

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Limitations] There is a need for long-term research across diverse geographies and cultural and socioeconomic contexts, as well as for additional syntheses addressing the identified limitations. These needs extend beyond the scope of this review. While we deliberately excluded pandemics, virus outbreaks, war, and armed conflict, these events significantly affect thousands of people worldwide as well, and studies confirm attendant mental health effects.7,102,103 Therefore, their long-term influences, which may follow similar patterns to natural and human-made disasters, also warrant careful scholarly attention.

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Implications] The accumulated body of knowledge on the mental health burden of disasters provides an invaluable starting point for public health and safety authorities, health care professionals, and other responders to prepare and implement preventive measures, mitigation strategies, or curative interventions across the disaster timeline. Our review, however, urges caution in forming firm general conclusions. Notably, we must make assumptions about differences in mental health risks according to disaster type or category with care. Further, the nature of disaster-related threats and losses, as well as vulnerability profiles of affected populations, can differ greatly across disaster settings, and thus, must be taken into account

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Implications] . Finally, perhaps the most profound practical implication is that, by relying on gradual post-disaster mental health improvement, we may have underestimated the long-term effects. The observed rise in mental health problems years after a disaster, suggests a “twin peaks” phenomenon. Nonetheless, given gaps in data beyond four years, the presence of multiple peaks is poorly understood, requiring validation and conscientious interpretation. In this context, it is notable that the increase identified in the combined longitudinal samples corresponds with findings from a systematic review of PTSD following the 9/11 terrorist attacks in New York City. This study reported declining mental health for responders and residents five to six years post-9/11.8

title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies
text: [Implications] It is important to better understand the combination of factors and the dynamics that contribute to mental health risks at later points in time. A cascading interplay of risk factors, reflected, for instance, in accumulated unmet health care needs, unresolved and new problems, life events, lack of support, and secondary stressors in the aftermath, may account for the increased mental health burden.17 In the years following a disaster, social relationships can deteriorate,15,18 and those affected may experience diminished recognition within their personal, professional, and community environments. The explanations described in the literature align with the factors identified by the authors of the included studies, who link them to elevated levels of mental health problems

text: [Implications] Beyond initial effects and despite extensive restoration efforts (e.g., repair of housing, infrastructure, schools, shops, and businesses), these examples and our review suggest that a substantial portion of the population in disaster-affected communities continues experiencing a mental health burden—largely invisible in scientific reporting until now, and more universal in nature than previously assumed. Such burden is part of the persistent lingering effects of disasters that, as described by Bonanno and colleagues,15 transcends the individual: “Disasters affect the nature and structure of families. They impact the communities in which they take place, taxing their institutions and sometimes challenging their survival

text: [Implications] . They impact the communities in which they take place, taxing their institutions and sometimes challenging their survival. The impact of a disaster can also ripple through larger segments of a society and sometimes alter the lives of people in remote regions far removed from the geographic loci of the event.” These potentially broad and enduring influences underscore the need for early, proactive, participation-driven recovery approaches. With support from long-term monitoring programs to guide shared decision-making, we can target at-risk communities to help alleviate the mental health burdens of disasters.

title: Atypical Cervical Myelopathy with Medullary Involvement from Intracranial Dural Arteriovenous Fistula: The Steroid Trap
text: In this report, we present a rare case of cervical myelopathy with medullary involvement as the initial manifestation of a cranial dural arteriovenous fistula, underscoring the need for a high index of suspicion in atypical or rapidly progressing myelopathy cases.

title: Atypical Cervical Myelopathy with Medullary Involvement from Intracranial Dural Arteriovenous Fistula: The Steroid Trap
text: A 40-year-old male presented with progressive paraplegia and respiratory insufficiency. The cervical spine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed long-segment hyperintensity involving the medulla as well as the cervical spinal cord, as shown in Figure 1a. The patient was evaluated for long-segment myelitis, and all the workup was negative. The patient’s neurological status deteriorated following administration of corticosteroids, consistent with steroid-induced worsening of venous-congestive myelopathy. However, on careful review of the MRI of the brain, there were some flow voids in the posterior fossa. Therefore, digital subtraction angiography (DSA) was performed, and a cranial dAVF was diagnosed as the cause of progressive cervical myelopathy

title: Atypical Cervical Myelopathy with Medullary Involvement from Intracranial Dural Arteriovenous Fistula: The Steroid Trap
text: . Therefore, digital subtraction angiography (DSA) was performed, and a cranial dAVF was diagnosed as the cause of progressive cervical myelopathy. The arterial feeders were from the middle meningeal artery and the dural branch of the occipital artery, with the venous pouch located along the sigmoid sinus, as shown in Figures 1b and 1c. The venous drainage from the pouch was into the spinal veins, as shown in Figures 1d–f, resulting in spinal venous congestion, which eventually led to T2 hyperintensity, i.e., vasogenic edema, in the cord. This resulted in paraparesis, and the medullary involvement was responsible for respiratory insufficiency. Following this, the patient was taken for embolization

title: Atypical Cervical Myelopathy with Medullary Involvement from Intracranial Dural Arteriovenous Fistula: The Steroid Trap
text: . Following this, the patient was taken for embolization. A microcatheter was advanced into the dural branch of the middle meningeal artery, and Onyx was injected into the arterial feeder, as shown in Figure 1g. We note penetration of the Onyx into the venous pouch and complete obliteration of the fistula, as shown in Figures 1g-i. On follow-up, there was improvement in bilateral lower-limb power to 4/5, with no respiratory insufficiency.

title: Atypical Cervical Myelopathy with Medullary Involvement from Intracranial Dural Arteriovenous Fistula: The Steroid Trap
text: dAVFs are classified based on their venous drainage patterns observed on DSA,[8910] most commonly using the Cognard classification system. Type I lesions exhibit anterograde drainage into a dural venous sinus. Type II lesions demonstrate impaired sinus drainage with reflux into adjacent sinuses (IIa), cortical veins (IIb), or both (IIa + b). Type III dAVFs drain directly into cortical veins without venous ectasia, while Type IV demonstrates similar drainage with associated venous ectasia

title: Atypical Cervical Myelopathy with Medullary Involvement from Intracranial Dural Arteriovenous Fistula: The Steroid Trap
text: . Type III dAVFs drain directly into cortical veins without venous ectasia, while Type IV demonstrates similar drainage with associated venous ectasia. Type V lesions—relevant to this case—drain into the spinal perimedullary veins.[67] dAVFs account for approximately 10%–15% of intracranial arteriovenous malformations and are typically diagnosed between the fifth and sixth decades of life.[6] They most frequently occur at the transverse–sigmoid sinus, cavernous sinus, superior sagittal sinus, anterior cranial fossa, and tentorium.[67]

title: Atypical Cervical Myelopathy with Medullary Involvement from Intracranial Dural Arteriovenous Fistula: The Steroid Trap
text: The clinical spectrum of dAVFs is diverse, driven by the lesion’s location and its venous outflow pattern. Cognard type V dAVFs are particularly notable for their potential to cause myelopathy, quadriparesis, cranial neuropathies, and brainstem dysfunction due to retrograde venous hypertension involving the craniocervical junction and brainstem.[10] Wrobel et al. reported cases of cranial dAVFs causing myelopathy via venous drainage into posterior spinal veins through the petrosal vein, affirming the pathophysiological role of venous hypertension rather than arterial insufficiency.[9]

title: Atypical Cervical Myelopathy with Medullary Involvement from Intracranial Dural Arteriovenous Fistula: The Steroid Trap
text: Radiologically, cranial and spinal dAVFs can both show longitudinal cord signal changes, expansion, and perimedullary flow voids. Importantly, spinal dAVFs can induce abnormalities remote from the fistulous site via the coronal venous plexus.[36] However, extension of such signal abnormalities into the medulla has not been documented with spinal dAVFs, as noted by Ernst et al.[8] This distinction underlines the need for cranial DSA when spinal angiography fails to identify a lesion in patients with progressive myelopathy.[67] Brunereau et al., in his series of patients with intracranial dAVFs, showed that spinal draining could only be followed to the cervical level, where the veins were drained into the epidural venous system via a medullary-radicular vein.[110]

title: Atypical Cervical Myelopathy with Medullary Involvement from Intracranial Dural Arteriovenous Fistula: The Steroid Trap
text: Clinically, patients typically present with insidiously progressive motor weakness, gait instability, and urinary dysfunction evolving over weeks to months. Symptoms may worsen with increased intrathoracic pressure during Valsalva maneuvers. MRI typically reveals longitudinally extensive T2 hyperintensities spanning more than three vertebral segments, often without any evidence of compressive pathology. In cases where imaging is equivocal, catheter angiography remains the diagnostic gold standard.[6]

title: Atypical Cervical Myelopathy with Medullary Involvement from Intracranial Dural Arteriovenous Fistula: The Steroid Trap
text: Therapeutically, prompt intervention—either via endovascular embolization or microsurgical disconnection—is essential to arrest disease progression and reverse venous hypertension. The selection of treatment modality is guided by the angioarchitecture of the fistula.[1] Transarterial or transvenous embolization can offer durable occlusion with low complication rates in appropriately selected cases. However, complete obliteration of the draining vein is critical; failure to do so may exacerbate cortical venous reflux or activate collateral shunting pathways. Incomplete treatment of the draining vein or merely targeting arterial feeders is often ineffective and may lead to disease progression

title: Atypical Cervical Myelopathy with Medullary Involvement from Intracranial Dural Arteriovenous Fistula: The Steroid Trap
text: . Incomplete treatment of the draining vein or merely targeting arterial feeders is often ineffective and may lead to disease progression. Microsurgical disconnection remains a viable alternative, particularly in anatomically unfavorable cases, and focuses on disconnecting the venous outflow of the fistula to achieve cure.[1348]

title: Atypical Cervical Myelopathy with Medullary Involvement from Intracranial Dural Arteriovenous Fistula: The Steroid Trap
text: This case underscores the imperative to consider cranial dAVFs in the differential diagnosis of progressive, unexplained cervical myelopathy—especially when radiological findings extend into the medulla. Early identification through comprehensive neurovascular imaging can dramatically alter clinical outcomes and prevent irreversible deficits. Importantly, corticosteroid administration should be withheld until vascular etiologies such as dAVFs are conclusively excluded, as steroids may transiently mask or worsen symptoms.

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [abstract] Lyme disease is zoonotic infection transmitted by Borrelia burgdorferi and, if left undiagnosed, can present in later stages with neurological manifestations. This review aims to consolidate evidence on stroke-like or similar cerebrovascular outcomes of Lyme neuroborreliosis (LNB) to aid early recognition and treatment.

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [abstract] A comprehensive search resulted in 90 patients meeting European Federation of Neurological Societies/Infectious Diseases Society of America/ American Academy of Neurology/American College of Rheumatology (EFNS/IDSA/AAN/ACR) criteria for LNB with radiologically or serologically confirmed cerebrovascular involvement. Data were charted descriptively.

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [abstract] Median age was 12 years among children and 52 years in adult cases. Tick exposure was reported in 89% of cases. Presentations included hemiparesis (51%), cranial-nerve palsy (38%; Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) facial 31%), and cognitive changes (26%). Common imaging findings were vasculitis (72%) and ischaemic stroke (51%), mainly in the cortical (56%) area. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) lymphocytic pleocytosis (median 73 cells/µL) with presence of intrathecal Borrelia Immunoglobulin G (IgG) appeared in the majority of cases. Antibiotics (mainly ceftriaxone) were used in 85% of cases and interventional management in 13% of cases. Ninety percent of cases improved after 6 months of treatment. Mortality and persistent tetraplegia were reported in 5% and 3% of cases, respectively.

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [abstract] LNB should be suspected in cases of cryptogenic stroke from endemic areas. Reduction in CSF pleocytosis with intrathecal Borrelia antibodies could predict a favorable antibiotic response, although some refractory cases were observed to improve only with interventional management. Prompt diagnosis and management can affect morbidity and mortality.

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Introduction] Lyme disease is a zoonotic infection caused by Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato complex genospecies (Bbsl), B. afzelii, and B. garinii.[1] It is transmitted via the bite of infected Ixodes tick species across the Eurasian and North American subcontinents. As per Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports, roughly 89,468 cases of Lyme disease were reported in 2023, with higher incidence in the mid-Atlantic, Northeast, and Upper Midwest regions in the United States.[23]

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Introduction] Lyme disease, if untreated, typically progresses through stages: early localized (erythema migrans, regional lymphadenopathy), early disseminated (cardiac, ophthalmologic, or musculoskeletal manifestations), and late disseminated (neurological and dermatological).[45] The key neurological manifestations include lymphocytic meningitis, radiculoneuritis, cranial neuropathies (commonly of cranial nerves VII, VIII, III, V, or VI), myelitis, radiculitis, or mononeuropathy multiplex.[6789]

text: [Introduction] Stroke and other cerebrovascular events secondary to Lyme neuroborreliosis (LNB) are infrequent and often mistaken for other common etiologies. The diagnostic approach (2020 American Academy of Neurology (AAN)/American College of Rheumatology(ACR)/Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) Guidelines) for suspected LNB, while nonlinear in clinical practice, begins with an assessment of presentation and exposure risk [Figure 1].[10]

text: [Introduction] This review focuses on the current evidence of clinical features, serological and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analyses, and traditional and novel approaches in the management of vasculitides and neurovascular sequelae associated with Lyme disease, with an aim to map existing consensus and bridge knowledge gaps. Given its complex diagnostic approach and potential for morbidity, LNB remains a challenging topic for clinical research and systematic evaluation.

text: [Search strategy] A comprehensive literature search was conducted to identify studies on neurovascular manifestations of LNB published from the inception of major databases up to February 2025 [Supplementary Tables 1-6] and was performed across PubMed, Embase, Google Scholar, CORE, Directory of Open Access Journals, and BASE using combinations of the following terms: “neuroborreliosis,” “cerebral vasculitis,” “intracranial hemorrhage,” “subarachnoid hemorrhage,” “venous thrombosis,” “aneurysm,” “transient ischemic attack,” “hemorrhagic stroke,” and “ischemic stroke.” The complete search strategy is provided in the Supplementary Tables 1-6.

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Eligibility criteria] This scoping review included studies published from the inception of the database to February 2025. Studies were eligible if they described pediatric (ages 18 or below) or adult patients diagnosed with LNB based on European Federation of Neurological Societies or IDSA/AAN/ACR guidelines.[1314] The study had to document neurovascular involvement with a causal association proposed by clinical reasoning, diagnostic workup, or imaging. Studies reporting co-infections (e.g., syphilis, babesiosis), autoimmune or neurodegenerative disorders (e.g., multiple sclerosis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, and dementia), psychiatric disorders, seizure disorders, or other cerebrovascular etiologies without exposure or serological evidence of LNB were excluded

text: [Results] A total of 71 manuscripts [IS1-IS71; Supplementary Table 7] was reviewed and studied 92 patients following the selection criteria [Figure 2]. Two patients (Cases 1 and 3) were excluded due to poor quality of evidence of cerebrovascular involvement secondary to NB as per JBI checklists (IS40). The analyses included 90 patients, with a median age of 12 years (Interquartile Range (IQR): 9–14) in the pediatric population and a median age of 52 (IQR: 39–60) in the adult population. There was no gender predominance, with 54% of cases being male. The majority of the cases were reported from the European continent (Germany [25.6%] and France [8.9%]), followed by the United States (16.7%) [Figure 3, Supplementary Table 8]

text: [Results] . The median time of onset of neurological symptoms was less than 1 day, ranging up to 730 days (IQR: 1–14). A history of residence or travel to a Lyme-endemic area was documented in 89% (n/N = 63/71) of cases, and 51% (n/N = 32/63) recalled a tick bite. Of the 35 patients where comorbidities were documented, hypertension was the most common (n = 15/35). Common neurological manifestations reported in the cases were unilateral or bilateral hemiparesis (51%), followed by cranial nerve palsies (38%), most notably lower motor neuron (LMN) facial paralysis (31%), cognitive impairment (26%), ataxia (23%), dysarthria (19%), and paraesthesia (17%). The least commonly reported symptoms were meningeal signs (7%), seizures (9%), and cerebellar signs (11%)

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Results] . The least commonly reported symptoms were meningeal signs (7%), seizures (9%), and cerebellar signs (11%). It was interesting to note a few cases reporting tetraplegia (5.6%) and locked-in syndrome (2.2%) [Table 1]. Radiologically confirmed final diagnoses showed that roughly three-quarters of the cases (n/N = 64/89) had evidence of vasculitis, 50.6% of cases had ischemic strokes, and 6.7% of cases had aneurysms. Rarer diagnoses of cerebrovascular involvement were cases with hemorrhagic-conversion strokes (5.6%), subarachnoid hemorrhage (6.7%), or cerebral venous sinus thromboses (5.6%). Two cases (2.2%) of isolated intracranial hemorrhage were reported. Only 2.2% of cases reported normal imaging findings

Brain regions most affected included the cerebral cortex (56.2%), particularly the parietal (16.9%), temporal (16.9%), and frontal lobes (11.2%). The brainstem was affected in 26/89 (29.2%) cases, and deeper brain structures such as the basal ganglia (23.6%), thalamus (13.5%), and internal capsule (7.9%) were involved in over two-fifth of reported cases [40/89]. Diencephalic (14.6%) and cerebellar (2.2%) regions were less commonly affected

Surgical interventions were necessary in 12/90 patients and included intra-arterial thrombolysis (33.3%), aneurysm embolization or clipping (16.6%), and stenting and decompressive craniectomy ([16.6%] each) [Table 4]. Regarding outcomes, the median follow-up was 4.5 months (IQR: 1.4–7.25 months) for serological monitoring and 6 months (IQR: 2–12 months) for neurological assessment. A reduction in serological markers was achieved in almost all cases (41/43 cases), while a majority (79/88 cases) showed improvement in neurological signs or imaging. text: [Discussion] This study reviews case studies and case series to provide clinicians with a descriptive review of expectations in a patient with probable LNB. A scoping review was undertaken to systematically identify reported cases and explore the heterogenous range of data, which could tend to be prone to bias due to the reliance of the review on case reports and series.

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] This extracellular spirochete causes a persistent infection by deploying specific virulence factors. In the tick midgut, it expresses outer surface protein (Osp) A and OspB, responsible for colonization and midgut adhesion, respectively. Once the tick feeds, OspC, shielded by the tick salivary protein Salp15, allows the spirochete to evade host antibodies and dampens the requirement for Natural Killer (NK) cells and macrophages.[18] In the human host, it survives through various adaptations, such as complement inhibition, antigenic variation, and immunomodulatory surface proteins.

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] The translocation of B. burgdorferi across the blood-brain barrier is a rare event, but its migration into brain parenchyma and the surrounding extracellular matrix can be influenced by chronic inflammation. The neurotropic nature is linked to the OspC, encoded by the ospC gene. Among the thirty-five identified genotypes, types A, B, I, and K strains have been implicated in cerebrovascular inflammation.[1920] The presence of antibodies against particular antigens (IgM against VlsE, p41, and OspC, or IgG against p100, vIsE, and p18) could predict probable cerebrovascular NB involvement.[21]

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] NB was first identified in the 1920s.[22] It is notifiable only in a few European countries, reflecting a surveillance gap. The individual manifestations of Lyme disease are not tracked, and neurological estimates rely on proportions rather than individual counts.[23] A bimodal pattern was observed in the age group of less than 20 years or between 40 and 60 years in 30% of the cases. This could be attributed to a likelihood of longer outdoor exposure and more extensive workup performed in younger age groups.

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] Although the review has noticed no predominance of a particular gender, previous population-based cohorts have noticed male adults with a higher incidence of presentations of Lyme disease and women appearing to be more prone to post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome.[2425] This discrepancy may reflect a limitation of the review’s reliance on case reports, which might have skewed gender representation. Most cases in the review have an exposure to endemic areas, but a recent trend of declining or stable incidence during nation-wide surveillance reports could be linked to environmental changes, vector ecology, or public health interventions.[2627]

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] Hypertension was a common comorbidity, reflecting a baseline prevalence rather than an additive burden. The lower representation of traditional stroke risk factors suggests the role of Bb in vascular inflammation. Comorbid conditions can play a role in the reporting of long-term symptoms and overall quality of life of Lyme disease patients and could be considered in the evaluation of these patients.[28] A lower subset of studies with this statistic proposes inclusion of complete vascular risk profiles in prospective studies to understand Borrelia-specific pathology from coincidental stroke mechanisms. The predominance of hemiparesis and other upper motor neuron signs over other symptoms supports the hypothesis of Lyme being a stroke mimic

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] . The predominance of hemiparesis and other upper motor neuron signs over other symptoms supports the hypothesis of Lyme being a stroke mimic. The relative scarcity of meningeal signs is reflective of a vasculitic over meningoencephalitic pathophysiology.

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] This review identified three vascular findings: (I) ischemic outnumbered hemorrhagic lesions, highlighting a probable inflammatory over hypertensive nature; (II) although the process is predominantly arterial, cerebral venous sinus thromboses can occur; and (III) Borrelia-mediated vasculitis can possibly weaken arterial walls to cause aneurysms, intracranial, and subarachnoid hemorrhages. Existing literature mentions that imaging in NB has heterogenous results, and its role is mainly to exclude other diagnoses.[293031] A quarter of the imaging reports showed concentric enhancement across multiple vascular beds, indicating a diffuse inflammatory arteriopathy rather than single-territory atherosclerosis

text: [Discussion] . Brain biopsy was done in two cases, one of which suspected intracranial masses as the cause of stroke (IS10, IS54). Although invasive, it provided an accurate diagnosis of the inflammatory origin of lesions, describing them as “perivascular cuffing with lymphocytes.”

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] As per guidelines, initial diagnostic testing should include two-tiered serologic testing (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay followed by confirmatory Western blot analysis), followed by lumbar puncture if indicated.[10] The review found varying patterns of serological findings, and CSF findings were relied upon for Borrelia infection interpretation. CSF analyses should focus on identifying lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein concentration, and an elevated CSF-to-serum Borrelia-specific antibody index ratio (AR). Increased Bb-specific CSF: serum (IgG) AR reflects ongoing intrathecal antibody production during NB. It was noticed that the LNB CSF findings were like a tuberculous meningitis profile. Our findings could reflect how the diagnostic yield of PCR testing is limited

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] . Our findings could reflect how the diagnostic yield of PCR testing is limited. Serum PCR positivity was low (4/16), and CSF PCR positivity was only modestly higher (6/20), consistent with the fact of low sensitivity of B. burgdorferi in CSF via PCR.[1314] This reinforces the need to interpret diagnostic tests in the context of clinical features and exposure. Elevated levels of neurofilament or CXCL13 in CSF were reported in seven cases, reflecting axonal loss typically corelated with neurodegenerative processes. This is consistent with findings from a trial, which supports the utility of serum neurofilament biomarker for acute-phase LNB.[3233] Future studies can focus on validating similar biomarkers for early diagnosis.

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] A diagnosis of definite LNB requires the convergence of clinical features, exposure history, positive CSF results, and supportive serologic findings. During tick-endemic seasons (i.e. summer, when people do tend to do more outdoor activities), most clinicians should try to include a tick profile: anything an Ixodes tick can transmit (identifying for Borrelia, Anaplasma, Babesia, and Ehrlichia).

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] Treatment typically has a prolonged course of antibiotics, with doxycycline or ceftriaxone being first-line options for central nervous system involvement. Clinicians prefer cephalosporins over doxycycline in most situations because of the historical belief of better blood–brain barrier penetration. If chosen, patients tend to be on doxycycline for a longer time compared to its penicillin counterpart.[34] However, recent studies have proven doxycycline to be safe and as effective as beta-lactams for children and adults.[3536] Uncertainty in the use of drugs for secondary prevention of stroke was reflected in this study, with only one-third of the cases utilizing them

text: [Discussion] . The IDSA guidelines do not endorse routine corticosteroid use as adjunctive therapy, and anticoagulants, antiepileptics, or acetazolamide were noticed to be used for supportive reasons.[10] Surgical interventions (endovascular approaches such as intra-arterial thrombolysis or stenting, aneurysm embolization or clipping) were utilized in about one in nine patients in the review. Selective cases with elevated intracranial pressure underwent decompressive craniectomy or hemicraniectomy. This could suggest earlier initiation of antibiotic treatment to prevent disease from progressing to requiring salvage surgical intervention

Although medical and interventional treatments are effective, no vaccine has yet been approved for the prevention of Lyme disease.[37] The Valneva–Pfizer “VLA15” is currently the only Lyme disease (LD) vaccine candidate in advanced clinical development (Phase III), with potential for better preventive control.

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] As neurological outcomes normalize later than serological markers, they may be followed up longer for assessing recovery. This was the trend observed in our review as well. The outcomes tend to be favorable in treated patients. Effective pathogen clearance is observed in almost all cases (90%), with either neurological or radiological improvement. The review suggests that vessel wall or parenchymal normalization could persist longer after functional recovery, with only 40% of cases achieving stable or reversed lesions. Atypical presentations of LNB are frequently subject to misdiagnosis and increased morbidity and mortality.[3839] A case reported an adult who presented with tetraplegia within hours. CSF analyses confirmed NB, and they were started on antibiotics

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] . CSF analyses confirmed NB, and they were started on antibiotics. Although respiratory and autonomic functions recovered, they remained tetraplegic (IS59).[40] Another patient was identified to have NB and received oral doxycycline, steroids, and cyclophosphamide for refractory vasculitis. Within 3 weeks, severe bi-hemispheric infarctions led to worsening cerebral edema with transtentorial and subfalcine herniation (IS35).[41] The patient had a prolonged onset of symptoms. Their condition worsened despite initiation of antibiotics, with further progression from stenosis to thrombosis of the basilar artery

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] . Their condition worsened despite initiation of antibiotics, with further progression from stenosis to thrombosis of the basilar artery. Tetraplegia persisted with anarthria and dysphagia (IS1).[42] The patient had multiple comorbidities, was admitted intubated and on vasopressors, and remained ventilator-dependent despite antibiotic therapy. Life support was withdrawn as per family wishes (IS15).[43] Another patient had escalating cerebral edema despite antibiotics and decompressive craniectomy and did not survive (IS8).[44] This patient had worsening of cerebral arterial stenoses and occurrence of a subdural hemorrhage despite interventional efforts, resulting in death (IS67).[45]

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] Another interesting presentation of NB with cerebrovascular manifestations is Syndrome of Inappropriate Anti-Diuretic Hormone (SIADH). In this review, Chehrenama et al.[46] reported a case in which the patient developed SIADH during the progression of the disease. Evidence for this association is limited, with a few case reports describing hyponatremia in conjunction with positive CSF findings for NB. This underscores the need to consider rare infections, such as borreliosis, as a possible cause of the neuroendocrine manifestation. The application of standardized clinical guidelines in LNB is not universally straightforward due to significant heterogeneity among reported cases. In instances of inconclusive labs or imaging, clinicians may have to rely on individual judgment

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] . In instances of inconclusive labs or imaging, clinicians may have to rely on individual judgment. Although a comparison of preceding non-neurological manifestations would have been valuable in identifying early clinical scenarios that warrant suspicion for NB, most reported cases in our review either presented primarily with neurological symptoms or did not provide sufficient detail on earlier systemic features. This limited the ability to characterize pre-neurological presentations. The reliance on case series limits the capacity to draw causal associations and is prone to reporting bias. Quality appraisal, while performed, could not be used to weigh studies, ranking low-quality reports the same as higher-quality ones

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Discussion] . Quality appraisal, while performed, could not be used to weigh studies, ranking low-quality reports the same as higher-quality ones. As a result, the findings should be interpreted as exploratory, owing to the study design’s constraints on performing advanced statistical analyses. Advanced imaging modalities have a limitation in identifying subtle or early-stage vascular involvement, particularly of those with a small caliber. Furthermore, there is a limited body of evidence supporting interventional approaches or adjunctive therapies. Despite a comprehensive search strategy, exclusion of studies in non-English languages or without available English translations could have limited the diversity of cases discussed.

title: Exploring Cerebrovascular Manifestations of Neuroborreliosis: A Scoping Review
text: [Conclusions] LNB can present with diverse cerebrovascular manifestations, mainly ischemic stroke. Given its potential for misdiagnosis, key diagnostic clues are essential for recognizing LNB. A high index of clinical suspicion and routine incorporation of Lyme serology and CSF analysis are recommended in the work-up of unexplained cerebrovascular events in individuals from endemic areas. Timely diagnosis and appropriate antimicrobial therapy should be considered to prevent irreversible neurological deficits and morbidity. Novel modalities of management, such as interventional techniques, could reduce morbidity and prevent mortality in affected patients.

text: [abstract] Developed at Bayer Technology Services, PK‐Sim and MoBi transitioned into the Open Systems Pharmacology (OSP) Suite, released as free open‐source software in 2017. An active community with stakeholders from academia, industries, and regulators contributes to the continuous improvement of open‐source model‐informed drug development (MIDD). This perspective summarizes the latest advancements presented at the second OSP Community Conference (OSP‐CC) hosted from 29 to 30th of September 2025 at Sanofi Paris, that gathered over 100 attendees from more than 40 institutions.

title: Open Systems Pharmacology Community Conference (OSP‐CC) Proceedings 2025
section: Human Intestinal Organoids and Potential Application for PBPK Modeling
text: [Human Intestinal Organoids and Potential Application for PBPK Modeling] Besides potential permeability and solubility limitations, active processes such as enzymatic metabolism and transporter activity may influence the observed bioavailability. Human intestinal organoids differentiated into functional epithelial monolayers were presented as an alternative to traditional Caco‐2 cell models. They express drug‐metabolizing enzymes like Cytochrome P450 (CYP) 3A4 and Uridine Diphosphate Glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs), showing metabolic capabilities accounting for the intestinal first‐pass effect. A good correlation between contextualized PBPK models with organoid‐based in vitro measures and clinically observed bioavailability was found, confirming gut wall metabolism as a potential contributor to bioavailability limitations.

section: Growing a Community‐Built Qualified OSP Suite Model Library
text: [Growing a Community‐Built Qualified OSP Suite Model Library] A qualified OSP‐model library (https://github.com/Open‐Systems‐Pharmacology/OSP‐PBPK‐Model‐Library) is the basis for reproducible workflows. New OSP features and software releases, such as updating expression data, require a systematic reevaluation of the library (currently > 30 drug molecules and DDI interactions) and recreating model specific OSP‐Qualification‐Reports (https://github.com/Open‐Systems‐Pharmacology/OSP‐Qualification‐Reports)

text: [Growing a Community‐Built Qualified OSP Suite Model Library] . Updating ADME protein expression values with the latest RNAseq expression databases (https://github.com/Open‐Systems‐Pharmacology/Gene‐Expression‐Databases) requires parameter reidentification via OSPSuite.ParameterIdentification (https://github.com/Open‐Systems‐Pharmacology/OSPSuite.ParameterIdentification) as expression changes impact the pharmacokinetic profile [3]. An automated workflow updating model parameters was presented ensuring high model quality and continuous improvement of the OSP software.

section: An Open Source In Silico Framework to Support Trial Design Decisions and Virtual Bioequivalence Assessments
text: [An Open Source In Silico Framework to Support Trial Design Decisions and Virtual Bioequivalence Assessments] The presented OSP Virtual‐bioequivalence (VBE) toolbox (https://github.com/Open‐Systems‐Pharmacology/OSPSuite.VBE‐Toolbox) integrates in vitro and in vivo data, enabling the generation of probabilistic predictions of drug exposure across formulations [4]. These analyses can inform bioequivalence trials and serve as a potential alternative to traditional bioequivalence studies that compare a test formulation with an established reference product to streamline drug development reducing the reliance on costly clinical trials.

section: Integrating Age‐ and BMI‐Related Changes to Form a Comprehensive Repository for Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic (PBPK) Modeling of Older People and People With Obesity
text: [Integrating Age‐ and BMI‐Related Changes to Form a Comprehensive Repository for Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic (PBPK) Modeling of Older People and People With Obesity] Underrepresentation of older adults and adults with obesity in clinical trials can be a challenge for drug efficacy and safety assessment. A comprehensive database integrating age‐ and body mass index (BMI)‐related changes was presented, including updates of organ weights, blood flows, glomerular filtration rate (GFR), and CYP metabolism [5]. Validation was performed for renally‐cleared and CYP3A4‐metabolized compounds showing improvements for adults with obesity and age‐related pharmacokinetic changes.

title: Open Systems Pharmacology Community Conference (OSP‐CC) Proceedings 2025
section: PBBM With OSP Suite: A Powerful Approach to Solving Bioequivalence Challenges in Regulated and Under Regulated Markets
text: [PBBM With OSP Suite: A Powerful Approach to Solving Bioequivalence Challenges in Regulated and Under Regulated Markets] In Latin American markets, regulatory requirements for bioequivalence vary significantly, creating challenges for product evaluation, particularly in countries where similar drug products reach the market without bioequivalence studies [6]. Physiologically‐based biopharmaceutics modeling (PBBM) was used in case studies for carvedilol, furosemide, omeprazole to predict bioequivalence and product development in both regulated and under‐regulated markets. In the presented examples, sex differences in gastrointestinal physiology were highlighted as critical for accurate bioequivalence predictions.

title: Open Systems Pharmacology Community Conference (OSP‐CC) Proceedings 2025
section: Bridging In Vitro Dissolution and In Vivo Pharmacokinetics: Application of a Novel Physiologically Based Biopharmaceutics Modeling (PBBM) Workflow to Vericiguat
text: [Bridging In Vitro Dissolution and In Vivo Pharmacokinetics: Application of a Novel Physiologically Based Biopharmaceutics Modeling (PBBM) Workflow to Vericiguat] A PBBM workflow (https://github.com/Open‐Systems‐Pharmacology/Oral‐PBBM‐Workflow) was presented utilizing a solubility toolbox for characterizing pH‐ and bile salt‐effects on solubilization. An in vitro dissolution model with mechanistic particle dissolution equations for the US Pharmacopeia (USP) 2 dissolution apparatus and enhanced human PBPK capabilities with updated GI tract parameters were applied to vericiguat. The workflow successfully predicted fasted and fed‐state pharmacokinetics and drug–drug interactions (DDI) with omeprazole and demonstrates potential for biowaiver support, formulation optimization, and virtual bioequivalence studies [7].

title: Open Systems Pharmacology Community Conference (OSP‐CC) Proceedings 2025
section: Accelerating Drug Discovery: Systematic Application of PBPK Modeling Supporting Candidate Selection
text: [Accelerating Drug Discovery: Systematic Application of PBPK Modeling Supporting Candidate Selection] Applying PBPK models in early drug discovery requires fast model building and analysis based on a seamless integration of required model parameters. An OSP‐based high‐throughput PBPK platform was presented integrating measured compound information and machine learning models for parameter prediction to accelerate drug discovery. The system automates data transfer of 48 in vitro assays using decision trees selecting appropriate physicochemical and ADME parameters, while incorporated machine learning models predict missing property values

text: [Accelerating Drug Discovery: Systematic Application of PBPK Modeling Supporting Candidate Selection] . Validation across 575 rat and 150 monkey IV studies demonstrated good predictive performance for extended clearance classification system (ECCS) class 2 compounds, enabling systematic candidate assessment and supporting portfolio‐wide screening for complex disposition mechanisms.

title: Open Systems Pharmacology Community Conference (OSP‐CC) Proceedings 2025
section: Prediction of Human Pharmacokinetics From Chemical Structure—Combining Mechanistic Modeling With Machine Learning
text: [Prediction of Human Pharmacokinetics From Chemical Structure—Combining Mechanistic Modeling With Machine Learning] Hybrid approaches combine machine learning with mechanistic modeling to predict pharmacokinetics directly from chemical structures. Combining graph convolutional neural networks (GNN) with PBPK models enabled prediction of key PK parameters (AUCiv, AUCpo, Cmax). Trained on ~10,000 compounds, a hybrid rat model was shown to achieve good exposure predictions after intravenous and oral administration [8]. The showcased approaches outperforms pure deep learning models and conventional scaling methods, particularly for oral exposure predictions, enabling early compound screening, prioritization, and dose predictions while reducing animal testing in accordance with 3R principles.

title: Open Systems Pharmacology Community Conference (OSP‐CC) Proceedings 2025
section: Integrating In Vitro and In Silico Approaches Enables Accurate Prediction of Drug‐Induced Liver Injury
text: [Integrating In Vitro and In Silico Approaches Enables Accurate Prediction of Drug‐Induced Liver Injury] Predicting drug‐induced toxicities as early as possible can help to focus on promising candidates and save valuable R&D resources. Combining in vitro toxicity assays with PBPK modeling was used to predict clinically known drug‐induced liver injury (DILI). Based on 241 drugs and in vitro toxicity assay data, clinical DILI outcomes were predicted using ratios of in vitro and PBPK model predicted Cmax values with good accuracy (ROC AUC 91%), outperforming simple heuristic screening rules (50%–70% accuracy). The presented approach demonstrates the potential of early DILI predictions aiming to reduce clinical failures and market withdrawals [9].

title: Open Systems Pharmacology Community Conference (OSP‐CC) Proceedings 2025
section: Tools and Workflows for Automated Reporting of PBPK Modeling With OSP
text: [Tools and Workflows for Automated Reporting of PBPK Modeling With OSP] Manual preparation of reports and submission files is time consuming and error prone. An automated reporting workflow using ospsuite (https://www.open‐systems‐pharmacology.org/OSPSuite‐R/) and osp.snapshots (https://github.com/esqLABS/osp.snapshots) R packages was presented. By using standardized tables, text blocks, and figures, an automated model documentation and report generation process could be developed that significantly reduces reporting time while improving consistency and reducing manual errors in regulatory documentation generation.

title: Open Systems Pharmacology Community Conference (OSP‐CC) Proceedings 2025
section: PBPK Modeling in Regulatory Submissions to the MHRA
text: [PBPK Modeling in Regulatory Submissions to the MHRA] Acceptance of modeling analysis is key for successful applications. PBPK modeling can help to reduce clinical trial burden by predicting DDI, population‐specific effects, and absorption mechanisms informing dose selection. Model qualifications are critical, with requirements proportional to regulatory impact and patient risk requiring individual evaluation for each application. Successful case examples involving CYP3A4 inhibition, pediatric dosing, gastric pH effects, and nasal absorption were presented. Stricter scrutiny for high‐risk applications like extrapolations requires a robust qualification to support regulatory decisions.

title: Open Systems Pharmacology Community Conference (OSP‐CC) Proceedings 2025
section: Software Verification, Validation, and Context of Use (CoU) Qualification of Open‐Source Modeling & Simulation Software for Regulatory Use in Translational MIDD
text: [Software Verification, Validation, and Context of Use (CoU) Qualification of Open‐Source Modeling & Simulation Software for Regulatory Use in Translational MIDD] The OSP platform uses GitHub for version control (https://github.com/Open‐Systems‐Pharmacology), automated testing, and code quality analysis. The community addresses regulatory challenges through open‐source transparency and community‐driven qualification. A three‐pillar approach encompasses software validation, CoU qualification, and installation verification. A qualification framework allows automatic re‐qualification with new releases or data. Examples of MIDD applications accepted by regulatory agencies and an outlook expanding to modular PBPK‐QSP integration were presented.

section: Integrating Population Approaches With Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Models: A Novel Framework for Parameter Estimation
text: [Integrating Population Approaches With Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Models: A Novel Framework for Parameter Estimation] The saemixPBPK (https://github.com/Sanofi‐Public/saemixPBPK) package was presented aiming to integrate population pharmacokinetic approaches in PBPK modeling. This hybrid approach combines the stochastic approximation expectation–maximization (SAEM) algorithm with mechanistic OSP models, enabling the estimation of individual parameters, quantification of interindividual variability, and assessment of covariate effects. The approach was evaluated using theophylline data with smoking status as a covariate and a drug–drug interaction study including itraconazole, resulting in more robust data‐informed predictions including population variability.

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [abstract] Paracetamol (PCM) is extensively metabolized in the liver via glucuronidation, sulfation, and oxidation. Although oral and intravenous PCM are commonly used interchangeably, a comprehensive evaluation of PCM metabolism across both routes is lacking. This study aimed to characterize the full pharmacokinetic (PK) profiles of PCM and its metabolites following oral and intravenous administration, accounting for presystemic and systemic metabolism. Concentrations of PCM, PCM‐glucuronide (PCM‐GLU), PCM‐sulfate (PCM‐SUL), PCM‐cysteine (PCM‐CYS), and PCM‐mercapturate (PCM‐MER) were pooled from three clinical studies, involving 53 adults with obesity and 16 adults without obesity (18–65 years, 53–198 kg)

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [abstract] . A semi‐physiological population PK model was developed with nonlinear mixed‐effects modeling, incorporating intestinal and liver compartments, and enterohepatic recirculation. A semi‐physiological PK model incorporating presystemic and systemic hepatic metabolism captured PK of PCM and PCM‐SUL following oral and intravenous administration. Intestinal oxidative metabolism for PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER and enterohepatic recirculation for PCM‐GLU were added to capture their full PK profiles. The estimated fraction of PCM absorbed was 0.745 (95% CI 0.699–0.792), with extensive first‐pass metabolism and faster metabolite formation after oral than after intravenous administration

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [abstract] . This semi‐physiological population PK model identified both hepatic and intestinal presystemic metabolism of PCM, as well as enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐GLU. Oral administration of PCM results in faster metabolite formation than intravenous dosing, mainly for the oxidative metabolites. This modeling approach may support the quantification of presystemic and systemic metabolism, which can be relevant for oral and intravenous dosing of drugs metabolized by multiple pathways.
