title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Introduction] Paracetamol (acetaminophen, PCM) is a widely used analgesic and antipyretic drug. It is extensively metabolized in the liver, mainly via glucuronidation (55%), sulfation (30%), and oxidation by cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes (5%–10%) [1, 2, 3, 4]. The oxidation pathway generates the toxic metabolite N‐acetyl‐p‐benzoquinone imine (NAPQI). Under normal conditions, this compound is detoxified by glutathione conjugation to form the harmless metabolites PCM‐cysteine (PCM‐CYS) and PCM‐mercapturate (PCM‐MER). When PCM is given at therapeutic doses, glutathione can sufficiently neutralize NAPQI. However, when glutathione is depleted (e.g., in cases of PCM overdose or malnutrition), this leads to increased accumulation of NAPQI, which can lead to liver failure.

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Introduction] PCM is rapidly absorbed after oral administration and undergoes first‐pass hepatic metabolism. Its pharmacokinetics have been extensively studied in diverse populations, including individuals with obesity [5], pregnant women [6], neonates [7], and older adults [8]. Several factors, including genetic polymorphisms and hepatic enzyme activity, contribute to interindividual and interethnic variability [4]. Patient weight is an important driver for PCM metabolism. Patients with obesity (BMI ≥ 30 kg m−2) have higher hepatic blood flow and increased expression of CYP2E1—the enzyme involved in the oxidative metabolism of PCM and the formation of NAPQI [5]

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Introduction] . As a result of increased CYP2E1‐mediated oxidation, glucuronidation, and sulfation, patients with obesity have an increased PCM clearance, whereas they also have a higher volume of distribution (Vd), leading to lower systemic PCM levels after standard dosing [5, 9]. In addition, patients with obesity show earlier and higher peak concentrations of PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER after the first dose. Despite these changes, the relative contribution of each metabolic pathway remains comparable to that of individuals with normal weight [5]

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Introduction] . Despite these changes, the relative contribution of each metabolic pathway remains comparable to that of individuals with normal weight [5]. In support of additional factors influencing the PK of PCM and its metabolites, studies have suggested the presence of CYP2E1 in the intestines [10] and enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐GLU in rats [11, 12], where deglucuronidation of PCM‐GLU and subsequent reabsorption of PCM in the gut were observed. These observations highlight the complex interplay between physiological factors and PCM metabolism and underscore the importance of studying presystemic and systemic processes across different routes of administration.

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Introduction] Although a recent physiologically–based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model studied PCM PK following both oral and intravenous administration, it did not account for metabolite formation [13]. Additionally, previous studies examined intravenous [5] and oral [9] PCM metabolism separately. Hence, a comprehensive combined evaluation of PCM metabolism following oral and intravenous administration to study presystemic and systemic metabolism is lacking. Therefore, this study aims to study the PK of PCM and its metabolites after oral and intravenous administration in patients using a semi‐physiological population PK approach.

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Study Design and Population] In this pooled study, data were obtained from three independent clinical studies on the PK of PCM and metabolites (see Table 1). Study 1 (PAPAYA Study) was a clinical trial conducted in the Netherlands, including patients with obesity planned to undergo a laparoscopic Roux‐en‐Y gastric bypass and healthy participants without obesity. Participants were excluded if they were pregnant, had liver disease, or had received PCM within 24 h prior to the study. Before participation, all participants provided written informed consent. This study was approved by the medical ethics committee of Erasmus Medical Center (NL70329.078.19) and the local scientific committee of Albert Schweitzer Hospital (2019–084)

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Study Design and Population] . The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and the Medical Research Involving Human Subjects Act (WMO) of the Netherlands. All included patients and healthy participants received 1000 mg of oral PCM (2 tablets of 500 mg from Teva, dispersed in 50–100 mL water prior to administration). Blood was drawn pre‐dose and at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 24 h following administration of PCM. text: [Study Design and Population] Study 2 was previously conducted in patients with obesity who were scheduled to undergo laparoscopic Roux‐en‐Y gastric bypass in the United States [9]. All patients received a single dose of 1500 mg oral PCM. For this PK analysis, only results from patients before surgery were included.

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Study Design and Population] Study 3 was a previously published study performed in the Netherlands, including patients with obesity planned to undergo a bariatric surgical procedure (laparoscopic Roux‐en‐Y gastric bypass or gastric sleeve) and patients without obesity undergoing oral and maxillofacial surgery [5]. All patients received 2000 mg of intravenous PCM just prior to the surgery. After 8 h, patients could receive PCM according to the standard postoperative pain protocol. Consequently, data from Study 3 included samples obtained after multiple doses of intravenous PCM. Detailed study designs and patient characteristics for Study 2 and Study 3 have been described previously [5, 9].

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Drug Assays] PCM, PCM‐GLU, PCM‐SUL, PCM‐CYS, and PCM‐MER were measured using high‐performance liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS). The analytical details of Study 1 were previously described by Flint et al. [14], and those of Study 2 were described by Chen et al. [9], and of Study 3 by Van Rongen et al. [5].

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Structural Model Development] The starting point for model development was the previously published model on the basis of intravenous PCM data from Study 3 [5]. In short, this model consisted of a one‐compartment model for PCM and PCM‐GLU, a combined one‐compartment model for PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER, and a two‐compartment model for PCM‐SUL, with linear eliminations for all metabolites. To incorporate oral data and account for potential route‐specific differences in PK, the model was extended in three steps.

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Structural Model Development] As a first step, an oral depot compartment with first‐order absorption was added to allow estimation of the fraction absorbed (Fa) and the absorption rate constant (ka). All other structural features and model assumptions were retained from the original intravenous model [5].

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Structural Model Development] In the second step, it was assessed whether presystemic metabolism accounts for differences in metabolite profiles following oral and intravenous administration. For this step, a semi‐physiological model was implemented on the basis of Brill et al. [15], incorporating gut wall, portal vein, and liver compartments. Hepatic metabolism was parameterized using the well‐stirred liver model, where the hepatic extraction ratio (EH) was estimated by the parameters intrinsic hepatic clearance (CLH,int) and liver blood flow (QH). Intestinal metabolism was modeled by estimating the gut wall extraction ratio (EG), incorporating villous blood flow (Qvilli) and permeability clearance through the enterocytes in the gut wall (CLperm) [16]

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Structural Model Development] . The intrinsic intestinal clearance (CLG,int) was estimated as a fraction of CLH,int. Drug‐specific parameters such as fraction unbound and CLperm were obtained from the literature [17, 18] and implemented in this semi‐physiological model. The previously assumed fraction of PCM cleared unchanged [5] was excluded from this model because of its minimal contribution to total clearance. Full details about the drug‐ and system‐specific parameters and semi‐physiological equations can be found in Table S1.

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Structural Model Development] In the third step, the inclusion of enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐GLU was evaluated to explain potential differences in PCM and PCM‐GLU concentrations following oral and intravenous administration. A gallbladder compartment was incorporated on the basis of a modified version of the model described by De Winter et al. [19]. In this model, PCM‐GLU entered into the gallbladder. The gallbladder emptied at a periodic interval of 3 h, releasing PCM back to the gut wall via a first‐order reabsorption process. Release times of pulsated gall release were allowed to vary across the datasets, reflecting different fasting states (fasted in Studies 2 and 3 and no restrictions of fasting in Study 1). This model assumed that all participants had an intact gallbladder and biliary system.

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Structural Model Development] Body size metrics, that is, total body weight or lean body weight (LBW), were initially retained from the original model of van Rongen et al. [5] and re‐evaluated in later phases of model development. To integrate these covariates into a model incorporating presystemic metabolism, the original LBW covariates previously applied to plasma clearances [5] were transformed to LBW covariates on CLH,int. LBW was calculated as described by Janmahasatian et al. [20].

text: [Stochastic Model Development] Residual variability was implemented as a combined proportional and additive error for PCM, PCM‐GLU, and PCM‐SUL, as shown in Equation (2):where C obs,ij is the observed concentration, C pred,ij is the predicted concentration, and where both proportional error ε p,ij and additive error ε a,ij have a mean of zero and a variance of σ 2 . To account for potential differences in the distribution of residual errors, separate error components were estimated for each study. For PCM‐CYS & PCM‐MER, a proportional error model was implemented for Studies 1 and 3, whereas an additive model was implemented for Study 2.

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Model Selection and Evaluation] Discrimination between models was guided by the precision of parameter estimates, shrinkages of omega and sigma (< 30%), a drop in objective function value (OFV, equal to minus two times log likelihood) with significance levels of p < 0.01 (decrease in OFV [dOFV] > 6.64) for hierarchical models, and parameter plausibility. Backward elimination was used to test whether a covariate could be left out (p < 0.01 or dOFV > 6.64). Goodness‐of‐fit (GOF) plots were stratified for route of administration (oral versus intravenous), study, and obesity status. To obtain parameter precision, sampling importance resampling (SIR) was used [21]. Internal model evaluation was further supported by stratified GOF plots and normalized prediction distribution error (NPDE) plots.

text: [Simulations] To illustrate the differences in PCM and metabolite profiles between oral and intravenous administration, simulations were performed with the final semi‐physiological population PK model. Concentration‐time curves at steady state (1000 mg four times daily) were simulated following both oral and intravenous administration in patients with and without obesity. Curves of four typical patients from the dataset of Study 1 were simulated, that is, those with total body weights of 60 kg, 92 kg, 120 kg, and 150 kg. The 60 kg and 92 kg patients represent the lower and higher interquartile ranges of patients without obesity, whereas the 120 kg and 150 kg patients represent lower and higher weights than the median of patients with obesity

text: [Patients and Data] Patient characteristics are summarized in Table 1. In total, 69 participants were included: 28 received PCM intravenously, and 41 received PCM orally. Notably, patients from Study 2 had comparable LBW and total body weight to those in the other studies but had a higher BMI.

text: [Patients and Data] Concentration‐time profiles of PCM and all metabolites are shown in Figure 1. From all observations, 13 individuals displayed double peaks in PCM concentration—9 after oral and 4 after intravenous administration—suggesting potential involvement of enterohepatic recirculation. In total, 782 PCM observations, 784 PCM‐GLU observations, 783 PCM‐SUL observations, and 766 PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER observations were available for analysis.

Observations of Study 3 after multiple dosing were left out in this plot for better visual comparison with Study 1 and 2. The plots are stratified by compound, study, and obesity status. title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Model Development] The previously published compartmental model for intravenous PCM and metabolites [5] extended with an oral depot compartment, was first applied to the entire dataset to assess its predictive performance. This initial model showed that the formation of metabolites was faster following oral administration compared to intravenous dosing, most distinctively for PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER. The NPDE plot shows that PCM concentrations were overpredicted, whereas metabolites were underpredicted following oral administration (example in Figure S1). This discrepancy suggested a substantial role for presystemic metabolism.

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Model Development] To address presystemic metabolism, hepatic and intestinal clearance were incorporated as a second step in model development. The addition of the well‐stirred liver model alone—reparameterized into QH and CLH,int—improved model predictions for PCM and its PCM‐GLU and PCM‐SUL metabolites (data not shown), but showed considerable misfit for PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER during the first 2 h after administration. Therefore, intestinal oxidative metabolism was also included in the model, which further improved the model fit, particularly for PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER in the first 2 h following oral dosing (Figure S2). The ratio of CLG,int to CLH,int was 0.00474 (95% CI 0.0032–0.0069) in our study, which was comparable to previous findings in patients receiving midazolam, where this ratio was 0.0012 [15]

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Model Development] . Unfortunately, no data about CLG,int of CYP2E1‐mediated metabolism are available. On the basis of mRNA and protein levels in different parts of the intestinal parts of humans [10, 24, 25], the low ratio of CLG,int to CLH,int was expected. Nonetheless, visual inspection of the NPDE plots suggested that the metabolite formation patterns still differed between oral and intravenous administration. Compared to intravenous dosing, oral dosing resulted in earlier conversions to PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER and reduced conversion to PCM‐GLU in the first 2 h after administration.

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Model Development] In the third model development step, enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐GLU was incorporated to address the misspecification in the PCM and PCM‐GLU profiles, particularly for Study 1. Several secondary peaks in PCM concentrations were observed between 3 and 6 h after oral dosing. Implementation of enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐GLU into the model strongly improved the fit for PCM and PCM‐GLU profiles (dOFV −143). In Study 1, where participants had no restrictions for fasting, gallbladder emptying was included at 1 h post‐dose and every 3 h subsequently. In contrast, emptying was delayed to 8 h post‐dose in Study 2 and to 6 h in Study 3, followed by 3‐h emptying intervals in both Studies 2 and 3

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Model Development] . In contrast, emptying was delayed to 8 h post‐dose in Study 2 and to 6 h in Study 3, followed by 3‐h emptying intervals in both Studies 2 and 3. These differences are consistent with known physiological effects of fasting and food intake on gallbladder motility [26, 27]. The gallbladder emptying times were fixed to the indicated values with a fixed IIV of 131% derived from the model of de Winter et al. [19] to avoid estimation problems, most likely because of overparameterization. The fraction of PCM‐GLU routed into the gallbladder was fixed at 0.1, representing 10% of the total PCM‐GLU formed. A sensitivity analysis was conducted, and no improvement of model fit was observed with alternative fractions eliminated via the gallbladder.

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Model Development] Despite taking into account the dose differences, patients in Study 2 consistently showed higher PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER concentrations and slower elimination of metabolites than those in Study 1. Other body size metrics (i.e., BMI and total body weight) were tested to address these differences, but did not improve the model. To account for the differences between these oral datasets, study‐specific effects were added on: elimination clearance of PCM‐GLU (dOFV −51.0), PCM‐SUL (dOFV −40.9), and both the elimination clearance and CLH,int of PCM‐CYS and MER (combined dOFV −40.9). The addition of study‐specific covariates on Fa and ka did not improve the model, on the basis of OFV and GOF plots.

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Model Development] The final structural model is shown in Figure 2, incorporating gut wall, portal vein, and liver compartments, and enterohepatic recirculation. The drug‐ and system‐specific parameters, along with the model equations, are shown in Table S1. The corresponding model code can be found in Material S3. Table 2 shows the parameter estimates of the final model. Fa was estimated at 0.745 (95% CI 0.699–0.792), and the fraction escaping gut metabolism (FG) can be derived from Qgut/(Qgut + CLG,int × fUG). For illustration, FG can be calculated at 0.9995 for a male individual weighing 60 kg (LBW 40.8 kg) and 0.9992 for a male individual weighing 120 kg (LBW 71.5 kg). The overall bioavailability (F) is the product of Fa, Fg, and fraction escaping hepatic metabolism (FH): F = Fa·FG·FH (Table S1)

text: [Model Development] . The overall bioavailability (F) is the product of Fa, Fg, and fraction escaping hepatic metabolism (FH): F = Fa·FG·FH (Table S1). Furthermore, ka was 0.0531 h−1 (95% CI 0.0415–0.0667), and Vd of PCM was 53.7 L (95% CI 50.2–57.0) for an individual with LBW 65.2 kg. The population CLH,int followed the expected hierarchy in metabolic routes, with glucuronidation being the most predominant pathway (CLH GLU 0.300 L min−1 [95% CI 0.278–0.327] for an individual with LBW 65.2 kg), followed by sulfation (CLH SUL 0.0667 L min−1 [95% CI 0.0608–0.0725] for an individual with LBW 65.2 kg), and oxidation (CLH CYS 0.0417 L min−1 [95% CI 0.0359–0.0486] for an individual with LBW 65.2 kg)

text: [Model Evaluation] Despite model refinements, some misspecification remained in the final semi‐physiological population PK model. PCM‐SUL was slightly underpredicted in patients with obesity after intravenous administration, whereas predictions for individuals without obesity receiving oral PCM matched the observations. In the original model on the basis of intravenous data (Study 3) [5], a covariate of LBW on plasma clearance to PCM‐SUL was incorporated. However, adding LBW or total body weight as a covariate on CLH,int to PCM‐SUL did not resolve this discrepancy in the final model with oral and intravenous data.

text: [Simulations] To illustrate the impact of the route of administration, concentration‐time profiles of PCM and metabolites were simulated in four representative male patients across the observed weight distribution (Section 2.4) under steady‐state conditions of 1000 mg four times daily, as shown in Figure 5. Following oral administration, metabolite formation was faster and led to earlier peak concentrations than following intravenous administration across all body weights. This effect was most prominent for oxidative metabolites (PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER). Because of rapid presystemic metabolism following oral administration, no delay in PCM‐GLU and oxidative metabolite formation was observed, whereas such a delay was apparent after intravenous administration.

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Discussion] To date, a comprehensive evaluation of intravenous versus oral PCM metabolism is lacking. This study provided insights into how presystemic and systemic metabolism and enterohepatic recirculation contribute to differences in parent drug and metabolite exposure between the two routes. It enhances our understanding of the relative roles of hepatic and intestinal presystemic metabolism.

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Discussion] The following key observations emerged from this analysis. First, oral administration led to faster metabolite formation, particularly via the oxidative metabolites (PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER). Second, presystemic hepatic metabolism alone was insufficient to capture the rapid formation of PCM‐CYS & PCM‐MER, highly suggesting a role for intestinal oxidative metabolism. Although intestinal CYP3A metabolism has been shown for midazolam [15] and identified in PBPK modeling [28], this is, to our knowledge, the first time intestinal oxidative metabolism has been described. This is supported by the presence of CYP2E1 in human mucosa cells [10]

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Discussion] . This is supported by the presence of CYP2E1 in human mucosa cells [10]. These results highlight the importance of presystemic metabolism—an effect that was underappreciated in prior PCM models that were developed using data upon either intravenous [5] or oral administration [29].

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Discussion] Third, following oral administration of PCM, relatively lower PCM‐GLU concentrations were observed in the first 2 h post‐dose compared to what is expected after intravenous administration. Together with the observed double peak PCM levels, this pattern indicated the occurrence of enterohepatic recirculation. Supporting this hypothesis, previous rat studies have demonstrated that PCM and PCM‐SUL formation were substantially delayed when PCM‐GLU was injected into more proximal intestinal regions [11, 12]. This phenomenon likely results from enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐GLU, which is converted back into PCM before undergoing further hepatic metabolism

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Discussion] In summary, this study describes PCM and metabolite PK following oral and intravenous administration using a semi‐physiological population PK model that allowed for the quantification of presystemic and systemic metabolism of the different pathways and enterohepatic recirculation. The results demonstrated that oral administration leads to faster metabolite formation, particularly through oxidative metabolism. This model could be used in the future to evaluate and predict special situations such as the influence of overdose or drug interactions (e.g., alcohol). Future PK studies in special populations, such as patients who have undergone metabolic and bariatric surgery, should explicitly evaluate both oral and intravenous PCM administration.

title: Semi‐Physiological Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Oral and Intravenous Paracetamol to Quantify Presystemic Metabolism and Enterohepatic Recirculation
text: [Conclusions] In this semi‐physiological population PK model, both hepatic and intestinal presystemic metabolism of PCM were characterized, along with enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐GLU and its subsequent deglucuronidation back to PCM. Oral administration of PCM results in faster and more extensive metabolite formation. These mechanistic insights are valuable not only for understanding PCM PK but could also support future PK evaluations of other drugs extensively metabolized via multiple routes.

title: Longitudinal Assessment of Executive and Visuospatial Function Recovery and Its Relationship with Functional Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke Patients
text: [abstract] Cognitive impairments in the executive and visuospatial domains are common after ischemic stroke and significantly affect a patient’s independence. These impairments can affect problem-solving abilities, planning, decision-making, and spatial awareness, which are critical for functional recovery. Understanding the trajectory of recovery and its association with functional outcomes is essential for improving the quality of life of stroke survivors. The Objectives of the study are to evaluate the recovery patterns of executive and visuospatial functions 90 days after ischemic stroke and to examine their relationship with functional outcomes.

title: Longitudinal Assessment of Executive and Visuospatial Function Recovery and Its Relationship with Functional Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke Patients
text: [abstract] In this longitudinal study, 401 patients with neuroimaging-confirmed ischemic stroke were assessed at admission and on Days 7, 30, and 90 post-stroke. Executive function was measured using the alternate Trail Making Test, and visuospatial function was assessed using the cube-copying and clock-drawing tests. Functional outcomes were evaluated using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) and Barthel Index. Repeated measures ANOVA (analysis of variance) was employed to assess cognitive recovery over time, and Spearman’s correlation was used to examine the relationship between cognitive and functional outcomes.

title: Longitudinal Assessment of Executive and Visuospatial Function Recovery and Its Relationship with Functional Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke Patients
text: [abstract] Significant improvements in executive and visuospatial functions were observed over the 90-day period, with the greatest gains noted within the first 30 days. A moderate-to-strong negative correlation between mRS and cognitive function was identified at all time points, peaking on Day 7.

title: Longitudinal Assessment of Executive and Visuospatial Function Recovery and Its Relationship with Functional Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke Patients
text: [abstract] Executive and visuospatial functions show dynamic recovery in the first 90 days post-stroke, particularly during the acute and subacute phases. Functional disability is closely associated with cognitive performance, underscoring the importance of early cognitive assessment.

title: Longitudinal Assessment of Executive and Visuospatial Function Recovery and Its Relationship with Functional Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke Patients
text: [Introduction] Ischemic stroke is one of the leading causes of long-term disability, significantly affecting the quality of life of survivors and placing considerable demands on caregivers and healthcare systems. Cognitive impairments, particularly in executive and visuospatial functions, represent some of the most challenging outcomes, as these areas are essential for performing daily activities and preserving independence.[12] These impairments result from localized cortical and subcortical brain lesions that disrupt neuronal networks essential for higher-order cognitive processes.[34]

title: Longitudinal Assessment of Executive and Visuospatial Function Recovery and Its Relationship with Functional Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke Patients
text: [Introduction] Visuospatial functions encompass the skills necessary for spatial awareness and the ability to pursue, integrate, and interpret visual information to guide actions, whereas executive functions involve processes such as problem-solving, goal-oriented behavior, decision-making, and adaptation to dynamic environments.[5] Stroke-related disruption of these intricate networks leads to significant cognitive and functional impairments, particularly when lesions involve the frontal lobe, parietal lobe, and subcortical structures.[6]

title: Longitudinal Assessment of Executive and Visuospatial Function Recovery and Its Relationship with Functional Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke Patients
text: [Introduction] The trajectory of executive and visuospatial function recovery following ischemic stroke is highly dynamic and influenced by several intrinsic and extrinsic factors, including stroke severity, lesion location, patient age, education level, comorbidities, and the quality and intensity of rehabilitation interventions.[789] Despite substantial advancements in understanding language and motor recovery, nuanced changes in executive and visuospatial recovery remain understudied.[10] Understanding these changes is critical, as executive and visuospatial functions influence problem-solving, planning, and navigation, which are key aspects of reintegration into personal, social, and professional life.

title: Longitudinal Assessment of Executive and Visuospatial Function Recovery and Its Relationship with Functional Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke Patients
text: [Introduction] This study aimed to address this gap by evaluating the recovery trajectories of executive and visuospatial functions in patients with ischemic stroke. It also aimed to provide information about cognitive recovery and its correlation with functional recovery over time by analyzing the recovery trajectory through longitudinal assessment.

title: Longitudinal Assessment of Executive and Visuospatial Function Recovery and Its Relationship with Functional Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke Patients
text: [Methods] This prospective longitudinal study was conducted at a tertiary care center in South India between February 2020 and November 2022. Adults aged ≥18 years with a confirmed diagnosis of ischemic stroke on neuroimaging were recruited following informed consent. Patients with significant pre-existing visual impairments unrelated to stroke were excluded to ensure a valid visuospatial assessment. This study was registered with the Clinical Trials Registry- India (CTRI) (CTRI/2020/01/022783). Ethical approval was obtained from the Kasturba Medical College and Kasturba Hospital Institutional Ethics Committee (approval number: 246/2019) to conduct the study.

title: Longitudinal Assessment of Executive and Visuospatial Function Recovery and Its Relationship with Functional Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke Patients
text: [Cognitive and functional assessments] Cognitive function was evaluated using standardized clinical tools. Executive functioning was assessed using the Alternate Trail Making Test, which required participants to alternate between numeric and alphabetic sequences. Visuospatial function was measured using the cube copying and clock drawing tests, with a composite score derived from performance across all tests. Each cognitive task was scored as binary (0 = incorrect, 1 = correct), with a cumulative score range of 0–5.[111]

title: Longitudinal Assessment of Executive and Visuospatial Function Recovery and Its Relationship with Functional Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke Patients
text: [Cognitive and functional assessments] Functional outcomes were assessed using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) and Barthel Index, both of which are validated tools for evaluating disability and independence in activities of daily living. Demographic, clinical, and radiological data were collected at baseline.

title: Longitudinal Assessment of Executive and Visuospatial Function Recovery and Its Relationship with Functional Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke Patients
text: [Data collection and follow-up] Participants were evaluated at four time points: admission (baseline), Day 7, Day 30, and Day 90 post-stroke. All assessments were conducted by trained personnel following a standardized protocol. Medical management and physiotherapy were provided according to institutional guidelines; however, the rehabilitation intensity was not quantitatively assessed.

text: [Statistical analysis] Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the baseline characteristics. Changes in cognitive function over time were analyzed using repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA), with post-hoc Tukey’s tests identifying significant pairwise differences. Spearman’s rank correlation assessed the relationship between cognitive scores and mRS at each follow-up point. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. Analyses were performed using EZR (Easy R statistical software version 1.61).

text: [Results] The study included 401 eligible patients with ischemic stroke who were admitted to the neurology ward between February 2020 and November 2022. The average age of the cohort was 62.3±12.45 (Mean ± standard deviation) years, with a male predominance of 277 patients (69.1%). Unemployment was present in 177 (43.9%) patients, and the median Kuppuswamy socioeconomic scale score was 13.00 (Interquartile Range [IQR]: 3.00–27.00) [Table 1]. The most prevalent comorbidities were hypertension and diabetes mellitus, affecting 65.6% and 41.6% of the patients, respectively [Table 2].

text: [Results] Infarctions were more common in the left cerebral hemisphere, affecting 172 (42.9%) of the patients. The left middle cerebral artery (MCA) was involved in 111 patients (27.8%) and the right MCA in 84 patients (20.9%). The median visuospatial and executive function scores were zero at admission but improved to 2 (IQR: 0–5) by Days 30 and 90 post-stroke [Table 3].

text: [Discussion] This study evaluated the recovery trajectories of executive and visuospatial functions in patients with ischemic stroke over 90 days and explored their association with functional outcomes. The results highlighted a dynamic, time-dependent recovery pattern, with significant gains observed mainly in the early post-stroke period.

title: Longitudinal Assessment of Executive and Visuospatial Function Recovery and Its Relationship with Functional Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke Patients
text: [Discussion] Our findings corroborate previous evidence that executive and visuospatial impairments are prevalent immediately after a stroke and tend to improve with time. The most substantial improvement occurred between admission and Day 30, aligning with the neuroplasticity window often observed during early stroke recovery.[12] Evidence suggests that the recovery trajectory is often nonlinear, with rapid improvements occurring during the acute and subacute phases, followed by a plateau in the chronic phase. Furthermore, another study suggested that the early recovery of visuospatial functions is often less pronounced than that of executive functions because of the complexity of the neural networks involved.[13]

text: [Discussion] The moderate-to-strong negative correlation between the mRS and cognitive scores at all time points reinforces the interconnectedness of physical and cognitive recovery. Notably, the strongest correlation on Day 7 suggests that functional disability during the acute phase may significantly impact early cognitive performance. Although the correlation was attenuated by Day 90, it remained statistically significant, indicating a persistent relationship. The slightly weaker correlation at Day 90 in our study aligns with existing research, which concluded that physical recovery may outpace cognitive recovery in some patients with ischemic stroke

Rehabilitation intensity was not quantified, and a more granular assessment of lesion characteristics and neural imaging markers could further elucidate the mechanisms underlying recovery.

title: Exploring the Role of Nuclear Factor Kappa B in the Immunobiology of Inflammatory Neuropathies
text: [abstract] Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) are inflammatory conditions, representing prototype examples of immune-mediated disorders of the peripheral nervous system. Activation of the nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) pathway is crucial for generating immune and inflammatory responses and creating an inflammatory milieu; however, this has not been studied in inflammatory neuropathies. We aimed to quantify the expression levels of two critical genes in the NF-κB pathway (Nfkb1 and Nfkb2), together with a prototype inflammatory gene, Tnfα, in inflammatory neuropathies.

title: Exploring the Role of Nuclear Factor Kappa B in the Immunobiology of Inflammatory Neuropathies
text: [abstract] Forty-nine patients with inflammatory neuropathies (GBS = 38, CIDP = 11) were recruited prospectively from a single neurology unit. Gene expression levels of Nfκb1, Nfκb2, and Tnfα were quantified using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction.

title: Exploring the Role of Nuclear Factor Kappa B in the Immunobiology of Inflammatory Neuropathies
text: [abstract] There were significantly increased expression levels of Nfκb1 in the inflammatory neuropathy group compared to healthy controls (P = 0.001), GBS versus healthy controls (P = 0.03), and CIDP versus healthy controls (P = 0.003). There were no significant differences in the expression levels of Nfκb2 and Tnfα genes between cases and controls. There was no correlation between the expression levels of these genes and the clinical severity scores.

title: Exploring the Role of Nuclear Factor Kappa B in the Immunobiology of Inflammatory Neuropathies
text: [abstract] The present study provides evidence for NF-κB pathway activation in inflammatory neuropathies, including both GBS and CIDP, suggesting that this spectrum of disorders may share a common central pathway for immune activation. Thus, the NF-κB pathway plays a critical role in the immunopathogenesis of inflammatory neuropathies; however, the molecular interacting partners within the immune system need to be studied to identify the differential immune trajectories in GBS and CIDP.

title: Exploring the Role of Nuclear Factor Kappa B in the Immunobiology of Inflammatory Neuropathies
text: [Introduction] Inflammatory neuropathies are a heterogeneous group of immune-mediated disorders of the peripheral nerves. They are defined pathologically by the abnormal infiltration of peripheral nerves, nerve roots, or both by inflammatory cells, followed by demyelination and/or axonal degeneration.[1] Inflammatory neuropathies are classified based on the tempo of clinical progression as acute, subacute, or chronic neuropathies.[2] Inflammation and autoimmunity are central to the pathogenesis of inflammatory neuropathies. Inflammation involves a series of coordinated processes mediated by cytokines, which act as initiators, mediators, and regulators, as well as intracellular signaling molecules and master regulator transcription factors of inflammatory cells

title: Exploring the Role of Nuclear Factor Kappa B in the Immunobiology of Inflammatory Neuropathies
text: [Introduction] . Most studies on inflammation in Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) have focused on the cytokines that function as initiators, mediators, and effectors of inflammatory responses. For example, altered levels of such cytokines related to inflammatory T helper (Th) 1 and Th17 have been reported in both GBS,[345] and CIDP.[67]

title: Exploring the Role of Nuclear Factor Kappa B in the Immunobiology of Inflammatory Neuropathies
text: [Introduction] Besides cytokines, the generation of an inflammatory response depends on the coordinated action of multiple extracellular and intracellular molecules. One of the most critical intracellular molecules of inflammation-related signaling is the nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB). NF-kB serves as the inducible regulator of inflammation. The NF-κB comprises a family of transcription factors involved in the induction of the expression of genes encoding proinflammatory molecules such as cytokines, chemokines, etc.[8] Apart from regulating inflammatory responses, the NF-κB also controls the activation, differentiation, and effector function of inflammatory T cells.[9] Given these functional attributes, the NF-κB appears to be a critical determinant of immune-inflammatory responses.

text: [Discussion] Immune activation is a consistent pathological basis for inflammatory neuropathies. Inflammation is a complex process, but the central mechanism is the activation of the NF-κB cascade, which is the prototype pathway that signals the generation of proinflammatory responses in the peripheral blood and various tissues in response to exogenous and endogenous triggers. Two members, p50 and p52, do not possess the transcriptional activation domain, while the remaining three, Rel-A, Rel-B, and c-Rel, contain a C-terminal transcriptional activation domain. The p50 and p52 homodimers remain transcriptionally repressive if they are not bound to Rel-A, Rel-B, or c-Rel. text: [Discussion] . NF-κB activation leads to the production of multiple inflammatory cytokines. Therefore, other inflammatory cytokine genes should be examined to understand the impact of elevated NF-κB expression on inflammatory markers. Though a similar expression of the Nfκb1 gene was observed in both GBS and CIDP, the downstream molecular pathways may be unique for GBS and CIDP, and these may govern their respective clinical courses. Thus, the molecular interacting partners of NF-κB within the immune system, particularly its inhibitor, I-κB, need to be explored to explain the differential immune trajectories that underlie GBS and CIDP. title: Exploring the Role of Nuclear Factor Kappa B in the Immunobiology of Inflammatory Neuropathies
text: [Conclusions] The present study provides evidence for the activation of the NF-κB signalling pathway in inflammatory neuropathies, both in GBS and CIDP, indicating that this spectrum of disorders share a common central pathway for immune system activation and the resulting inflammatory response. The findings of the present study must be confirmed in larger cohorts and patients derived from different populations for further validation. Longitudinal assessment, combined with the simultaneous evaluation of protein levels and genetic polymorphisms, may provide better insights into the role of this pathway in inflammatory neuropathies.

text: [Introduction] A squalene-based adjuvant, such as AddaVax™, an analogue of clinically approved MF59, has been widely used in licensed vaccines and shown to enhance antigen uptake and immune activation [2829]. However, classical adjuvants exhibit several disadvantages, including limited capacity to induce strong cellular immunity, potential reactogenicity and reduced efficacy in elderly or immunocompromised individuals [30]. These limitations highlight the need for innovative immunostimulatory strategies.

title: Immunogenicity of SARS-CoV-2 vaccine prototype based on virus-like particles of hepatitis B core antigen from genotype G and interleukin 12 expressing Semliki Forest virus as a genetic adjuvant
text: [Introduction] Genetic adjuvants, particularly those based on cytokine expression, have emerged as promising alternatives, demonstrating advantages such as sustained local production, targeted immune modulation and reduced systemic toxicity [31]. Vector-based delivery of cytokines, such as IL-12, enables precise orchestration of immune responses by promoting Th1 polarization, enhancing cytotoxic T lymphocyte activity and supporting the development of long-lasting, high-quality antibody responses characterized by the promotion of IgG2a class switching – a factor associated with effective antiviral immunity [3234]

title: Immunogenicity of SARS-CoV-2 vaccine prototype based on virus-like particles of hepatitis B core antigen from genotype G and interleukin 12 expressing Semliki Forest virus as a genetic adjuvant
text: [Introduction] . The cytokine-expressing viral vectors offer a potent means of enhancing immune responses not only by the cytokine delivery, but also by the intrinsic induction of innate anti-vector immunity at sites of the vaccine injection. These effects are particularly valuable in the context of antiviral immunity, where both humoral and cellular responses are critical for pathogen clearance.

title: Immunogenicity of SARS-CoV-2 vaccine prototype based on virus-like particles of hepatitis B core antigen from genotype G and interleukin 12 expressing Semliki Forest virus as a genetic adjuvant
text: [Introduction] Replication-deficient Semliki Forest virus (SFV) vectors were shown previously to modulate anti-cancer immune response in murine models by delivery of IL-12, IFN-γ and other cytokines [3537]. The advantages of the replication-deficient SFV vectors include high-transient gene expression, the absence of the vector pre-immunity in a large part of the human population, safety (low pathogenicity) and ability to induce immunogenic cell apoptosis in infected cells [37]. However, the use of SFV vectors as adjuvants for subunits or VLP-based vaccines has been less investigated. The present study explores the immunogenic potential of a novel VLP-based vaccine candidate constructed from the HBc/G ‘two-tail’ vector displaying the RBM motif from a viral spike protein

The immunological enhancement provided by the SFV-IL12 genetic adjuvant, alone or in combination with AddaVax™, was assessed to determine the most effective strategy for eliciting balanced and protective immune responses. Findings from this investigation potentially contribute to the ongoing refinement of modular VLP-based vaccine platforms and support the rational use of combinatory adjuvant approaches in future vaccine development.

text: [Discussion] Adjuvants play a vital role in enhancing immune response, particularly when dealing with subunit or VLP-based vaccines containing poorly immunogenic components. Classical adjuvants like AddaVax, a squalene-based oil-in-water emulsion similar to MF59, are known to enhance antigen uptake and presentation [53]. However, such adjuvants may lack the ability to sufficiently stimulate robust cellular immunity, particularly Th1 responses, and can be associated with reactogenicity/toxicity or reduced efficacy in vulnerable populations [5455]. The exploration of novel immunostimulatory strategies, particularly cytokine-based genetic adjuvants, represents a promising direction in vaccine development.

title: Concatenated modular BK channel constructs reveal divergent stoichiometry in gating control by LRRC26 (γ1), pore, and selectivity filter
text: [abstract] Big-conductance, Ca²+-activated K+ (BK) channels consist of Ca²+- and voltage-sensing, pore-forming α (BKα) subunits and regulatory auxiliary β or γ subunits. Concatenated subunit constructs are powerful tools for elucidating subunit stoichiometry in ion channel gating and regulation, allowing control over subunit arrangement, stoichiometry, and mutation. However, the additional S0 transmembrane segment in BKα places its N- and C-termini on opposite sides of the membrane, preventing tandem BK channel subunit construction by conventional methods

text: [abstract] . To investigate the atypical ‘all-or-none’ modulatory function of γ subunits and the subunit stoichiometry of BK channel gating, we developed concatenated constructs containing 2 or 4 BKα subunits by splicing them into modular forms that can be co-expressed to form functional channels. These constructs retained voltage and Ca²+ gating properties similar to intact BK channels. By fusing the LRRC26 (γ1) subunit to the N-terminus of tandem BKα constructs, we found that a single γ1 subunit per α subunit tetramer is sufficient to fully modulate the channel. Furthermore, the L312A mutation in the deep pore region exhibited a stoichiometrically graded effect on voltage-gated BK channel activation

text: [abstract] . Furthermore, the L312A mutation in the deep pore region exhibited a stoichiometrically graded effect on voltage-gated BK channel activation. In contrast, a V288A mutation at the selectivity filter induced channel inactivation only when present in all four BKα subunits. Thus, by engineering concatenated BKα constructs, we identified three distinct stoichiometric modes of BK channel gating control by LRRC26, the pore, and the selectivity filter. This study offers new molecular tools and advances our understanding of subunit stoichiometry in BK channel gating and modulation.

title: Concatenated modular BK channel constructs reveal divergent stoichiometry in gating control by LRRC26 (γ1), pore, and selectivity filter
text: [Introduction] The big-conductance, calcium- and voltage-activated K+ (BK) channel is a unique member of the potassium channel family, characterized by exceptionally large single-channel conductance and dual regulation by membrane voltage and intracellular free Ca2+ (Salkoff et al., 2006). The BK channel is a homotetramer composed of four identical pore-forming, Ca2+- and voltage-sensing α (BKα) subunits (~130 kDa) and variable auxiliary subunits. BK channels exhibit prominent features in molecular architecture (Tao and MacKinnon, 2019; Tao et al., 2023) and allosteric gating mechanisms (Horrigan and Aldrich, 2002; Xia et al., 2002)

title: Concatenated modular BK channel constructs reveal divergent stoichiometry in gating control by LRRC26 (γ1), pore, and selectivity filter
text: [Introduction] . In the transmembrane (TM) domains, BK channels differ from most voltage-gated K+ (Kv) channels by possessing an extra S0 TM helix, lacking domain swapping between the S1-S4 voltage-sensing domain (VSD) and the S5-S6 pore-gate domain (PGD), and exhibiting tight VSD-PGD packing via extensive S4-S5 interactions (Tao and MacKinnon, 2019). The BKα subunit also contains a large cytosolic C-terminus composed of two tandem RCK domains (RCK1, RCK2) responsible for Ca2+ and Mg2+ sensing (Xia et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2010; Hite et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2002; Yusifov et al., 2008)

text: [Introduction] . The RCK domains from all BKα subunits assemble into a tetrameric two-layer gating ring that expands and shifts toward the membrane in response to Ca2+ bindings, leading to S6 movement and channel opening (Hite et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2017).

title: Concatenated modular BK channel constructs reveal divergent stoichiometry in gating control by LRRC26 (γ1), pore, and selectivity filter
text: [Introduction] BK channel function is regulated by auxiliary β and γ subunits and by LINGO1, conferring tissue-specific gating and pharmacological properties (Solaro and Lingle, 1992; Wallner et al., 1995; Brenner et al., 2000; Yan and Aldrich, 2010; Yan and Aldrich, 2012; Guan et al., 2017; Dudem et al., 2020). The four γ subunits (γ1-γ4), also known as LRRC26, LRRC52, LRRC55, and LRRC38, are leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-containing membrane proteins (Yan and Aldrich, 2010; Yan and Aldrich, 2012). The γ subunits facilitate BK channel activation by shifting the voltage dependence of channel activation in the hyperpolarizing direction by ~140 mV (γ1), 100 mV (γ2), 50 mV (γ3), and 20 mV (γ4), in terms of half-maximal activation voltage (V1/2) in the absence of Ca2+

All γ subunits share a common topology, including an N-terminal signal peptide, an extracellular LRR domain, a single TM segment, and a short intracellular C-terminus (Yan and Aldrich, 2010; Yan and Aldrich, 2012; Chen et al., 2022). text: [Introduction] A fundamental question in ion channel gating and regulation is the structural and functional subunit stoichiometry. BK channel modulation by the γ subunits exhibits an atypical binary ‘all-or-none’ phenotype: voltage-dependence (V1/2) is either fully shifted or unchanged under limited γ1 expression (Chen et al., 2022; Gonzalez-Perez et al., 2014). In tetrameric ion channels, auxiliary proteins typically follow fourfold symmetry, producing graded modulation based on subunit stoichiometry relative to the pore-forming principal subunit, as observed with BK β subunits (Wang et al., 2002), KCNE subunits on KCNQ channels (Nakajo et al., 2010), and KChIP subunits on Kv4 channels (Kitazawa et al., 2014)

text: [Introduction] To address this, we engineered modular BKα constructs that reassemble into functional concatenated channels with biophysical properties comparable to intact BK channels. Using these, we demonstrate that a single γ1 subunit per BKα tetramer is sufficient to fully modulate the channel. Given the central role of the PGD in BK channel gating, we further applied this system to mutational analyses of the deep pore and selectivity filter. We revealed distinct stoichiometric requirements for gating control by LRRC26, the pore, and the selectivity filter. This study provides new molecular tools and mechanistic insights into the stoichiometry of BK channel gating and regulation.

text: [A single LRRC26 (γ1) subunit per channel is sufficient to fully modulate BK channels] The γ1 subunit’s ‘all-or-none’ modulatory effect on BK channels has remained mechanistically elusive, despite the recent availability of 3D structures of the BKα/γ1 complexes. To directly investigate the functional stoichiometry of BK channel modulation by the γ1 subunit, we fused the C-terminus of the γ1 subunit to the N-terminus of the first αM repeat in the αMM and αMMMM constructs, generating the BKγ1αMM (BKγ1αM(dual)) and BKγ1αMMMM (BKγ1αM(quad)) fusion constructs (Figure 2B). text: [A single LRRC26 (γ1) subunit per channel is sufficient to fully modulate BK channels] . Upon co-expression of these constructs with αΔM-GFP in HEK293 cells, we observed that the N-terminally fused γ1 subunit induced a V1/2 shift of 125 mV with the BKγ1αMM construct (V1/2 = 62 ± 5 mV) and 145 mV with the BKγ1αMMMM construct (V1/2 = 38 ± 4 mV) in the virtual absence of Ca2+ (Figure 2D and E). These large V1/2-shifting effects in stoichiometrically defined γ1:α=1:2 and 1:4 channel complexes clearly indicate that a single γ1 subunit per tetrameric channel is sufficient to fully modulate BK channels. This ‘one-subunit-sufficient’ effect provides a mechanistic explanation for the observed binary, all-or-none modulation by the γ1 subunit when its expression is limited.

section: L312A mutation reveals stoichiometrically graded gating and confirms functional integrity of concatenated constructs
text: [L312A mutation reveals stoichiometrically graded gating and confirms functional integrity of concatenated constructs] To ensure that the concatenated αM constructs are suitable for studying the stoichiometry of BK channel gating and regulation, the constructs must demonstrate two additional aspects of functional integrity beyond simply forming functional channels. First, each αM repeat within the construct should contribute equally to channel formation. Second, the concatenated dual and quadruple αM repeats in the αM(dual) and αM(quad) constructs should assemble primarily as complete units, that is two αM(dual) constructs or one αM(quad) construct should form a single channel. The latter ensures that heterogeneous channels with uncontrolled subunit stoichiometry are unlikely to form and confound the results.

text: [Discussion] In conclusion, our study employed an innovative strategy to generate concatenated subunit constructs and investigate the subunit stoichiometry and modulation of BK channels. Using these concatenated constructs, we identified three distinct types of subunit stoichiometry in BK channel modulation: an additive (independent) type and two contrasting all-or-none types, namely, ‘one-subunit-sufficient’ and ‘all-subunit-required’. text: [abstract] The rate of cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD) varies considerably from person to person. Numerous epidemiological studies point to the protective effects of cognitive, social, and physical enrichment as potential mediators of cognitive decline in AD; however, there is much debate as to the mechanism underlying these protective effects. The retrosplenial cortex (RSC) is one of the earliest brain regions with impaired functions during AD pathogenesis, and its activity is affected by cognitive, social, and physical stimulation, making it a particularly interesting region to investigate the influences of an enriched lifestyle on AD pathogenesis

These changes in cognitive performance coincided with restored functional connectivity of the RSC and preserved PV-IN density within this region. text: [Introduction] . As the most abundant source of GABAergic signaling in the RSC, PV-INs are critical for maintaining the excitatory–inhibitory balance of this region and are thus crucial for many higher-order cognitive processes. Several reports have identified impaired activity and expression of PV-INs in AD, particularly in the RSC (Hof et al., 1991; Bernstein et al., 2011; Terstege and Epp, 2023; van Heusden et al., 2023). Impaired PV-IN activity in the RSC arises earliest during AD pathogenesis in females, with this earlier susceptibility having been proposed as a causal factor influencing sex differences in AD vulnerability (Terstege et al., 2025).

text: [Y maze spontaneous alternation] Spatial working memory ability was assessed using a Y maze spontaneous alternation task (Kraeuter et al., 2019; Khan et al., 2024). The arms of the Y maze apparatus were 41.5 cm long, 7.5 cm wide, and 12.5 cm tall and were cleaned with 70% EtOH before and after each trial. Mice were placed at the end of one arm of the Y maze allowed 5 min to explore the apparatus. During this trial, a spontaneous alternation was defined as a sequence in which mice entered each of the three arms of the maze without re-entering either of the two previously entered arms. The number of spontaneous alternations was expressed as a percentage of the total number of arm entries, with the first two arm entries excluded, for statistical comparisons between groups.

The conditioning chamber had black and white vertical stripes along the walls and metal bars along the floor and was cleaned with 30% isopropyl alcohol before and after each trial. During a conditioning trial, mice were allowed to explore the chamber for 3 min prior to the onset of a 20 s tone (2,700 Hz). section: Female 5xFAD mice housed under enriched conditions do not show cognitive impairments
text: [Female 5xFAD mice housed under enriched conditions do not show cognitive impairments] The 5xFAD mouse model of AD has a well-characterized timeline of pathological progression and cognitive impairments. At 6 months of age, we observed the expected high density of amyloid-β plaque deposition in the RSC of 5xFAD mice (Fig. S1A). Enrichment did not influence the accumulation of amyloid-B plaques compared with standard housing (Fig. S1B; see Fig. 1A for schematic of enrichment cage). Based on previous characterization of the 5xFAD mice, we also expected that deficits in spatial and conditioned memory should arise by 6 months of age (Terstege et al., 2025; see Fig. 1B for timeline of behavioral testing in the current manuscript). Spatial memory performance assessed in the Y maze spontaneous alternation task supported these previous findings

Spatial memory performance assessed in the Y maze spontaneous alternation task supported these previous findings. Here, no effects of genotype or housing condition were observed in 4-month-old mice (Fig. 1C). However, by 6 months, we observed a lower proportion of spontaneous alternations in 5xFAD mice and an increase in spontaneous alternations in mice housed under enriched conditions (Fig. 1D). Subsequent analyses of the effect sizes of these changes by housing condition revealed that the performance of 5xFAD mice was only impaired relative to WT controls when housed under standard conditions.

section: Female 5xFAD mice housed under enriched conditions do not show cognitive impairments
text: [Female 5xFAD mice housed under enriched conditions do not show cognitive impairments] Following spatial memory testing, mice were trained on a trace contextual fear memory protocol. This protocol allows for the assessment of both cued and contextual memory. In 6-month-old WT and 5xFAD mice, no differences were observed in the rate of freezing behavior during the initial conditioning trial (Fig. S1C,D). Following tone presentation during a trace testing trial 24 h later, 5xFAD mice housed under control conditions displayed decreased freezing, indicating impaired retrieval of the cued memory (Fig. 1E). Subsequent reintroduction to the original conditioned context revealed that these impairments extended to contextual memory performance, with 5xFAD mice housed under standard conditions exhibiting decreased freezing during this trial (Fig. 1F)

text: [Density and synaptic connectivity of PV-INs in the RSC are preserved in female 5xFAD mice under enriched housing conditions] To assess the functional consequences of this decrease in PV-IN expression density across the RSC, we stained the tissues from 6-month-old mice for synaptotagmin-2 (SYT2; Fig. 3C). SYT2 is a marker with high specificity for presynaptic contacts from PV-INs; therefore, its expression density provides insight into the ability of PV-INs to regulate both its own activity and the activity of pother cell populations across the region (Sommeijer and Levelt, 2012). Here, a significant genotype × housing condition interaction revealed impaired expression density of SYT2 across the RSC of only the 5xFAD mice which were housed under control conditions (Fig. 3D).

text: [The density of RSC PV-INs in the clinical AD cases is anticorrelated with the amyloid burden in this region] The relationship between increased amyloid-β load and RSC PV-IN density can also be studied in clinical AD populations through histological analyses of postmortem tissue samples (Fig. 5A). By labeling PV-INs across postmortem tissue samples from the RSC, we found that the density of these cells is decreased in women with AD compared with CN controls (Fig. 5B). Furthermore, the density of RSC PV-INs in tissue samples obtained from women with AD was anticorrelated with the coverage of amyloid-β burden, wherein higher amyloid-β load was associated with a decreased density of RSC PV-INs (Fig. 5C).

text: [Discussion] Previous studies have identified relationships between enrichment and increased resiliency to cognitive decline in AD (Oveisgharan et al., 2020; Simone et al., 2023). However, there is little consensus as to the mechanism underlying this effect. As the incidence of AD rises, it is critical to gain a better understanding of these accessible lifestyle interventions which could be integrated into AD prevention strategies.

title: Environmental Enrichment Preserves Retrosplenial Parvalbumin Density and Cognitive Function in Female 5xFAD Mice
text: [Discussion] While the mechanisms mediating the protective effects of enrichment on cognitive decline in AD are largely unknown, several neurological correlates predictive of AD onset have been identified (Dubois et al., 2023; Hansson et al., 2023; Jia et al., 2024). Altered RSC activity may predict the onset of cognitive impairment in AD (Ash et al., 2016; Ziontz et al., 2021; Walsh et al., 2022; Veréb et al., 2023). The RSC is important for learning and memory, and its activity can be modulated through learning, social interactions, and physical exercise (Vann et al., 2000; Holschneider et al., 2007; Holzschneider et al., 2012; Todd et al., 2015; Pan et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2024)

The current study examined whether multimodal enrichment could improve cognitive outcomes and preserve RSC function in the 5xFAD mouse model of AD. With enrichment beginning early, prior to the establishment of significant RSC amyloid pathology and the onset of cognitive impairments, the study mimicked a preventative approach.

text: [Discussion] After enrichment, 5xFAD mice showed improved spatial working memory and contextual memory compared with 5xFAD mice in standard housing. 5xFAD mice in enriched housing also did not display RSC hyperactivity during contextual memory recall like the 5xFAD mice housed under standard conditions. Furthermore, the density of anticorrelated functional connections formed with the RSC during contextual memory recall was low in 5xFAD mice housed under enriched conditions. This mimicked the density of these connections in WT mice and sharply contrasted the high density of anticorrelated connections observed in 5xFAD mice housed under standard conditions. Anticorrelated activity involving this region has been reported during early stages of AD, while other reports have shown decreases in RSC anticorrelated activity with physical exercise (Voss et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019). text: [Discussion] To further examine the protective effects of WFA+ PNNs against amyloid infusion, RSC PNNs were directly manipulated using ChABC. No loss of PV-INs occurred in response to amyloid infusion, unless WFA+ PNNs had been depleted beforehand. Interestingly, the percentage of PV-INs enrobed by WFA+ PNNs decreased with ChABC treatment; however, combined amyloid and ChABC treatments did not alter this percentage. These results suggest that surviving PV-INs were those that maintained their WFA+ PNN expression, further demonstrating the protective role of these structures.

text: [Discussion] To elucidate the relationship between enrichment, PNNs, and PV-IN resilience to AD pathology, ChABC was expressed across RSC PV-INs of WT and 5xFAD mice housed under enriched conditions. Without RSC PNNs, the protective effect of enriched housing conditions on RSC PV-IN density in 5xFAD mice was lost. These findings point toward PNN stability as a potential mechanism mediating the protective effects of enrichment on RSC PV-INs.

WFA staining binds the N-acetylgalactosamine moiety of chondroitin sulfate glycosaminoglycans, a critical constituent of PNNs, and is the most commonly used marker to visualize these structures (Härtig et al., 1999; Fawcett et al., 2019; Lupori et al., 2023). Additionally, PNNs are also defined by an aggrecan core, which can be visualized with ACAN staining (Giamanco et al., 2010; Ueno et al., 2018). In WFA-labeled PNNs, while Acan gene expression often correlates highly with WFA diffuse fluorescence, the extent to which these immunofluorescent labels colocalize is highly variable (Yamada and Jinno, 2017; Ueno et al., 2018; Lupori et al., 2023). In some regions, such as CA3 of the hippocampus, many PNNs label positively for ACAN but do not stain with WFA (Härtig et al., 2022). In the RSC, however, many more PNNs are WFA+ than not (Härtig et al., 2022). As such, we focused on WFA+ PNNs.

text: [Discussion] The current study was conducted in female mice. Sex differences are prominent in AD, with women having an increased risk of developing AD (Gao et al., 1998; Andersen et al., 1999). Furthermore, PV-INs are vulnerable in the early stages of AD pathogenesis and highly sensitive to changes occurring during aging in women (Povysheva et al., 2019; Gilfarb and Leuner, 2022). Previous findings identified PV-INs as being particularly susceptible to AD pathogenesis in females, particularly in the RSC where sex-specific impairments of PV-INs occur earlier than in many other neuroanatomical regions commonly associated with AD (Terstege and Epp, 2023; Terstege et al., 2025). As such, the current study was focused on environmental enrichment and its role in mediating this sex-specific vulnerability.

text: [Discussion] The current study highlights the relationship between enrichment and the proportion of WFA+ PNNs enrobing PV-INs in AD; however, they have implications which could shed light on a multitude of neuroscience research topics. In the hippocampus, alterations in PNN and PV-IN colocalization have been shown to impact the ability to form and maintain memories (Liu et al., 2023; Ramsaran et al., 2023). In the entorhinal cortex, impaired coverage of PNNs around PV-INs has been associated with the development of epilepsy (Rogers et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2022). While these relationships have been well characterized, there have been relatively few studies identifying means through which the density of WFA+ PNNs can be restored or protected

text: [Discussion] While many studies have reported associations between cognitive, social, and physical enrichment on resilience to cognitive decline in AD; several studies have failed to replicate these results (Jankowsky et al., 2005; Hüttenrauch et al., 2017; Butler et al., 2018; Griñán-Ferré et al., 2018; Oveisgharan et al., 2020). In our results, it is important to highlight potential confounds which may contribute to variability in the literature. One key contributor may be protocol duration (Kallio et al., 2017; Vasquez et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022). Generally, shorter enrichment protocols have yielded smaller effects (Hampshire et al., 2019). Moreover, the variety of enrichment is important (Kelly et al., 2014), and early intervention is most effective in slowing cognitive decline

title: Environmental Enrichment Preserves Retrosplenial Parvalbumin Density and Cognitive Function in Female 5xFAD Mice
text: [Conclusion] Our findings demonstrate that prolonged cognitive, social, and physical enrichment abolishes cognitive deficits observed in 6-month-old female 5xFAD mice. Our results also suggest that these conditions are sufficient to preserve functional connectivity of the RSC and protect PV-INs in this region, even in the absence of differences in amyloid pathology. Together, these results provide support for the maintenance of PV-INs in the RSC as a potential mechanism mediating the protective effects of enrichment against cognitive decline in AD.
